pbb15a84e33.title: How Wind and Water Change Rock
pbb15a84e33.text:
[Diagram: A tall rock on the left breaks into small pieces. Arrows show wind and a river carrying the pieces to a low beach on the right.]

Weathering
Weathering is the slow breaking of rock into smaller pieces. Rain, ice, and plant roots can crack even the hardest stone over many years.

Erosion
Erosion happens when wind or moving water carries those pieces away. A powerful river can move sand and pebbles a long distance from the place where they started.

Deposition
Deposition is the last step. The wind or water slows down and drops the pieces in a new location. Over time, the pieces can build a sandy beach or an enormous dune.

All three changes are slow. People rarely notice them in one day, but together they alter the shape of the land.

p28052297c9.title: Two Kinds of Change on a Mountain
p28052297c9.text:
Slow Change
On the mountains of southwestern Saudi Arabia, soil moves downhill a tiny bit every year. Scientists call this slow movement creep. Fence posts and old walls begin to lean, but nobody actually sees them move. Families have years to notice the problem and repair their land.

Fast Change
A landslide is very different. After several days of severe rain, the soil becomes heavy with water. Suddenly, an entire hillside can slide down in less than a minute. Roads may collapse, and homes can be buried.

How They Are Alike
Both creep and landslides are caused by gravity pulling soil and rock downhill. Both are more likely on steep slopes with few plants to hold the ground in place.

[Diagram: Two hills side by side. The left hill shows leaning fence posts labeled "Creep: years." The right hill shows a pile of mud at the bottom labeled "Landslide: minutes."]

pd1ff354ed3.title: Lina's Plan
pd1ff354ed3.text:
Lina and Sara had been best friends since the first day of first grade. When Ms. Huda announced the school art exhibition, Lina immediately clapped her hands. “We will paint one enormous picture together, and I have already chosen the colors,” she said.

Sara secretly wanted to create her own clay camel, but she only nodded politely. At home, she stared at the lump of clay sitting on her desk, and her stomach felt tight. If she told Lina the truth, would her friend feel disappointed?

The next morning, Lina proudly waved a sketch of the picture in the air. “You can paint the sky,” she announced. Sara opened her mouth, then closed it again. She held her clay camel behind her back and took a deep breath.

p060aa61661.title: The Same Saturday
p060aa61661.text:
Yousef had practiced his football kicks for weeks, so when Coach Adel posted the tryout date, his heart did a flip. Then he read the date again. The tryouts were on the same Saturday as the city chess tournament.

Majed, his partner on the chess team, was already making confident plans. “We are definitely going to win the gold cup this time,” Majed said. “I registered us as a pair, so you cannot back out now.”

Yousef felt like he was caught between a rock and a hard place. He loved chess, but playing football for the school had always been his dream. That night he could not sleep a wink. Finally, he knocked quietly on his grandfather's door.

“Tell Majed honestly how you feel,” Grandfather said gently. “A real friend will listen, even if the news is difficult to hear.”

The next morning, Yousef found Majed beside the school gate. He took a deep breath and spoke from the heart.

p7bed208d17.title: Businesses Can Be Good Neighbors
p7bed208d17.text:
A business needs to earn money, but it can also help the people around it. In fact, helping others can make a business stronger.

Sharing Food
A bakery in Dammam gives its extra bread to a food bank every evening. Families in need get fresh bread, and nothing goes to waste.

Teaching Skills
A computer shop offers free weekend classes for older people. Many grandparents have learned to video call their families.

Earning Trust
When customers see a shop helping others, they want to shop there again. Kindness brings in new customers.

Every business should find one way to give back. It is good for the community and good for the business.

p0fae783b94.title: Why Giving Can Be Good Business
p0fae783b94.text:
Some people believe a company must keep every riyal it earns to be successful. However, the story of a small sports shoe company in Jeddah shows another path.

A Simple Promise
In 2021, the company made a promise: for every pair of shoes sold, it would give one pair to a child who needed shoes. Many shoppers liked this idea and chose the company over larger brands.

The Numbers Tell the Story
[Bar graph: Pairs of Shoes Sold. 2021: 2,000 pairs. 2022: 5,000 pairs. 2023: 9,000 pairs.]
As the graph shows, sales grew every year after the promise began. The company also donated thousands of pairs to schools.

A Lesson for Others
This example proves that a business does not have to choose between profit and kindness. When companies help people, customers often reward them with their loyalty.

pb26555d356.title: Built for the Desert
pb26555d356.text:
[Photo: A small sand cat with wide ears sits beside a sand dune. Caption: The sand cat's large ears help it hear prey moving under the sand.]

Staying Cool
The Arabian desert is extremely hot during the day. Many animals, such as the sand cat, rest in underground burrows when the sun is strong. They come out to hunt at night, when the air is much cooler.

Finding Water
Water is difficult to find in the desert. The Arabian oryx can survive for weeks without drinking. It gets the water it needs from the plants it eats.

Moving on Sand
Soft sand is hard to walk on. The camel has wide, flat feet that do not sink, so it can travel long distances across the dunes.

These special features are called adaptations. They help desert animals survive in a place with very little water and terrible heat.

pb5cb4afce9.title: Masters of Disguise in the Red Sea
pb5cb4afce9.text:
The coral reefs of the Red Sea are full of color, but they are also full of danger. Many animals survive there because of camouflage, a kind of adaptation that helps them blend into their surroundings.

Changing Colors
The octopus can change the color and pattern of its skin in less than a second. When a shark swims near, the octopus can look exactly like a rock or a patch of sand.

Hiding in Shape
The stonefish does not change color, but its lumpy body looks like a rock covered with algae. Small fish swim right up to it, and the stonefish swallows them in a flash.

[Photo: A stonefish resting on the sea floor. Caption: Can you find the fish? Its rough skin matches the rocks around it.]

Whether they are hiding from predators or waiting for prey, these animals show how camouflage helps them stay alive.

p1020c19a4a.title: The Bee and the Butterfly
p1020c19a4a.text:
CHARACTERS: BEE, a busy worker; BUTTERFLY, her carefree friend; NARRATOR

SETTING: A colorful flower garden on a warm spring morning.

NARRATOR: Bee flies from flower to flower, carrying sweet nectar back to her hive.
BUTTERFLY (stretching her wings): Bee, why are you always so busy? Come and relax in the sunshine with me!
BEE: I cannot rest yet, because I must store honey before the cold days come.
BUTTERFLY (laughing): The cold days are far away, and there is plenty of time.
NARRATOR: Weeks pass. The flowers fade, and a chilly wind blows through the empty garden.
BUTTERFLY (shivering): Bee, the flowers have disappeared, and I have nothing to eat!
BEE (opening the door of her hive): Come in, friend. I saved enough for both of us. Next spring, we will work together.

pc91d49c757.title: The Well in the Oasis
pc91d49c757.text:
CHARACTERS: SAMI, a careful farmer; RAED, his neighbor; NARRATOR

SETTING: Two date farms side by side in a green oasis. A deep well stands between them.

NARRATOR: It is the cool season, and the well is full of water.
SAMI (digging a channel to a storage tank): I am saving water now, because the hot summer always brings a terrible drought.
RAED (lying in the shade of a palm tree): Why worry, Sami? The well has never run dry. Come and join me for a cup of tea.
SAMI: Thank you, but this storage tank will not fill itself.
NARRATOR: Summer arrives. The sun burns, and the water in the well sinks lower every day.
RAED (looking at his drooping palm trees, frustrated): My trees are dying, and I do not know what to do!
SAMI (turning the tap on his tank): My tank is full, neighbor. Take whatever you need, and this winter we will build a tank for your farm too.
RAED (quietly): Thank you, Sami. I will never laugh at hard work again.

p06bc9c8d5e.title: The Desert Falcon
p06bc9c8d5e.text:
Above the golden dunes the falcon circles, calm and slow,
Her outstretched wings are silver sails that catch the winds below.
Her eyes are polished lanterns, searching every rocky ledge,
She hovers like a question mark beside the canyon's edge.

Then suddenly she tumbles down, an arrow from the sky,
The frightened lizards scatter as the hunter rushes by.
I watch her from my window, and I hold my breathing still,
I wish that I could travel with her courage and her skill.

pd36c85b991.title: The Camel's Song
pd36c85b991.text:
You call me slow and clumsy when I wander through the sand,
But I can cross the empty miles that you will never understand.
My humps are patient storehouses that keep me strong for days,
My lashes are like curtains that protect me from the haze.

You hurry in your noisy trucks and grumble at the heat,
While I go gently forward on my wide and padded feet.
The desert is my library, the stars are my old friends,
I carry every caravan until the journey ends.

p65602d96d2.title: The Box of Pencils
p65602d96d2.text:
Every November, when the first clouds gather over our town, I think about the morning the valley flooded. I was eight years old then.

Two years ago, the rain fell for an entire night. By sunrise, brown water was rushing through the streets, and furniture was scattered across the road like broken toys. From our balcony, I watched my neighbor, Mr. Fahad, wading gingerly through the water as he carried his daughter's schoolbag above his head.

Now I am ten, and our class is collecting supplies for families who lost their homes in a storm far away. My teacher assigned me to sort the pencils and notebooks. As I pack each box, I remember Mr. Fahad's careful steps, and I add an extra eraser, just in case.

pa6dadff859.title: Two Views of the Drive
pa6dadff859.text:
When the storm damaged the coastal village of Al-Bahar, local organizations asked residents of nearby towns to donate blankets, food, and books. Majid, who was twelve, immediately emptied his shelf of adventure novels into a carton.

His sister Reem frowned. “Those families need roofs and clean water,” she argued. “What good are a few old books?”

Majid did not answer at first. Instead, he showed her a photograph from the newspaper. A small boy was sitting on a pile of broken bricks, reading a damaged magazine as if it were a precious treasure.

Reem studied the picture for a long time. Then she walked to her room and returned with her favorite atlas and a box of colored pencils. “Maybe a roof protects you from the rain,” she said quietly, “but a story protects you from boredom and fear.”

pc77cca06b4.title: The Woman Who Planted Forests
pc77cca06b4.text:
Wangari Maathai grew up in the green hills of Kenya, where clear streams ran past fig trees. When she returned home in the 1960s after studying in the United States, she was shocked. Many forests had been cut down, the streams were muddy, and families had to walk far to find firewood.

Wangari believed this was a serious injustice, because poor families suffered the most. In 1977 she started the Green Belt Movement, which paid village women a small amount to plant trees. Some officials disliked her ideas and even had her arrested, but she refused to quit.

Over the years, the women she trained planted millions of trees. In 2004, Wangari became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Her life shows that one determined person can help heal an entire land.

[Timeline: 1940 Wangari is born in Kenya · 1971 she earns a doctorate · 1977 she starts the Green Belt Movement · 2004 she wins the Nobel Peace Prize]

p0ff43c2ae5.title: The Scientist Who Heard the Silence
p0ff43c2ae5.text:
Rachel Carson loved the ocean long before she ever saw it. She was born in 1907 on a farm in Pennsylvania. As a girl, she read every sea story she could find. Later she became a qualified marine biologist and worked for the government.

In the 1950s, Carson noticed something alarming. Farmers and towns were spraying strong chemicals to kill insects. The poison was also harming birds, fish, and other wildlife. In 1962 she published Silent Spring, a book that warned readers about this danger.

Some chemical companies attacked her. They called her emotional and unscientific. But Carson had checked her facts carefully, and she calmly defended her work before government leaders. In my view, her quiet courage was more powerful than any loud protest, because her careful evidence changed how a whole nation thought about nature.

[Timeline: 1907 Carson is born · 1951 her best-selling book about the sea appears · 1962 Silent Spring is published · 1964 Carson dies]

p537b526cd0.title: School Gardens Grow Better Students
p537b526cd0.text:
Every school should have its own vegetable garden. Gardens teach valuable lessons that no textbook can teach alone.

Learning by Doing
In a garden, students measure the planting beds, count seeds, and record how quickly their vegetables grow. These activities turn mathematics and science into real experiences.

Healthier Choices
Children who grow carrots and tomatoes are more likely to taste them. Teachers report that gardening students choose fruit and vegetables at lunch more often.

Answering the Concerns
Some parents worry that gardens cost too much money. However, a small garden needs only soil, seeds, and water, and many local farms gladly donate supplies.

[Map: a school campus with the garden beside the cafeteria and a water tap near the playground]

p211914520b.title: Every Drop Counts
p211914520b.text:
Farmers in dry countries should switch to drip irrigation, a watering system that delivers water directly to the roots of plants.

Saving Water
Traditional sprinklers spray water into the air, where much of it evaporates in the desert heat. Drip tubes, however, release small amounts slowly into the soil, so plants use almost every drop.

Stronger Crops
Because leaves stay dry, plants grown with drip systems often show greater resistance to some diseases. Farmers in Saudi Arabia have used these advancements to grow dates, tomatoes, and cucumbers in places that once seemed impossible to farm.

What Critics Say
Some people disagreed with this plan, arguing that the equipment is expensive. Yet the savings on water usually pay for the tubes within a few seasons.

[Map: the Arabian Peninsula with green dots marking farms that use drip irrigation near Al-Kharj and Al-Qassim]

p08842b2f09.title: When the Lights Went Out
p08842b2f09.text:
Signals Go Dark
One summer afternoon, a storm knocked out the power in a busy part of the city. Instantly, every traffic light at the main intersection (in-ter-SEK-shun) went completely dark.

Confusion on the Roads
Because no signal told drivers when to stop, cars crept forward from four directions at once. Horns honked, buses blocked the crosswalk, and frightened walkers waited on the corners. As a result, a trip that usually took five minutes eventually took nearly an hour.

Order Returns
Finally, police officers arrived and directed traffic with whistles and hand signals. Drivers followed their instructions, and the cars began moving smoothly again. That afternoon showed everyone that simple rules protect people every single day.

p29063037cb.title: How Football Got Its Rules
p29063037cb.text:
Many Games, Many Rules
Two hundred years ago, football in England was a confusing sport. Each school played its own version (VUR-zhun) of the game. At some schools, players could carry the ball; at others, they could only kick it. When teams from different schools met, they often argued instead of playing.

Writing It Down
In 1863, club leaders met in London to solve the problem. After several heated meetings, they agreed on a single set of laws, and handling the ball was mostly forbidden. Because of this agreement, teams could finally compete fairly.

Changing the Laws
The rules have changed many times since then. For example, the penalty kick was added in 1891 after players kept stopping goals with unfair fouls. Each change was like an amendment (uh-MEND-ment), a small improvement to an important set of rules.

pc914799736.title: The Wire Comes to Millbrook
pc914799736.text:
In the spring of 1905, workers strung black wires along the dusty main road of Millbrook. Ten-year-old Clara watched from the porch of the general store as a man climbed a tall wooden pole. Her father, the town doctor, stood beside her with his arms folded.

“Some people say the telephone will ruin good conversation,” said Mr. Hale, the storekeeper. “Why talk to a box when you can walk to a neighbor's door?”

Clara's father shook his head. “When a farmer's child is sick ten miles away, walking takes hours. With a telephone, I could hear about it in minutes.”

Clara looked at the gleaming new bell on the store wall. She wondered who would be the first person to ring it, and she hoped the news would be good.

p8350cb08be.title: The Night the Bell Rang
p8350cb08be.text:
For nearly a decade, my uncle Samuel had been tinkering with batteries and bells in his small workshop, so when our town finally built a telephone exchange, he volunteered to run it. I was eleven, and I squirmed with impatience every evening until he let me watch him work. The switchboard sat in a narrow room above the bakery.

One stormy night in 1912, the exchange bell rang so suddenly that I nearly dropped my lamp. A shaky voice on the line said that the bridge on the river road had washed away. My uncle connected the call to the sheriff, and within minutes riders were directing wagons onto a safer path.

Before that night, I had thought the switchboard was just a noisy machine full of tangled cords. Now I understood that it was a kind of lifeline, stretching invisibly from house to house.

p764161edac.title: The Wobbly Bicycle
p764161edac.text:
Each afternoon, Yusuf carefully rolled his bicycle down the quiet, sandy lane behind his house,
and each afternoon he wobbled, tipped, and tumbled sideways to the ground.
“Try again,” his sister whispered, holding tightly to the back of the seat.

His knees were scraped and dusty, and his cheeks were burning with embarrassment;
he wanted to leave the bicycle forever beside the garden gate.
“Try again,” his sister whispered, “every rider falls at first.”

On the seventh day, the wheels kept turning, smooth and straight and steady,
and the wind rushed past his smiling face like an excited cheering crowd.
“I did it!” Yusuf shouted, and his triumph echoed down the lane.

p7b7ea624d7.title: The Patient Pen
p7b7ea624d7.text:
Mariam's pen kept hovering above the paper like a nervous honeybee,
while drops of ink were dangling from its tip like tiny, dark tears.
Her letters leaned and wobbled, and her circles looked like broken eggs.

“Slow and steady,” Grandfather said, as he gently guided her hand.
“A beautiful line is not a gift; it is a path you walk each day.”
So every evening after dinner, Mariam practiced at the kitchen table.

The weeks went by like quiet camels crossing the golden sand,
and slowly, stroke by careful stroke, her letters learned to stand.
When at last she wrote her name, it curled across the page like ribbon,
and Grandfather smiled, for she had worked so hard to attain her goal.

p893220406d.title: A Closer Look at Sand
p893220406d.text:
A handful of beach sand looks plain and gritty to the naked eye. Under a microscope, however, it becomes a surprising little world. A good lens can magnify each grain fifty times or more, revealing tiny shells, bits of coral, and glassy crystals in many colors.

[Photograph: Colorful grains of sand seen through a microscope. Caption: Some “grains” are really broken pieces of sea shells and coral.]

Scientists study sand to learn where it came from. Dark grains often come from volcanic rock, while pale grains on many tropical beaches come from crushed coral and shells. By looking closely at a single sample, a researcher can begin to read the history of a beach that took thousands of years to form.

p3bb85e808b.title: The Story of the Microscope
p3bb85e808b.text:
Around the year 1021, the scientist Ibn al-Haytham studied how light bends in curved glass. No one had built a microscope yet. Centuries later, around 1590, Dutch eyeglass makers put lenses at both ends of a tube. Small objects looked much larger!

In 1665, the English scientist Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork. He named the tiny boxes he saw “cells.” A few years later, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made his own strong lenses and saw tiny living things in a drop of pond water.

During the 1930s, engineers built the electron microscope. It uses beams of tiny particles instead of light. Today, scientists can magnify objects more than a million times and watch germs cling to a cell.

[Timeline: 1021 Ibn al-Haytham studies light; 1590 first tube microscope; 1665 Hooke names cells; 1670s tiny living things observed; 1930s electron microscope]

p9a37e20dc6.title: The Big Race
p9a37e20dc6.text:
Rami checked the wheels of his racing wheelchair twice before the big race. The left wheel made a tiny clicking sound, but he decided it was nothing. The sky above the track was a gray blanket, and a cool wind was beginning to blow.

When the starter's whistle sounded, Rami shot forward like an arrow. He passed one racer, then another. His teammate Kareem cheered from the side, his voice as loud as a drum.

Halfway around the track, the clicking grew louder. Rami felt the chair pull to the left, and he slowed down to keep from crashing. Two racers zoomed past him. His chest burned with disappointment, but he gripped the wheels and pushed on toward the finish line.

p187d7b120c.title: The Empty Seat
p187d7b120c.text:
Every Saturday, Lina's older brother, Adam, drove her to wheelchair basketball practice and stayed to watch. This week, however, he kept glancing at his phone, and his knee bounced like a restless rabbit. “I might have to leave early,” he mumbled.

During the scrimmage, Lina looked toward the bleachers after every basket. Adam's seat was empty. Her confidence melted like ice on a hot sidewalk, and she missed three easy shots in a row.

That evening, Lina finally told Adam how disappointed she felt. He was quiet for a moment. “I've been distant lately,” he admitted. “I was helping my friend study for a big test, but I should have told you.” Lina nodded, and the knot in her stomach slowly loosened. Next Saturday, Adam promised, he would be in the front row.

p4ed38de1c6.title: Digging Up the Past
p4ed38de1c6.text:
For many years, people believed that the fort at Jamestown had been washed away by the James River. Then, in 1994, an archaeologist named William Kelso began to dig near the riverbank. Before long, his team began to uncover pieces of pottery, tools, and coins. In 1996, they found dark stains in the soil left by the fort's wooden walls.

[Sidebar: What Do Archaeologists Do? Archaeology is the study of the past through objects people left behind. Archaeologists dig carefully, record where each object is found, and compare it with old documents.]

Since then, researchers have found more than a million objects at the site. Each item is evidence about how the settlers lived, what they ate, and how they traded with the Powhatan people. Together, these discoveries have changed what historians know about this era.

p3a1c4d519d.title: The First Years at Jamestown
p3a1c4d519d.text:
In December 1606, three small ships left England carrying 104 men and boys on a long expedition across the Atlantic Ocean. After about four months at sea, they reached Virginia in April 1607. In May, the colonists chose a spot on the James River and began building a fort.

The first summer brought tremendous hardships. The river water was salty and unsafe, food ran low, and many settlers became sick. In September 1608, John Smith became the colony's leader and made a strict rule: those who did not work would not eat.

The winter of 1609 to 1610 was so terrible that it became known as the “Starving Time.” Yet the colony survived, and Jamestown became the first permanent English settlement in North America.

[Map: Three ships sail from England across the Atlantic Ocean to the Chesapeake Bay, then up the James River to Jamestown.]

pc1897319ab.title: Power from the Playground Roof
pc1897319ab.text:
Last year, the students at Al-Noor School noticed that their classrooms used a lot of electricity. The air conditioners ran all day, and the lights stayed on even when rooms were empty. The students wanted to find a cleaner way to get energy.

The school decided to put solar panels on the roof. Workers installed forty panels in just two days. Now the panels catch sunlight and turn it into electricity for the classrooms.

The students also made a few new rules. They turn off lights when they leave a room. They close the doors so cool air stays inside. Small choices like these help the school save energy and money.

[Sidebar: How Does a Solar Panel Work? A solar panel is made of special cells. When sunlight hits the cells, they make a small electric current.]

p2e08ca9990.title: Wind at Work
p2e08ca9990.text:
People have used wind for energy for a very long time. Centuries ago, windmills in Persia used moving air to grind grain into flour. Today, tall wind turbines do a different job. Their long blades spin when the wind blows, and a machine inside the turbine converts that motion into electricity.

Wind power has many benefits. Wind is renewable, so it will never run out, and turbines do not send smoke into the air. However, wind energy also has problems. The wind does not blow all the time, so turbines cannot make electricity every hour of the day. Some people also feel that long rows of turbines spoil the view of open land.

Engineers are working to solve these problems. Some are building large batteries that store extra electricity for calm days.

[Sidebar: Did You Know? The blades of many wind turbines are longer than a basketball court.]

p4235d51fa4.title: The Biofuel Debate
p4235d51fa4.text:
Mr. Hamdan's fourth-grade class was preparing for a debate about biofuels. Biofuels are fuels made from plants or from waste such as used cooking oil. Half of the class would argue that biofuels are a good choice, and the other half would argue against them.

Reem's team found several advantages. Plants grow back each season, so biofuels are renewable. Turning waste into fuel also keeps old oil out of drains and rivers.

Faisal's team discovered problems. Growing fuel crops takes a great deal of land and water. In a dry country, that water might be needed more for food. Some biofuels also cost more to make than gasoline.

On the day of the debate, both teams spoke clearly and listened politely. In the end, the class agreed on one thing. Every energy source has costs and benefits, and wise choices come from comparing them carefully.

p46c5a2d6d4.title: The Caravan at Hail
p46c5a2d6d4.text:
In the spring of 1870, a long caravan of camels moved slowly toward the town of Hail. Twelve-year-old Salim walked beside his father. The sun was hot, and the wind blew sand into his eyes. Salim found the sand irritating, but he did not complain.

Salim's father was searching for his older brother, Khalid. The two brothers had been apart for twenty years. Khalid had left home to trade horses in the north, and no letters had come back.

When the caravan reached the town well, a gray-bearded man was filling a water skin. He looked up, and his eyes grew wide. “Ahmad?” he whispered. Salim's father dropped the rope he was holding. The two brothers hugged for a long time, and Salim smiled. His family was whole again.

pc909660c82.title: Waiting on the Pearl Coast
pc909660c82.text:
In the summer of 1925, the town of Darin sat quietly beside the warm waters of the Gulf. Most of the men had sailed away months earlier to dive for pearls. Only women, children, and old men remained in the narrow lanes between the coral-stone houses.

Every evening, Mariam climbed onto the flat roof of her home and watched the sea. Her father's boat had been gone since spring. The heat during the day was so intense that even the cats slept in the shade, but the evening breeze carried the smell of salt and seaweed.

At last, one evening in September, white sails appeared on the horizon. People rushed down to the beach, shouting and waving. Mariam ran faster than she had ever run. When her father stepped onto the sand, tired and thin, she held his hand and would not let it go.

pf364024714.title: Many Voices
pf364024714.text:
In the year 1150, the great geographer al-Idrisi was working on a map of the known world in the city of Palermo. Travelers from many lands came to his workshop to describe the rivers, mountains, and cities they had seen.

Yusuf, a boy who spoke both Arabic and Greek, was hired to help. At first he found the work dull. Many sailors spoke too quickly, and some argued about distances. Yusuf despised the long afternoons of copying numbers.

One day, an old sailor from a distant island described a harbor that no one in the workshop had ever heard of. Yusuf carefully translated every word, and al-Idrisi added the harbor to the map. The geographer thanked him warmly. “A map is made by many voices,” he said. “Without you, this harbor would be missing.”

From then on, Yusuf listened to every traveler with patience, proud to be one of those voices.

p364070461c.title: Up the Green Mountain
p364070461c.text:
Early in the morning, my whole family climbs the mountain path near Abha.
The mist wraps around our shoulders like a soft gray blanket.
My father walks in front, steady and slow, a camel who never tires.
My little sister skips ahead, then stops to pick tiny yellow flowers.

The old juniper trees lean over the trail and whisper secrets to the wind.
When we reach the top, the clouds lie below us like a sleeping sea.
My grandmother opens a basket, and we gobble warm bread with honey.
I look at my family, laughing together in the cool mountain air,
and I know this mountain will always hold a piece of us.

pfd34e0164a.title: My Name Is Yasmin
pfd34e0164a.text:
Grandmother named me Yasmin after the jasmine vine on our garden wall.
Each spring, it climbs higher, reaching for the sun with tiny green fingers.
My cousins all have names from old family stories, but mine came from a flower.
At first, I wished my name were as grand and famous as theirs.

Now I watch the vine wrap itself around the wall like a gentle hug,
and its white blossoms fill the evening air with sweetness.
Like the jasmine, I keep climbing, even when the wall feels too tall.
My name is not a story from the past; it is a promise still growing.
It is my own, and it belongs to no one else.

paa29df0378.title: Two Views from the Dune
paa29df0378.text:
Brother: The desert at night is empty and silent, and I miss my bright city lights.
The cold wind bites my ears, and the sand creeps into everything I own.
I count the long hours until we pack the tent and drive back home.

Sister: The desert at night is a giant theater, and the stars are the audience.
The wind hums an old song that my grandfather once taught me.
I hope this night stretches on forever, like the dunes around our tent.

p4ec5d8a2a6.title: A Naturalist's Notebook
p4ec5d8a2a6.text:
Naturalists are scientists who study plants and animals where they live. One of their most important tools is a simple notebook called a field journal. In it, they record the date, the weather, and everything they observe.

A field journal is a primary source because it is written by the person who saw the events firsthand. Here is an entry from a student naturalist who visited a mangrove forest on the Red Sea coast:

[Journal entry: “March 3. Low tide. I saw at least twenty small crabs waving one giant claw. When a heron landed nearby, they all ran into their holes at once!”]

Later, a writer might use journals like this one to write a book about mangroves. That book would be a secondary source, because its author did not see the events herself.

p3fc0e47934.title: The Plant Traveler
p3fc0e47934.text:
Ibn al-Baitar was born in Málaga, in Al-Andalus, around the year 1197. As a boy, he walked through the hills with an herbalist who taught him the names of wild plants. Because of these early lessons, he became fascinated by the natural world.

When he was about twenty, he left home to study plants in other lands. He traveled across North Africa and into Egypt and Syria. Wherever he went, he gathered plants, questioned local healers, and checked whether earlier books were correct. As a result, he found many mistakes that older writers had made.

His careful work led to a huge book that described more than 1,400 plants and other natural medicines. Scholars used his book for generations, and some of his notes were translated into other languages centuries later.

pfa872087d4.title: Shields of the Shore
pfa872087d4.text:
Along the coasts of the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, mangrove trees grow where the land meets salty water. Their tangled roots rise above the mud like the legs of a giant spider. These roots slow down waves, so the shore behind them washes away less during storms. The roots also trap mud, leaves, and other debris, which slowly builds up new land.

For many years, people cut down mangroves to build roads and harbors. As a result, some coasts lost their natural shield, and fish that once hid among the roots became harder to find.

Today, scientists and volunteers are planting millions of young mangroves. Naturalists who study these new forests have noticed a spectacular change. Birds are nesting in the branches again, and young fish are returning to the shallow water.

p247e735717.title: The Mint Garden
p247e735717.text:
Huda loved the scent of fresh mint, but the small grocery on her street had stopped selling it. Now mint was scarce in the neighborhood, and her grandmother complained that her afternoon tea tasted ordinary without it.

Huda had an idea: she could grow mint on the flat roof of their apartment building and sell fragrant bundles to her neighbors. Unfortunately, there was a problem, because she needed pots, soil, and seeds, and she did not have enough money to buy them.

Huda counted her savings. She had only half of what she needed. Then her older brother offered her a small loan. “You can repay me when you sell your first bundles,” he explained.

Six weeks later, bright green leaves overflowed from every pot. Huda sold her mint at the door each afternoon, and soon she had paid back her brother and earned a small profit.

p6ceab6b37f.title: The Bicycle Doctor
p6ceab6b37f.text:
Every afternoon, Faris watched the younger children in his neighborhood push bicycles with flat tires and loose, rattling chains. The only repair shop in town was far away, and few families could afford the bus fare to get there.

Faris knew how to repair bicycles because his uncle, a patient mechanic, had taught him. He decided to open a small repair stand in front of his apartment building, charging a few riyals for each repair to cover the cost of tubes and tools.

On the first Saturday, nobody came. Faris began to wonder whether the stand had been a foolish waste of his savings. Then his friend Majid suggested a practical solution. “People do not know you are here,” he said, “so let's make colorful signs.”

They painted bright signs and placed them near the school entrance and the neighborhood mosque. By the following weekend, a long line of children stood waiting, each one holding a broken bicycle.

p3e16cc8955.title: Dates for the Fair
p3e16cc8955.text:
For several weeks, the twins Lama and Dana had been planning a stall for their school's charity fair. They intended to sell homemade date cookies and donate every riyal of profit to the children's hospital. But two days before the fair, they had a serious disagreement.

Lama wanted to bake two hundred cookies. “The more we make, the more money we will raise,” she insisted. Dana shook her head firmly. “Flour and dates are expensive, and if we cannot sell them all, we will waste our savings,” she argued. Neither sister would change her mind, and the kitchen grew uncomfortably silent.

That evening, their mother asked each girl to explain her reasoning. After listening carefully, she suggested a compromise. They would bake one hundred cookies first and make more only if the first batch sold quickly.

At the fair, every cookie had disappeared by noon. The twins agreed that next year they would plan together from the very beginning.

pb7297831e4.title: Tablets Belong in Every Classroom
pb7297831e4.text:
Every student in our country should have a tablet for schoolwork. Tablets give young readers access to thousands of books, and they help students advance at their own speed.

Faster Access to Information
A tablet can hold an entire library, so a student in a small village can read the same books as a student in a big city. Teachers can also send new lessons and practice activities to their classes in seconds.

What the Numbers Show
[Bar graph: Average minutes of reading per day. Students with paper books only: 18 minutes. Students with tablets and paper books: 27 minutes.]
In one survey of four hundred students, those who used tablets read nine more minutes each day. This data suggests that tablets encourage reading.

Answering the Critics
Some parents worry that bright screens can tire children's eyes. That is a fair counterpoint, but schools can easily require short screen breaks every twenty minutes.

pa2df712388.title: Why Families Need Screen-Free Evenings
pa2df712388.text:
Families should switch off their devices for at least one evening each week. Phones and tablets certainly have benefits, but their drawbacks grow when they take over the hours that families spend together.

Less Talk at the Table
A recent study by a children's health organization found that families who used phones during dinner talked to each other for only half as long. Researchers cite this loss of conversation as one reason children feel disconnected at home.
[Line graph: Minutes of family conversation per evening. No devices: 40 minutes. One device at the table: 28 minutes. Three or more devices: 19 minutes.]

A Fair Counterpoint
Some people argue that video calls allow children to talk with grandparents who live far away. This is true, and those calls are valuable. However, a screen-free evening does not ban such calls; it simply protects one night for talking face to face.

A Simple Start
Choose one evening, place every device in a basket, and let the conversation begin.

pdb33ddaa7d.title: A Plan for a Stronger Nation
pdb33ddaa7d.text:
A Weak First Government
After the American Revolution, the thirteen states agreed to a plan called the Articles of Confederation. Under this plan, the national government could not collect taxes, so it had no money to pay its soldiers or its debts.

Meeting in Philadelphia
In May 1787, representatives from twelve states gathered in Philadelphia for a convention. George Washington was chosen to lead the meetings. Large states wanted more votes in Congress because they had more people, but small states feared that they would be ignored.

The Great Compromise
To resolve this debate, the delegates accepted a proposal from the state of Connecticut. Congress would have two parts. In the Senate, every state would have two members, while in the House of Representatives, states with larger populations would have more members.

[Timeline: 1781, Articles of Confederation approved. May 1787, convention begins. September 1787, Constitution signed. 1788, enough states approve the Constitution.]

p874c9c0e5e.title: Seven Emirates, One Nation
p874c9c0e5e.text:
A Difficult Situation
In 1968, Britain announced that it would leave the Gulf region by the end of 1971. The small emirates along the coast suddenly faced a serious problem. Each one was too small to protect itself and to build modern schools, hospitals, and roads alone.

Talking Together
Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi and Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum of Dubai met and agreed to work as partners. They invited the other rulers to join them, and for nearly four years the leaders discussed how a union of the emirates could work fairly for everyone.

A New Country
On 2 December 1971, six emirates formed the United Arab Emirates, and Sheikh Zayed became its first president. Ras Al Khaimah joined a few weeks later, in February 1972.

[Timeline: 1968, Britain announces it will leave. February 1968, Abu Dhabi and Dubai agree to unite. December 1971, the UAE is formed. February 1972, Ras Al Khaimah joins.]

p298d81be04.title: The Lost Net of the Singing Sea
p298d81be04.text:
Long ago, in a village where the sea sang softly to the shore each evening, there lived an old woman who made beautiful fishing nets. One night a jealous wind snatched her finest net and carried it far across the water.

Her son Hamad, determined to recover it, set out at dawn in his small wooden boat. The waves grumbled and pushed against him, but he kept rowing. On the third day, exhausted and hungry, he met an old fisherman sitting alone on a rock in the middle of the water. “Follow the gulls,” the fisherman said, “and do not turn back when the sea grows angry.”

Hamad thanked him and followed the gulls. Soon black clouds marched across the sky, and the furious sea roared around his tiny boat. Hamad's arms ached, yet he remembered the old man's words. At last he detected a flash of silver between two rocks. There, caught on a jagged reef, was his mother's precious net, shining like the moon above the water.

pbde2d23737.title: The Mountain That Kept Its Secrets
pbde2d23737.text:
Long ago, a young weaver named Salma lived at the foot of a tall mountain whose stony face frowned down on her village. Every spring, the village well ran dry, and the people walked for hours to fetch water.

One morning, an old traveler stopped at Salma's door. In gratitude for the bread she shared, he told her a secret. “A spring sleeps beneath the eagle's rock near the summit,” he said. “Wake it, and your village will never be thirsty again.”

Salma packed a rope and a small hammer and began the long, dangerous climb. As she climbed, the wind tugged at her scarf and tried to pull her backward, and loose stones whispered warnings under her feet. Twice she slipped on the crumbling path, and twice she stood up again, determined to continue.

Near the summit, after many exhausting hours, she finally discovered the eagle's rock. She pressed her ear against it and heard water murmuring inside. Salma lifted her hammer.

p0e72a1df8e.title: The Boy Who Planted Shade
p0e72a1df8e.text:
Young Faris watched the children waiting daily underneath the burning summer sun,
So he decided he would plant a little tree for every single one.
His ambitious plan seemed foolish to the neighbors living on his crowded street,
Who laughed and said a desert boy could never hope to beat the heat.
He carried heavy buckets every morning, watering each tiny seed,
And whispered, “One small tree today is all the waiting children need.”
He whispered it through windy autumn, whispered it through winter rain,
“One small tree today,” he promised, planting carefully again.
The seasons turned, the branches spread, and cooling shadows touched the ground,
And now the children rest beneath the leafy shelter Faris found.

p4bb076cd10.title: What My Sister Carried
p4bb076cd10.text:
On Fridays my sister walked to the community kitchen beside the busy harbor.
She carried bags of rice, lentils, and dates that she had collected from our neighbors.
I asked her why she bothered, since one person could hardly change anything important.
She did not answer; she simply handed me a heavy bag and said, “Come and see.”
I watched an elderly fisherman accept a warm meal with trembling, grateful hands.
I watched a little boy smile as he balanced a bowl of soup against his chest.
Now every Friday, I carry the heavier bag,
and I understand the satisfaction my sister never needed to explain.

pfc8e96ced5.title: A Week in Kuala Lumpur
pfc8e96ced5.text:
Yousef had not wanted to leave Jeddah for his father's work trip. He would miss the football tournament, and he was sure that Malaysia would feel strange and lonely.

On the first morning, his father's colleague, Mr. Lim, took them to a crowded breakfast stall beside a colorful neighborhood market. Yousef frowned at the bowl of rice cooked in coconut milk. “I don't eat spicy food,” he blurted, before he had even tasted it.

Mr. Lim only laughed and pushed a plate of sliced cucumber toward him. “Try a little with the cucumber,” he suggested. Yousef took a small bite, then another. The rice was warm, rich, and fragrant, and it was only slightly spicy after all.

That afternoon, they watched boys playing sepak takraw, kicking a woven ball over a high net without using their hands. Yousef's eyes widened with surprise and excitement. When one boy flipped upside down to strike the ball, Yousef cheered louder than anyone.

“Maybe,” he admitted that evening, “this trip is not so bad after all.”

pbbe7a27da9.title: The Market in Marrakesh
pbbe7a27da9.text:
Amira expected the trip to Marrakesh to be exactly like home. After all, people there spoke Arabic too. However, on her first visit to the market, she discovered that the Moroccan Darija the shopkeepers used sounded very different from her own dialect.

When a carpet seller said something quickly, Amira thought he was being rude and turned away. Her grandmother gently caught her sleeve. “He was complimenting your scarf,” she explained. “He said its colors remind him of the desert at sunset.”

Amira's cheeks grew warm. She realized that the misunderstanding had been her own fault, not the seller's. She walked back, smiled, and thanked him in careful, slow Arabic. The seller laughed kindly and taught her three new Darija words.

By the end of the week, Amira had filled a notebook with phrases, recipes, and sketches of tiled fountains. She no longer wanted everything to be like home.

p75b18c48d7.title: Fences on the Water
p75b18c48d7.text:
When a ship leaks oil near a coast, the oil spreads across the water in a thin, shiny layer that can stretch for many kilometers. It can coat the feathers of seabirds and wash onto beaches where turtles lay their eggs. Workers must act quickly to stop the oil from spreading.

One of the first tools that cleanup crews usually depend on is a boom. A boom is a long, floating tube that works like a fence on the water. Crews in small boats pull the boom around the oil to trap it in one place.

Next, powerful machines called skimmers go to work beside the floating booms. A skimmer glides across the surface and lifts the oil off the water, the way a spoon lifts cream from the top of milk. The oil is pumped into tanks so that it can be carried away safely.

Booms and skimmers do not solve every problem, but they give workers valuable time to protect the shore and the animals living there.

p40ce8b8261.title: Borrowing Ideas from Nature
p40ce8b8261.text:
Oil and water do not mix, yet separating them after a spill is surprisingly difficult. Ordinary sponges soak up both liquids, so they quickly fill with seawater and stop working. For years, this obstacle frustrated engineers who wanted a simple way to remove oil from the ocean.

Some researchers found an answer by studying the lotus plant. Water rolls off a lotus leaf in round drops because the leaf is covered with tiny bumps and a waxy coating. Scientists designed an artificial sponge that mimics this surface. Its fibers push water away but grab oil and hold it inside.

The new sponges are also flexible. Workers can squeeze the oil out, collect it in a container, and use the same sponge again many times. Because the design copies a function found in nature, it creates less waste than older methods.

Inventors call this approach biomimicry. Instead of starting from nothing, they ask how plants and animals already solve similar problems.

p0b5580559a.title: Small Tokens, Big Ideas
p0b5580559a.text:
Long before people wrote words, they still needed to keep records. I believe that small clay tokens found in ancient Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, were one of the earliest record systems in the world.

Archaeologists have found thousands of these tokens. Some are shaped like cones, some like balls, and some like tiny jars. Each shape seems to stand for a different good, such as grain, oil, or sheep. A farmer who owed ten jars of oil could be given ten jar-shaped tokens.

There is more evidence for this idea. Some tokens were sealed inside hollow clay balls. Marks pressed on the outside of the balls matched the tokens inside, so anyone could check the count without breaking the ball.

These simple objects show that people found clever ways to record information. They also may have led to one of the greatest inventions of all: writing.

peb11b07b18.title: Save the Past in Pixels
peb11b07b18.text:
Every year, ancient objects in museums become a little weaker. Cloth fades, wood cracks, and paper crumbles into fragments. In my view, every museum should create detailed digital copies of its oldest treasures before more of them are lost.

First, digital copies protect the originals. When students and researchers can study a three-dimensional scan on a screen, curators can keep the real object preserved in a dark, cool room where light and touch cannot harm it.

Second, scans allow people everywhere to learn. A historian in Riyadh could examine a scroll stored in London without traveling at all.

Some people argue that a copy can never replace the real thing, and they are partly right. Standing in front of an intact object from a distant era is a powerful experience. However, a scan does not replace the original; it simply makes sure that the original survives for future generations to see.

p327f624df4.title: A Voice for Readers Who Could Not See
p327f624df4.text:
Louis Braille was born in a small French village in 1809. When he was three years old, he hurt his eye with a tool in his father's workshop. An infection spread, and by age five he was blind in both eyes.

At that time, blind children rarely went to school. Louis was lucky. He won a place at a special school for blind students in Paris, more than thirty kilometers from his home. The school owned only a few books, and each one used huge raised letters that were slow to read.

Louis sought a better way. At age fifteen, he created a code of raised dots that fingers could read quickly. Some teachers preferred the old method, but Louis continued improving his system patiently.

[Photograph: A young student runs her fingers across a page of raised dots. Caption: Today, millions of people around the world read with Louis Braille's six-dot code.]

Louis Braille gave blind readers something they had always deserved: the freedom to read on their own.

p8287f2324e.title: Helen Keller: Speaking for Others
p8287f2324e.text:
Helen Keller was not yet two years old when an illness left her unable to see or hear. For several years she lived in a silent, dark world, and she often became angry because no one could understand her.

Everything changed in 1887, when a teacher named Anne Sullivan arrived. Anne spelled words into Helen's hand with her fingers. One day, as cool water poured over one hand, Anne spelled w-a-t-e-r into the other. Suddenly Helen understood that every object had a name, and she was eager to learn them all.

Helen went on to graduate from college, a remarkable achievement for anyone at that time. She did not stay quiet about what she had learned. She traveled to more than thirty countries, giving outspoken speeches about the rights of people with disabilities.

[Photograph: Helen Keller sits beside a table, reading a book with her fingers. Caption: Keller believed that every child, whatever their challenges, was entitled to an education.]

Her life proves that courage can open doors that seem permanently locked.

pf8db9fcac0.title: The Missing Compass
pf8db9fcac0.text:
[Setting: A tent at a desert campsite just after sunset. A lantern hangs from the center pole, and sleeping bags cover the floor.]

SAMI: (searching through his backpack) Grandfather's brass compass was right here in the front pocket, and now it has completely vanished!

HUDA: (calmly) Don't panic, Sami. Think carefully about every place that you visited this afternoon.

SAMI: We climbed the enormous dune, we fed the camels, and then we helped Grandfather build the evening fire.

GRANDFATHER: (entering with a smile) Haste makes waste, children. Searching wildly will only scatter everything further.

HUDA: (pointing at the sand near the door) Look at those wide, padded tracks leading directly toward the camels!

SAMI: (astounded) Do you think a camel carried my compass away?

GRANDFATHER: (laughing) Not exactly, but a curious young camel loves pulling shiny objects from open pockets.

p0d4e3d1036.title: The Tortoise Who Disappeared
p0d4e3d1036.text:
[Setting: A school garden on a hot morning. A low wooden fence surrounds a patch of grass, a water dish, and a pile of leafy lettuce that nobody has touched.]

MARYAM: (kneeling by the fence, perplexed) Our tortoise, Qamar, was inside this fence yesterday afternoon. The gate is closed, so how could she possibly escape?

OMAR: (folding his arms, suspicious) I saw Khalid standing near the garden after school. Maybe he took her home without asking.

KHALID: (hurrying in) I heard my name! I was only filling her water dish, and I locked the gate when I left.

MARYAM: Let's not jump to conclusions, Omar. We should interpret the clues before we blame anyone.

KHALID: (crouching to examine the ground) Look at this freshly dug soil under the lettuce. Tortoises dig shallow holes to stay cool when the weather becomes too hot.

OMAR: (embarrassed) I suppose I should reconsider what I said. Appearances can be deceiving.

MARYAM: (gently brushing away the soil) Here she is, concealed beneath the leaves and perfectly safe!

p6d596d429d.title: Keeping the Sea
p6d596d429d.text:
Before the long vacation ends, I wander slowly by the shore,
collecting every shining shell the tide delivered here before.
The waves are silver ribbons that unravel on the sand;
I hold the warm and golden afternoon like water in my hand.

The seagulls are writing messages in circles on the sky,
and all the fishing boats are sleepy whales that drift nearby.
I fill a jar with memories, with laughter, salt, and light,
so I can open summer on a gray December night.

p7210f35dd0.title: After the Rain in the Desert
p7210f35dd0.text:
For months the valley was barren and brown,
a dusty page that nobody wanted to open or read,
where the restless wind wrote only lonely messages of sand.

Then one evening the heavy clouds arrived,
gray plumes of feathers drifting slowly over the silent hills,
and the rain began a patient conversation with the thirsty ground.

By morning, tiny green fingers were reaching upward everywhere.
Purple flowers opened like delicate umbrellas,
and the bees were humming, busy as merchants in a crowded market.

The land had not been empty after all.
It had been waiting quietly, holding its seeds like precious secrets,
for the wonderful moment when it could finally speak.

pcc25fad132.title: Al-Biruni Measures Earth
pcc25fad132.text:
About a thousand years ago, a scholar named Al-Biruni wanted to know the size of Earth. Other thinkers had tried before, but their methods needed long trips across deserts. Al-Biruni found a simpler way.

First, he measured the height of a mountain near the town of Nandana. Next, he climbed to the top and looked at the horizon, the line where the land seems to meet the sky. He measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line.

[Diagram: A large circle shows Earth. A tall mountain stands on its edge. A dotted line runs from the mountaintop to the horizon, and a small label reads “angle of dip.”]

With these two numbers and a careful calculation, he worked out the size of the whole planet. His answer was approximately the same as the one scientists use today. He showed that a clever idea can be as useful as a long and difficult journey.

p0b1697f571.title: Weather Balloons
p0b1697f571.text:
Every day, at hundreds of stations around the world, scientists release weather balloons at the same time. Each balloon carries a small box of instruments called a radiosonde. As the balloon rises, the radiosonde measures temperature, air pressure, and moisture. It sends this data back to the ground by radio every few seconds.

[Diagram: A large balloon at the top is labeled “filled with helium.” A string hangs below it to a small parachute. Below the parachute hangs a box labeled “radiosonde.”]

The air pressure gets lower as the balloon climbs higher. Because of this, the balloon slowly swells until it is several times wider than when it left the ground. At about 30 kilometers high, it finally bursts. The parachute then opens, and the radiosonde drifts gently back to Earth. Forecasters use the data to predict storms and plan safe flights.

p8da50d3d0c.title: Watching Earth from Space
p8da50d3d0c.text:
Before the space age, scientists could study only small pieces of Earth at a time. A thermometer on a rooftop recorded the temperature of one city, and a ship could measure the waves of one patch of sea. Nobody could watch the whole planet working together.

Satellites changed that. Circling high above the surface, these machines photograph clouds, oceans, forests, and ice every day. Some carry instruments that sense heat, which allows researchers to measure the temperature of the atmosphere and the sea from far away. The first satellite, launched in 1957, was about the size of a beach ball.

The data has revealed patterns that were once invisible. Researchers have watched sea ice shrink, deserts spread, and enormous dust storms travel thousands of kilometers across oceans.

Today, satellites give scientists a view of Earth as one connected system rather than a collection of separate places.

pc2511f6260.title: The Soup Pot, 1932
pc2511f6260.text:
In the winter of 1932, Papa lost his job at the shoe factory, and the family's small savings disappeared within a few months. Mama started making soup from whatever was left in the cupboard. Some nights it was only potatoes and water with a little salt.

One evening, Ruth noticed that old Mr. Kaplan next door had not lit his stove for several days. She looked at the steaming pot, and then she looked at her little brother's hungry face, wondering whether it was fair to ask.

“Mama,” she asked quietly, “could we share some of our supper with Mr. Kaplan, since he lives all alone?”

Mama sighed and rubbed her tired eyes. “We barely have enough for ourselves, Ruth, and winter is far from over.”

Ruth did not argue. She simply poured half of her own bowl into a glass jar and wrapped it carefully in a towel to keep it warm. Then she pulled on her thin coat, tiptoed past the kitchen, and stepped quietly into the cold, dark hallway.

peedd45ab34.title: Leo's Plan
peedd45ab34.text:
Leo was twelve years old in 1935, and he was tired of watching his father search for work that never seemed to come. Each morning Pa left before sunrise, and each evening he came home with empty hands and a tired smile.

“I could sell newspapers on the corner,” Leo suggested at dinner, “because plenty of boys my age already do it.”

Pa shook his head. “Your job is school, and I won't have you leave it for any reason.”

Leo pushed his beans around his plate. He felt caught between two things he cared about. He loved his lessons, especially arithmetic, but he hated seeing his family worry about every penny.

That night, he lay awake considering possibilities until a solution finally appeared. He would sell papers for one hour before school and still be in his seat when the bell rang. In the morning, he explained his plan carefully. After a long, thoughtful silence, Pa smiled and said, “You drive a hard bargain, son, so just keep your grades up.”

p162612962c.title: Black Sunday
p162612962c.text:
By April of 1935, the wind on the plains had become an enemy. It lifted the dry soil from the fields and carried it for miles, leaving fences buried and crops ruined. Mae's family had stayed on their farm through three hard years, but every storm tested their patience.

On a quiet Sunday afternoon, Mae was hanging laundry when the birds suddenly went silent. She glanced toward the north and froze. A black wall of dust, taller than any building she had ever seen, was rolling across the horizon.

Dropping a sheet into the basket, she shouted for her grandfather as loudly as she could.

Grandpa appeared on the porch, studied the sky, and wasted no time. “Get the animals into the barn, and then wet some cloths and press them against every window in the house,” he ordered calmly.

Mae ran toward the chickens with her heart pounding. Over the years she had learned an important lesson: panic helped no one, but courage and quick thinking almost always could.

p95e75f4b38.title: Lionfish Do Not Belong Here
p95e75f4b38.text:
Lionfish are beautiful fish with striped fins and long spines. They come from the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea, where they live in balance with other animals. In the Atlantic Ocean, however, they cause serious trouble.

Why Are Lionfish a Problem?

In the Atlantic, lionfish have no natural enemies. They eat huge numbers of small reef fish, and each female can lay thousands of eggs. As a result, their numbers have grown quickly along many coasts.

[Chart: Young reef fish on one Atlantic reef. Before lionfish arrived: 100. Five weeks after: 21.]

What Can People Do?

I believe divers and fishers should catch as many lionfish as they possibly can. Some restaurants now serve lionfish, which gives people another good reason to hunt them. Protecting our reefs is worth the effort.

p87c22977fe.title: A Welcome Newcomer
p87c22977fe.text:
Not every plant or animal from another land causes harm. The honeybee is a good example. Honeybees first came from Europe, Africa, and Asia, yet today they live on farms all around the world.

How Do Honeybees Help Farmers?

Many crops cannot make fruit unless pollen moves from flower to flower, a job that wind alone cannot do well. Honeybees carry that pollen as they collect nectar. Farmers who grow almonds, apples, and melons often rent hives from beekeepers during the short blooming season so that their trees produce more fruit.

[Chart: How much each crop depends on bees. Almonds: very high. Apples: high. Melons: high. Wheat: none.]

Should We Worry About Them?

Some people point out that honeybees compete with wild bees for flowers. That concern is fair, and scientists should keep studying it. Still, the agricultural benefits that honeybees provide to farmers everywhere are enormous. In my view, honeybees have earned their place in our fields.

pb0098258d3.title: A Tree That Went Too Far
pb0098258d3.text:
Decades ago, planners in parts of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula faced a serious problem: the desert was creeping toward villages. They chose a solution that seemed perfect. Mesquite, a tough tree from the Americas, could thrive with very little rain, hold sand in place, and provide firewood.

What Went Wrong?

The mesquite grew far better than anyone expected. Its seeds spread through animal droppings, and thick thorny forests soon covered grazing land, riverbanks, and farm fields. In some regions, native trees declined as mesquite took their water.

[Chart: Land covered by mesquite in one dry region. 1980: small. 2000: medium. 2020: very large.]

What Should We Learn?

I am convinced that mesquite teaches a clear lesson. Before introducing a species, communities must study how it might behave many years later. A quick fix can become a widespread problem that costs far more to solve.

p5965fa89fb.title: The Victory Garden
p5965fa89fb.text:
Nora knelt in the dirt and pulled a fat orange carrot from the ground. She smiled, remembering the day the garden began.

Back in the spring of 1943, Nora had felt useless. Her brother had joined the navy, and her mother worked long hours at the factory. Nora asked Grandpa what a ten-year-old could possibly do to help. Without a word, he handed her a heavy shovel and pointed at the empty, weedy yard behind the house. If families grew their own vegetables, he explained, the farms could send more food to the soldiers.

All summer, Nora watered and weeded under the hot sun. Some days her back ached, and she wanted to quit.

Now, as she filled her basket, she finally understood. Her small garden was feeding not only her own family but also two elderly neighbors down the street. Even a girl with a shovel could make a difference.

p5d932c002e.title: The Scrap Drive
p5d932c002e.text:
The truck pulled away, piled high with old pots, broken bicycles, and rusty tools. Tom waved until it turned the corner, and then he looked down at his empty wagon and grinned proudly.

Three weeks earlier, he had stood in the same spot feeling foolish. The town bulletin had asked every family to donate scrap metal so that factories could build more ships. Tom had dragged his wagon from house to house, but most neighbors simply shook their heads and closed their doors. One man even laughed and said a boy could not help win a war.

That evening, Tom almost gave up. Instead, he painted a cheerful sign that read “Every pot builds a ship” and tied it firmly to his wagon before trying again the next morning. Gradually, doors began to open. Mrs. Lee contributed a dented kettle, the baker added two battered trays, and the mechanic donated an entire box of discarded engine parts.

By the end of the month, Tom's wagon had made forty trips across town. He had learned that patience could turn a closed door into an open one.

pbc92f84967.title: The Night Shift
pbc92f84967.text:
Grandmother Ellen turned the old radio dial slowly, as if it might still carry secrets. “I was only nineteen,” she told me, “when I learned to listen for a living.”

In 1942, she had joined hundreds of young women at a quiet station by the sea. Their task was to intercept coded enemy messages and copy every letter exactly. The work was dull and exhausting. Night after night, she sat with headphones pressed to her ears, writing down strings of letters that meant nothing to her. She never learned what most of them said.

Years later, she discovered that her careful notes had helped others crack the codes and protect ships at sea. No one had thanked her at the time, and she had not expected it.

“Every small task mattered,” she said, switching off the radio. “Even the ones nobody could see.”

p90cda904d4.title: Lights in the Deep
p90cda904d4.text:
Sunlight cannot reach the deep ocean. Below about 1,000 meters, the water is completely dark. Because there is no light, many deep-sea animals make their own. This glow is called bioluminescence.

Animals use their light in different ways. The anglerfish has a glowing lure that hangs above its mouth. Small fish swim toward the light, and the anglerfish quickly snaps them up. Some shrimp spray a cloud of glowing liquid when a predator comes near. The bright cloud confuses the hunter, so the shrimp can escape into the darkness.

Light can also help animals find each other in the endless dark. Some fish flash special patterns of light, much like a secret code that only their own kind can read.

p02b457151f.title: Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor
p02b457151f.text:
In 1977, scientists in a small submarine called Alvin made a surprising discovery near the Galápagos Islands. Deep on the ocean floor, they found cracks that poured out hot water full of minerals. These openings are called hydrothermal vents.

[Map: The eastern Pacific Ocean. A red line marks a long ridge on the sea floor. Stars along the ridge show vent sites. The Galápagos Islands sit close to one of the stars.]

Vents form where the plates of Earth's crust slowly pull apart. Seawater sinks into the cracks, is heated by melted rock below, and then shoots back up. Because the water carries chemicals, tiny bacteria can turn them into food. As a result, tubeworms, crabs, and clams live near the vents even though sunlight never reaches them.

pf91e87a5bc.title: The Warm Deep of the Red Sea
pf91e87a5bc.text:
Most of the deep ocean is frigid, with temperatures barely above freezing. The Red Sea is a remarkable exception. Even two thousand meters down, its water stays at about 21 degrees Celsius.

[Map: The Red Sea is a long, narrow sea between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. At its southern end, a shallow passage called Bab el-Mandeb connects it to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.]

Why is the deep water so warm? The answer lies at the southern entrance. Bab el-Mandeb is shallow, so the icy deep currents of the Indian Ocean cannot flow over it. Meanwhile, the desert sun causes so much evaporation that the surface water becomes extra salty and heavy. This warm, salty water slowly sinks and fills the deep basin.

This unusual warmth has consequences. Many deep-sea animals from the Indian Ocean need cold water, so they cannot survive in the Red Sea's depths. As a result, its deep waters hold fewer species, yet several of them are found nowhere else.

p69c601df82.title: The Library Door
p69c601df82.text:
Every afternoon the library door opens its patient arms and invites me inside,
where quiet shelves whisper stories of oceans, mountains, and faraway villages.
I choose a heavy atlas, and the pages flutter like eager birds beneath my fingers.

Suddenly I am standing in a crowded market in Morocco, where copper lanterns glow,
and a merchant offers me sweet mint tea in exchange for a friendly conversation.
Then I am sailing across the cold green sea toward the islands of Norway,
where the wind sings a long, low song and the waves slap the sides of the wooden boat.

When the clock on the wall announces closing time, I return the atlas to its shelf,
but I carry every country home with me, folded carefully inside my imagination.
I have never needed a ticket or a suitcase to discover the wonderful world.

pb77194a6a6.title: The Errand to the Harbor
pb77194a6a6.text:
Grandfather hands Layla a basket of dates and sends her on an errand to the harbor.
The morning sun stretches its golden fingers across the sleepy rooftops of the town,
and far away the ferry horn blares twice, warning the travelers to hurry aboard.

On the crowded dock, a tired sailor from a distant island rests beside his heavy bag.
Layla offers him the sweetest dates, and he smiles and opens a small wooden box.
Inside are seashells, smooth and pale, that sing of beaches she has never visited.

She carries the seashells home, and Grandfather listens as she describes the stranger.
“Sometimes,” he says, “a simple exchange becomes a bridge between two different worlds.”
Layla places the shells on her windowsill, where they whisper of the open ocean every evening.

p4dfb0a23a2.title: The Final Round
p4dfb0a23a2.text:
Yusuf and Karim had been inseparable friends since second grade, when they had learned chess together at the neighborhood community center. Now both boys had reached the final round of the city tournament, and only one of them could win the trophy.

The night before the match, Yusuf sat at his desk, pensive and silent. He worried that beating Karim might damage their friendship. Karim felt the same way, but he also knew that holding back would be a kind of insult.

When the match began, neither boy tried to evade a difficult position or settle for an early, comfortable draw. Karim launched a barrage of attacks, and Yusuf defended calmly, move after move. After two exhausting hours, Yusuf won by a single pawn.

Karim stood, shook his friend's hand, and smiled warmly. “You earned this victory fairly,” he said, “but next year I'm definitely coming for that trophy.” Both boys laughed, and they walked home together, just as they always had.

pff04555547.title: Two Gloves, One Goal
pff04555547.text:
For three years, Reem and Dana had shared everything: lunch, homework, and a perpetual argument about which football team was better. Then the coach announced that the school team needed only one goalkeeper, and the two friends became rivals overnight.

During tryouts, Dana noticed that Reem kept protecting her left wrist. Dana could have stayed silent, since an injured rival would make her own victory almost certain. Instead, she quietly told the coach, who sent Reem to the school nurse.

Eventually, the coach selected Dana for the position, explaining that her reflexes were remarkably quick. Reem was disappointed, and for a few days the silence between them felt devastating. Finally, Reem knocked on Dana's door holding two pairs of gloves.

“You could have won without saying anything,” Reem said. “You chose my health over an easy victory, and I won't forget that.” Then she grinned and offered to help her friend practice every afternoon before the championship season.

p138fc1ace6.title: The Boy Who Gave Books Fingertips
p138fc1ace6.text:
Louis Braille was born in a small French village in 1809. At the age of three, he injured his eye with a sharp tool in his father's workshop, and an infection soon left him completely blind.

At ten, Louis entered a school for blind children in Paris. The school's few books used huge raised letters that were slow and difficult to read by touch. Then a soldier named Charles Barbier visited and shared a code of raised dots designed for reading messages at night.

Barbier's system was complicated, but Louis recognized its possibilities. Working with determination, he simplified it into a small cell of just six dots. By 1824, when he was only fifteen, his new alphabet was ready.

Louis later became a teacher and continued improving his code. Today, braille is used around the world, and millions of blind readers can enjoy books independently because of a teenager's persistence.

p8008ff57eb.title: The Windmill Builder
p8008ff57eb.text:
In 2001, a severe drought struck Malawi, and William Kamkwamba's family, like many farming families, could barely find enough food. Unable to pay school fees, fourteen-year-old William had to leave school.

Instead of giving up on learning, he visited a small village library. There he discovered a science book with a picture of windmills on its cover. Although his English was limited, he studied the diagrams carefully and imagined building one himself.

Neighbors laughed as William collected scrap metal, an old bicycle frame, and plastic pipes from a junkyard. He persevered anyway. In 2002, his windmill turned in the wind and powered a few small lights in his family's home. Later, he built a larger windmill to pump water for crops.

William's achievement attracted international attention, and he eventually completed his education at a university in the United States. His story shows that curiosity and persistence can contribute more to success than expensive equipment.

p61b8676db5.title: The Lemon Tree
p61b8676db5.text:
Noura found the chrysalis hanging beneath a leaf of her grandmother's lemon tree. It looked like a tiny green lantern, smooth and still, and it seemed to conceal a precious secret.

“Be patient,” Grandmother said. “Something wonderful is happening inside, even if you cannot see it.”

Every morning before school, Noura checked the chrysalis. Every morning, she also practiced the speech she would give on the school stage at the end of the month. Her voice trembled, and her hands felt cold and clumsy.

On the day of the speech, Noura woke early and hurried to the tree. The chrysalis had split open, and a butterfly was slowly drying its delicate orange wings in the warm sunlight. After a few quiet minutes, it lifted gracefully into the air.

That afternoon, Noura stepped onto the stage, took a deep breath, and began to speak in a clear, steady voice.

p638fcbf34e.title: The Borrowed Shell
p638fcbf34e.text:
During his first week in the coastal town, Ali spent every afternoon alone on the rocks, pretending to study the tide pools so that no one would notice how lonely he felt. His old friends were a thousand kilometers away, and the new school felt enormous.

One afternoon he spotted a hermit crab dragging a cracked, cramped shell across the sand. The crab paused beside an empty whelk shell, examined it cautiously, and then, in one quick, fragile moment, abandoned its old home. For a few seconds it was soft and completely unprotected. Then it slipped into the larger shell and marched away, almost proudly.

Ali watched for a long time. The next morning, he left his comfortable silence behind and asked the boy beside him about the school's robotics club. His voice shook, but the boy grinned and invited him to the meeting.

p79290f2131.title: Sadu
p79290f2131.text:
My grandmother sits beside the tent with her loom stretched across the sand,
pulling crimson and black threads through her experienced fingers as patiently as the desert waits for rain.
She weaves triangles like mountains and diamonds like distant stars,
and narrow white borders that wander across the cloth like the footprints of camels traveling at dawn.

Every pattern remembers somebody important: an adventurous sister, a difficult journey, a winter of violent storms.
When I ask her to teach me, she laughs and places my clumsy hands upon the threads,
and together we tie the knots that her mother tied, and her mother's mother before her.

Someday the radiant colors will gradually fade and the edges will grow frayed and soft,
but the memories inside the weaving will remain as brilliant as the morning.

p4c5a01fe89.title: Grandfather's Net
p4c5a01fe89.text:
Each evening on the harbor wall, my grandfather repairs his fishing net,
knotting broken cords with fingers that are cracked and brown as driftwood.
The net spreads across his knees like a map of every voyage he remembers,
its torn places marking storms, its tight knots marking calm and generous seas.

He never hurries, never complains; he simply hums an ancient sailors' melody
while the sunset pours its copper light across the patient water.

I used to imagine the net was ordinary rope, a simple instrument for catching silver fish,
but now I understand that it is also a library of his decisions,
and every knot he teaches me is a sentence I will someday read to my children.

pab61410431.title: The Last Crate
pab61410431.text:
Every June, Tariq's family followed the harvest to a different farm, and this year it was a date farm near the edge of the desert. The work began before sunrise, while the air was still cool and the palm leaves rustled in the breeze.

Tariq's job was to carry heavy crates of dates to the waiting truck. By noon his arms ached and the fierce sun burned the back of his neck, yet he still enjoyed the quiet rows of palm trees and the sweet smell of the ripening fruit.
