questions.stem: True or false: An antonym of “mingle” is “separate.”
questions.why: To mingle is to mix together; to separate is to keep apart.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “magnify”? Choose two.
questions.why: Magnify means make bigger, so shrink and reduce are opposites.

questions.stem: “The new student did not mingle with the others at first. She stood alone near the door, but by lunchtime she was chatting and laughing in a group.” Which phrase is an antonym clue for “mingle”?
questions.why: Standing alone is the opposite of mingling.

questions.stem: Put these steps for looking at onion cells with a microscope in order.
sequence: Place a thin slice of onion on a glass slide.
Set the slide under the microscope's lens.
Turn the knob to focus on the magnified cells.
Look closely and draw the cells you see.
questions.why: You prepare the slide, place it, focus, and then observe.

questions.stem: In each sentence, is “typical” used correctly or incorrectly?

rows.text: Hot weather is typical in Riyadh in August.
Snow in Makkah is typical every summer.
A typical football match lasts about ninety minutes.
It is typical for fish to climb trees.

questions.why: Typical describes what usually happens.

questions.stem: Match each key word to its antonym: “gritty,” “humid,” “cling,” “typical,” and “magnify.”
questions.why: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Which word is the BEST antonym for “typical” in this sentence: “A typical summer day in Abha is mild, but last July was far hotter than normal”?
questions.why: Exceptional means very different from what is typical.

questions.stem: Under the microscope, the drop of pond water came alive. Tiny creatures swam past each other, and green threads of algae seemed to ____ with them. Nothing was standing still.
questions.why: Mingle means mix together, which fits creatures moving among the algae.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about a beach trip.
segments: The air near the Red Sea was warm and humid.
Sand made our sandwiches feel gritty.
Barnacles cling tightly to the rocks so the waves cannot pull them away.
I used a hand lens to dissolve a tiny crab so I could see its legs.
questions.correction: I used a hand lens to magnify a tiny crab so I could see its legs.
questions.why: A lens magnifies things; it does not dissolve them.

questions.stem: Part A: “Most rocks feel solid and smooth, but this beach rock was gritty; tiny grains rubbed off on my fingers.” What does “gritty” mean as it is used here?

partA.stem: Part A: “Most rocks feel solid and smooth, but this beach rock was gritty; tiny grains rubbed off on my fingers.” What does “gritty” mean as it is used here?

options.label: A
options.text: soft and light

options.label: B
options.text: rough with tiny grains

options.label: C
options.text: wet and slippery

options.label: D
options.text: smooth and shiny

partB.stem: Part B: Which words in the beach-rock sentence help show the meaning of “gritty”?

options.label: A
options.text: “on my fingers”

options.label: B
options.text: “tiny grains rubbed off”

options.label: C
options.text: “Most rocks”

options.label: D
options.text: “this beach rock”

questions.why: Tiny grains rubbing off show that gritty means rough with tiny grains, the opposite of smooth.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “cling” mean to hold on tightly or to keep believing in something?

rows.text: The koala clings to the branch while it sleeps.
Grandmother clings to the old family traditions.
Wet clothes cling to your skin after swimming.
Rami clung to the hope that his team would win.

questions.why: Cling can describe holding with the body or holding on to an idea.

questions.stem: Which word completes the analogy? magnify : shrink :: humid : ____
questions.why: Magnify and shrink are antonyms, so humid pairs with dry.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences describe a substance that dissolves? Choose three.
options: Oil floats in a layer on top of water.
Sand settles to the bottom of a jar.
Salt grains vanish when stirred into soup.
A spoon of honey disappears into warm tea.
A fizzy tablet vanishes in a glass of water.
Pebbles sit at the bottom of a fish tank.
questions.why: A substance that dissolves mixes into a liquid and disappears from view.

questions.stem: Choose the most precise word: “Scientists use an electron ____ to see viruses, which are thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand.”
questions.why: A microscope is used to see very tiny things.

questions.stem: True or false: “Humid” and “arid” are antonyms, because humid air is moist and arid air is very dry.
questions.why: Arid means very dry, the opposite of humid.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “magnify” means “to make a problem seem bigger than it really is.”

segments.text: Worrying too much can magnify a small mistake.
A hand lens can magnify a leaf's veins.
Telescopes magnify the craters on the Moon.
The camera can magnify faraway birds.

questions.why: Magnify can also mean to make something seem more important or serious.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Dana felt disappointed when the rain canceled the class trip to the zoo.” What does “disappointed” mean?
options: sad that a hope did not come true
tired from a long and busy day
happy that a wish finally came true
afraid of a loud, sudden noise
questions.why: Disappointed means sad because something you hoped for did not happen.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “determined,” “encourage,” “frustrated,” and “cooperate.”

pairs.right: to give someone hope and support
upset because you cannot do something

questions.why: These words describe feelings and teamwork.

questions.stem: True or false: A confident player believes she can do well.
questions.why: Confident means sure of yourself.

questions.stem: Faisal fell off his bike many times, but he was ____ to learn, so he kept trying.
questions.why: Determined people keep trying and do not give up.

questions.stem: Does each action “encourage” a teammate or not?

rows.text: saying “Great shot! Keep going!”
clapping when a friend scores
laughing when a teammate misses
ignoring a friend who asks for help

questions.why: To encourage is to give support and hope.

questions.stem: “After he broke the vase, Omar went to his mother to apologize.” What does “apologize” mean?
questions.why: To apologize is to say you are sorry.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show players who “cooperate”? Choose two.
options: Each player tried to keep the ball to himself the whole game.
The players passed the ball so everyone had a turn to shoot.
The team shared the water bottles fairly during the break.
Two players argued loudly about who should be the captain.
questions.why: To cooperate is to work together and share.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “distant,” “frustrated,” or “confident” in it.

pairs.left: My cousin seems distant lately and hardly talks to me.
Lulu felt frustrated when her kite would not fly.
Ziyad felt confident before the spelling test.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the way the word is used.

questions.stem: The mountains looked small because they were so ____ from our car on the highway.
questions.why: Distant means far away.

questions.stem: True or false: If two friends cooperate on a project, they refuse to work together.
questions.why: Cooperate means to work together.

questions.stem: “Rana was frustrated. She tried to tie the knot five times, and each time it came undone, so she threw the rope on the ground.” Which clue helps you understand “frustrated”?
options: “she threw the rope on the ground”
questions.why: Throwing the rope shows she was upset and annoyed.

questions.stem: In each sentence about feeling “frustrated” or “confident,” is the comparison a simile or a metaphor?

rows.text: Her anger was a boiling pot.
He felt as confident as a lion.
Frustration buzzed in her head like a swarm of bees.
His confidence was a shining shield.

questions.why: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “encourage”?
questions.why: After “kind,” we need the noun encouragement.

questions.stem: Complete the simile: “After weeks of practice, Jana felt as ____ as an eagle soaring over the mountains.”
questions.why: A soaring eagle suggests feeling confident and strong.

questions.stem: True or false: “My brother was a distant star, far away and hard to reach” is a metaphor.
questions.why: It says the brother was a star without using like or as.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “confident”? Choose two.
questions.why: Unsure and doubtful mean the opposite of confident.

questions.stem: “Fahd was determined to finish the race. His legs ached, but he never gave up, and he crossed the line at last.” Which phrase best shows what “determined” means?
questions.why: Determined people never give up.

questions.stem: Put these events in order to show how Laila and her best friend Sara stopped feeling “distant.”
sequence: Sara started sitting with other girls at lunch.
Laila felt hurt and frustrated, but she said nothing.
One afternoon, Laila told Sara honestly how she felt.
Sara apologized, and the two friends laughed together again.
questions.why: The friends grow distant, then honest talk brings them close again.

questions.stem: In each sentence, is “cooperate” used correctly or incorrectly?

rows.text: The ants cooperate to carry a large crumb to their nest.
Doctors and nurses cooperate to help patients.
The sleepy boy cooperated alone in his bed all day.
The rock cooperated quickly down the hill.

questions.why: Cooperate needs people or animals working together.

questions.stem: Match each key word to its synonym: “determined,” “disappointed,” “encourage,” and “apologize.”
questions.why: Synonyms have nearly the same meaning.

questions.stem: In “Yasmin's disappointment was a heavy stone she carried all week,” what does the metaphor suggest?
options: Her sadness lasted and weighed her down.
She was strong enough to lift heavy rocks.
She liked to collect heavy stones from the beach.
Her bag was full of rocks from science class.
questions.why: The heavy stone stands for a sad feeling that stayed with her.

questions.stem: At first, the new goalkeeper was quiet and shy. But each time he blocked a shot, his teammates cheered. By the end of the season, he stood in the goal like a wall of stone, ____ and calm.
questions.why: The cheering and the strong wall simile show he became confident.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about a robotics team.
segments: The robotics team worked hard to cooperate on their machine.
When the robot's arm broke, Huda felt frustrated.
Her teammates were distant and said, “You can fix it — we believe in you!”
Encouraged, she repaired the arm, and the team won second place.
questions.correction: Her teammates were encouraging and said, “You can fix it — we believe in you!”
questions.why: Kind, hopeful words are encouraging, not distant.

questions.stem: Part A: “Mazen's words were warm sunshine on his little sister's face after her team lost the match.” What does this metaphor suggest Mazen's words did?

partA.stem: Part A: “Mazen's words were warm sunshine on his little sister's face after her team lost the match.” What does this metaphor suggest Mazen's words did?

options.label: A
options.text: They made her even more disappointed.

options.label: B
options.text: They made her feel too hot.

options.label: C
options.text: They told her about the weather.

options.label: D
options.text: They encouraged and comforted her.

partB.stem: Part B: Which words in the sentence about Mazen best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “warm sunshine”

options.label: B
options.text: “Mazen's words”

options.label: C
options.text: “his little sister's”

options.label: D
options.text: “lost the match”

questions.why: Warm sunshine suggests comfort and encouragement.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use “distant” to mean far away in space or cold and unfriendly in behavior?

rows.text: We saw a distant ship on the Arabian Gulf.
Since the argument, Noura has been distant with her cousin.
Distant thunder rumbled over the mountains.
The new neighbor gave a distant nod and walked away.

questions.why: Distant can describe space or how close people feel.

questions.stem: Which word completes the analogy? encourage : discourage :: confident : ____
questions.why: Encourage and discourage are opposites, so confident pairs with unsure.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences are similes that describe being “determined”? Choose three.
options: The runner felt determined and strong.
Sami kept climbing like a goat on a rocky cliff.
He pushed forward as steady as a camel crossing the desert.
His determination was an iron wall.
She held on to her goal like a falcon gripping its prey.
Nada was determined to win the race.
questions.why: Similes use like or as to compare.

questions.stem: Choose the most precise word: “When the referee made an unfair call, the captain did not shout. Instead, she stayed calm and ____ with the referee and the other team to solve the problem.”
questions.why: Working together to solve a problem is cooperating.

questions.stem: True or false: “Saying ‘I apologize’ was a bridge that brought the two friends back together” is a simile because it uses “like” or “as.”
questions.why: It is a metaphor; it says the apology was a bridge without like or as.

questions.stem: Select the TWO sentences that use a metaphor to show someone feeling “frustrated.”

segments.text: Tariq was a volcano ready to explode when his puzzle fell apart.
Tariq's frustration was a knot tightening in his chest.
Tariq felt frustrated like a bird in a small cage.
Tariq was frustrated because the puzzle was hard.

questions.why: Metaphors say a feeling is something else without like or as.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Archaeology helps us learn how people lived long ago by studying old tools and buildings.” What is “archaeology”?
options: the study of stars and planets in space
the study of how plants grow in the desert
the study of weather and rain clouds
the study of the past through old objects
questions.why: Archaeology studies old objects to learn about the past.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “document,” “era,” “expedition,” and “permanent.”

pairs.right: a long period of time in history
a journey made for a special purpose
lasting for a very long time

questions.why: These words help you read about history.

questions.stem: True or false: Footprints in the mud can be evidence that an animal walked by.
questions.why: Evidence is a sign that shows something is true.

questions.stem: The divers hoped to ____ an old shipwreck buried under the sand of the Red Sea.
questions.why: To uncover is to find something that was hidden.

questions.stem: Is each thing “permanent” or temporary?

rows.text: henna on a hand that fades in two weeks
the pyramids of Giza
a sandcastle at the beach
a stone mountain

questions.why: Permanent things last a very long time.

questions.stem: “The new stadium is tremendous; it can hold more than sixty thousand fans.” Which word means about the same as “tremendous”?
questions.why: Tremendous means very large.

questions.stem: Which TWO are examples of a “document”? Choose two.
questions.why: A document is an official paper with information.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “era,” “expedition,” or “evidence” in it.

pairs.left: The era of steam trains lasted many years.
pairs.right: a period of time in history

pairs.left: The team went on an expedition to the Empty Quarter.
pairs.right: a long trip with a purpose

pairs.left: The muddy shoes were evidence that Bader had been outside.
pairs.right: signs that show something is true

questions.why: Each meaning fits the way the word is used.

questions.stem: Scientists packed food, tents, and maps for their ____ to study the glaciers of Antarctica.
questions.why: An expedition is a journey with a purpose.

questions.stem: True or false: Something “tremendous” is very tiny and hard to see.
questions.why: Tremendous means very large or great.

questions.stem: “Archaeologists dig slowly and carefully. They brush away the soil with small brushes so they do not break the objects they uncover.” Which clue helps you understand “uncover”?
options: “so they do not break the objects”
questions.why: Brushing away soil uncovers, or reveals, what is under it.

questions.stem: Sort these sayings an expedition leader might use. Does each mean “check the evidence before you believe” or “keep working little by little”?

rows.text: “Don't judge a book by its cover.”
“Slow and steady wins the race.”
“Seeing is believing.”
“Rome wasn't built in a day.”

questions.why: Adages give advice in a few memorable words.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “permanent”?
questions.why: To describe how the maps are kept, use the adverb permanently.

questions.stem: During a long expedition, the guide reminded the tired team, “Slow and ____ wins the race.”
questions.why: The adage means patient, steady work leads to success.

questions.stem: True or false: The adage “Where there's smoke, there's fire” means a small piece of evidence may point to something bigger.
questions.why: Smoke is evidence that a fire is nearby.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms of “tremendous”? Choose two.
questions.why: Tremendous means very great or very large.

questions.stem: “The castle has stood for eight hundred years. It is a permanent part of the town, and no one plans to tear it down.” Which clue helps you understand “permanent”?
questions.why: Lasting eight hundred years shows the castle is permanent.

questions.stem: Put these steps of an archaeology dig at an ancient desert town in order.
sequence: Researchers study old documents that mention the town.
They choose a spot and carefully dig away the sand.
They uncover pottery, coins, and tools.
They write a report that explains the evidence.
questions.why: Archaeologists research, dig, find objects, and then explain what they found.

questions.stem: In each sentence, is “era” used correctly or incorrectly?

rows.text: The Abbasid era was a time of great learning in Baghdad.
In the era of the internet, news travels fast.
I ate a quick era for breakfast this morning.
Please put the era on the shelf next to the books.

questions.why: An era is a period of time, not an object.

questions.stem: Match each key word with its synonym: “permanent,” “tremendous,” “uncover,” and “evidence.”
questions.why: Synonyms have nearly the same meaning.

questions.stem: An archaeologist says, “We cannot say who lived here yet. One coin is not enough evidence.” Which adage best matches her idea?
options: “One swallow does not make a summer.”
“Don't count your chickens before they hatch.”
questions.why: One sign alone is not enough to prove something.

questions.stem: In 1922, a team searching the Valley of the Kings in Egypt found a hidden staircase. Beneath it lay the tomb of a young king, filled with gold. The find gave historians a ____ amount of new information about ancient Egypt.
questions.why: Tremendous means very great, which fits a huge discovery.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about a museum visit.
segments: At the National Museum in Riyadh, we saw objects from a much earlier era.
A guide showed us an old expedition written on animal skin.
She explained that archaeology helps us uncover the past.
Some rock carvings are permanent clues about life thousands of years ago.
questions.correction: A guide showed us an old document written on animal skin.
questions.why: Something written down is a document, not an expedition.

questions.stem: Part A: Before an expedition, a team leader tells the explorers, “Don't put all your eggs in one basket.” What does she most likely mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Before an expedition, a team leader tells the explorers, “Don't put all your eggs in one basket.” What does she most likely mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Pack the lightest things at the very bottom.

options.label: B
options.text: Spread supplies in several bags in case one is lost.

options.label: C
options.text: Bring plenty of eggs to eat during the long journey.

options.label: D
options.text: Use only one strong basket for all the food.

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail would best support the answer to Part A about the expedition?

options.label: A
options.text: Eggs are a healthy food that gives explorers energy.

options.label: B
options.text: If one camel runs off, the team still has food and water in other packs.

options.label: C
options.text: Heavy items should go in the strongest bag.

options.label: D
options.text: Baskets are easy to carry on long trips.

questions.why: The adage warns against risking everything in one place.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use “document” as a noun (a paper) or a verb (to record)?

rows.text: The scientists document every bone they find.
Keep this document in a safe place.
The old document showed the date the fort was built.
Photographers document the rare birds of the Farasan Islands.

questions.why: Document can name a paper or the action of recording.

questions.stem: Which pair has the same relationship as “uncover : hide”?
questions.why: Uncover and hide are antonyms, like permanent and temporary.

questions.stem: Which THREE finds would be “evidence” that people once lived at a desert site? Choose three.
options: fresh tire tracks in the sand
the ashes of old cooking fires
questions.why: Old objects made by people are evidence of life long ago.

questions.stem: Choose the most precise word: “The pyramids have stood for over four thousand years, so people think of them as ____ structures.”
questions.why: Standing for thousands of years shows the pyramids are permanent.

questions.stem: True or false: The adage “Patience is a virtue” fits archaeologists who spend years slowly uncovering one ancient site.
questions.why: Archaeology needs patience, so the adage fits.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “uncover” means “to discover a hidden fact,” not “to remove a covering from an object.”

segments.text: The detective worked to uncover the truth about the missing map.
Grandmother lifted the cloth to uncover the warm bread.
Workers will uncover the pool before summer.
The wind began to uncover the buried stone steps.

questions.why: Uncover can mean to find out a secret or hidden fact.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Workers installed new lights in the school gym last week.” What does “installed” mean?
questions.why: To install something is to put it in place so it can be used.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “consume,” “converted,” “efficient,” and “incredible.”

pairs.right: changed from one form into another

questions.why: Each word names an idea you meet when reading about energy.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Sunlight is a renewable source of energy,” the word “renewable” means it can be replaced naturally and will not run out.
questions.why: Renewable sources, such as sunlight and wind, are replaced by nature.

questions.stem: It was a ____ that Salma and her cousin wore the same green dress to the party without planning it.
questions.why: A coincidence is when two things happen together by chance.

questions.stem: Is each energy source “renewable” or not renewable?

rows.text: wind that turns a turbine
sunlight on a solar panel
oil pumped from deep underground
coal dug from a mine

questions.why: Renewable sources are replaced by nature; oil and coal take millions of years to form.

questions.stem: “Big trucks consume a lot of fuel on long trips.” Which word means the same as “consume”?
questions.why: To consume fuel is to use it up.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe something “efficient”? Choose two.
options: Hessa’s new lamp gives bright light but uses very little electricity.
The car used a full tank of fuel to drive one short street.
Omar packed his school bag in two minutes without forgetting anything.
The old heater wasted most of its energy as noise and smoke.
questions.why: Efficient things do a job well without wasting time or energy.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “consequences,” “installed,” or “converted” in it.

pairs.left: Littering has bad consequences for sea turtles.
Dad installed a fan in the kitchen.
pairs.right: put in place to be used

pairs.left: The old barn was converted into a library.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.

questions.stem: The tallest tower in Riyadh looked ____ from the airplane window, and Yousef could not stop staring at it.
questions.why: Incredible means amazing or hard to believe.

questions.stem: True or false: If a family installed solar panels on the roof, they took the panels down and threw them away.
questions.why: Installed means put in place, not removed.

questions.stem: “The farmers converted the dry field into a green garden. They dug channels, added water, and planted seeds.” Which clue helps you understand “converted”?
questions.why: The words “into a green garden” show the field was changed into something new.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “efficient”?
questions.why: After “the,” we need the noun form, efficiency.

questions.stem: Is each pair made of a key word and its synonym or its antonym: consume, renewable, incredible, efficient?

rows.text: consume — use up
renewable — limited
incredible — ordinary
efficient — not wasteful

questions.why: Synonyms mean the same; antonyms mean the opposite.

questions.stem: “Leaving the tap running can have serious consequences in a dry country.” What are “consequences”?
questions.why: Consequences are the results that come after an action.

questions.stem: Our class garden uses a pump that is so ____ that it waters every plant with just a few liters of water.
questions.why: An efficient pump does its job without wasting water.

questions.stem: Which TWO words belong to the same word family as “consume”? Choose two.
questions.why: Consumer and consumption share the base of consume.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “By coincidence, the bus and the rain arrived at the very same moment” uses “coincidence” correctly.
questions.why: Two things happening together by chance is a coincidence.

questions.stem: Put these steps in order to show how wind energy is “converted” into light in a home.
sequence: The wind spins the blades of a turbine.
The spinning turbine produces electricity.
Wires carry the electricity to a house.
A lamp changes the electricity into light.
questions.why: Energy is converted step by step from motion to electricity to light.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “incredible” correctly?
options: We incredible our lunch together at noon on every school day.
Please incredible the classroom door carefully before you leave.
The falcon dove at an incredible speed to catch its prey.
The incredible spoon was resting quietly inside the kitchen drawer.
questions.why: Incredible describes something amazing, like a falcon’s speed.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that shows a “consequence” of wasting energy.

segments.text: Ali left every light on all night.
Because of this, the family’s electricity bill doubled.
His sister likes to read under a lamp.

questions.why: A consequence is the result of an action, here the higher bill.

questions.stem: The prefix “re-” means “again.” How does this help you understand “renewable” energy?
options: It is very old, so it can never change at all.
It can be made new again by nature.
It can never be used even one single time.
It is made only one time, by people in factories.
questions.why: Re- (again) + new shows that renewable energy is replaced again and again.

questions.stem: The prefix “in-” can mean “not,” but in some words it means “in” or “into.” Sort each word by the meaning of its prefix.

rows.text: incredible (not believable)
installed (put into place)
incorrect (not right)
inside (in the side)

questions.why: Incredible uses in- as “not,” but installed uses in- as “into.”

questions.stem: The prefix “co-” means “together.” A ____ happens when two events come together by chance.
questions.why: Co- (together) + incidence (happening) gives coincidence.

questions.stem: Which THREE key words begin with the Latin prefix “con-”? Choose three.
questions.why: Consequences, converted, and consume all begin with con-.

questions.stem: Complete each analogy about energy words by matching its first half with the best ending.

pairs.left: Waste is to save as consume is to ___
Install is to remove as build is to ___
Renewable is to wind as limited is to ___

questions.why: Analogies keep the same relationship on both sides.

questions.stem: Which word BEST completes the sentence? “The new bus engine is so ____ that it travels twice as far on the same amount of fuel.”
questions.why: Efficient is exact: it means getting more work from less energy.

questions.stem: Read: “Our school installed solar panels last year. Now the building consumes less electricity from the city. The panels are efficient on sunny days. The sun is a renewable source, so it will coincidence one day.” Which part uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: Now the building consumes less electricity
The panels are efficient on sunny days
so it will coincidence one day
questions.correction: so it will never run out
questions.why: Coincidence is a noun for chance events; the sentence needs “never run out.”

questions.stem: Part A: In “The speaker made an incredible claim that cars would soon run on water,” what does “incredible” most likely mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The speaker made an incredible claim that cars would soon run on water,” what does “incredible” most likely mean?

options.label: A
options.text: very exciting

options.label: B
options.text: hard to believe

options.label: C
options.text: easy to prove

options.label: D
options.text: very old

partB.stem: Part B: Which clue in the word supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: the prefix in- means “not,” and cred means “believe”

options.label: B
options.text: the prefix in- always means “inside”

options.label: C
options.text: the suffix -ible means “full of joy”

options.label: D
options.text: the root cred means “car”

questions.why: In- (not) + cred (believe) + -ible (able) means not able to be believed.

questions.stem: In a debate, Noura argued that burning coal has harmful ____ for the air, so the city should build wind farms instead.
questions.why: Consequences are the results of an action, such as pollution from coal.

questions.stem: Is “converted” or “installed” the more precise word for each sentence?

rows.text: The engineers ___ the parking roof into a solar farm.
A technician ___ a new meter beside our door.
The mill ___ wheat into flour.

questions.why: Converted means changed into something else; installed means put in place.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Grandfather showed us old photos of our ancestors who lived in the village long ago.” What are “ancestors”?

family members who lived long before us
questions.why: Ancestors are relatives from long ago.

questions.stem: “It is an honor to carry our school flag at the sports day.” Which word means the same as “honor”?

questions.stem: “Climbing the mountain took great endurance, but the hikers kept going for ten hours.” What does “endurance” mean here?

disliked
despised
questions.why: Despised is the strongest form of dislike.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which someone “retreated.”

despised

questions.stem: Put these words in order from the mildest to the strongest feeling, ending with “despised.”
sequence: bothered
irritated
angry
despised
questions.why: Words with similar denotations can show different intensity of feeling.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “honor” with its meaning “to keep or respect a promise or rule”? Choose two.
options: Ali always honors his word to his friends.
She won an honor for her science project.
It is an honor to meet the famous author.
The shop will honor the coupon until Friday.
questions.why: Honor can mean a special award or respect, or to keep a promise.

questions.stem: Complete each analogy about honor and retreat by matching its first half with the best ending.

pairs.left: Advance is to forward as retreat is to ___

questions.why: Analogies keep the same relationship on both sides.

questions.stem: Which word BEST completes the sentence? “The marathon runner’s ____ helped her keep going even when her legs ached.”
questions.why: Endurance is exact: it means the ability to keep going through difficulty.

questions.stem: Many people ____ the loud, smoky trucks on their quiet street, but the drivers did not seem to notice.

questions.stem: True or false: “The intensity of her voice” and “the loudness and force of her voice” have nearly the same denotation.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The hungry goats gobble the grass in seconds.” What does “gobble” mean?
questions.why: To gobble is to eat something very fast.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “mist,” “roots,” “gobble,” and “individuality.”

what makes a person different from others

questions.why: Knowing each word helps you understand poems about family and nature.

questions.stem: True or false: In “A light mist covered the mountains of Taif in the morning,” the word “mist” means thin, cloudy air with tiny drops of water.

questions.stem: The palm tree’s ____ reach deep into the ground to find water.
questions.why: Roots grow underground and take in water.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe “mist” or not?

rows.text: Tiny water drops float over the river at dawn.

questions.why: Mist is made of tiny drops of water in the air.

questions.stem: “Each student painted a different picture to show their individuality.” Which word means the same as “individuality”?
questions.why: Individuality is what makes each person unique.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences are examples of “personification”? Choose two.
options: The old door groaned when we pushed it.
The door was made of wood.
The wind whispered secrets to the palm trees.
The wind blew from the north.
questions.why: Personification gives human actions to things that are not human.

questions.stem: Match each line with the poetry tool it uses: “metaphor,” “personification,” or “imagery.”

The moon smiled down at the sleeping town.

questions.why: Each line uses a different tool.

questions.stem: The writer used rich ____, so I could almost smell the fresh bread and hear the sizzling pan.
questions.why: Imagery uses words that appeal to the senses.

questions.stem: True or false: A poem written in free verse must rhyme at the end of every line.
questions.why: Free verse does not follow a set rhyme or rhythm.

questions.stem: “The baby birds gobble every worm their mother brings. In a moment, the food is gone.” Which clue helps you understand “gobble”?
options: “In a moment, the food is gone”
questions.why: Food gone in a moment shows the birds eat quickly.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “individuality”?
questions.why: Before the noun “markings,” we need the adjective individual.

questions.stem: Is each line a “metaphor” or “personification”?

rows.text: The classroom was a beehive of busy students.
The sun yawned and slowly woke up.
Her smile is a lantern in the dark.
The stream sang a happy song.

questions.why: A metaphor says one thing is another; personification gives human traits to things.

questions.stem: “The traditions of my family are my roots.” What does “roots” mean in this sentence?
options: the answers to a hard math problem
the underground parts of a tall palm tree
the first letters of words in a line
the family history a person comes from
questions.why: Here roots means the history and heritage a person comes from.

questions.stem: Lama wrote her poem in ____, with lines of different lengths and no rhyme, so it sounded like natural speech.
questions.why: Free verse has no fixed rhyme or rhythm.

questions.stem: Which TWO lines use “imagery” that appeals to the sense of sound? Choose two.
options: Waves crashed and hissed against the rocks.
The sky was deep purple at sunset.
The rose petals felt soft as silk.
The kettle whistled loudly on the stove.
questions.why: Sound imagery uses words for what we hear.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “Wearing her own colorful scarf showed Reem’s individuality” uses “individuality” correctly.
questions.why: Individuality is shown by things that make a person unique.

questions.stem: Put these weather descriptions in order from the lightest to the thickest, starting with “mist.”
sequence: a thin mist over the lake
a gray fog that hides the trees
a thick cloud that hides the whole mountain
questions.why: Mist is the lightest; fog and clouds are thicker.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “gobble” correctly?
options: The car gobbled very quietly down the road toward the city.

questions.why: Gobble means to eat very quickly.

questions.stem: Select the line that is an example of “metaphor.”

My grandmother is a tall palm tree, giving us shade.
We walked slowly through the market.

questions.why: The line says grandmother is a palm tree, which is a metaphor.

questions.stem: In the line “The fire gobbled the dry branches,” why is “gobble” an example of personification?
options: The line compares fire to the branches by using the word “like.”
Fire cannot really eat, so it is given an action of a living thing.
Fire is really a hungry animal that lives deep in the forest.

questions.why: Giving fire the action of eating is personification.

questions.stem: Is “roots” used with its literal meaning or its figurative meaning in each sentence?

Our love of poetry has deep roots in our family.
The farmer pulled the weed out by its roots.

questions.why: Literal roots are plant parts; figurative roots are a person’s origins.

questions.stem: In the line “A soft ____ wrapped the hills like a gray blanket,” the poet uses a simile to describe the morning.

questions.stem: Which THREE lines use “imagery,” “metaphor,” or “personification” to describe nature? Choose three.
options: Cool, sweet water trickled over smooth stones.
Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen.
The night is a black cloak over the city.
The mountain wore a crown of snow.
questions.why: Figurative language and imagery create pictures; facts do not.

questions.stem: Complete each analogy about nature and poetry by matching its first half with the best ending.

pairs.left: Gobble is to eat as sprint is to ___

questions.why: Analogies keep the same relationship on both sides.

questions.stem: True or false: “Sheer” has the same meaning in “a sheer scarf” and “a sheer cliff.”

questions.stem: Which word has the MOST positive connotation for describing a waterfall?
questions.why: Spectacular suggests strong admiration and wonder.

questions.why: An encounter is a meeting, here with an animal.

questions.stem: “The workers received their wages every Thursday.” Which word means the same as “wages”?
questions.why: Wages are the pay people receive for working.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “prosper,” “profit,” or “risk” in it.

questions.stem: Put these steps in order to show how a young seller might earn a “profit.”
