questions.why: Knowing these words helps you understand poems about goals and feelings.

questions.stem: True or false: “Cat” and “hat” rhyme because they end with the same sound.
questions.why: Words rhyme when their ending sounds match.

questions.stem: Musa ____ when the cold wind blew through his thin jacket.
questions.why: Shuddered means shook from cold or fear.

questions.stem: Does each pair of words “rhyme” or not?

rows.text: sand / hand
moon / spoon
camel / desert
sea / fish

questions.why: Rhyming words have the same ending sound.

questions.stem: “Amal is ambitious; she wants to become an astronaut one day.” What does “ambitious” mean?
questions.why: An ambitious person has big goals.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe a feeling of “satisfaction”? Choose two.
options: Nasser smiled after finishing the puzzle all by himself.
Rami frowned when he lost his favorite pen.
Jamal was bored waiting for the long bus ride to end.
Hind felt proud and happy when her plant finally bloomed.
questions.why: Satisfaction is the good feeling after doing something well.

questions.stem: A poem that tells a story with characters and events is called a ____ poem.
questions.why: A narrative poem tells a story.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term — “repetition,” “free verse,” “rhyme,” “narrative” — with its meaning.

pairs.right: using the same word or line again
poetry with no set rhyme or beat
words with the same ending sound
a poem that tells a story

questions.why: These terms describe how poems are built.

questions.stem: True or false: A poem written in “free verse” must rhyme at the end of every line.
questions.why: Free verse does not need to rhyme or follow a set beat.

questions.stem: “After weeks of practice, Saeed felt great satisfaction when he finally scored a goal; he grinned all the way home.” What does “satisfaction” most likely mean?
questions.why: Grinning after scoring shows pleasure at success.

questions.stem: Is each line an example of “repetition,” “rhyme,” or neither?

rows.text: Run, run, run to the shore.
The sun is bright; the stars are light.
My cat sleeps on the chair by the window.
Again and again and again the waves come.

questions.why: Repetition repeats words; rhyme matches ending sounds.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “ambitious”?
questions.why: Before a noun like “student,” we need the adjective ambitious.

questions.stem: Fahad ____ all the capital cities of Asia and could name them in one minute.
questions.why: Naming them quickly from memory shows he memorized them.

questions.stem: Part A: “The puppy shuddered in the rain, its whole body shaking until we wrapped it in a towel.” What does “shuddered” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: “The puppy shuddered in the rain, its whole body shaking until we wrapped it in a towel.” What does “shuddered” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: slept

options.label: B
options.text: trembled

options.label: C
options.text: ran

options.label: D
options.text: barked

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the sentence about the puppy best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “wrapped it in a towel”

options.label: B
options.text: “in the rain”

options.label: C
options.text: “The puppy”

options.label: D
options.text: “its whole body shaking”

questions.why: Shaking is the clue that shuddered means trembled.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “ambitious”?
questions.why: A lazy person has no wish to work toward goals, the opposite of ambitious.

questions.stem: Which TWO words belong to the same word family as “repetition”? Choose two.
questions.why: Repeat, repeatedly, and repetition share the same base.

questions.stem: Put these steps for performing a poem in order, using “rhyme,” “repetition,” and “memorized.”
sequence: Choose a short poem with rhyme and repetition.
Read it aloud slowly several times.
Once you have memorized it, practice without the paper.
Recite it to the class with a clear voice.
questions.why: You must read a poem many times before it is memorized.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The ambitious team trained before sunrise every day to win the cup,” the clue “trained before sunrise every day” supports the meaning of “ambitious.”
questions.why: Working very hard toward a big goal shows ambition.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term — “narrative,” “free verse,” “repetition,” “rhyme” — with an example of it.

pairs.right: a poem about a fisherman's long day at sea
lines of different lengths with no set beat
“tall” ending one line and “wall” ending the next

questions.why: Examples help you recognize each poetry term.

questions.stem: In “The cold wind made Ali shudder as he tried to wind the old clock,” the two uses of “wind” are homographs. What does the second “wind” mean?
questions.why: Homographs are spelled the same but differ in meaning; to wind a clock is to turn its key.

questions.stem: Does “present” mean “a gift” or “to show formally” in each sentence about poetry?

rows.text: Each student will present a narrative poem to the class.
Mona's present was a book of rhyme and riddles.
Grandfather gave me a present: a notebook for free verse.
We will present our memorized poems at the festival.

questions.why: Present is a homograph: PREZ-ent (a gift) and pre-ZENT (to show).

questions.stem: Which sentence in this paragraph about a poetry contest uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: Dana wrote a narrative poem about her grandfather's trip across the desert by camel.
She used repetition, starting each stanza with “Step by step.”
Her poem was free verse, so every line ended with a perfect rhyme.
She memorized it and won first prize.
questions.correction: Her poem was free verse, so the lines did not need to rhyme.
questions.why: Free verse does not follow a rhyme pattern.

questions.stem: The poet chose ____ instead of rhyme, letting each line end wherever the thought ended.
questions.why: Free verse lets lines end freely without rhyme.

questions.stem: “Tear” is a homograph. Which TWO sentences use “tear” to mean “a drop from the eye”? Choose two.
options: The ambitious builder had to tear down the old wall first.
When she memorized the sad poem, a tear fell onto the page.
Be careful not to tear the poster about rhyme and rhythm.
A tear of satisfaction rolled down the runner's cheek at the finish line.
questions.why: Tear (TEER) is a drop from the eye; tear (TAIR) means to rip.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: shuddered is to fear as smiled is to ____.
questions.why: People shudder from fear and smile from joy.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The poet will record her narrative poem, and it may set a new record for listeners,” what does the first “record” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The poet will record her narrative poem, and it may set a new record for listeners,” what does the first “record” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: to break something into pieces

options.label: B
options.text: the best result ever reached

options.label: C
options.text: to save sounds to play later

options.label: D
options.text: a list of names and dates

partB.stem: Part B: Which clue in that sentence about the poet shows the second “record” is a different word?

options.label: A
options.text: It comes after the word “poet.”

options.label: B
options.text: It is spelled the same way.

options.label: C
options.text: It comes after “a new” and names a thing.

options.label: D
options.text: It ends with the same letter d.

questions.why: Homographs change meaning and part of speech; “a new record” is a noun.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes this paragraph: “Nadia was ____. She wanted to win the science fair, learn three languages, and build a robot. Her friends admired how hard she worked toward big goals.”
questions.why: Having many big goals and working hard shows Nadia is ambitious.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “satisfaction” has the most precise and fitting meaning.

segments.text: After fixing the bicycle by himself, Yaser felt deep satisfaction.
Yaser felt satisfaction when he dropped his phone in the pool.
The satisfaction of the storm broke three windows.
Yaser satisfaction the bicycle with new tires.

questions.why: Satisfaction is the pleased feeling after doing something well.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The poets who live in Abha gave a live reading of their rhyming poems,” the two uses of “live” are homographs that are spelled the same but pronounced differently.
questions.why: Live (LIV) means to dwell; live (LYVE) means happening in real time.

questions.stem: “Rashid blurted out the answer before the teacher finished the question.” What does “blurted” mean?
questions.why: To blurt is to say something suddenly without thinking.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “appreciation,” “congratulate,” “critical,” and “cultural.”

pairs.right: a feeling of thanks or valuing something
to tell someone you are happy about their success
about the customs of a group of people

questions.why: Knowing these words helps you read about people and places.

questions.stem: True or false: When you congratulate a friend, you tell her you are happy about her success.
questions.why: Congratulating means praising someone's success.

questions.stem: Grandmother was ____ my drawing, saying the colors were beautiful.
questions.why: Saying something nice about someone's work is complimenting.

questions.stem: Is each sentence an example of “complimenting” someone or not?

rows.text: “Your handwriting is so neat!”
“You did a great job on the poster.”
“Please close the door.”
“What time is it?”

questions.why: A compliment is a kind remark that praises someone.

questions.stem: “The Janadriyah festival shows cultural traditions such as sword dancing, poetry, and old crafts.” What does “cultural” mean?
options: about the customs of a group
about the weather of a place
questions.why: Cultural means related to a group's customs and arts.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show a “misunderstanding”? Choose two.
options: Khalid and his brother both agreed to share the toys.
Ali thought the trip was on Monday, but it was really on Sunday.
Sara thought her friend was angry, but he was only tired.
The class understood the directions and finished on time.
questions.why: A misunderstanding is a mistake about what is true or what someone meant.

questions.stem: The audience clapped to show their ____ for the children's beautiful song.
questions.why: Clapping shows appreciation, or valuing something.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “contradicted,” “critical,” or “blurted” in it.

pairs.left: Omar contradicted his friend about the score.
The judge was critical of the messy drawing.
Lina blurted the surprise by accident.

questions.why: Each meaning fits how the word is used.

questions.stem: True or false: If your brother contradicted you, he agreed with every word you said.
questions.why: To contradict is to say the opposite.

questions.stem: “Ahmed said the museum opened at nine, but his sister contradicted him, saying it opened at ten.” What does “contradicted” most likely mean?
questions.why: His sister gave a different time, so she said the opposite.

questions.stem: Is each pair made of a key word and its synonym or its antonym: appreciation, critical, complimenting, contradicted?

rows.text: appreciation — thanks
critical — approving
complimenting — praising
contradicted — agreed

questions.why: Synonyms mean the same; antonyms mean the opposite.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “congratulate”?
questions.why: The sentence needs a past-tense verb, congratulated.

questions.stem: The coach was ____ of our passing, pointing out every mistake we made in the game.
questions.why: Pointing out mistakes means being critical.

questions.stem: Part A: “There was a misunderstanding: Majed thought the party was at his uncle's house, but it was really at the park.” What does “misunderstanding” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: “There was a misunderstanding: Majed thought the party was at his uncle's house, but it was really at the park.” What does “misunderstanding” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: a mistake about what is true

options.label: B
options.text: a long trip to see family

options.label: C
options.text: a game played in the park

options.label: D
options.text: a happy surprise at a party

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the sentence about Majed best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “There was”

options.label: B
options.text: “the party was”

options.label: C
options.text: “but it was really at the park”

options.label: D
options.text: “his uncle's house”

questions.why: “But it was really” shows that Majed's idea was a mistake.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “critical” in “The judge was critical of the painting”?
questions.why: Praising is the opposite of finding fault.

questions.stem: Which TWO words belong to the same word family as “appreciation”? Choose two.
questions.why: Appreciate, appreciative, and appreciation share the same base.

questions.stem: Put these events in order to show how a “misunderstanding” was fixed at a family dinner.
sequence: Nora blurted, “This soup is too hot!”
Her aunt thought Nora did not like the soup.
Nora explained that she loved it but needed it to cool.
Her aunt laughed, and the misunderstanding was over.
questions.why: A misunderstanding starts, grows, is explained, and then ends.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Instead of criticizing my essay, the teacher kept complimenting the strong opening,” the word “Instead” signals that complimenting is the opposite of criticizing.
questions.why: “Instead of” is an antonym clue.

questions.stem: Match each key word — “congratulate,” “complimenting,” “critical,” “cultural,” “contradicted” — with a word from its family.
questions.why: Words in a family share a base and a related meaning.

questions.stem: “Critical” can mean “finding fault” or “extremely important.” In which sentence does it mean “extremely important”?
options: Don't be so critical of your little brother.
My cousin is critical of every meal I cook.
Clean water is critical for a healthy town.
The critic was critical of the new film.
questions.why: Water is extremely important for health.

questions.stem: Hamad did not mean to be rude; he was so excited that he ____ the surprise before his mother could open the gift.
questions.why: Blurted means said suddenly without thinking, which fits being excited and not meaning it.

questions.stem: Which sentence in this paragraph about a visit to Morocco uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: During our trip to Morocco, we learned about many cultural traditions.
We showed our appreciation by thanking our hosts for the delicious meal.
My father congratulated the cook on her wonderful couscous.
I contradicted my sister when I agreed with everything she said.
questions.correction: I contradicted my sister when I said the market closed earlier than she thought.
questions.why: To contradict is to disagree, not to agree.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: complimenting is to praising as contradicting is to ____.
questions.why: Contradicting means opposing what someone says.

questions.stem: Which kind of context clue explains “appreciation,” “cultural,” and “critical” in each sentence?

rows.text: Her appreciation, or thankful feeling, showed in her smile.
Cultural events, such as folk dances and craft fairs, filled the week.
Unlike his kind, approving uncle, the judge was critical.

questions.why: Context clues can define, give examples, or show an opposite.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences give a context clue showing that “blurted” means “said suddenly without thinking”? Choose two.
options: The words burst out before Lina could stop them; she had blurted the answer.
Mona blurted something to her friend yesterday.
Without stopping to think, Yousef blurted the secret.
Faris blurted the answer during the quiz.
questions.why: Clues like “without stopping to think” and “burst out” explain the meaning.

questions.stem: Part A: “At first, Tariq felt little appreciation for the old market; he called it noisy and crowded. By the end of the day, however, he was complimenting the spice sellers and praising the handmade lanterns.” How does Tariq's appreciation change?

partA.stem: Part A: “At first, Tariq felt little appreciation for the old market; he called it noisy and crowded. By the end of the day, however, he was complimenting the spice sellers and praising the handmade lanterns.” How does Tariq's appreciation change?

options.label: A
options.text: It disappears completely.

options.label: B
options.text: It stays the same all day.

options.label: C
options.text: It turns into anger at sellers.

options.label: D
options.text: It grows from little to great.

partB.stem: Part B: Which word in those sentences about Tariq signals the change?

options.label: A
options.text: “however”

options.label: B
options.text: “crowded”

options.label: C
options.text: “noisy”

options.label: D
options.text: “handmade”

questions.why: “However” signals a contrast between before and after.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes this paragraph: “When Leen's family moved to Japan, she bowed to greet people, just as her neighbors did. She also learned to remove her shoes indoors. Learning these ____ customs helped her make friends quickly.”
questions.why: Bowing and removing shoes are cultural customs.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “congratulate” is used correctly.

segments.text: The principal stood up to congratulate the students who won the robotics contest.
We congratulate the team for losing the key to the gym.
Please congratulate the window before the sandstorm.
The cat will congratulate under the bed.

questions.why: We congratulate people for their success.

questions.stem: True or false: A misunderstanding can happen when people from different cultural backgrounds use the same hand gesture to mean different things.
questions.why: Different customs can cause people to misunderstand each other.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The museum garden has artificial flowers made of silk, so they never need water.” What does “artificial” mean?
questions.why: Artificial things are made by people instead of growing naturally.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “collaborate,” “flexible,” “obstacle,” and “mimic.”

pairs.right: to copy how something looks or acts

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you read about teamwork and problem-solving.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Divers used special techniques to clean the feathers of the seabirds,” the word “techniques” means ways of doing a job.
questions.why: Techniques are skilled ways of doing something.

questions.stem: The gymnast is so ____ that she can touch her toes without bending her knees.
questions.why: Flexible means able to bend easily.

questions.stem: Is each thing “artificial” or natural?

rows.text: plastic grass on a football field
a date palm growing in an oasis
a lake made by building a dam
a coral reef in the Red Sea

questions.why: Artificial things are made by people; natural things are not.

questions.stem: “Parrots can mimic the sounds people make, like a phone ringing or a person laughing.” What does “mimic” mean?
questions.why: To mimic is to copy a sound or action.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show people who “collaborate”? Choose two.
options: Firefighters and nurses work together to help after a fire.
Each runner races alone to be the first to finish.
Omar paints a picture alone in his room after school.
Three classmates share the work to build one model volcano.
questions.why: People who collaborate work together toward one goal.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “obstacle,” “function,” or “dedicated” in it.

pairs.left: A fallen tree was an obstacle on the mountain road.
The function of a kettle is to boil water.
Nora is a dedicated swimmer who trains every morning.
pairs.right: working hard and caring a lot

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.

questions.stem: The ____ nurse stayed late at the clinic every night to care for sick children.
questions.why: A dedicated person gives time and effort to something important.

questions.stem: True or false: If a robot can mimic a cat, it acts nothing like a cat.
questions.why: To mimic means to copy, so the robot acts like a cat.

questions.stem: “The new bridge has many functions. It carries cars, lets people walk across, and holds pipes that bring water to the town.” What does “functions” mean in these sentences?
questions.why: The examples list the jobs the bridge does.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “collaborate”?
questions.why: After “a,” the noun form collaboration is needed.

questions.stem: Is each pair a synonym or an antonym of “flexible,” “mimic,” “dedicated,” “artificial,” or “obstacle”?

rows.text: flexible — stiff
mimic — imitate
dedicated — committed
artificial — natural
obstacle — barrier

questions.why: Synonyms mean the same; antonyms mean the opposite.

questions.stem: The coach showed the team new ____ for passing the ball quickly, such as the one-touch pass and the wall pass.
questions.why: The examples are ways of passing, so they are techniques.

questions.stem: The Latin root “flex” means “to bend,” as in “flexible.” Which TWO words come from the same root? Choose two.
questions.why: Reflex and flexibility both come from the root meaning bend.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “Scientists collaborate when they share ideas and tools to solve one problem” uses “collaborate” correctly.
questions.why: Sharing ideas and tools to solve a problem is collaborating.

questions.stem: Put these chess players in order from the least to the most “dedicated.”
sequence: plays chess once and then forgets about it
plays chess with friends on some weekends
practices chess every day and studies famous games
questions.why: The more time and effort someone gives, the more dedicated they are.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “flexible”?
questions.why: Rigid means stiff, the opposite of flexible.

questions.stem: Match each form of “function,” “artificial,” and “techniques” with its meaning.

pairs.right: in a way made by people
having to do with special skills or tools

questions.why: Suffixes such as -al and -ly change a word's form.

questions.stem: Engineers designed the robot arm to ____ the way a human hand grips and lifts small objects.
questions.why: The arm copies the hand, so mimic fits.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “flexible” is to “rubber band” as “artificial” is to ____.
questions.why: A rubber band is flexible, and a wax apple is artificial.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “function” mean a job or purpose, or a formal event?

rows.text: The function of the heart is to pump blood.
The embassy held a function to welcome the new students.
This button's function is to turn off the alarm.
Guests wore their best clothes to the evening function at the hotel.

questions.why: Function is a multiple-meaning word: a purpose or a formal gathering.

questions.stem: A sandstorm buried part of the highway near Riyadh. Road crews had to ____ with police officers and truck drivers to clear it. No single team could have finished the job alone.
questions.why: The clue “no single team… alone” shows the groups worked together.

questions.stem: In these sentences about a falcon trainer, which sentence misuses “techniques,” “dedicated,” “obstacle,” or “flexible”?
segments: The trainer used patient techniques to teach the young falcon.
She was dedicated and worked with it every morning.
A tall fence was an obstacle the bird learned to fly over.
Soon the falcon could flexible the calls of other birds.
questions.correction: Soon the falcon could mimic the calls of other birds.
questions.why: Flexible describes bending; copying calls is mimic.

questions.stem: The Latin root “fac” or “fic” means “make,” as in “artificial.” Which THREE words share this root? Choose three.
questions.why: Factory, manufacture, and beneficial all contain the root meaning make or do.

questions.stem: “Obstacle” comes from Latin parts meaning “to stand against.” Which sentence uses “obstacle” in a way that best matches this origin?
options: A huge boulder stood across the trail, blocking the climbers.
A guide gave the climbers a map of the safest trail route.
The climbers rested beside a cool spring halfway up the trail.
The view from the top of the trail was wide and beautiful.
questions.why: An obstacle stands in the way, like a boulder across a trail.

questions.stem: Engineers built the stadium roof from a ____ material that bends in strong wind instead of cracking.
questions.why: The clue “bends instead of cracking” points to flexible.

questions.stem: “Ibn al-Haytham tested light with careful techniques, such as shining it through small holes into a dark room.” What does “techniques” mean in this sentence?

partA.stem: “Ibn al-Haytham tested light with careful techniques, such as shining it through small holes into a dark room.” What does “techniques” mean in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: mistakes made by beginners

options.label: B
options.text: rooms used for science

options.label: C
options.text: tools made of glass

options.label: D
options.text: methods for doing something

partB.stem: Which words from the sentence best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “such as shining it through small holes”

options.label: B
options.text: “careful”

options.label: C
options.text: “Ibn al-Haytham tested light”

options.label: D
options.text: “into a dark room”

questions.why: The example shows a method, so techniques are ways of doing something.

questions.stem: Match each Latin root with its meaning: “flex” in “flexible,” “funct” in “function,” “art” in “artificial,” and “labor” in “collaborate.”
questions.why: Latin roots carry meaning into many English words.

questions.stem: Does “mimic” have a positive or negative feeling in each sentence?

rows.text: The young artist learned by mimicking the brushstrokes of great painters.
Hamad hurt his brother's feelings by mimicking his voice to make others laugh.
Scientists built a robot that mimics a fish to study coral reefs safely.
A rude boy mimicked the new student's accent in a mocking way.

questions.why: Mimic can be positive (learning, science) or negative (making fun of someone).

questions.stem: “The archaeologist carefully brushed sand away from an old clay pot buried in the desert.” What is an “archaeologist”?
options: a doctor who treats sick animals at the city zoo
a pilot who flies heavy cargo planes over the desert
a chef who cooks traditional meals
a scientist who studies objects from long ago
questions.why: An archaeologist digs up and studies things from the past.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “fragments,” “intact,” “preserved,” and “remnants.”

pairs.right: kept safe from harm or decay
small parts that are left over

questions.why: These words describe old objects and what is left of them.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The vase fell, but it stayed intact,” the word “intact” means the vase broke into many pieces.
questions.why: Intact means whole, so the vase did not break.

questions.stem: My grandfather kept his old school notebooks in a dry box, so they were well ____.
questions.why: Preserved means kept safe so something lasts.

questions.stem: Is each object “intact” or in “fragments”?

rows.text: a teacup with no cracks or chips
a mirror shattered into tiny pieces
a clay tablet found whole after 3,000 years
a plate that broke into many sharp bits

questions.why: Intact means whole; fragments are broken pieces.

questions.stem: “A historian read old letters and diaries to learn how people lived in Makkah long ago.” What does a “historian” do?
options: sells old coins at the market
questions.why: A historian studies and writes about the past.

questions.stem: Which TWO things could be called “remnants”? Choose two.
options: the stone walls left from an ancient fort
a few crumbs left on the plate after lunch
a brand-new bicycle still in its box
a full tank of water for the garden
questions.why: Remnants are the small parts left over.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “era,” “reconstruct,” or “preserved” in it.

pairs.left: The era of steam trains lasted many years.
pairs.right: a long period of time in history

pairs.left: Engineers will reconstruct the old bridge.
Salt preserved the fish for the long voyage.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.

questions.stem: After the earthquake, workers will ____ the school using the original plans so it looks the same as before.
questions.why: To reconstruct is to build again.

questions.stem: True or false: The age of the dinosaurs could be called an “era.”
questions.why: An era is a long period of time in history.

questions.stem: “Divers found fragments of an old ship on the seabed near Jeddah. The broken pieces of wood and pottery were scattered across the sand.” Which words are a clue to the meaning of “fragments”?
questions.why: The next sentence restates fragments as broken pieces.

questions.stem: The ancient letter was so damaged that the historian had to ____ the missing words by studying other letters from the same time.
questions.why: The historian rebuilds the missing words, so reconstruct fits.

questions.stem: Is each pair a synonym or an antonym of “intact,” “preserved,” “fragments,” or “reconstruct”?

rows.text: intact — whole
intact — broken
preserved — protected
fragments — pieces
reconstruct — demolish

questions.why: Synonyms mean the same; antonyms mean the opposite.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “preserved”?
questions.why: After “way of,” the -ing form preserving is needed.

questions.stem: Read: “Unlike the crumbling walls nearby, the gate of the old fort at Al-Ula was still intact, with every stone in place.” Which TWO clues help you know what “intact” means? Choose two.
questions.why: A contrast clue and a restatement clue both show intact means whole.

questions.stem: True or false: An “archaeologist” would most likely study the remnants of an ancient village.
questions.why: Archaeologists study what is left of past places.

questions.stem: Put in order the steps an archaeologist follows to reconstruct a broken pot found at a dig.
sequence: dig carefully at the site
collect the fragments that are found
clean and label each piece
reconstruct the pot from the pieces
questions.why: The pieces must be found and cleaned before the pot can be rebuilt.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “preserved”?
questions.why: Ruined is the opposite of preserved.

questions.stem: Match each form of “historian” and “archaeologist” with its meaning.

pairs.right: a person who studies the past
the study of ancient objects and sites

questions.why: Words in the same family share a base meaning.

questions.stem: In the ____ before cars, travelers crossed the Arabian desert on camels.
questions.why: An era is a period of time.

questions.stem: Which word best describes a building that still has all its walls, roof, and doors after 500 years?
questions.why: A building that is still whole is intact.

questions.stem: Which kind of context clue explains the key word in each sentence about “remnants,” “intact,” “fragments,” or “era”?

rows.text: The remnants, or leftover pieces, of the cloth were used to make a small bag.
Unlike the shattered jar beside it, this jar was intact.
The museum shows fragments such as broken arrowheads, bits of pottery, and pieces of glass.
An era, a long period in history, can last hundreds of years.

questions.why: Context clues can define, contrast, or give examples.

questions.stem: Floodwater swept through the old market. When it drained away, only ____ of the wooden stalls remained: a few posts, a torn awning, and scattered boards. The merchants promised to rebuild.
questions.why: The list of leftover parts shows that remnants fits.

questions.stem: In these sentences about a museum visit, which sentence misuses “historian,” “fragments,” “era,” or “intact”?
segments: The guide was a historian who knew many facts about the past.
She showed us fragments of a clay lamp from an early era.
The lamp was broken, so it was completely intact.
We learned a lot about life long ago.
questions.correction: The lamp was broken, so it was not intact.
questions.why: A broken object cannot be intact.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “reconstruct” correctly? Choose three.
options: The kitten will reconstruct when it is tired.
Scientists reconstruct a dinosaur skeleton from its bones.
Please reconstruct your juice before it gets warm.
Police reconstruct a car accident to learn exactly how it happened.
After the storm, the town worked to reconstruct the damaged harbor.
questions.why: Reconstruct means to build or put together again.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “historian” is to “the past” as “astronomer” is to ____.
questions.why: A historian studies the past; an astronomer studies the stars.

questions.stem: The dry air of the Egyptian desert ____ papyrus scrolls for thousands of years, so scholars can still read them today.
questions.why: The scrolls can still be read, so the air kept them safe.

questions.stem: “Most of the old manuscript had crumbled to dust; only a few fragments survived, and the historian worked for months to piece together their meaning.” What does “fragments” mean in this sentence?

partA.stem: “Most of the old manuscript had crumbled to dust; only a few fragments survived, and the historian worked for months to piece together their meaning.” What does “fragments” mean in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: whole books in good shape

options.label: B
options.text: long journeys across land

options.label: C
options.text: careful readers of history

options.label: D
options.text: small pieces of something

partB.stem: Which phrase best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “their meaning”

options.label: B
options.text: “the historian”

options.label: C
options.text: “had crumbled to dust”

options.label: D
options.text: “worked for months”

questions.why: Something that crumbled leaves only small pieces behind.

questions.stem: Match each phrase in capital letters with the key word that could replace it: “era,” “remnants,” “intact,” or “archaeologist.”

pairs.left: The Abbasid PERIOD was famous for its scholars.
Only the LEFTOVER PARTS of the city wall still stand.
One tower is STILL WHOLE after centuries.
A SCIENTIST WHO STUDIES ANCIENT SITES mapped the ruins.

questions.why: Each key word can replace a longer phrase with the same meaning.

questions.stem: Is “era,” “reconstructed,” “historians,” or “fragments” used correctly in each sentence?

rows.text: The era of the Hejaz Railway began in the early 1900s.
The archaeologist reconstructed the meal so she could eat it.
Historians use letters, maps, and diaries as evidence.
The fragments were whole and had no cracks.

questions.why: Check whether each word's meaning fits the sentence.

questions.stem: “Hessa was full of anticipation the night before the school trip to the aquarium, and she could hardly sleep.” What does “anticipation” mean?
questions.why: Anticipation is excited waiting for something to happen.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “neutral,” “outspoken,” “reserved,” and “sought.”
questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you describe people and actions.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The referee stayed neutral during the final match,” the word “neutral” means the referee did not favor either team.
questions.why: A neutral person does not take sides.

questions.stem: Khalid is quiet and ____, so he rarely speaks first in class discussions.
questions.why: Reserved describes a quiet person who keeps to himself.

questions.stem: Does each person sound “outspoken” or “reserved”?

rows.text: Maha always shares her opinion loudly in meetings.
Yousef listens quietly and keeps his thoughts to himself.
The team captain openly tells the coach when a rule seems unfair.
Noura prefers to watch before joining a conversation.

questions.why: Outspoken people speak up; reserved people stay quiet.

questions.stem: “The sailors sought a safe harbor when the storm grew stronger.” What does “sought” mean?
questions.why: Sought is the past tense of seek, meaning looked for.

questions.stem: Which TWO situations are “unequal”? Choose two.
options: One player gets three turns while another gets only one.
Each runner starts the race at the same line.
Both teams have eleven players on the field.
One child gets a large slice of cake and the other a tiny one.
questions.why: Unequal means not the same in amount or treatment.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “defy,” “entitled,” or “anticipation” in it.

pairs.left: The tiny plant seemed to defy the desert heat and kept growing.
pairs.right: to resist or stand up against

pairs.left: Every student is entitled to a free library card.
The crowd waited in anticipation for the fireworks.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.

questions.stem: Every student who finishes the reading challenge is ____ to a certificate.
questions.why: Entitled means having a right to something.

questions.stem: True or false: If you “defy” a rule, you follow it carefully.
questions.why: To defy a rule is to refuse to obey it.

questions.stem: “Unlike his outspoken sister, Hamad was reserved; he rarely shared his ideas unless someone asked him.” Which phrase is a clue to the meaning of “reserved”?
questions.why: Rarely sharing ideas describes a reserved person.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about “unequal” practice time has a prefix error?
questions.why: The prefix un- is used with equal to make unequal.

questions.stem: Is each part of “unequal,” “anticipation,” “outspoken,” and “neutrality” a prefix or a suffix?

rows.text: un- in unequal
-ion in anticipation
out- in outspoken
-ity in neutrality

questions.why: Prefixes go at the beginning of a word; suffixes go at the end.

questions.stem: When the coach asked who started the argument, Faris stayed ____ and did not take either player's side.
questions.why: Not taking a side means staying neutral.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “outspoken”? Choose two.
questions.why: Reserved and shy people do not speak out openly.

questions.stem: True or false: “The explorers sought fresh water for days and finally found a spring” uses “sought” correctly.
questions.why: The explorers looked for water, so sought is correct.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order from the least to the most “anticipation” Rashid feels about Eid.
sequence: Rashid barely remembers that Eid is next week.
Rashid marks the date of Eid on his calendar.
Rashid counts the hours until Eid and cannot sit still.
questions.why: Counting the hours shows the strongest anticipation.

questions.stem: Which word is a synonym of “defy”?
questions.why: To defy is to resist.

questions.stem: Match each form of “entitled,” “neutral,” and “anticipation” with its meaning.

pairs.right: the state of not taking sides
to expect or look forward to

questions.why: Suffixes such as -ment, -ity, and -ion change a word's form.

questions.stem: The new rule was ____ because older students got twice as much computer time as younger students.
questions.why: Getting twice as much time is not equal.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “reserved” to mean “set aside for someone”?
options: He gave a reserved smile when he met the new teacher.
The reserved boy sat alone and read his book quietly.
The front row is reserved for the guests of honor.
Salma is reserved and seldom speaks in large groups.
questions.why: Reserved can mean shy or set aside; seats are set aside.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “entitled” mean “has a right to” or “has the title”?

rows.text: The book is entitled “Stars Over the Desert.”
Each player is entitled to one water break.
Her poem, entitled “Morning Rain,” won first prize.
Workers are entitled to rest on their days off.

questions.why: Entitled is a multiple-meaning word.

questions.stem: The village council discussed where to dig the new well. Some members wanted it near the farms; others wanted it near the school. The chairman stayed ____, listening to both groups before making a fair decision.
questions.why: Listening to both groups without choosing shows he was neutral.

questions.stem: In these sentences about a debate club, which sentence misuses “outspoken,” “reserved,” “sought,” or “defy”?
segments: Lina is outspoken and always shares her views in debates.
Her friend Dana is more reserved and speaks softly.
Before the contest, both girls sought advice from their coach.
They decided to defy the coach's helpful tips by following them closely.
questions.correction: They decided to follow the coach's helpful tips closely.
questions.why: To defy means to go against, not to follow.

questions.stem: The prefix “un-” means “not,” as in “unequal.” Which THREE words use “un-” with the same meaning? Choose three.
questions.why: In unfair, unknown, and unsafe, un- means not.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “outspoken” is to “reserved” as “equal” is to ____.
questions.why: Outspoken and reserved are opposites, like equal and unequal.

questions.stem: The young scientist ____ advice from experts, asking them to check her findings about desert locusts before she shared them.
questions.why: She looked for advice first, so sought fits best.

questions.stem: “Instead of giving up, the small fishing boat seemed to defy the waves, climbing over each one and pushing on toward the shore.” What does “defy” mean in this sentence?

partA.stem: “Instead of giving up, the small fishing boat seemed to defy the waves, climbing over each one and pushing on toward the shore.” What does “defy” mean in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: to calmly follow

options.label: B
options.text: to slowly forget

options.label: C
options.text: to sink below

options.label: D
options.text: to boldly resist

partB.stem: Which phrase best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “Instead of giving up”

options.label: B
options.text: “toward the shore”

options.label: C
options.text: “each one”

options.label: D
options.text: “the small fishing boat”

questions.why: Not giving up shows the boat resisted the waves.

questions.stem: Match each affix with its meaning: “-ion” in “anticipation,” “un-” in “unequal,” “out-” in “outspoken,” and “-al” in “neutral.”
questions.why: Affixes add meaning to base words.

questions.stem: Does “defy” have a positive or negative feeling in each sentence?

rows.text: The athlete defied the doctors' predictions and walked again within a year.
The driver defied the traffic signals and put people in danger.
The tiny desert flower defies the heat and blooms each spring.
The student defied the safety rules in the lab and spilled acid.

questions.why: Defy can show courage or careless rule-breaking.

questions.stem: “The inquisitive kitten sniffed every box and peeked into every bag in the new house.” What does “inquisitive” mean?
questions.why: Inquisitive means curious and eager to find out.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “astounded,” “concealed,” “perplexed,” and “precise.”
questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you describe mysteries and clues.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The squirrel concealed its nuts under the leaves,” the word “concealed” means hid.
questions.why: To conceal something is to hide it.

questions.stem: Hamad was ____ when he saw his little brother solve the hard puzzle in just one minute.
questions.why: Astounded means very surprised.

questions.stem: Is each thing “concealed” or in plain sight?

rows.text: a key taped under a flowerpot
a stop sign at a busy corner
a lizard whose colors match the sand
a bright poster on the classroom door

questions.why: Concealed things are hidden from view.

questions.stem: “The directions were so confusing that the tourists looked perplexed and kept turning the map around.” What does “perplexed” mean?
questions.why: Confusing directions leave people puzzled.

questions.stem: Which TWO measurements are the most “precise”? Choose two.
questions.why: Precise measurements are exact.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “suspicious,” “interpret,” or “reconsider” in it.

pairs.left: The guard grew suspicious when he saw the open gate at night.
Can you interpret the signs on this old map?
Please reconsider your answer before you hand in the test.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.

questions.stem: Sara was ____ of the strange email that asked for her password, so she deleted it.
questions.why: Suspicious means feeling that something may be wrong.

questions.stem: True or false: An “inquisitive” student never asks any questions.
questions.why: Inquisitive students are curious and ask many questions.

questions.stem: “At first Omar wanted to quit the swim team, but after talking with his coach, he thought about it again and decided to reconsider.” Which words help you understand “reconsider”?
questions.why: To reconsider is to think about something again.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “precise”?
questions.why: After “great,” the noun precision is needed.

questions.stem: Is each pair a synonym or an antonym of “concealed,” “precise,” “perplexed,” “inquisitive,” or “astounded”?

rows.text: concealed — hidden
precise — vague
perplexed — confused
inquisitive — uninterested
astounded — amazed

questions.why: Synonyms mean the same; antonyms mean the opposite.

questions.stem: Detectives must ____ small clues, such as footprints or a torn ticket, to figure out what happened.
questions.why: To interpret clues is to explain what they mean.

questions.stem: Which TWO sights would make a neighbor “suspicious”? Choose two.
options: a child riding a bike to school in the morning
a stranger peeking into parked cars at night
a door left wide open while the family is away
the mail carrier delivering letters at noon
questions.why: Suspicious things make people think something is wrong.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The magician astounded the audience by pulling a long ribbon out of an empty box” uses “astounded” correctly.
questions.why: The audience was greatly surprised, so astounded fits.

questions.stem: Put these reactions to a shooting star in order from the least surprised to “astounded.”
sequence: noticed it calmly
was a little surprised
was astounded
questions.why: Astounded is the strongest kind of surprise.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “concealed”?
questions.why: Shown is the opposite of concealed.

questions.stem: Match each form of “suspicious,” “precise,” “interpret,” and “inquisitive” with its meaning.

pairs.right: a feeling that something is wrong

questions.why: Words in the same family share a base meaning.

questions.stem: The doctor gave a ____ time for taking the medicine: exactly 8:00 in the morning.
questions.why: Exactly 8:00 is a precise time.

questions.stem: The proverb “Curiosity is the key to knowledge” best describes which kind of person?
questions.why: An inquisitive person is curious, and curiosity leads to learning.

questions.stem: Which key word best matches the lesson of each proverb: “reconsider” or “suspicious”?

rows.text: It is never too late to change your mind.
If something sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
Sleep on it before you decide.
All that glitters is not gold.

questions.why: Some proverbs warn us to think again; others warn us to doubt appearances.

questions.stem: The weather station recorded a sudden drop in air pressure, darker clouds, and a shift in the wind. The forecaster had to ____ these signs carefully before warning fishermen to stay in port.
questions.why: The forecaster explains what the signs mean, so interpret fits.

questions.stem: In these sentences about a science fair, which sentence misuses “inquisitive,” “precise,” “perplexed,” or “astounded”?
segments: Fahad is inquisitive and loves asking how machines work.
For his project, he made precise measurements with a ruler.
The judges were perplexed because his results were so clear and easy to understand.
In the end, they were astounded by his clever robot.
questions.correction: The judges were impressed because his results were so clear and easy to understand.
questions.why: Perplexed means confused, which does not fit clear results.

questions.stem: The proverb “Measure twice, cut once” teaches people to be “precise.” Which TWO situations follow this advice? Choose two.
options: A tailor cuts the cloth first and measures it afterward.
A painter splashes paint quickly without looking.
A baker weighs the flour carefully before adding it to the dough.
A carpenter checks the length of a board again before sawing it.
questions.why: Checking carefully before acting is being precise.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “concealed” is to “hidden” as “perplexed” is to ____.
questions.why: Concealed and hidden are synonyms, like perplexed and confused.

questions.stem: The scientist was not just surprised; she was ____ to find a living fish in a desert pool that had been dry for years.
questions.why: “Not just surprised” calls for a stronger word: astounded.

questions.stem: “The old saying ‘Still waters run deep’ fits my uncle. He is quiet, but when he speaks, his ideas surprise everyone.” How would you interpret this saying?

partA.stem: “The old saying ‘Still waters run deep’ fits my uncle. He is quiet, but when he speaks, his ideas surprise everyone.” How would you interpret this saying?

options.label: A
options.text: Calm water is never dangerous.

options.label: B
options.text: Loud people are always wise.

options.label: C
options.text: Quiet people may have deep thoughts.

options.label: D
options.text: Rivers are deeper than lakes.

partB.stem: Which phrase best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “Still waters”

options.label: B
options.text: “The old saying”

options.label: C
options.text: “fits my uncle”

options.label: D
options.text: “when he speaks, his ideas surprise everyone”

questions.why: The uncle is quiet but has deep ideas, which explains the saying.

questions.stem: Match each proverb with the key word whose idea it best expresses: “precise,” “reconsider,” “suspicious,” or “inquisitive.”

pairs.left: Not everything that shines is gold.
Curiosity is the mother of discovery.

questions.why: Proverbs express ideas that key words can name.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “suspicious” describe someone who feels doubt or something that causes doubt?

rows.text: The cat was suspicious of the new vacuum cleaner.
A suspicious bag was left near the airport gate.
Mother was suspicious when the cookie jar was suddenly empty.
The man's suspicious behavior made the guard watch him closely.

questions.why: Suspicious can describe a person who doubts or a thing that seems wrong.

questions.stem: “After months without rain, the field was barren; nothing grew there at all.” What does “barren” mean?
questions.why: Barren land has no plants growing on it.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “plumes,” “stanza,” “lyric,” and “alliteration.”

pairs.right: a group of lines in a poem
a short poem that shares feelings
repeating the first sound in nearby words

questions.why: These words help you talk about poems and images.

questions.stem: True or false: “Sami's silly snake slid south” is an example of alliteration.
questions.why: Many nearby words begin with the same s sound.

questions.stem: The peacock spread its bright blue and green ____ to show off in the garden.
questions.why: Plumes are large, showy feathers.

questions.stem: Is each place “barren” or full of life?

rows.text: a rocky hill with no plants or animals
a green oasis with palm trees and birds
an empty salt flat under the hot sun
a coral reef crowded with colorful fish

questions.why: Barren places have little or no life.

questions.stem: “Her smile was an expression of pure joy when she saw her grandparents at the airport.” What does “expression” mean here?
options: a rule that must be followed
a way of showing a feeling
questions.why: An expression shows what someone feels.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe something “meaningful”? Choose two.
options: Majed tapped his pencil on the desk without thinking about it.
Fatima glanced at an ad on a bus and forgot it a moment later.
Volunteering at the food bank made Reem feel her work truly mattered.
Ali keeps the pen his grandfather gave him because it reminds him of their talks.
questions.why: Meaningful things are important and full of purpose.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “meter,” “stanza,” or “lyric” in it.

pairs.left: Her poem has a steady meter, like a ticking clock.
pairs.right: the pattern of beats in a line of poetry

pairs.left: The second stanza describes the sea at night.
pairs.right: a group of lines in a poem

pairs.left: She wrote a lyric about missing her old home.
pairs.right: a short poem that expresses personal feelings

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word in its sentence.

questions.stem: The tired traveler finally saw green fields after crossing the ____ desert where nothing grew.
questions.why: Nothing grew there, so the desert was barren.

questions.stem: True or false: A “stanza” is a single word that rhymes at the end of a line.
questions.why: A stanza is a group of lines in a poem.

questions.stem: “The ostrich shook its plumes, and soft feathers drifted across the sand.” Which words help you understand “plumes”?
questions.why: Soft feathers explain what plumes are.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “meaningful”?
questions.why: An adjective, meaningful, describes the noun way.

questions.stem: Is each line describing “plumes” or a “barren” place a simile or a metaphor?

rows.text: The clouds were plumes of white smoke.
The barren hill was like a bald head.
The barren desert was a sea of silent sand.
The kite's tail floated like a feathery plume.

questions.why: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.

questions.stem: The line “Big brown bears bounce on blue balls” uses ____ because many words begin with a “b” sound.
questions.why: Repeating the first sound in nearby words is alliteration.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms of “barren”? Choose two.
questions.why: Bare and lifeless both describe land where little grows.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The poet read a lyric that shared her love of the sea” uses “lyric” correctly.
questions.why: A lyric is a short poem that shares feelings.

questions.stem: Put these parts from the smallest to the largest: a word, a line, a “stanza,” and a whole poem.
sequence: a word
a line
a stanza
a whole poem
questions.why: Words make lines, lines make stanzas, and stanzas make a poem.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “barren”?
questions.why: Fertile land grows many plants, the opposite of barren.

questions.stem: Match each form of “expression” and “meaningful” with its meaning.

pairs.right: to show or tell a feeling

questions.why: Suffixes such as -ive, -ful, and -less change a word's meaning.

questions.stem: When you clap along to a poem and feel a steady beat, you are noticing its ____.
questions.why: Meter is the pattern of beats in poetry.

questions.stem: Which line uses a metaphor to describe a “barren” place?
options: The plain was barren and very dry.
The barren plain looked like a page.
The barren plain was a blank page.
Nothing grew on the barren plain.
questions.why: A metaphor says one thing is another without like or as.

questions.stem: Sort each line by its figurative device: simile, metaphor, or “alliteration.”

rows.text: The heron's plumes were like silver smoke.
Summer is a golden coin I keep in my pocket.
Wild winds whistle while we wait.
Her voice was as gentle as rain.

questions.why: Similes use like or as, metaphors compare directly, and alliteration repeats first sounds.

questions.stem: Grandmother's old photo album is ____ to our family. Each picture holds a memory of a trip, a wedding, or a holiday. We look through it together every Eid.
questions.why: Something full of memories and importance is meaningful.

questions.stem: In these sentences about a poetry contest, which sentence misuses “lyric,” “stanza,” “meter,” or “alliteration”?
segments: Rana wrote a lyric about her love for the sea.
Each stanza had four lines that rhymed.
She counted the beats to keep a steady meter.
Her alliteration was a line where every word rhymed with “blue.”
questions.correction: Her alliteration was a line where every word began with the letter b.
questions.why: Alliteration repeats beginning sounds, not rhymes.

questions.stem: Which THREE lines are similes or metaphors that give “expression” to a feeling? Choose three.
options: My heart was a drum before the race.
His anger was a storm in the room.
He was angry about the broken vase.
Her joy bubbled like a fountain.
She felt happy after the race.
questions.why: Similes and metaphors express feelings through comparisons.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “stanza” is to “poem” as “paragraph” is to ____.
questions.why: A stanza is part of a poem, as a paragraph is part of an essay.

questions.stem: Above the factory, gray ____ of smoke curled into the evening sky.
questions.why: Plumes can also mean feather-shaped clouds of smoke.

questions.stem: A poet writes: “The desert after summer is a barren drum, / it waits in silence for the rain to come.” What does the metaphor “a barren drum” suggest about the desert?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: It is green and wet.

options.label: C

options.label: D

partB.stem: Which words best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “The desert”

options.label: B
options.text: “for the rain”

options.label: C
options.text: “after summer”

options.label: D

questions.why: A barren drum that waits in silence is empty and quiet.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term with an example of it: “alliteration,” “meter,” “stanza,” and “lyric.”

pairs.right: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM, a steady beat
four lines grouped together, then a space
a short, song-like poem about missing home

questions.why: Each term names a different part or feature of poetry.

questions.stem: Is “meter” or “expression” used with its poetry meaning or an everyday meaning in each sentence?

rows.text: Each line of her poem has a meter of three beats.
The taxi meter showed twenty riyals.
Rhymes and similes are tools of poetic expression.
His expression changed when he heard the good news.

questions.why: Meter and expression are multiple-meaning words.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The Moon takes about a month to orbit Earth, traveling around it again and again.” What does “orbit” mean?
options: to travel in a path around something
to stay still in one spot
to shine brightly in the dark night sky
to fall slowly toward the ground
questions.why: To orbit is to move in a curved path around another object.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “spheres,” “diameter,” “approximately,” and “evaluate.”

pairs.right: the distance straight across a circle through its center
to judge how good something is

questions.why: Each word names an idea scientists use when they study space.

questions.stem: True or false: If you measure the diameter of a round pizza, you measure straight across it from one edge to the other through the middle.
questions.why: A diameter goes across a circle and passes through its center.

questions.stem: The bus ride from Riyadh to Qassim takes ____ four hours, give or take a few minutes.
questions.why: “Give or take a few minutes” shows the time is approximate, not exact.

questions.stem: Is each object one of the “spheres,” or is it not a sphere?

rows.text: a football
an orange
a cereal box
a sheet of paper

questions.why: Spheres are round in every direction, like a ball.

questions.stem: Huda added the cost of the juice and the bread to find the total. Her calculation showed she needed twelve riyals. What is a “calculation”?
options: a guess made without any thinking
the work of finding an answer with numbers
a picture drawn carefully to show an idea
a list of things to buy at a shop
questions.why: A calculation uses math to find an answer.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show someone who is about to evaluate something? Choose two.
options: The boy tossed his old shoes into the closet.
The coach watched each runner to judge who was fastest.
The teacher read the posters to decide which ones were clearest.
The cat slept in a sunny corner all afternoon.
questions.why: To evaluate means to look closely and judge the quality of something.

questions.stem: For the art contest, the judges listed their ____: neat work, bright colors, and a clear idea.
questions.why: Criteria are the rules or standards used to judge something.

questions.stem: True or false: An astronomical object is something found in space, such as a star or a planet.
questions.why: Astronomical describes things related to stars, planets, and space.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “orbit,” “criteria,” or “calculation” in it.

pairs.left: Satellites orbit Earth high above the clouds.
The criteria for the prize were speed and safety.

questions.why: Each meaning fits how the word is used in its sentence.

questions.stem: “The old well in the village is approximately ten meters deep. No one has measured it exactly, but it is close to that.” Which clue helps you understand “approximately”?
questions.why: “Close to that” tells you approximately means nearly, not exactly.

questions.stem: Before choosing a new school bag, Faisal made an ____ of three bags, comparing their weight, pockets, and price.
questions.why: The noun form “evaluation” fits after “an”; it means a careful judgment.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “approximately”?

rows.text: roughly
about
exactly
precisely

questions.why: Approximately means about; exactly is its opposite.

questions.stem: True or false: “The criteria for joining the swim team were that you could float, swim one lap, and follow the coach's rules” uses “criteria” correctly.
questions.why: Criteria are the standards someone must meet, and this sentence lists them.

questions.stem: Which TWO things would a scientist most likely measure by finding their diameter? Choose two.
options: the round opening of a telescope tube
the weight of a bag of rice
a circular crater on the Moon
the length of a straight road
questions.why: Diameter is used for round things like circles and spheres.

questions.stem: “Astronomers study comets, planets, and distant galaxies. These astronomical wonders can only be seen clearly with strong telescopes.” What does “astronomical” mean in this sentence?
options: having to do with old machines
having to do with objects in space
having to do with ocean animals
having to do with tall city buildings
questions.why: The examples comets, planets, and galaxies show that astronomical refers to space.

questions.stem: To find how many tiles the classroom floor needs, the builder must ____ the area carefully.
questions.why: The verb “calculate” fits after “must”; a calculation is the result of that work.

questions.stem: Match each vocabulary word with its antonym (opposite): “approximately,” “evaluate,” and “spheres.”
questions.why: An antonym has the opposite meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The new satellite will orbit the classroom desk,” the word “orbit” is used correctly.
questions.why: Satellites orbit planets in space, not desks in a classroom.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order for a class that wants to evaluate three model rockets using clear criteria.
sequence: Agree on the criteria, such as height and safety.
Launch each rocket and record the results.
Do the calculations to compare the heights.
Evaluate which rocket met the criteria best.
questions.why: You set criteria first, then gather data, calculate, and finally judge.

questions.stem: The Greek root “astro” means “star.” Which word shares this root with “astronomical” and names a person who travels into space?
questions.why: Astronaut has the root astro, meaning star, just like astronomical.

questions.stem: Sort these words by the Greek root they share with “diameter” (meter = measure) or “spheres” (sphere = ball).

rows.text: thermometer
speedometer
hemisphere
atmosphere

questions.why: Words with meter measure something; words with sphere describe a ball or round layer.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this short paragraph: “Scientists use many criteria to judge a planet. They measure its diameter to know its size. They track how long it takes to orbit the Sun. Then they spheres the data to decide if life could exist there.”
segments: Scientists use many criteria to judge a planet.
They measure its diameter to know its size.
They track how long it takes to orbit the Sun.
Then they spheres the data to decide if life could exist there.
questions.correction: Then they evaluate the data to decide if life could exist there.
questions.why: Spheres are round objects; evaluate means to judge, which fits the sentence.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “diameter” is to “measure across” as “orbit” is to ____.
questions.why: Diameter names a distance measured across a circle; to orbit is to travel around something.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “The engineers needed an exact answer, not a guess. A single mistake in their ____ could send the satellite off course, so they checked every number twice.” Which word BEST fits the blank?
questions.why: Calculations are math work that must be exact; checking numbers twice fits.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “astronomical” correctly.

segments.text: The astronomical team watched an eclipse through special glasses.
The astronomical sandwich was made with cheese and tomato.
My little brother astronomical his shoes before school.
We planted astronomical seeds in the school garden.

questions.why: Astronomical relates to studying space, like watching an eclipse.

questions.stem: Match each Greek root with its meaning and a key word that contains it: “astro,” “sphere,” and “meter.”
questions.why: Knowing Greek roots helps you figure out science words.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The price of the telescope was astronomical, so Salem saved for two years,” what does “astronomical” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The price of the telescope was astronomical, so Salem saved for two years,” what does “astronomical” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: easy to find

options.label: B
options.text: very small

options.label: C
options.text: extremely large

options.label: D
options.text: related to stars

partB.stem: Part B: Which clue in the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “saved for two years”

options.label: B
options.text: “the telescope”

options.label: C
options.text: “Salem”

options.label: D
options.text: “the price of”

questions.why: Here astronomical is used in a figurative way to mean huge, like the distances in space.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “approximately” in the most precise and fitting way? Choose two.
options: She approximately smiled at her friend across the yard.
Approximately half of the students chose the science club.
The camel caravan traveled approximately forty kilometers before sunset.
questions.why: Approximately fits estimates, not exact numbers or actions like smiling.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about a science fair: “The judges had three criteria for the projects. They wanted to evaluate how creative each idea was. One student built a model of the planets as small spheres. He showed that Earth takes approximately one day to orbit the Sun.”
segments: The judges had three criteria for the projects.
They wanted to evaluate how creative each idea was.
One student built a model of the planets as small spheres.
He showed that Earth takes approximately one day to orbit the Sun.
questions.correction: He showed that Earth takes approximately one year to orbit the Sun.
questions.why: Earth needs about one year, not one day, to orbit the Sun.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “You can rely on Grandpa; he always picks us up from school on time.” What does “rely” mean?
questions.why: To rely on someone is to trust and depend on them.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “assume,” “guarantee,” “nominate,” and “sympathy.”

pairs.right: a promise that something will happen
to suggest someone for a job or prize

questions.why: Each word describes a way people think about or treat others.

questions.stem: True or false: A supportive friend helps and encourages you when things get hard.
questions.why: Supportive means giving help and encouragement.

questions.stem: The sky was full of dark clouds and thunder, so it was ____ going to rain.
questions.why: Obviously means clearly; dark clouds and thunder make rain easy to see coming.

questions.stem: Does each sentence show “sympathy” or not?

rows.text: Noura hugged her sister after she fell off her bike.
Ali said, “I'm sorry your bike broke.”
Sami laughed when his friend tripped.
Reem ignored her crying cousin.

questions.why: Sympathy means caring about someone else's sadness or trouble.

questions.stem: “My class will nominate Majed for team captain because he is fair and kind.” What does “nominate” mean?
options: to teach someone a new game
to give someone a heavy bag
to remove someone from a sports team
to name someone for a position
questions.why: To nominate is to suggest someone for a role.

questions.stem: Which TWO words mean almost the same as “guarantee”? Choose two.
questions.why: A guarantee is a firm promise or pledge.

questions.stem: The tiny kitten was a ____ at first, but after weeks of good food it grew strong.
questions.why: A weakling is someone or something that is weak.

questions.stem: True or false: If you assume your friend is at home, you know for sure because you saw him there.
questions.why: To assume is to believe without proof, not to know for sure.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “rely,” “supportive,” or “obviously” in it.

pairs.left: Farmers rely on rain to water their crops.
Her supportive parents cheered at every match.
He was obviously tired; he yawned all morning.

questions.why: Each meaning fits how the word is used in its sentence.

questions.stem: “Don't assume the shop is open just because the lights are on. Check the sign first, because guessing could waste your trip.” Which clue helps you understand “assume”?
questions.why: The clue links assuming with guessing, which is believing without checking.

questions.stem: Our teacher asked us to write a ____ for the student who helps others the most.
questions.why: The noun “nomination” fits after “a”; it is the act of naming someone for an honor.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “supportive”?

rows.text: encouraging
helpful
discouraging
unkind

questions.why: Supportive means helpful; unkind and discouraging mean the opposite.

questions.stem: True or false: “The new phone came with a two-year guarantee, so the shop will fix it for free if it breaks” uses “guarantee” correctly.
questions.why: A guarantee is a promise that something will be repaired or replaced.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe someone a team can rely on? Choose two.
options: Lama always finishes her part of the group project on time.
Yousef often forgets the meeting time.
Hamad comes to every practice and never misses a pass.
Dana leaves early whenever the game gets hard.
questions.why: You can rely on people who are steady and keep their promises.

questions.stem: “After the flood, neighbors brought food and blankets to the families who lost their homes. Everyone showed great sympathy.” What does “sympathy” mean here?
options: feeling proud of winning a prize
being angry with others for all their mistakes
sharing the sadness of others and wanting to help
questions.why: Bringing food and blankets shows care for people in trouble.

questions.stem: It was ____ that Maha had practiced; she played the oud without a single mistake.
questions.why: The adjective “obvious” fits after “was”; “obviously” is the adverb form.

questions.stem: Match each vocabulary word with its antonym (opposite): “weakling,” “assume,” and “supportive.”
questions.why: An antonym has the opposite meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The weakling lifted the heavy cupboard all by himself,” the word “weakling” is used correctly.
questions.why: A weakling lacks strength, so he would not lift a heavy cupboard alone.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order for how a school club chooses a leader after students nominate classmates.
sequence: Students nominate classmates they rely on.
Each nominated student gives a short speech.
Everyone votes for one nominee.
The winner thanks the supportive members.
questions.why: Nominations come first, then speeches, a vote, and thanks.

questions.stem: In “When our team lost, Coach said we were all in the same boat, so we must rely on each other,” what does the idiom “in the same boat” mean?
options: sailing together on a fishing trip
questions.why: “In the same boat” is an idiom meaning everyone faces the same problem.

questions.stem: Does each idiom describe being “supportive” or not being supportive?

rows.text: to have someone's back
to lend a hand
to give someone the cold shoulder
to leave someone out in the cold

questions.why: Idioms about helping show support; idioms about ignoring do not.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph: “When Omar broke his arm, his classmates showed sympathy. They carried his books and helped him with notes. His supportive friends visited him every day. Obviously, they treated him like a weakling and refused to help.”
segments: When Omar broke his arm, his classmates showed sympathy.
They carried his books and helped him with notes.
His supportive friends visited him every day.
Obviously, they treated him like a weakling and refused to help.
questions.correction: Obviously, they treated him like a true friend and never refused to help.
questions.why: The last sentence contradicts the supportive actions described before it.

questions.stem: Which word BEST completes the sentence? “The doctor cannot ____ that the medicine will work for everyone, but it has helped most patients.”
questions.why: Guarantee means to promise for certain, which the doctor cannot do.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “Many people ____ that a small player cannot score. However, Bader is quick and clever. He proved them wrong in the final match.” Which word BEST fits the blank?
questions.why: People assume, or believe without proof, something that later turns out to be wrong.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “guarantee” in an idiom-like way to show strong certainty.

segments.text: “I guarantee you'll laugh at my uncle's stories,” said Rana.
The store guarantee covered the broken fan.
We read the guarantee printed on the box.
The guarantee expired after one year.

questions.why: Here “I guarantee” is a common expression meaning “I'm sure,” not a written promise.

questions.stem: Match each idiom with its meaning in a sentence that uses a key word: “Mona didn't want to be a weakling, so she decided to…”

pairs.right: keep going and not give up
accept the results of her actions
do her fair share of the work

questions.why: Idioms have meanings that are different from their exact words.

questions.stem: Part A: In “Don't throw in the towel now — we can rely on our best runner in the last lap,” what does the idiom “throw in the towel” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In “Don't throw in the towel now — we can rely on our best runner in the last lap,” what does the idiom “throw in the towel” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: give up

options.label: B
options.text: dry off

options.label: C
options.text: clean up

options.label: D
options.text: start over

partB.stem: Part B: Which part of the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the towel”

options.label: B
options.text: “now”

options.label: C
options.text: “we can rely on our best runner in the last lap”

options.label: D
options.text: “our best runner”

questions.why: Relying on the best runner shows there is still hope, so the speaker says not to give up.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “obviously” with the most fitting shade of meaning? Choose two.
options: The puppy was obviously happy, wagging its tail wildly.
The cake was obviously burned; black smoke filled the kitchen.
The answer was obviously hidden where nobody could find it.
He obviously whispered so that no one would notice.
questions.why: Obviously means easy to see, so it does not fit hidden or secret actions.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about a family business: “During hard times, the family had to rely on one another. The children were supportive and helped in the shop. Their father nominated that business would get better soon. His hope gave everyone strength.”
segments: During hard times, the family had to rely on one another.
The children were supportive and helped in the shop.
Their father nominated that business would get better soon.
questions.correction: Their father assumed that business would get better soon.
questions.why: Nominate means to name someone for a role; assume means to believe something will happen.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Date palms thrive in the hot sun of Al-Ahsa and give plenty of fruit.” What does “thrive” mean?
options: move away to a brand-new place
questions.why: Plants that thrive grow well.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “agricultural,” “declined,” “identify,” and “widespread.”

pairs.right: to find out or name what something is

questions.why: These words help you talk about nature and farming.

questions.stem: True or false: If a room is in disorder, everything is neat and in its proper place.
questions.why: Disorder means a messy state without order.

questions.stem: The birthday party was a surprise, so Lina's smile showed it was completely ____.
questions.why: Unexpected means not planned for or known about ahead of time.

questions.stem: Is each place or job “agricultural” or not agricultural?

rows.text: a wheat farm
a date palm orchard
a shoe store
a computer office

questions.why: Agricultural things have to do with farming and growing crops or animals.

questions.stem: “With dark clouds gathering, rain this afternoon is probable.” What does “probable” mean?
questions.why: Probable means likely.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe something widespread? Choose two.
options: Sand from the storm covered streets all across the city.
A single bird sat on the fence.
The cold spread to almost every class in the school.
One leaf fell on the doorstep.
questions.why: Widespread things reach many people or places.
