questions.stem: The number of sea turtles ____ after their nesting beaches were covered with trash.
questions.why: Declined means went down in number.

questions.stem: True or false: A bird watcher uses a guidebook to identify the birds she sees.
questions.why: To identify is to figure out what something is.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “thrive,” “disorder,” or “unexpected” in it.

pairs.left: The wind left the tents in disorder.
An unexpected visitor knocked at night.

questions.why: Each meaning fits how the word is used in its sentence.

questions.stem: “Scientists could not identify the strange fish at first. They studied its fins, colors, and teeth before they learned its name.” Which clue helps you understand “identify”?
questions.why: Learning its name shows that to identify is to find out what something is.

questions.stem: Using smart water pumps has improved ____ in the Qassim region, where farmers grow wheat and vegetables.
questions.why: The noun “agriculture” (farming) fits here; agricultural is the adjective form.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “declined”?

rows.text: decreased
dropped
increased
grew

questions.why: Declined means went down, so increased and grew are opposites.

questions.stem: True or false: “The weeds became widespread, covering every field in the valley” uses “widespread” correctly.
questions.why: Covering every field shows the weeds are widespread.

questions.stem: Which TWO plants or animals most likely thrive in a hot, dry desert? Choose two.
options: a camel that can go days without drinking
a polar bear with thick fur
a water lily that floats in ponds
questions.why: Living things thrive where they are suited to the environment.

questions.stem: “The new beetle caused a widespread problem. It ate crops on farms in many different villages, not just one.” What does “widespread” mean here?
questions.why: Many villages, not just one, shows the problem was widespread.

questions.stem: It is ____ that the team will win, because they have won all their games this year.
questions.why: The adjective “probable” fits after “is”; probably is the adverb form.

questions.stem: Match each vocabulary word with its antonym (opposite): “thrive,” “unexpected,” and “disorder.”
questions.why: An antonym has the opposite meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The plants declined in the healthy, well-watered garden and grew taller every week,” the word “declined” is used correctly.
questions.why: Declined means became weaker or fewer, which does not match growing taller.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order for how scientists might handle an unexpected new weed spreading near a farm.
sequence: Identify what kind of plant the weed is.
Measure how widespread it has become.
Decide on the most probable way to stop it.
Check that the crops thrive again.
questions.why: Scientists first identify, then measure, plan, and check results.

questions.stem: The prefix “dis-” means “not” or “opposite of.” Which meaning does “disorder” have when the root word is “order”?
questions.why: Dis- + order means a lack of order, or a mess.

questions.stem: Sort these words by the root word they share with “unexpected” (expect) or “widespread” (spread).

rows.text: expectation
unexpectedly
spreading
outspread

questions.why: Finding the root word inside a longer word helps you understand it.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about invasive plants: “A new vine arrived in the valley by accident. Its growth was unexpected and fast. Soon the vine was widespread, and native plants declined. Farmers worked hard to help the vine thrive and cover even more land.”
segments: A new vine arrived in the valley by accident.
Its growth was unexpected and fast.
Soon the vine was widespread, and native plants declined.
Farmers worked hard to help the vine thrive and cover even more land.
questions.correction: Farmers worked hard to stop the vine from spreading and covering even more land.
questions.why: Farmers would try to stop a harmful vine, not help it thrive.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “thrive” is to “healthy forest” as “declined” is to ____.
questions.why: Thrive matches growth; declined matches something getting smaller.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “The scientists studied the dying coral. They found that warm water was the most ____ cause. They were not completely sure, but the evidence pointed strongly to it.” Which word BEST fits the blank?
questions.why: Probable means likely; the scientists were not sure but strongly believed it.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “identify” correctly.

segments.text: The ranger helped us identify the tracks as belonging to a fox.
We identify the sandwiches into four pieces for lunch.
The kite will identify higher if the wind is strong.
My sister identified the cake with chocolate frosting.

questions.why: To identify is to recognize or name what something is.

questions.stem: Match each word with its root word and the meaning of its prefix or suffix: “unexpected,” “disorder,” and “agricultural.”
questions.why: Splitting words into roots and affixes reveals their meanings.

questions.stem: Part A: In “Our class declined the invitation to the museum because the trip was on exam day,” what does “declined” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In “Our class declined the invitation to the museum because the trip was on exam day,” what does “declined” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: became weaker

options.label: B
options.text: went down in number

options.label: C
options.text: arrived late

options.label: D
options.text: politely said no

partB.stem: Part B: Which clue best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the invitation”

options.label: B
options.text: “our class”

options.label: C
options.text: “because the trip was on exam day”

options.label: D
options.text: “to the museum”

questions.why: Declined can also mean refused; the exam-day clue explains why the class said no.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “disorder” with the meaning “a sickness or problem in how something works”? Choose two.
options: A blood disorder made the patient feel tired often.
After the party, the kitchen was in disorder.
The students left the books in disorder on the shelf.
The doctor treated a sleep disorder that kept the man awake.
questions.why: Disorder can mean a mess or a health problem; context tells which.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about a farm: “The agricultural fair showed new ways to grow food. One farmer used fish to fertilize his crops. Visitors were surprised by this unexpected idea. It is probable that his vegetables declined because they grew so large.”
segments: The agricultural fair showed new ways to grow food.
One farmer used fish to fertilize his crops.
Visitors were surprised by this unexpected idea.
It is probable that his vegetables declined because they grew so large.
questions.correction: It is probable that his vegetables thrived because of the fish.
questions.why: His vegetables grew so large, so they thrived; declined means they got worse.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The school bulletin told parents that sports day would be on Thursday.” What is a “bulletin”?
options: a kind of shoe worn for sports
a short news report or notice
questions.why: A bulletin is a short announcement of news.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “contributions,” “enlisted,” “recruits,” and “survival.”

pairs.right: things given to help a cause
joined the military or a group

questions.why: These words help you talk about communities working together.

questions.stem: True or false: A goalkeeper who catches the ball before it reaches the net is trying to intercept it.
questions.why: To intercept is to stop something on its way to somewhere.

questions.stem: Water and shade are important for ____ in the desert.
questions.why: Survival means staying alive; water and shade help with that.

questions.stem: Do these items show “diversity” or no diversity?

rows.text: a garden with roses, cacti, and palms
a class with students from many countries
a box of identical red pencils
a wall painted one plain color

questions.why: Diversity means having many different kinds.

questions.stem: “The hospital's operations ran smoothly, from the kitchen to the emergency room.” What does “operations” mean here?
options: the ways work is carried out
the loud noises of the machines
questions.why: Operations are the activities and work that keep something running.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe contributions? Choose two.
options: The boy kept all his toys to himself.
Neighbors donated food to families in need.
Students gave books to the new library.
The shop closed early on Friday.
questions.why: Contributions are things people give to help.

questions.stem: The new ____ practiced marching every morning at the training camp.
questions.why: Recruits are new members who are still being trained.

questions.stem: True or false: If Khalid enlisted in the scouts, he decided not to join them.
questions.why: Enlisted means joined, not refused to join.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “bulletin,” “intercept,” or “diversity” in it.

pairs.left: The radio gave a weather bulletin.
The defender jumped to intercept the pass.
The market showed a diversity of spices.

questions.why: Each meaning fits how the word is used in its sentence.

questions.stem: “The rescue team ran operations all night. They searched buildings, carried supplies, and guided people to safety.” Which clue helps you understand “operations”?
options: “searched buildings, carried supplies, and guided people”
questions.why: The list of actions shows that operations are planned activities.

questions.stem: Every ____ to the charity drive, even a single coin, helped buy blankets for families.
questions.why: The noun “contribution” fits after “every”; contribute is the verb.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “survival”?

rows.text: staying alive
endurance
death
extinction

questions.why: Survival means continuing to live; death and extinction are opposites.

questions.stem: True or false: “The army enlisted many young volunteers during the war” uses “enlisted” correctly.
questions.why: Enlisted can mean signed up people to serve.

questions.stem: Which TWO things would a new team member most likely need, as one of the recruits? Choose two.
options: a gold medal for twenty years of service
questions.why: Recruits are new, so they need training and gear, not retirement items.

questions.stem: “The coral reef has great diversity: hundreds of fish, crabs, sea stars, and plants live there together.” What does “diversity” mean?
questions.why: Hundreds of different living things show diversity.

questions.stem: The sailors tried to ____ the enemy's secret message before it reached the ship.
questions.why: The base verb “intercept” fits after “tried to.”

questions.stem: Match each vocabulary word with its antonym (opposite): “enlisted,” “diversity,” and “recruits.”
questions.why: An antonym has the opposite meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The bulletin was a large building with ten floors,” the word “bulletin” is used correctly.
questions.why: A bulletin is a news notice, not a building.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a city sent help after a storm, using “bulletin,” “recruits,” and “operations.”
sequence: A news bulletin warned that a storm was coming.
The city asked for recruits to help clean up.
The new volunteers were trained quickly.
Rescue operations began the next morning.
questions.why: First a warning, then volunteers, training, and finally operations.

questions.stem: Which homophone correctly completes this sentence about recruits? “The recruits waited for ____ captain to arrive.”
questions.why: “Their” shows that the captain belongs to the recruits.

questions.stem: Choose the correct homophone for each sentence about survival in the desert.

rows.text: The traveler drank the ____ bottle of water to aid his survival.
He dug a ____ in the sand to find cool shade for survival.
The ____ group's survival depended on the guide.
Survival experts said a ____ in the tent let in the sand.

questions.why: Whole means all of something; hole means an opening.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph: “The bakery made bread for the soldiers. Their contributions were a big help. The baker used flower and water to make the dough. Everyone's work was important for survival.”
segments: The bakery made bread for the soldiers.
Their contributions were a big help.
The baker used flower and water to make the dough.
Everyone's work was important for survival.
questions.correction: The baker used flour and water to make the dough.
questions.why: Flour is ground grain for baking; a flower is part of a plant.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “recruits” is to “team” as “contributions” is to ____.
questions.why: Recruits are added to a team; contributions are added to a fund.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “The navy wanted to stop the supply ship before it reached the port. Its plan was to ____ it at sea. The captains studied maps for days.” Which word BEST fits the blank?
questions.why: Intercept means to stop something on its way.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses the homophone correctly with the word “operations.”

segments.text: The operations team worked for one week without a break.
The operations team worked for one weak without a break.
The operations team worked four one week without a break.
The operations team worked for won week without a break.

questions.why: Week (seven days), for (a preposition), and one (the number) are correct here.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about bulletins with the correct homophone meaning.

pairs.left: The bulletin board was painted red.
The herd of camels appeared in the bulletin photo.

questions.why: Homophones sound alike but have different meanings and spellings.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The surgeon performed two operations on the patient's knee,” what does “operations” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The surgeon performed two operations on the patient's knee,” what does “operations” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: math problems

options.label: B
options.text: business activities

options.label: C
options.text: medical surgeries

options.label: D
options.text: military actions

partB.stem: Part B: Which clue best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the surgeon” and “the patient's knee”

options.label: B
options.text: “performed”

options.label: C
options.text: “two”

options.label: D
options.text: “on the”

questions.why: A surgeon and a knee show the medical meaning of operations.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “diversity” with the most precise meaning? Choose two.
options: The diversity of birds on the island amazed scientists.
Our school celebrates the diversity of its students' languages.
The diversity of the plain white wall was boring.
He ate one diversity of rice at lunch.
questions.why: Diversity means variety, so it must describe many different kinds.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about wartime: “Many young men enlisted in the army. The recruits trained hard. They listened to the daily bulletin for news. Their intercept was to help their country.”
segments: Many young men enlisted in the army.
They listened to the daily bulletin for news.
Their intercept was to help their country.
questions.correction: Their goal was to help their country.
questions.why: Intercept is a verb meaning to stop something on its way; goal fits the sentence.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The agile goat jumped quickly from rock to rock on the mountain.” What does “agile” mean?
options: too heavy to climb up steep rocks
able to move quickly and easily
questions.why: Agile describes moving with speed and ease.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “cache,” “dormant,” “forage,” and “frigid.”

pairs.right: inactive or asleep for a time

questions.why: These words describe how animals live in nature.

questions.stem: True or false: Bears hibernate by sleeping through the cold winter months.
questions.why: To hibernate is to spend the winter in a deep sleep.

questions.stem: A thick wool blanket ____ you from the cold winter air.
questions.why: Insulates means protects from heat or cold.

questions.stem: Is each place “frigid” or not frigid?

rows.text: the ice of Antarctica
a frozen mountain top
a sunny Riyadh afternoon
a warm kitchen oven

questions.why: Frigid places are extremely cold.

questions.stem: “Squirrels forage for nuts and seeds before winter comes.” What does “forage” mean?
questions.why: To forage is to look for food.

questions.stem: Which TWO animals hibernate during winter? Choose two.
questions.why: Some bears and hedgehogs sleep through winter; camels and falcons stay active.

questions.stem: The squirrel buried a ____ of acorns under the tree so it could eat them later.
questions.why: A cache is a hidden supply.

questions.stem: True or false: A dormant volcano is erupting with hot lava right now.
questions.why: Dormant means inactive for now, not erupting.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “adaptation,” “insulates,” or “agile” in it.

pairs.left: A camel's hump is a helpful adaptation.
pairs.right: a body feature that helps survival

pairs.left: The agile cat climbed the fence.

questions.why: Each meaning fits how the word is used in its sentence.

questions.stem: “Some seeds stay dormant in the dry desert sand for years. They do not grow at all until heavy rain finally wakes them.” Which clue helps you understand “dormant”?
options: “do not grow at all until heavy rain”
questions.why: Not growing until something wakes them shows dormant means inactive.

questions.stem: Thick fur is an ____ that helps arctic foxes live in the snow.
questions.why: The noun “adaptation” fits after “an”; it names a helpful feature.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “frigid”?

rows.text: icy
freezing
scorching
hot

questions.why: Frigid means very cold; scorching and hot are its opposites.

questions.stem: True or false: “Penguins huddle together in the frigid wind to stay warm” uses “frigid” correctly.
questions.why: Frigid wind is extremely cold wind.

questions.stem: Which TWO things insulate an animal from the cold? Choose two.
questions.why: Fat and feathers trap warmth and insulate the body.

questions.stem: “Deep in the ocean, the octopus is agile. It squeezes through tiny cracks and darts away from danger in a flash.” What does “agile” mean here?
questions.why: Darting and squeezing through cracks show quick, easy movement.

questions.stem: The tortoise digs a burrow where it will ____ until spring returns.
questions.why: The base verb “hibernate” fits after “will.”

questions.stem: Match each vocabulary word with its antonym (opposite): “agile,” “dormant,” and “frigid.”
questions.why: An antonym has the opposite meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Fish forage in the desert sand for water,” the word “forage” is used correctly.
questions.why: Fish forage in water, not in desert sand.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how a chipmunk gets ready to hibernate.
sequence: It forages for nuts and seeds in autumn.
It hides a cache of food in its burrow.
It lines the burrow with leaves that insulate it.
It sleeps through the frigid winter.
questions.why: Gathering, storing, insulating, and then sleeping is the order.

questions.stem: “Unlike the busy hummingbird, which flies all day, the bat in the cave remained dormant all winter long.” Which word signals a context clue of contrast for “dormant”?
questions.why: “Unlike” tells you dormant means the opposite of busy.

questions.stem: Is the context clue for each key word a definition clue or an example clue?

rows.text: “Blubber insulates, or keeps warm, the whale's body.”
“A cache, or hidden supply, was found in the tree.”
“Adaptations, such as webbed feet and gills, help animals swim.”
“Animals forage for food like berries, insects, and roots.”

questions.why: Definition clues explain the word; example clues give examples of it.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about polar bears: “Polar bears live in frigid places. Thick fur insulates their bodies. They are agile swimmers and hunt seals. In summer they forage in the warm cache of the Arctic sea.”
segments: Polar bears live in frigid places.
They are agile swimmers and hunt seals.
In summer they forage in the warm cache of the Arctic sea.
questions.correction: In summer they forage in the cold waters of the Arctic sea.
questions.why: A cache is a hidden supply, not a body of water.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “hibernate” is to “bear” as “forage” is to ____.
questions.why: Bears hibernate; a hungry goat forages for food.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “The scientist found a hidden ____ of seeds inside a hollow log. A small mouse had stored them there. It would eat them when food was hard to find.” Which word BEST fits the blank?
questions.why: A cache is a hidden store, which matches the stored seeds.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “cache” as a hidden supply.

segments.text: The crow kept a cache of shiny stones in its nest.
We sat in the cache at the beach.
The runner was cache and quick.
Our teacher will cache the class to the park.

questions.why: Cache is a noun naming a hidden collection.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the context clue type that explains “adaptation,” “frigid,” or “agile.”

pairs.left: “An adaptation is a feature that helps an animal survive.”
“The frigid water, unlike the warm bath, made him shiver.”
“The agile monkey, which leaped and swung easily, reached the fruit.”

questions.why: Writers use definitions, contrasts, and descriptions as clues.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The deep ocean is frigid; no sunlight reaches it, and the water is near freezing,” what does “frigid” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The deep ocean is frigid; no sunlight reaches it, and the water is near freezing,” what does “frigid” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: very cold

options.label: B
options.text: very dark

options.label: C
options.text: very deep

options.label: D
options.text: very salty

partB.stem: Part B: Which clue best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the deep ocean”

options.label: B
options.text: “the water is near freezing”

options.label: C
options.text: “is”

options.label: D
options.text: “no sunlight reaches it”

questions.why: Near freezing directly shows that frigid means very cold.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “insulates” with the most precise meaning? Choose two.
options: The ice insulates the lake by melting it quickly.
The sun insulates the desert sand until it burns.
Snow insulates a rabbit's burrow by keeping the cold wind out.
A whale's blubber insulates it in icy seas.
questions.why: Insulates means keeps heat in or cold out, not heats or melts.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about deep-sea life: “Some sea animals have an amazing adaptation. They glow in the dark to find food. Others stay dormant to save energy. The squid is frigid, darting fast to catch its prey.”
segments: Some sea animals have an amazing adaptation.
They glow in the dark to find food.
Others stay dormant to save energy.
The squid is frigid, darting fast to catch its prey.
questions.correction: The squid is agile, darting fast to catch its prey.
questions.why: Agile means quick and nimble; frigid means very cold.

questions.stem: “The car horn blares outside the bakery, and everyone jumps.” What does “blares” mean?
options: plays a soft and gentle tune
questions.why: Something that blares makes a loud, harsh sound.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “blares,” “errand,” “exchange,” and “connection.”

pairs.right: a short trip to do a job
to give one thing and get another back
a link between people or things

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you understand the word in any sentence.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Mama sent Khalid on an errand to buy fresh bread,” the word “errand” means a short trip to get something done.
questions.why: An errand is a short trip to do a task for someone.

questions.stem: At the book fair, Sara and Lina ____ their favorite books so each girl has something new to read.
questions.why: To exchange is to give something and get something back.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use “imagery” (words that help you see, hear, smell, taste, or feel), or not?

rows.text: The golden dunes glowed under a pink evening sky.
We went to the market on Tuesday.
Warm cardamom coffee steamed in the tiny cups.
The meeting lasted one hour.

questions.why: Imagery uses sense details to paint a picture in the reader's mind.

questions.stem: Which word means almost the same as “connection”?
questions.why: A connection is a link between things or people.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term—“personification,” “assonance,” “consonance,” and “imagery”—with an example line.

pairs.right: The wind whispered secrets to the palms.
Go slow over the open road.
The black truck struck the rock.
Cold, salty spray stung my cheeks.

questions.why: Each poetry device creates a different effect in a line.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The radio blares the morning news so loudly that the baby wakes up” uses “blares” correctly.
questions.why: A very loud radio blares, which could wake a baby.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use personification? Choose two.
options: The old clock struck twelve at noon.
Big waves washed over the sand castle.
The old clock grumbled as it struck noon.
The sea reached out and grabbed the sand castle.
questions.why: Personification gives human actions, like grumbling or grabbing, to things that are not human.

questions.stem: Grandpa's tales about life in Jeddah long ago gave me a strong ____ to my family's past.
questions.why: A connection is a link, here between a child and family history.

questions.stem: “Noor had one more errand before dinner. She still needed to pick up her brother's shoes from the repair shop.” What does “errand” most likely mean?
options: a short trip to get something done
a long holiday spent far away from home
a gift brought for a family
questions.why: Picking up shoes is a short trip to do a job, which is an errand.

questions.stem: Is the key word (“exchange,” “blares,” or “connection”) used as a noun or a verb in each sentence?

rows.text: The student exchange brought pupils from Oman to Riyadh.
Let's exchange phone numbers with the new neighbors.
The loudspeaker blares the start of the race.
A strong connection keeps the video call clear.

questions.why: A noun names a thing; a verb shows an action.

questions.stem: The phrase “the cool blue moon” is an example of ____ because the “oo” vowel sound repeats.
questions.why: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Pick a thick black stick,” the repeated “ck” sound at the ends of words is an example of consonance.
questions.why: Consonance is the repetition of consonant sounds, often at the ends of words.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “blares” when talking about sound? Choose two.
questions.why: Whispers and murmurs are soft, the opposite of blares.

questions.stem: “Our class did a cultural exchange with a school in Japan. We sent dates and Arabic calligraphy, and they sent us paper cranes.” What does “exchange” mean here?
options: traveling by airplane to a faraway country
a race between two teams of pupils
giving and receiving things in return
a test given at the end of the year
questions.why: Each school gave and received gifts, which is an exchange.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “connection”?
questions.why: After “will” we need the verb connect, not the noun connection.

questions.stem: Put these sounds in order from the softest to the one that blares the loudest.
sequence: a cat purring on the sofa
a teacher speaking to the class
a fire alarm that blares in the hall
questions.why: Blares describes the loudest, harshest sound.

questions.stem: Does each line show personification, assonance, or consonance?

rows.text: The tired sun sank into its sandy bed.
Low tones float over the old boat.
The milk spilled and filled the hall.

questions.why: Personification gives human traits; assonance repeats vowels; consonance repeats consonants.

questions.stem: True or false: “Imagery” is language that appeals only to the sense of sight.
questions.why: Imagery can appeal to all five senses: sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch.

questions.stem: Which word best shows that the siren is very loud and harsh? “The siren ____ through the empty streets at midnight.”
questions.why: Blares carries the strongest sense of a loud, harsh noise.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “exchange” mean “a swap or trade” or “a place where money or goods are traded”?

rows.text: The stock exchange opened at ten o'clock.
We exchange gifts with our cousins at Eid.
Travelers changed riyals at the currency exchange in the airport.
The players exchange shirts after the match.

questions.why: Exchange has several meanings; the rest of the sentence shows which one fits.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: whispers is to quiet as blares is to ____.
questions.why: Whispers are quiet; something that blares is loud.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “The old door groaned when we pushed it, / and the wind sighed softly through the hall.” Which device do these lines mainly use?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “The old door groaned when we pushed it, / and the wind sighed softly through the hall.” Which device do these lines mainly use?

options.label: A
options.text: rhyme

options.label: B
options.text: personification

options.label: C
options.text: assonance

options.label: D
options.text: consonance

partB.stem: Part B: Which word from the lines about the door and the wind best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: old

options.label: B
options.text: hall

options.label: C
options.text: pushed

options.label: D
options.text: sighed

questions.why: Doors and wind cannot really groan or sigh; giving them human actions is personification.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about an errand: “Hessa ran a quick errand to buy milk for her grandmother. At the shop, she gave coins in exchange for a cold bottle. Outside, a car horn imagery loudly at a slow driver. Hessa smiled and hurried home.”
segments: Hessa ran a quick errand to buy milk for her grandmother.
At the shop, she gave coins in exchange for a cold bottle.
Outside, a car horn imagery loudly at a slow driver.
questions.correction: Outside, a car horn blared loudly at a slow driver.
questions.why: A horn blares; imagery is a writing device, not a sound.

questions.stem: Which TWO lines use personification to show the desert's mood? Choose two.
options: The dunes slept peacefully under a blanket of stars.
The dunes were as gold as honey in the sunset.
Thousands of stars shone above the quiet dunes.
The hot wind complained as it pushed across the sand.
questions.why: Sleeping and complaining are human actions, so those lines use personification.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “Our pen-pal letters built a warm ____ between students in Abha and students in Kenya, even though they never met.”
questions.why: A connection is a bond or link between people.

questions.stem: Which word gives the fridge a human action (personification)? “All night the old fridge ____ in the dark kitchen, keeping the milk cold.”
questions.why: Snoring is something people do, so it personifies the fridge.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a paragraph that uses “imagery” and “connection.”
sequence: Fatima opened a book about life in Morocco.
Rich imagery let her almost smell the spices in the busy markets.
She felt a new connection to children who lived far away.
The next day, she wrote her own poem about the trip she imagined.
questions.why: The paragraph moves from reading, to the imagery, to the feeling, to a result.

questions.stem: True or false: The line “Slow boats float home” uses both assonance and personification.
questions.why: The long “o” sound is assonance, but nothing is given a human action, so there is no personification.

questions.stem: “Huda's mother is an activist who works to protect sea turtles on the Red Sea coast.” What is an “activist”?
options: a person who sells goods at a market
a person who writes reports for TV news
a person who repairs cars and trucks
a person who works for a cause or change
questions.why: An activist works hard to bring about change for a cause.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “advocate,” “initiative,” “persevere,” and “contribute.”

pairs.right: to speak up in support of something
the ability to start something on your own

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you use the words correctly.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Faisal showed determination by practicing his assembly speech every day until it was perfect,” the word “determination” means refusing to give up.
questions.why: Determination is a firm purpose to reach a goal.

questions.stem: Each student will ____ one book to the new class library.
questions.why: To contribute is to give something to help a shared goal.

questions.stem: Does each action show the ability to persevere, or does it show giving up?

rows.text: Salem kept fixing his robot after it failed five times.
Reem stopped learning to swim after one try.
The runner finished the marathon despite sore legs.
Omar quit the puzzle when it got hard.

questions.why: To persevere is to keep trying even when it is hard.

questions.stem: Which word means almost the same as “inspire”?
questions.why: To inspire is to motivate someone to act.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show someone taking initiative? Choose two.
options: Noor waited for someone else to fix the broken swing.
Badr cleaned his room after his father asked him three times.
Without being asked, Lama organized a beach cleanup.
Ziyad started a reading club when he saw the library was empty.
questions.why: Initiative means starting something on your own, without being told.

questions.stem: Planting trees around the school had a big ____ on summer temperatures in the yard.
questions.why: An impact is a strong effect.

questions.stem: True or false: An advocate for clean water is someone who argues against having clean water.
questions.why: An advocate speaks up in support of something.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “inspire,” “impact,” or “determination” in it.

pairs.left: The coach's speech inspired the team.
pairs.right: filled with the desire to do something

pairs.left: The meteor's impact left a deep crater.
pairs.right: the force of one object hitting another

pairs.left: Her determination helped her finish the climb.
pairs.right: firm purpose to reach a goal

questions.why: Context shows the meaning of each word.

questions.stem: “Ali wanted to contribute to the charity drive. He gave half of his savings and spent Saturday packing food boxes.” What does “contribute” mean?
options: to watch something from far away
to count items in a large box
to collect money and food from others
to give or add something to help
questions.why: Giving savings and time are ways to contribute.

questions.stem: Is the key word (“advocate,” “inspire,” “impact,” or “contribute”) used as a noun or a verb in each sentence?

rows.text: Teachers advocate for safer crossings near schools.
She is a strong advocate for reading.
Their kindness will inspire others.
The project's impact was huge.
Your help will contribute a lot.

questions.why: Some words, like advocate, can be either a noun or a verb.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence uses the wrong form of “determination”?
segments: to finish the science fair project
questions.why: After “Her” we need the noun determination.

questions.stem: The student council took the ____ to start a recycling program before anyone asked them.
questions.why: Taking the initiative means starting something on your own.

questions.stem: Which TWO words or phrases are antonyms of “persevere”? Choose two.
questions.why: To persevere is to keep going, so quit and give up are opposites.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to “advocate” in “Dr. Rania is an advocate for children's health”?
questions.why: An advocate is a champion or supporter of a cause.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The heavy rain had an impact on the football schedule, so the match was moved to Friday” uses “impact” correctly.
questions.why: The rain had an effect on the schedule, so impact fits.

questions.stem: Put these steps of a young activist's beach campaign in order.
sequence: Noticing plastic litter piling up on the beach.
Taking the initiative to form a cleanup team.
Persevering through weeks of hot weekend work.
Seeing the impact: a cleaner beach and returning crabs.
questions.why: A campaign moves from a problem, to action, to effort, to results.

questions.stem: Match each form of “inspire,” “contribute,” “persevere,” and “activist” with its meaning.

pairs.right: something that gives you courage or ideas
continuing even when it is hard
action taken to bring about change

questions.why: Suffixes such as -tion, -ance, and -ism form nouns.

questions.stem: True or false: A person with determination usually gives up as soon as a task becomes difficult.
questions.why: Determination means sticking with a goal.

questions.stem: Which word best describes someone who publicly speaks up for a cause, rather than simply agreeing with it?
questions.why: An advocate actively speaks up in support of a cause.

questions.stem: In each sentence, does “impact” mean “a strong effect” or “a hit or collision”?

rows.text: The new library had a positive impact on reading scores.
The impact of the ball cracked the window.
Social media has a big impact on how teens shop.
Seat belts protect riders during the impact of a crash.

questions.why: Impact has a literal and a figurative meaning.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: teacher is to educate as advocate is to ____.
questions.why: A teacher educates; an advocate supports a cause.

questions.stem: Part A: “At eleven, Tariq noticed that older neighbors could not carry groceries up the stairs. Without waiting for adults, he organized a delivery team of friends.” Which word best describes Tariq?

partA.stem: Part A: “At eleven, Tariq noticed that older neighbors could not carry groceries up the stairs. Without waiting for adults, he organized a delivery team of friends.” Which word best describes Tariq?

options.label: A
options.text: showing initiative

options.label: B
options.text: showing laziness

options.label: C
options.text: showing fear

options.label: D
options.text: showing pride

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase about Tariq's delivery team best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: older neighbors

options.label: B
options.text: Without waiting for adults

options.label: C
options.text: carry groceries

options.label: D
options.text: up the stairs

questions.why: Acting without waiting to be told shows initiative.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this paragraph: “Rawan is an activist who works to save mangrove forests. She advocates for laws that protect the coastline. Her speeches inspire many students to volunteer. Sadly, her hard work has had no impact, because the forests are now growing again.”
segments: Rawan is an activist who works to save mangrove forests.
She advocates for laws that protect the coastline.
Her speeches inspire many students to volunteer.
Sadly, her hard work has had no impact, because the forests are now growing again.
questions.correction: Her hard work has had a great impact, because the forests are now growing again.
questions.why: If the forests are growing again, her work had a strong impact.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show both determination and initiative? Choose two.
options: Maha finished her homework because her teacher checked it.
Fahad noticed his school had no ramp, wrote to the principal himself, and kept writing until one was built.
Without being told, Dana designed a water filter and kept improving it after each failure.
Saad started a garden but quit after the first plant died.
questions.why: Initiative is starting on your own; determination is not quitting.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “The village's water problem was solved because each family agreed to ____ a few riyals every month to repair the well.”
questions.why: Families gave money to help, so contribute is precise.

questions.stem: True or false: “Persevere” and “determination” are close in meaning, but “persevere” names an action while “determination” names a quality.
questions.why: Persevere is a verb; determination is a noun naming a quality.

questions.stem: Put these actions in order from the smallest to the largest contribution to a food bank.
sequence: donating one can of beans
volunteering for a single afternoon
organizing a citywide food drive as an activist
questions.why: A larger contribution gives more time, effort, or goods.

questions.stem: Which word makes this sentence most precise? “Her brave speech ____ hundreds of students to start recycling clubs at their schools.”
questions.why: To inspire is to move people to act.

questions.stem: “The firefighter showed great courage when he ran into the burning building to save a cat.” What does “courage” mean?
options: fear of being in the dark
questions.why: Courage is bravery in a dangerous or hard situation.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “courage,” “sacrifice,” “compassion,” and “criteria.”
questions.why: These words help describe and judge heroes.

questions.stem: True or false: In “A selfless volunteer gave her weekends to help at the animal shelter,” the word “selfless” means caring more about others than oneself.
questions.why: Selfless people put others' needs first.

questions.stem: The ____ lifeguard swam through rough waves at a Jeddah beach to rescue a struggling swimmer.
questions.why: Valiant means very brave.

questions.stem: Does each action show “compassion” or not?

rows.text: comforting a crying younger child
laughing at someone who tripped
visiting a sick neighbor with soup
ignoring a classmate who needs help

questions.why: Compassion is caring about others who suffer.

questions.stem: “Hind showed perseverance; she practiced the hard math problems every day until she could solve them.” Which word means the same as “perseverance”?
questions.why: Perseverance means continuing until you succeed.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show a “sacrifice”? Choose two.
options: Saad ate his favorite dessert after dinner.
Maha spent her savings on medicine for her sick cat.
Ali gave up his football match to help his father at the shop.
Noor bought a new game for herself at the mall.
questions.why: A sacrifice means giving up something you value.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “distinguish,” “criteria,” or “valiant” in it.

pairs.left: Can you distinguish a falcon from a hawk?
The judges used three criteria to score projects.
The valiant guard stood firm in the storm.

questions.why: Each meaning fits the word's sentence.

questions.stem: Twins can look so alike that even their teacher cannot ____ one from the other.
questions.why: To distinguish is to tell things apart.

questions.stem: True or false: A person with no compassion feels sorry for people who are suffering.
questions.why: Compassion is that feeling of care; without it, a person does not feel sorry.

questions.stem: “The coach listed the criteria for joining the team: good attendance, teamwork, and a positive attitude.” Which clue best helps you understand “criteria”?
questions.why: The list shows the standards a player must meet.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “courage”?

rows.text: bravery
boldness
cowardice
fear

questions.why: Courage means bravery, so cowardice and fear are opposites.

questions.stem: The ____ young girl spoke up when she saw a classmate being teased.
questions.why: The adjective courageous describes the girl.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about a doctor uses the wrong form of “compassion”?
questions.why: The adjective compassionate describes the voice.

questions.stem: True or false: “The team showed perseverance by quitting after the first loss” uses “perseverance” correctly.
questions.why: Perseverance means continuing, not quitting.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “selfless”?
questions.why: Selfless means caring for others; selfish is its opposite.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are closest in meaning to “valiant”? Choose two.
questions.why: Valiant means brave and heroic.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in order to show a climber's “perseverance.”
sequence: Turki set a goal to climb Jabal Sawda, one of the highest peaks in Saudi Arabia.
On his first try, he turned back because of heavy fog.
He trained for three more months to build his strength.
On his second try, he reached the top and watched the sunrise.
questions.why: Perseverance means trying again after a setback.

questions.stem: Match each form of “distinguish” with its meaning.
questions.why: Suffixes change both the form and the meaning.

questions.stem: The judges' main ____ for the science fair were creativity, accuracy, and clear explanation.
questions.why: Criteria are the standards used to judge.

questions.stem: Which word suggests the greatest bravery, often in a battle or a serious emergency?
questions.why: Valiant suggests heroic bravery in great danger.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: generous is to selfish as compassion is to ____.
questions.why: Generous and selfish are opposites; so are compassion and cruelty.

questions.stem: Which sentence in this paragraph about a flood rescue misuses a vocabulary word (courage, sacrifice, compassion, distinguish)?
segments: During the flood, a teenager showed courage by guiding neighbors to safety.
He made a sacrifice by leaving his own belongings behind.
His compassion for the elderly was clear as he carried their bags.
People could hardly distinguish his valiant actions, so they gave him an award.
questions.correction: People admired his valiant actions, so they gave him an award.
questions.why: Distinguish means tell apart; the sentence needs admired.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “criterion” and “criteria” correctly?
options: “One criterion is honesty; the other criteria are courage and kindness.”
“One criterias is honesty; the other criterion is courage and kindness.”
“One criterion are honesty; the other criteria is courage and kindness.”
“One criteria is honesty; the other criterion are courage and kindness.”
questions.why: Criterion is singular and criteria is plural.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe a hero by “courage” or by “compassion”?

rows.text: He climbed a smoky stairway to reach trapped children.
She sat for hours with a lonely patient.
He drove into a sandstorm to bring water to stranded travelers.
She shared her lunch with a hungry classmate every day.

questions.why: Courage faces danger; compassion shows care.

questions.stem: In “Some say heroes must be famous, but the true test is whether a person acts selflessly when no one is watching,” which criteria for a hero does the writer support?

partA.stem: In “Some say heroes must be famous, but the true test is whether a person acts selflessly when no one is watching,” which criteria for a hero does the writer support?

options.label: A
options.text: appearing often on television

options.label: B
options.text: winning many awards and prizes

options.label: C
options.text: being known by many people

options.label: D
options.text: helping others without wanting praise

partB.stem: Which phrase best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “acts selflessly when no one is watching”

options.label: B
options.text: “Some say heroes must be famous”

options.label: C
options.text: “whether a person”

options.label: D
options.text: “the true test”

questions.why: Acting when no one is watching means helping without wanting praise.

questions.stem: The Latin root “cor” means “heart.” Which TWO statements explain how “courage” connects to this root? Choose two.
options: Courage means having a weak or tired heart.
Courage is a medical word for a heart illness.
A courageous person acts with a strong heart even when afraid.
Courage comes from inner strength, as if from the heart.
questions.why: Courage is strength that comes from the heart.

questions.stem: Doctors who stayed at their hospital for weeks during the outbreak, far from their families, made a great ____.
questions.why: Giving up time with family for others is a sacrifice.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in order so the argument about heroes and their “criteria” makes sense.
sequence: Many people call sports stars heroes.
However, a hero should meet clear criteria, such as courage and selflessness.
Scoring goals does not require risking anything for others.
Therefore, nurses and rescuers fit the word better than most athletes.
questions.why: The argument states a common view, counters it with criteria, gives a reason, then concludes.

questions.stem: True or false: “Valiant” and “brave” are similar, but “valiant” sounds more formal and heroic.
questions.why: Valiant has a stronger, more formal connotation.

questions.stem: Daniel stayed up late watching TV. The next day, he was so tired that he couldn't focus in class. Would you say the late night affected him?
options: No, because watching TV cannot change how a person feels.
No, because he still went to school the next day.
Yes, because he watched his favorite show that night.
Yes, because staying up late changed how well he could focus.
questions.why: To affect something means to change or influence it.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “affect,” “bout,” “clarify,” “emerge,” and “improvise.”

pairs.right: a short contest or period of activity
to make something up without planning

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you understand how people act under pressure.

questions.stem: Jason and his little brother played video games together for a few minutes before dinner. Would you describe this as a bout?
options: Yes, because a bout can be a short period of an activity or a contest.
Yes, because the brothers played before they sat down to eat.
No, because a bout must last for several days without any breaks.
No, because only adults are allowed to take part in a bout.
questions.why: A bout is a short period of activity, such as a match or a contest.

questions.stem: True or false: When a diver comes up out of the water, you could say the diver emerges from the sea.
questions.why: To emerge means to come out of something and into view.

questions.stem: The magician covered the empty box with a cloth, and a moment later a white dove began to ____ from it.
questions.why: The dove comes out into view, so it emerges.

questions.stem: The teacher explained the math problem quickly, but the students were even more confused afterward. Would you say the explanation gave the students clarity?
options: No, because the teacher should not explain math problems.
Yes, because every math explanation gives students clarity.
No, because the students were more confused instead of understanding.
Yes, because the teacher explained the problem very quickly.
questions.why: To clarify means to make clear; confused students did not get clarity.

questions.stem: Is each person acting “pensively” or not?

rows.text: Huda gazed at the sea for a long time, quietly thinking about her grandfather's advice.
The fans cheered and jumped when their team scored a goal.
Yousef sat still with his chin in his hand, wondering which school club to join.
The children raced across the playground, shouting happily.

questions.why: Acting pensively means being quiet and deep in thought.

questions.stem: Our scout leader forgot the tent poles, so he had to ____ by tying the tent between two palm trees.
questions.why: Making a solution on the spot without planning is improvising.

questions.stem: After the heavy rain stopped, a rainbow began to appear in the sky. Would you say the rainbow started to emerge?
options: No, because a rainbow can only emerge from under the ground.
Yes, because the rainbow was coming into view in the sky.
Yes, because rainbows are always seen after a heavy storm.
No, because the rain had to stop before anything could happen.
questions.why: To emerge means to appear or come into view.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the word “affect” correctly? Choose two.
options: Mona will affect her finished homework to the teacher tomorrow.
The loud construction noise affected Reem's ability to concentrate on her reading.
The new medicine had a quick affect on Grandfather's cough.
Drinking enough water affects how energetic athletes feel during a match.
questions.why: Affect is a verb meaning to change or influence; the noun is effect.

questions.stem: The band followed the music exactly as they had practised for weeks, using all their regular instruments. Would you say the drummer had to improvise?
options: Yes, because drummers always make up their music as they play.
No, because the band played exactly what they had practised.
Yes, because the band had been practising for many weeks.
No, because a drummer is not a real member of the band.
questions.why: To improvise is to make something up on the spot, not to follow a plan.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Before answering, Dana asked her teacher to clarify the instructions, because she was not sure whether to write one paragraph or two.” What does “clarify” mean?

partA.stem: Read the sentence: “Before answering, Dana asked her teacher to clarify the instructions, because she was not sure whether to write one paragraph or two.” What does “clarify” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: repeat louder

options.label: B
options.text: make clearer

options.label: C
options.text: make shorter

options.label: D
options.text: change completely

partB.stem: Which part of the sentence best helps the reader understand “clarify”?

options.label: A
options.text: asked her teacher

options.label: B
options.text: the instructions

options.label: C
options.text: Before answering

options.label: D
options.text: she was not sure whether to write one paragraph or two

questions.why: Dana was unsure, so she needed the instructions made clearer.

questions.stem: Sarah and her friends laughed loudly while telling jokes during lunch. Would you say Sarah was thinking pensively?
options: Yes, because people often think pensively while eating lunch.
No, because Sarah was sitting with a large group of friends.
Yes, because she had to think of funny jokes to tell her friends.
No, because she was laughing loudly instead of quietly thinking.
questions.why: Pensively means in a quiet, deeply thoughtful way.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses the word “bout” correctly.

segments.text: The two wrestlers shook hands before their first bout began.
Ahmad put the bout in his backpack before school.
We went on a long bout to the mountains last summer.
The teacher wrote a bout on the board for us to copy.

questions.why: A bout is a match or contest, like one between two wrestlers.

questions.stem: Does each sentence need “affect” (a verb) or “effect” (a noun)?

rows.text: The cold weather can ____ how fast plants grow.
The new playground had a positive ____ on recess.
Will the sandstorm ____ our flight to Jeddah?
One ____ of daily exercise is better sleep.

questions.why: Affect is usually the action (verb); effect is the result (noun).

questions.stem: In the middle of the school show, the actor forgot his lines, but he managed to ____ a funny speech, and the audience never noticed.
questions.why: He made up a speech on the spot, so he improvised.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to show how a chick emerges from its egg.
sequence: A tiny crack appears on the shell.
The chick pecks a small hole and pushes against the shell.
The chick finally emerges, wet and tired, from the broken egg.
questions.why: The chick emerges only after it breaks through the shell.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who reads a message pensively is most likely skimming it quickly while chatting with friends.
questions.why: Reading pensively means reading slowly and thoughtfully.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “emerge,” “clarify,” “pensively,” and “improvise.”
questions.why: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the coach uses a word incorrectly?
segments: the rules for the new players
so that no one would be confused.
questions.why: The coach wanted to make the rules clear, so clarify is correct.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “bout” mean “a short period of illness”?
options: Our karate bout ended in a tie after six minutes.
Grandmother is resting after a bout of the flu.
The boxing bout lasted for three hard rounds.
The chess players shook hands before the final bout.
questions.why: A bout can be a match, but “a bout of the flu” is a short time of being sick.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “Explain” is to “clarify” as “appear” is to ____.
questions.why: Explain and clarify are synonyms; appear and emerge are also synonyms.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph about Nasser's chess game. Which sentence uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: Nasser stared pensively at the chessboard for five minutes.
He knew one careless move could affect the whole game.
When his plan failed, he had to improvise a new one.
His little sister cheered pensively when he won.
questions.correction: His little sister cheered loudly when he won.
questions.why: Cheering is loud and lively, not pensive.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “The power went out during the school performance. Without lights or music, the actors had to improvise, using flashlights from the audience to light the stage.” Which word best describes the actors?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “The power went out during the school performance. Without lights or music, the actors had to improvise, using flashlights from the audience to light the stage.” Which word best describes the actors?

options.label: A
options.text: careless

options.label: B
options.text: resourceful

options.label: C
options.text: rehearsed

options.label: D
options.text: silent

partB.stem: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The power went out

options.label: B
options.text: during the school performance

options.label: C
options.text: Without lights or music

options.label: D
options.text: using flashlights from the audience to light the stage

questions.why: Improvising with flashlights shows the actors were resourceful.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “emerge” to mean “to become known” rather than “to come out into view”?
options: After the investigation, new facts began to emerge about the old fort.
The bright sun finally emerged from behind the thick gray clouds.
A baby turtle slowly emerged from the warm sand on the beach at night.
Hundreds of bats emerge from the dark cave every evening at sunset.
questions.why: Facts emerge when they become known; animals and the sun emerge into view.

questions.stem: Identify the part of speech of the form of “improvise,” “pensively,” “emerge,” or “clarify” in each sentence.

rows.text: The band's improvisation surprised the audience.
Ali looked pensively out the window.
New leaves emerge after the first rain.
The coach gave a clarification of the new rule.

questions.why: Suffixes such as -tion (noun) and -ly (adverb) show a word's part of speech.

questions.stem: Which TWO situations would most likely require someone to improvise? Choose two.
options: A tour guide's microphone breaks just as she begins speaking to a large group.
A chef discovers there are no eggs left halfway through baking a cake for guests.
A pilot follows the checklist exactly before every flight, as she always does.
A student reads her speech word for word from carefully prepared notes.
questions.why: People improvise when something unexpected ruins their plan.

questions.stem: The judge asked the witness to ____ his statement, since his first answer could be understood in two different ways.
questions.why: An answer with two possible meanings needs to be made clear.

questions.stem: Arrange these ways of looking at a problem from the least thoughtful to the most thoughtful, ending with “studying it pensively.”
sequence: glancing at it carelessly
looking at it briefly
studying it pensively
questions.why: Pensively describes the deepest, most careful kind of thinking.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Years of drought can affect a village in ways that emerge only slowly, as wells dry up and families move away.” How do “affect” and “emerge” work together in this sentence?
options: The drought ends quickly, and the families return to the village right away.
The village improvises new wells, so nothing in the village really changes.
The drought is explained clearly before anyone in the village is touched by it.
The drought changes the village, and the results become noticeable over time.
questions.why: Affect shows the change; emerge shows the results slowly becoming visible.

questions.stem: A caterpillar wrapped itself tightly inside a cocoon, waiting to grow into a butterfly. Would you say it was inside a chrysalis?
options: Yes, because it was in a protective case while changing into a butterfly.
No, because caterpillars only stay inside a nest made by their parents.
No, because a chrysalis is a kind of flower that caterpillars eat.
Yes, because it was wrapped tightly and wanted to stay warm forever.
questions.why: A chrysalis is the protective case where a caterpillar changes into a butterfly.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “chrysalis,” “compulsion,” “contrary,” “crave,” and “thrill.”

pairs.right: the case a caterpillar rests in while it changes
a strong urge that is hard to resist

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you describe feelings and changes.

questions.stem: Ben took another piece of candy from the jar, but he could have easily stopped himself if he wanted. Would you say he acted from a compulsion?
options: No, because a compulsion is an urge that is very hard to stop.
Yes, because anyone who eats candy is acting from a compulsion.
Yes, because the candy jar was full and easy for Ben to reach.
No, because Ben only took one more piece instead of the whole jar.
questions.why: A compulsion is an urge a person can hardly resist; Ben could easily stop.

questions.stem: After a long day of fasting in Ramadan, Hamad began to ____ a cold glass of water.
questions.why: To crave something is to want it very much.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who feels a thrill is feeling bored and sleepy.
questions.why: A thrill is a sudden feeling of excitement.

questions.stem: Everyone in the group agreed that pizza was the best choice for lunch, and Sarah agreed with them. Would you say Sarah's opinion was contrary to the others?
options: Yes, because people's opinions about food are always different.
No, because Sarah did not want to eat any lunch at all.
Yes, because Sarah gave her opinion after the others did.
No, because her opinion was the same as everyone else's.
questions.why: Contrary means opposite; Sarah's opinion matched the group's.

questions.stem: Does each experience give a person a “thrill” or not?

rows.text: Seeing a whale shark swim beside the boat in the Red Sea
Waiting in a long, quiet line at the bank
Scoring the winning goal in the last minute of the final
Folding the same pile of towels as on every other day

questions.why: A thrill comes from something exciting, not something dull.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses the word “contrary” correctly.

segments.text: Contrary to the weather forecast, the afternoon was sunny and calm.
The contrary children agreed happily with every suggestion.
She contraried the cake into four equal pieces.
We walked contrary the hallway to reach our class.

questions.why: “Contrary to” means opposite to what was expected.

questions.stem: After dinner, Mia felt completely full and had no desire to eat dessert. Would you say she began to crave dessert?
options: No, because to crave something is to want it very much.
Yes, because dessert is served after dinner in most homes.
Yes, because people always crave sweet food after dinner.
No, because Mia did not know what the dessert was going to be.
questions.why: Mia had no desire for dessert, so she did not crave it.

questions.stem: Put the stages of a butterfly's life in order, ending with the moment it leaves the chrysalis.
sequence: A tiny egg is laid on a leaf.
A caterpillar hatches and eats many leaves.
The caterpillar forms a chrysalis around itself.
An adult butterfly breaks out of the chrysalis.
questions.why: The chrysalis stage comes between the caterpillar and the butterfly.

questions.stem: As the roller coaster raced down the track, Jacob felt his heart pound with excitement. Would you say he felt a thrill?
options: Yes, because the roller coaster was very long and fast.
Yes, because a thrill is a sudden rush of excitement.
No, because roller coasters only make people feel afraid.
No, because a thrill is a feeling of being calm and sleepy.
questions.why: A pounding heart full of excitement is a thrill.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “Rashid felt a compulsion to check his phone every few minutes. Even when he promised himself to stop, he reached for it again.” What does “compulsion” mean?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “Rashid felt a compulsion to check his phone every few minutes. Even when he promised himself to stop, he reached for it again.” What does “compulsion” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: a strong urge that is hard to resist

options.label: B
options.text: a polite request from a friend

options.label: C
options.text: a careful plan made in advance

options.label: D
options.text: a reward for good behavior

partB.stem: Which part of the sentences best helps the reader understand “compulsion”?

options.label: A
options.text: Even when he promised himself to stop, he reached for it again

options.label: B
options.text: Rashid felt

options.label: C
options.text: every few minutes

options.label: D
options.text: to check his phone

questions.why: Not being able to stop shows a compulsion.

questions.stem: My little brother is so ____ that if I say the sky is blue, he insists it is green.
questions.why: A contrary person says or does the opposite.

questions.stem: Which TWO words or phrases are synonyms of “crave”? Choose two.
questions.why: To crave is to long for or strongly desire something.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “contrary,” “crave,” “thrill,” and “compulsion.”
questions.why: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Is “thrill” used as a noun (a feeling) or a verb (to excite) in each sentence?

rows.text: Riding a camel for the first time was a real thrill.
The fireworks over the corniche thrilled the crowd.
Winning the spelling bee gave Lama a thrill she never forgot.
The acrobats' daring jumps will thrill the audience.

questions.why: Thrill can name a feeling (noun) or an action (verb).

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “On the first day of school, the new students stayed quiet and kept to themselves, like caterpillars hidden inside a chrysalis.” What does the comparison to a chrysalis suggest?
options: They were wearing hard, shiny costumes for a school event.
They were hungry and only wanted to eat their lunches.
They were growing taller much faster than the other students.
They were staying hidden until they felt ready to come out.
questions.why: A chrysalis protects something that will change and come out later.

questions.stem: True or false: The phrase “on the contrary” introduces an idea that is the opposite of what was just said, as in “The test was not easy; on the contrary, it was very hard.”
questions.why: “On the contrary” signals the opposite idea.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about Lina's dessert uses a word incorrectly?
segments: she thrilled a bowl of fresh fruit.
questions.correction: she craved a bowl of fresh fruit.
questions.why: Lina wanted the fruit, so she craved it.

questions.stem: Watching the eagle dive toward the water gave the young birdwatchers a sudden ____.
questions.why: A sudden exciting feeling is a thrill.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “contrary” mean “stubborn and likely to do the opposite of what is asked”?
options: The fishing boat sailed against contrary winds all morning long.
Contrary to popular belief, camels do not store water in their humps.
The two teams held contrary opinions about the new tournament rule.
The contrary goat walked backward whenever the farmer pulled it.
questions.why: A contrary animal or person stubbornly does the opposite.

questions.stem: Arrange these phrases from the weakest desire to the strongest, using the words “crave” and “compulsion.”
sequence: a mild wish
a strong craving
an uncontrollable compulsion
questions.why: A compulsion is stronger than a craving, which is stronger than a wish.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph about Khaled's science project. Which sentence uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: Khaled's science project was about butterflies.
He explained that a caterpillar rests inside a chrysalis while its body changes.
Contrary to what many people think, the caterpillar is not asleep.
When the butterfly finally craved out, Khaled felt a thrill.
questions.correction: When the butterfly finally emerged, Khaled felt a thrill.
questions.why: Craved means wanted; the butterfly came out, or emerged.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Long after the race ended, Majed still craved the thrill of crossing the finish line first.” What does “craved” suggest about Majed?

partA.stem: Read the sentence: “Long after the race ended, Majed still craved the thrill of crossing the finish line first.” What does “craved” suggest about Majed?

options.label: A
options.text: He could not remember anything about the race.

options.label: B
options.text: He was afraid to take part in another race.

options.label: C
options.text: He was tired of racing and wanted to quit.

options.label: D
options.text: He strongly wanted to feel that excitement again.

partB.stem: Which word in the sentence most strongly shows Majed's desire?

options.label: A
options.text: crossing

options.label: B
options.text: ended

options.label: C
options.text: craved

options.label: D
options.text: first

questions.why: Craved shows a strong desire for the thrill.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of the key word (“chrysalis,” “thrill,” or “compulsion”) as it is used.

pairs.left: The moth rested inside its chrysalis for two weeks.
Her quiet first year was a chrysalis before she became team captain.
pairs.right: a stage of hidden growth before a big change

pairs.left: The roller coaster's final drop was a thrill.
Nawaf felt a compulsion to tidy every desk he passed.
pairs.right: an urge that is hard to resist

questions.why: A word like chrysalis can have a literal and a figurative meaning.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “crave” or “craved” correctly? Choose two.
options: The museum guide craved the visitors toward the exit.
After the long hike, the scouts craved shade and cold water.
The tailor craved a neat pattern into the leather belt.
Many children crave praise from the adults they admire.
questions.why: To crave is to want something strongly.

questions.stem: The scientist's results were ____ to what she had predicted; instead of growing faster, the plants grew more slowly.
questions.why: Results that are the opposite of a prediction are contrary to it.

questions.stem: Is “compulsion” used correctly in each sentence?

rows.text: He felt a compulsion to wash his hands again and again.
The compulsion of the cake was chocolate and cream.
Some gamers struggle with a compulsion to play late at night.
We built a compulsion out of sticks for the science fair.

questions.why: A compulsion is an urge that is hard to control.

questions.stem: Which word suggests an urge that a person struggles to control, giving it the most negative connotation compared with “compulsion,” “aspiration,” “enthusiasm,” and “preference”?
questions.why: A compulsion is an urge a person cannot easily control, so it sounds negative.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The thrill of discovery kept the explorers searching the desert for weeks,” the word “thrill” refers to a fear that made the explorers want to quit.
questions.why: Here thrill means excitement, which kept the explorers going.

questions.stem: During the war, soldiers used large guns that could fire heavy shells across long distances. Would you say they were using artillery?
options: Yes, because artillery means large, heavy guns used in war.
No, because artillery is only used by ships far out at sea.
No, because artillery means the uniforms that soldiers wear.
Yes, because the soldiers were fighting during a long war.
questions.why: Artillery is large guns, such as cannons, used in war.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “frayed,” “oblong,” “ripen,” “somber,” and “taut.”

pairs.right: worn and torn at the edges

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you picture objects and moods.

questions.stem: Max's backpack was brand new, and the straps were smooth and strong with no signs of damage. Would you say the straps were frayed?
options: No, because Max had not used his backpack at school yet.
Yes, because backpack straps are usually frayed when new.
Yes, because the straps were strong enough to hold books.
No, because frayed things are worn and torn at the edges.
questions.why: New, smooth straps are not frayed.

questions.stem: True or false: When a diver jumps headfirst into the sea, she makes a plunge.
questions.why: A plunge is a sudden jump or dive into something.

questions.stem: The farmer waited for the dates to ____ in the hot summer sun before picking them.
questions.why: Fruit ripens when it becomes ready to eat.

questions.stem: On the table sat a melon that was much longer than it was wide, shaped almost like an egg. Would you describe it as oblong?
options: No, because an oblong shape is perfectly round, like a ball.
No, because melons are always too heavy to be called oblong.
Yes, because the melon was sitting on top of the table.
Yes, because an oblong shape is longer than it is wide.
questions.why: Oblong means longer than it is wide.

questions.stem: Is each object “taut” or loose?

rows.text: a drum skin stretched tightly over the frame
a jump rope lying on the ground
a tent rope pulled tight against the wind
an old belt hanging from a hook

questions.why: Taut means stretched or pulled tight.

questions.stem: Sam carefully walked down the pool steps into the water. Would you say he made a plunge?
options: Yes, because any way of entering a pool is called a plunge.
No, because a plunge is a sudden jump or dive, not a slow walk.
No, because Sam did not know how to swim in deep water.
Yes, because Sam ended up in the water of the swimming pool.
questions.why: Walking down slowly is not a sudden plunge.

questions.stem: The edges of Grandfather's old prayer rug were ____ after many years of use.
questions.why: Cloth that is worn and loose at the edges is frayed.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that describes an oblong object.

segments.text: The rugby ball is longer than it is wide, with rounded ends.
The coin is perfectly round and flat.
Each side of the square tile is the same length.
The warning sign has three equal sides.

questions.why: An oblong object is longer than it is wide.

questions.stem: The green bananas slowly turned yellow and soft, ready to eat. Would you say they began to ripen?
options: Yes, because bananas are a popular yellow fruit.
No, because the bananas were green at the start.
Yes, because ripening means becoming ready to eat.
No, because bananas ripen only after they are cooked.
questions.why: Fruit that turns soft and ready to eat is ripening.

questions.stem: At the birthday party, people laughed loudly, played games, and wore bright clothing. Would you say the mood was somber?
options: No, because the party was held in the middle of the day.
No, because a somber mood is serious or sad, not cheerful.
Yes, because birthday parties are always quiet and serious.
Yes, because the guests wore clothing in many bright colors.
questions.why: Laughter and bright colors create a cheerful mood, not a somber one.

questions.stem: Put these events in order to show how a mango ripens.
sequence: The small mango is hard and green.
The mango grows larger on the branch.
Its skin turns yellow and its flesh becomes soft and sweet.
questions.why: A fruit ripens as it grows and softens.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “The rope bridge was taut, so it barely moved when the hikers crossed it. Earlier in the day, when it had been loose, it swung wildly.” What does “taut” mean?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “The rope bridge was taut, so it barely moved when the hikers crossed it. Earlier in the day, when it had been loose, it swung wildly.” What does “taut” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: very old

options.label: B
options.text: falling apart

options.label: C
options.text: brightly painted

options.label: D
options.text: stretched tight

partB.stem: Which part of the sentences best helps the reader understand “taut”?

options.label: A
options.text: the hikers crossed it

options.label: B
options.text: Earlier in the day

options.label: C
options.text: when it had been loose, it swung wildly

options.label: D
options.text: The rope bridge

questions.why: Loose is the opposite of taut, so the contrast is the clue.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “taut,” “somber,” “frayed,” and “plunge.”
questions.why: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: The rope hanging from the tree was loose and sagging toward the ground. Would you describe it as taut?
options: No, because the rope was tied to a branch of the tree.
Yes, because the rope reached all the way to the ground.
No, because a taut rope is pulled tight, not sagging.
Yes, because ropes that hang from trees are always taut.
questions.why: A sagging rope is slack, not taut.

questions.stem: Does each scene have a “somber” mood or a cheerful mood?

rows.text: Guests stood silently in gray clothes as rain tapped on the windows.
Children sang and clapped at the Eid celebration.
The empty, dim hallway echoed with slow footsteps.
Bright balloons floated above the laughing crowd.

questions.why: Somber scenes feel dark, quiet, and serious.

questions.stem: When the cold front arrived, temperatures began to ____ from 30 degrees to 12 degrees in just a few hours.
questions.why: A sudden, large drop is a plunge.
