questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the sewing project uses a word incorrectly?
segments: so they would not come apart.
questions.why: Edges that are coming apart are frayed.

questions.stem: True or false: Artillery refers to small hand tools that farmers use for planting seeds.
questions.why: Artillery means large guns used in war.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “plunge” mean “a sudden fall in amount or value”?
options: He finally decided to take the plunge and join the robotics club.
The swimmers took a plunge into the cool pool after practice.
Shoppers noticed a plunge in the price of strawberries.
The falcon made a fast plunge toward the rabbit in the grass.
questions.why: A plunge in price is a sudden drop in value.

questions.stem: After three hours of waiting in the noisy airport, the travelers' nerves were ____.
questions.why: Frayed nerves is a figurative way to say people are worn out and irritated.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “ripen” in a figurative way, meaning “to develop fully over time”? Choose two.
options: The figs ripened on the tree near the end of the long summer.
The friendship between the two neighbors ripened as they worked side by side.
Over years of practice, his talent for calligraphy ripened into true skill.
Tomatoes ripen faster when they are left in a warm, sunny room.
questions.why: Talents and friendships ripen figuratively; fruit ripens literally.

questions.stem: Arrange these ropes from the loosest to the most taut.
sequence: a slack rope lying in loose loops
a rope pulled until it is almost straight
a taut rope stretched so tight it hums when plucked
questions.why: Taut is the tightest state of a rope.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “The old flag on the fortress wall was frayed and faded. Its torn edges flapped weakly in the somber gray light.” What feeling do the words “frayed” and “somber” create together?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “The old flag on the fortress wall was frayed and faded. Its torn edges flapped weakly in the somber gray light.” What feeling do the words “frayed” and “somber” create together?

options.label: A
options.text: a sad, worn-out feeling

options.label: B
options.text: an exciting, joyful feeling

options.label: C
options.text: a calm, hopeful feeling

options.label: D
options.text: a silly, playful feeling

partB.stem: Which other detail best adds to that feeling?

options.label: A
options.text: in the gray light

options.label: B
options.text: The old flag

options.label: C
options.text: Its torn edges flapped weakly

options.label: D
options.text: on the fortress wall

questions.why: Weak, torn edges add to the sad, worn-out feeling.

questions.stem: Is each item a type of “artillery”?

rows.text: a large cannon on wheels
a soldier's water bottle
a heavy gun that fires shells many kilometers
a pair of binoculars

questions.why: Artillery means large, heavy guns.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the analogy? “Loose” is to “taut” as “cheerful” is to ____.
questions.why: Loose and taut are opposites; cheerful and somber are also opposites.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph about the old fortress. Which sentence uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: The old fortress still had two pieces of artillery on its walls.
Their long barrels pointed toward the sea.
Visitors walked through the oblong courtyard in somber silence.
A guide explained that the cannons would plunge the town during attacks.
questions.correction: A guide explained that the cannons had protected the town during attacks.
questions.why: Plunge does not mean protect; the cannons protected the town.

questions.stem: The pattern on Aunt Huda's tablecloth was made of ____ shapes, each twice as long as it was wide.
questions.why: A shape twice as long as it is wide is oblong.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “taut” or “ripen” as it is used.

pairs.left: Her taut face showed how worried she was.
The plan ripened over several months.

questions.why: Taut and ripen each have a literal and a figurative meaning.

questions.stem: After months of saving, Layla finally bought her own guitar to play at school. Would you say she managed to acquire a guitar?
options: Yes, because to acquire something means to get it.
No, because to acquire means to borrow for a day.
Yes, because she wanted to play music at school.
No, because Layla had to save money for months.
questions.why: To acquire is to get or gain something.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “acquire,” “circuit,” “detect,” “foreman,” and “savor.”

pairs.right: a complete route that ends where it began
the worker in charge of a group of workers

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you understand stories about work and travel.

questions.stem: The runners jogged halfway around the stadium and then stopped to rest before reaching the starting point. Would you say they completed a circuit?
options: No, because the runners stopped to rest and drink water.
No, because a circuit goes all the way around to the start.
Yes, because the runners jogged around part of the stadium.
Yes, because any run inside a stadium is called a circuit.
questions.why: A circuit is a complete route that returns to where it began.

questions.stem: True or false: If you move hesitantly, you move quickly and without any doubt.
questions.why: Moving hesitantly means moving slowly because you are unsure.

questions.stem: Grandmother likes to ____ each sip of her hot cardamom coffee instead of drinking it all at once.
questions.why: To savor is to enjoy something slowly.

questions.stem: A smoke alarm went off when it sensed a small fire in the kitchen. Would you say the alarm could detect the smoke?
options: No, because smoke alarms can only detect very large fires.
Yes, because to detect means to notice or sense something.
No, because the fire was small and stayed in the kitchen.
Yes, because the alarm was making a very loud noise.
questions.why: The alarm sensed the smoke, so it detected it.

questions.stem: Does each person act “hesitantly” or confidently?

rows.text: Nora stopped at the edge of the diving board and looked down for a long time.
Talal marched to the board and solved the problem in seconds.
The new student paused at the classroom door before stepping inside.
The captain shouted clear orders to her team.

questions.why: Pausing and holding back show hesitation.

questions.stem: At the construction site, one of the workers quietly followed instructions from the person in charge. Would you call that worker the foreman?
options: Yes, because the foreman is any worker who follows the instructions.
Yes, because the worker was quiet and worked hard all day long.
No, because the foreman is the person in charge who gives the instructions.
No, because a construction site does not need anyone in charge.
questions.why: The foreman leads the workers; this worker was following orders.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses the word “acquire” correctly.

segments.text: The museum hopes to acquire an ancient Arabic manuscript next year.
Please acquire the lights when you leave the room.
The bird acquired across the sky in a straight line.
We acquired loudly at the funny cartoon.

questions.why: To acquire is to get or gain something, such as a manuscript.

questions.stem: The ____ checked the workers' progress every hour and told them which field to harvest next.
questions.why: The foreman is in charge of the workers.

questions.stem: When asked to speak in front of the class, Lina paused, took a deep breath, and slowly walked to the front. Would you say she moved hesitantly?
options: Yes, because she was asked to speak in front of others.
Yes, because she paused and moved slowly, as if unsure.
No, because a deep breath shows that she felt excited.
No, because she walked to the front of the class at last.
questions.why: Pausing and moving slowly show that Lina moved hesitantly.

questions.stem: Omar swallowed the cookie in two quick bites without paying attention to its taste. Would you say he wanted to savor it?
options: No, because Omar did not share his cookie with anyone.
No, because to savor is to enjoy something slowly.
Yes, because people always savor sweet cookies.
Yes, because Omar ate the whole cookie very fast.
questions.why: Eating quickly without tasting is the opposite of savoring.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “A metal detector can detect coins buried deep in the sand. When it finds metal, it beeps loudly.” What does “detect” mean?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “A metal detector can detect coins buried deep in the sand. When it finds metal, it beeps loudly.” What does “detect” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: clean or polish

options.label: B
options.text: bury or hide

options.label: C
options.text: discover or sense

options.label: D
options.text: sell or trade

partB.stem: Which part of the sentences best helps the reader understand “detect”?

options.label: A
options.text: A metal detector

options.label: B
options.text: coins

options.label: C
options.text: buried deep in the sand

options.label: D
options.text: When it finds metal, it beeps loudly

questions.why: “When it finds metal” shows that detect means discover.

questions.stem: Put these steps in order to show how a runner completes one circuit of the track.
sequence: She starts at the white starting line.
She runs around the first curve and down the far side.
She rounds the second curve toward the home stretch.
She crosses the same white line where she began.
questions.why: A circuit ends where it began.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “acquire,” “hesitantly,” “savor,” and “detect.”
questions.why: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Identify the part of speech of the form of “acquire,” “detect,” or “hesitant” in each sentence.

rows.text: The bank installed machines to detect fake bills.
Rana answered hesitantly when the teacher called on her.
The library's newest acquisition is a rare map.
Sniffer dogs help with the detection of hidden items.

questions.why: Suffixes such as -tion (noun) and -ly (adverb) change a word's part of speech.

questions.stem: Doctors use X-rays to ____ broken bones that cannot be seen from the outside.
questions.why: X-rays help doctors discover, or detect, hidden injuries.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The electrician fixed the circuit so the lights would work again,” the word “circuit” means the complete path that electricity travels through.
questions.why: An electrical circuit is a complete path for electricity.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the young goalkeeper uses a word incorrectly?
questions.why: Someone unsure moves hesitantly.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe someone who is about to savor something? Choose two.
options: Huda slowly breathes in the smell of fresh bread before taking a small bite.
Mona skips dessert because she is far too full to eat anything else.
After a long trip, Yasser sits quietly to enjoy every moment of being home.
Sami swallows his juice in one gulp so he can run back outside to play.
questions.why: To savor is to enjoy something slowly and fully.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “circuit” mean “a regular route of places that a person travels to”?
options: The judge traveled a circuit of nearby towns each month.
The race cars sped around the circuit for fifty exciting laps.
The science class built a simple circuit with a battery and a bulb.
A broken wire stopped the circuit, so the fan would not turn.
questions.why: A judge's circuit is a regular route from town to town.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “Gain” is to “acquire” as “notice” is to ____.
questions.why: Gain and acquire are synonyms; notice and detect are also synonyms.

questions.stem: Is “savor” used with its literal meaning (taste) or its figurative meaning (enjoy an experience) in each sentence?

rows.text: Ali savored the sweet dates one at a time.
The team savored their victory for days.
She savored the quiet morning before the house woke up.
Grandpa savored the spicy lentil soup slowly.

questions.why: Savor can describe enjoying food or enjoying a moment.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph about farm workers. Which sentence uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: The farm workers moved from place to place on a yearly circuit.
At each farm, a foreman told them where to work.
Over the years, they acquired many useful skills.
Some of them could savor a ripe melon just by tapping it.
questions.correction: Some of them could detect a ripe melon just by tapping it.
questions.why: Tapping helps a person detect, or notice, ripeness.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The new worker hesitantly raised his hand to ask the foreman a question.” What does “hesitantly” suggest about the worker?
options: He felt unsure or nervous about speaking up.
He already knew every answer that he needed.
He was in a hurry to finish work and go home.
He was angry with the foreman for being unfair.
questions.why: Doing something hesitantly shows uncertainty or nervousness.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “At the market, the foreman tasted a grape from each crate. He could detect even a slightly sour batch, and he refused to acquire any fruit that was not perfect.” Which word best describes the foreman?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “At the market, the foreman tasted a grape from each crate. He could detect even a slightly sour batch, and he refused to acquire any fruit that was not perfect.” Which word best describes the foreman?

options.label: A
options.text: forgetful

options.label: B
options.text: careful

options.label: C
options.text: shy

options.label: D
options.text: careless

partB.stem: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: he refused to acquire any fruit that was not perfect

options.label: B
options.text: At the market

options.label: C
options.text: from each crate

options.label: D
options.text: a slightly sour batch

questions.why: Refusing imperfect fruit shows that the foreman is careful.

questions.stem: Which TWO words could replace “acquire” in the sentence “The school plans to acquire new laptops for the computer lab”? Choose two.
questions.why: To acquire is to obtain or get, often by buying.

questions.stem: Arrange these ways of eating from the fastest to the slowest, ending with the way that shows someone savors the food.
sequence: gulp the food in seconds
eat the food at a normal pace
savor the food bite by bite
questions.why: Savoring is the slowest, most careful way of enjoying food.

questions.stem: The engineer asked the electricians to check every part of the ____, because one loose wire could stop the whole system from working.
questions.why: Electricity flows through a complete circuit.

questions.stem: In which sentence is “foreman” used with its correct meaning?
options: The museum displayed a foreman, an ancient tool for grinding wheat.
The foreman gave each worker a different row of trees to prune.
The foreman of a sentence is always the very first word in it.
Our team's foreman is the smallest bird in the whole flock.
questions.why: A foreman is the person in charge of a group of workers.

questions.stem: The teacher said Ali's success in math was because of his hard work and practice. Would you say his success could be an attribute of his effort?
options: No, because only a student can attribute success, not a teacher.
No, because success in math has nothing to do with effort.
Yes, because the teacher attributes his success to his hard work.
Yes, because Ali is good at every single subject in school.
questions.why: To attribute something is to say it is caused by something else.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “diverge,” “merit,” “subvert,” “sundry,” and “vehemently.”

pairs.right: worth or value that deserves praise
to secretly work against or weaken

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you describe people and their choices.

questions.stem: The two paths in the forest started together, but then one turned left and the other turned right. Would you say the paths began to diverge?
options: No, because the two paths started at the very same place.
Yes, because the paths split and went in different directions.
No, because paths in a forest always stay close together.
Yes, because the forest was very large and full of trees.
questions.why: To diverge means to go in different directions.

questions.stem: True or false: A box of sundry items holds many different kinds of things.
questions.why: Sundry means various or of different kinds.

questions.stem: Fatima's science fair project had so much ____ that the judges awarded it first place.
questions.why: Merit is worth or value that deserves praise.

questions.stem: Mariam's essay was messy, confusing, and full of mistakes. Would you say it showed great merit?
options: Yes, because Mariam finished writing the whole essay.
No, because Mariam did not write about a serious topic.
No, because merit means high quality that deserves praise.
Yes, because every essay a student writes has great merit.
questions.why: A messy, confusing essay does not show great merit.

questions.stem: Does each person speak “vehemently” or calmly?

rows.text: The fan shouted, “That was NOT a foul!” and waved his arms wildly.
The librarian whispered the directions to the reading room.
Saad pounded the table as he argued that the plan was unfair.
The nurse gently explained how to take the medicine.

questions.why: Speaking vehemently means speaking with strong, forceful feeling.

questions.stem: The student reminded everyone to follow the school rules and encouraged his classmates to obey them. Would you say he was trying to subvert the rules?
options: Yes, because he talked to his classmates about the rules.
Yes, because students always try to change school rules.
No, because he did not know what the school rules were.
No, because to subvert rules is to work against them.
questions.why: Supporting the rules is the opposite of subverting them.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to show how two camel tracks diverge.
sequence: Two camel tracks begin side by side at the oasis.
For a few kilometers, the tracks run next to each other.
At a large rock, the tracks diverge, one heading north and one heading east.
questions.why: Tracks diverge when they split apart.

questions.stem: The souvenir shop in the old souq sold ____ items, from brass lanterns to woven baskets and spice jars.
questions.why: Many different kinds of items are sundry items.

questions.stem: In the market, the shop sold fruits, clothes, toys, and many other small items. Would you say the shop had sundry goods?
options: No, because a market shop cannot sell clothes.
Yes, because the shop was busy with shoppers.
No, because sundry means only one kind of item.
Yes, because sundry means many different kinds.
questions.why: A shop with many kinds of goods has sundry goods.

questions.stem: When the team lost, the coach calmly spoke to the players and gently told them what to do better next time. Would you say he reacted vehemently?
options: Yes, because coaches always react strongly after a loss.
No, because vehemently means with strong, forceful feeling.
Yes, because the team lost the match and the coach spoke.
No, because the coach did not watch the whole match.
questions.why: A calm, gentle reaction is not vehement.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “Some players tried to subvert the coach's plan by secretly passing only to their friends. Because of this, the team's strategy fell apart.” What does “subvert” mean?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “Some players tried to subvert the coach's plan by secretly passing only to their friends. Because of this, the team's strategy fell apart.” What does “subvert” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: to openly support

options.label: B
options.text: to copy exactly

options.label: C
options.text: to secretly weaken or undermine

options.label: D
options.text: to explain clearly

partB.stem: Which part of the sentences best helps the reader understand “subvert”?

options.label: A
options.text: the coach's plan

options.label: B
options.text: the team's strategy fell apart

options.label: C
options.text: their friends

options.label: D
options.text: Some players

questions.why: The plan falling apart shows it was weakened, or subverted.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses the word “diverge” correctly.

segments.text: The friends' opinions began to diverge when they discussed which club to join.
The two streams diverge into one large river near the city.
Please diverge your homework to the teacher by Thursday.
The kitten diverged a ball of yarn across the floor.

questions.why: Opinions diverge when they become different.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “diverge,” “merit,” “vehemently,” and “sundry.”
questions.why: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Is “attribute” used as a noun (a quality) or a verb (to credit as a cause) in each sentence?

rows.text: Patience is an important attribute of a good teacher.
Scientists attribute the coral damage to warmer water.
Honesty was her strongest attribute.
The coach attributes the win to hard training.

columns.text: Verb: to credit as a cause

questions.why: Attribute can name a quality or mean to say something caused a result.

questions.stem: The two scientists agreed about the problem, but their solutions began to ____ when they discussed the cost.
questions.why: Ideas that become different diverge.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the poetry contest uses a word incorrectly?
questions.why: Merit means value; sundry means various.

questions.stem: True or false: A student who vehemently disagrees with a rule feels only a little unsure about it.
questions.why: Vehemently means with very strong feeling.

questions.stem: Which TWO actions would subvert a school's recycling program? Choose two.
options: Secretly throwing plastic bottles into the paper bin
Placing clear labels on each recycling bin
Collecting cans at lunch and sorting them correctly
Telling classmates that recycling is useless so they stop sorting trash
questions.why: Actions that weaken a program subvert it.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “merit” mean “to deserve” rather than “value”?
options: There is real merit in learning a second language.
His plan has some merit, but it is too costly.
The judges discussed the merit of each design.
Her careful research merits a prize.
questions.why: As a verb, merit means to deserve.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “Join” is to “merge” as “separate” is to ____.
questions.why: Join and merge are synonyms; separate and diverge are also synonyms.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph about twins. Which sentence uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: Twins often share many attributes, such as eye color and height.
However, their interests can diverge as they grow older.
One twin might subvert music, while the other prefers sports.
Many twins vehemently insist on being seen as individuals.
questions.correction: One twin might love music, while the other prefers sports.
questions.why: Subvert means to weaken; it does not mean to enjoy.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “The two brothers looked exactly alike, yet their talents diverged. One wrote sundry poems about the sea, and the other built model engines.” What does “diverged” show about the brothers?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “The two brothers looked exactly alike, yet their talents diverged. One wrote sundry poems about the sea, and the other built model engines.” What does “diverged” show about the brothers?

options.label: A
options.text: Their talents developed in different directions.

options.label: B
options.text: Their talents were exactly the same.

options.label: C
options.text: They shared every hobby with each other.

options.label: D
options.text: They argued vehemently about hobbies.

partB.stem: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: model engines

options.label: B
options.text: The two brothers looked exactly alike

options.label: C
options.text: about the sea

options.label: D
options.text: One wrote sundry poems about the sea, and the other built model engines

questions.why: Different hobbies show that their talents diverged.

questions.stem: Which word fits each sentence better: “vehemently” or “mildly”?

rows.text: The villagers ____ protested the plan to cut down the ancient palm grove, shouting and holding signs.
Dad ____ suggested that we might leave a little earlier.
The lawyer ____ denied the false accusation, raising her voice.

questions.why: Vehemently shows strong feeling; mildly shows gentle feeling.

questions.stem: Which word has the most negative connotation when describing what someone does to a plan?
questions.why: Subvert suggests secretly working to destroy a plan.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are the best synonyms for “sundry”? Choose two.
questions.why: Sundry means assorted or various.

questions.stem: Arrange these reactions to a new school rule from the weakest feeling to the strongest, including “vehemently protested.”
sequence: quietly mentioned a concern
mildly disagreed
firmly objected
vehemently protested
questions.why: Vehemently describes the strongest feeling.

questions.stem: Historians ____ the city's rapid growth to its location on an important trade route.
questions.why: To attribute something to a cause is to say it caused the result.

questions.stem: Match each word form related to “diverge,” “merit,” “subvert,” and “vehemently” with its meaning.

pairs.right: trying to weaken a system secretly

questions.why: Word families share a root meaning.

questions.stem: The stadium can only hold 500 people during a football match. Would you say the stadium has a large capacity?
options: No, because the stadium is used only for football.
Yes, because a stadium is always a very large building.
No, because 500 people is a small number for a stadium.
Yes, because football matches attract many fans.
questions.why: Capacity is the most something can hold; 500 is small for a stadium.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “capacity,” “coalesce,” “compatible,” “rigid,” and “scenario.”

pairs.right: to come together to form one thing
stiff, or not able to change
an imagined situation or series of events

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you read science and technology texts.

questions.stem: Several small streams stayed separate and flowed in different directions without joining together. Would you say the streams began to coalesce?
options: Yes, because there were several small streams of water.
No, because to coalesce means to come together into one.
Yes, because all streams eventually turn into rivers.
No, because streams only flow during the rainy season.
questions.why: Streams that stay apart do not coalesce.

questions.stem: True or false: A rigid ruler bends easily, like a piece of string.
questions.why: Rigid means stiff and hard to bend.

questions.stem: The water tank on the roof has a ____ of 1,000 liters, so it cannot hold any more than that.
questions.why: Capacity is the most a container can hold.

questions.stem: The new phone works with many different chargers and connects easily to a variety of earphones. Would you say the phone is compatible with many devices?
options: No, because the phone needs chargers to keep working.
Yes, because the phone is new and costs a lot of money.
Yes, because it works well with many other devices.
No, because new phones never work with older earphones.
questions.why: Compatible means able to work well together.

questions.stem: Is each object “rigid” or flexible?

rows.text: a steel beam
a rubber band
a frozen block of ice
a cotton scarf

questions.why: Rigid objects are stiff and do not bend.

questions.stem: The teacher followed the schedule exactly and did not allow any changes. Would you say the schedule was rigid?

questions.stem: Put these events in order to show how raindrops coalesce into a puddle.

Nearby drops touch and join into bigger drops.
The bigger drops coalesce into one wide puddle.
questions.why: Drops coalesce as they join together.

questions.stem: The teacher asked the students to imagine what they would do if the internet stopped working for a week. Would you say the teacher gave them a scenario?
options: Yes, because the teacher asked a homework question.
No, because the internet never stops working.
No, because a scenario must be a true event.
Yes, because a scenario is an imagined situation.
questions.why: Imagining what would happen in a situation is thinking about a scenario.

questions.stem: Which TWO pairs are compatible? Choose two.

a phone and a charger made for that same phone model
two classmates who enjoy working together and share ideas easily
a square peg and a round hole that is too small for it
questions.why: Compatible things work well together.

questions.stem: Identify the part of speech of the form of “rigid,” “compatible,” or “coalesce” in each sentence.

rows.text: The rigidity of the frame kept the tent standing.
These two apps are not compatible.
Fog droplets coalesce on cold windows.
Engineers tested the compatibility of the parts.

questions.why: Suffixes such as -ity turn adjectives into nouns.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The new sports hall has a seating capacity of 8,000.” What does “capacity” mean in this sentence?
options: the number of games played there each year
the price of a ticket to enter the hall
the height of the ceiling in the hall
the largest number of people it can hold
questions.why: Seating capacity is how many people a place can hold.

questions.stem: The museum's rules were so ____ that visitors were not allowed to take even one photo.
questions.why: Rules that allow no exceptions are rigid.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the engineers' test uses a word incorrectly?
segments: a thousand people jumped at once
questions.why: Capacity names how much the floor can hold.

questions.stem: True or false: A scenario is something that has already happened and been proven true.
questions.why: A scenario is an imagined or possible situation.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “capacity” mean “a role or position” rather than “the amount something can hold”?
options: She spoke in her capacity as team captain.
The school bus has a capacity of fifty passengers.
The bottle's capacity is half a liter of water.
The hall was filled to capacity for the graduation.
questions.why: “In her capacity as” means in her role as.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “Soft” is to “clay” as ____ is to “steel.”
questions.why: Clay is soft; steel is rigid.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph about the footbridge test. Which sentence uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: Engineers tested a new footbridge in a careful scenario.
Hundreds of volunteers coalesced in the middle of the bridge.
The bridge's rigid steel frame barely moved under their weight.
The test showed that the bridge's compatible was large enough for big crowds.
questions.correction: The test showed that the bridge's capacity was large enough for big crowds.
questions.why: Capacity is the amount something can hold.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “The coach's rigid schedule left no time for rest. When several players became exhausted, he refused to change a single practice.” What does “rigid” suggest about the coach?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “The coach's rigid schedule left no time for rest. When several players became exhausted, he refused to change a single practice.” What does “rigid” suggest about the coach?

options.label: A
options.text: He wanted the players to rest more.

options.label: B
options.text: He was unwilling to change his plans.

options.label: C
options.text: He forgot to plan the practices.

options.text: He was kind and flexible with players.

partB.stem: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: he refused to change a single practice

options.label: B
options.text: several players became exhausted

options.label: C
options.text: for rest

options.label: D
options.text: The coach's schedule

questions.why: Refusing to change shows a rigid attitude.

questions.stem: Does “rigid” describe something physical (stiff) or a way of behaving (strict) in each sentence?

rows.text: The rigid plastic case protected the camera.
Her rigid rules about bedtime never changed, even on holidays.
The frozen towel was as rigid as a board.
His rigid thinking stopped him from trying new ideas.

columns.text: Behavior: strict or unwilling to change

questions.why: Rigid can describe objects or attitudes.

questions.stem: Which TWO words could best replace “coalesce” in the sentence “Over time, the scattered villages began to coalesce into a single town”? Choose two.
questions.why: To coalesce is to merge or unite.

questions.stem: What does the phrase “worst-case scenario” mean in “In the worst-case scenario, the flight will be delayed until tomorrow”?
options: a short story with a happy ending
a plan that has already been finished
the outcome most people expect to happen
the worst outcome that could happen
questions.why: A worst-case scenario is the worst possible outcome.

questions.stem: Arrange these containers from the smallest capacity to the largest.
sequence: a teaspoon
a drinking glass
a bucket
a swimming pool
questions.why: Capacity is how much a container can hold.

questions.stem: Doctors check that a donor's blood type is ____ with the patient's before a transfusion.
questions.why: Blood types must be able to work together, or be compatible.

questions.stem: Match each key word with the example that best shows it: “capacity,” “scenario,” “coalesce,” and “compatible.”

pairs.right: Imagine the power goes out during a storm.
Drops of oil join into one big drop.

questions.why: Examples help show what each word means.

questions.stem: Even though they disagreed, both students spoke politely and listened to each other. Would you say they showed civility?
options: No, because the students did not agree in the end.
Yes, because civility means being polite and respectful.
No, because people who disagree cannot show civility.
Yes, because they were both students at the same school.
questions.why: Civility is polite, respectful behavior.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “perceive,” “persist,” “repercussion,” “severe,” and “tolerance.”

pairs.right: to notice or become aware of
a result of an action, usually a bad one
acceptance of different ideas or people

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you discuss how people treat each other.

questions.stem: Thick fog covered the valley, making it impossible to see anything below, even the nearby trees. Would you say you could perceive the city?
options: No, because there were no trees in the city.
No, because the fog made it impossible to see anything.
Yes, because the city was in the valley below.
Yes, because cities are large and always easy to notice from above.
questions.why: To perceive is to see or notice; the fog blocked everything.

questions.stem: True or false: A severe sandstorm is a mild breeze that causes no problems.
questions.why: Severe means very serious or harsh.

questions.stem: Even though the puzzle was hard, Rakan decided to ____ until he finished it.
questions.why: To persist is to keep going.

questions.stem: The little plant stopped growing because it had very little water and sunlight. Would you say the plant continued to persist?
options: No, because the plant stopped growing instead of continuing.
No, because the plant was much too small for anyone to notice it.
Yes, because the plant still had a little bit of sunlight.
Yes, because plants always keep growing without water.
questions.why: To persist is to continue; the plant stopped.

questions.stem: Does each action show “civility” or not?

rows.text: Holding the door open for an elderly neighbor
Interrupting a classmate who is speaking
Thanking the bus driver at the end of the ride
Pushing ahead of others in the lunch line

questions.why: Civility means polite, respectful behavior.

questions.stem: After shouting at his friend, he later faced the negative results of his choice. Would you say he experienced a repercussion?
options: No, because a repercussion is a kind of loud noise.
No, because he only shouted at his friend one time, not many times.
Yes, because he and his friend were in an argument.
Yes, because a repercussion is a result of an action.
questions.why: A repercussion is a result, often a bad one, of an action.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses the word “tolerance” correctly.

segments.text: The club shows tolerance by welcoming members with different opinions.
Ahmed poured tolerance into his glass of water.
The tolerance of the race was fifteen kilometers.
She wrote her name with a sharp tolerance.

questions.why: Tolerance is accepting people and ideas that are different.

questions.stem: Arrange these weather events from the least severe to the most severe.
sequence: a light breeze
a strong gust
a powerful sandstorm
a destructive hurricane
questions.why: Severe weather is the most serious and harmful.

questions.stem: The storm caused only a few leaves to fall from the trees and did not damage anything. Would you say the storm was severe?
options: Yes, because some leaves fell from the trees during the storm.
No, because a severe storm is serious and causes harm.
Yes, because all storms are severe and dangerous.
No, because the storm happened during the day.
questions.why: A storm with no damage is not severe.

questions.stem: The teacher allowed students to share different opinions without getting upset. Would you say the teacher showed tolerance?
options: No, because teachers should not allow different opinions.
Yes, because tolerance means accepting different views.
Yes, because the teacher was in charge of the class.
No, because the students shared too many opinions.
questions.why: Accepting different opinions calmly shows tolerance.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “From the top of the tower, Dana could perceive tiny boats far out at sea. With her binoculars, she could even see the flags on their masts.” What does “perceive” mean?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “From the top of the tower, Dana could perceive tiny boats far out at sea. With her binoculars, she could even see the flags on their masts.” What does “perceive” mean?

options.label: D

questions.why: “Could even see” shows that perceive means see or notice.

questions.stem: Match each word with its antonym: “civility,” “persist,” “severe,” and “tolerance.”
questions.why: Antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Which TWO situations could lead to a repercussion for the person involved? Choose two.
options: Ziad finishes his chores and then reads a book.
Kareem copies his friend's homework, and the teacher notices.
Maha thanks her coach after a long practice.
Leen ignores the safety rules and breaks a lab beaker.
questions.why: Repercussions follow choices, especially poor ones.

questions.stem: Identify the part of speech of the form of “persist,” “perceive,” or “tolerance” in each sentence.

rows.text: Her persistence helped her win the race.
Owls perceive movement in the dark.
The teacher is tolerant of honest mistakes.
Our perception of the problem changed after the meeting.

questions.why: Suffixes such as -ence, -tion, and -ant change a word's part of speech.

questions.stem: If the cough continues to ____ for more than a week, you should visit a doctor.
questions.why: A cough that persists keeps going.

questions.stem: True or false: Talking calmly and respectfully during a disagreement is an example of civility.
questions.why: Civility is polite, respectful behavior, even in disagreement.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about cheating on exams uses a word incorrectly?
segments: that cheating on exams has serious civility,
questions.correction: that cheating on exams has serious repercussions,
questions.why: Results of an action are repercussions.

questions.stem: The doctor warned that the burn was ____ and needed treatment right away.
questions.why: A burn that needs treatment right away is severe.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “severe” mean “very plain, without decoration”?
options: The coach gave a severe warning to the team.
The office had a severe, plain gray design.
Kamal had a severe headache after the long trip.
The storm caused severe damage along the coast.
questions.why: Severe can also describe a plain, undecorated style.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: “Rudeness” is to “civility” as “quit” is to ____.
questions.why: Rudeness and civility are opposites; quit and persist are opposites too.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph about the football league. Which sentence uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: Our football league started a program to build tolerance among players.
Coaches asked everyone to show civility, even after a tough loss.
Players learned that cheating can have lasting repercussions.
Anyone who persists in breaking the rules will perceive a severe penalty.
questions.correction: Anyone who persists in breaking the rules will receive a severe penalty.
questions.why: Perceive means notice; a penalty is received.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “Although the critics laughed at her first designs, the young architect persisted. Ten years later, her buildings stood in cities across the region.” What does “persisted” suggest about the architect?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “Although the critics laughed at her first designs, the young architect persisted. Ten years later, her buildings stood in cities across the region.” What does “persisted” suggest about the architect?

options.label: A
options.text: She stopped designing for ten years.

options.label: B
options.text: She agreed with the critics completely.

options.label: C
options.text: She kept working despite criticism.

options.label: D
options.text: She gave up and chose a new career.

partB.stem: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: the young architect

options.label: B
options.text: Ten years later, her buildings stood in cities across the region

options.label: C
options.text: her first designs

options.label: D
options.text: the critics laughed

questions.why: Her later success shows she persisted.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes each sentence: “perceive” or “persist.”

rows.text: Bats use sound to ____ objects in the dark.
If the pain should ____, call the clinic.
Some people ____ the color red as exciting.
Weeds ____ in the garden no matter how often we pull them.

questions.why: Perceive means notice; persist means continue.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “tolerance” to mean “the ability to handle something difficult” rather than “respect for differences”?
options: The festival promoted tolerance among neighbors.
Camels have a high tolerance for heat and thirst.
Tolerance helps people from many cultures live together.
Our class values tolerance for different opinions.
questions.why: Tolerance can also mean the ability to endure something hard.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are the closest synonyms of “repercussion”? Choose two.
questions.why: A repercussion is a consequence or aftereffect.

questions.stem: Arrange these responses to a classmate's mistake from the least civility to the most civility.
sequence: mocking the classmate in front of everyone
ignoring the classmate completely
kindly offering to help fix the mistake
questions.why: Kind, respectful responses show the most civility.

questions.stem: Because she had a nut allergy, Huda had zero ____ for peanuts; even a tiny amount made her sick.
questions.why: Here tolerance means the body's ability to handle something.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the key word it best illustrates: “perceive,” “repercussion,” “civility,” and “persist.”

The guard noticed a faint smell of smoke.
After skipping practice, Omar was benched for the final.
The two debaters shook hands and thanked each other.

questions.why: Each example shows one word's meaning in action.

questions.stem: The sailor disobeyed a direct order from the captain on a 17th-century ship. As a result, he was sentenced to twenty lashes in front of the crew. Would you say the sailor underwent a flogging for his actions?
options: Yes, because he was punished by being whipped twenty times.
No, because a flogging is a long prison sentence on land far from the sea.
No, because the captain only gave an order and did not punish anyone.
Yes, because he had to clean the deck of the ship for twenty days.
questions.why: A flogging is a punishment of beating someone with a whip or stick.

questions.stem: Match each Concept Vocabulary word from “I Am Malala” with its meaning: “flogging,” “heritage,” “represent,” and “siege.”

pairs.right: a punishment of beating with a whip
traditions and history passed down from earlier generations
to speak or act for someone
surrounding a place to cut off its supplies

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you discuss history, culture, and conflict.

questions.stem: Sarah's family has lived in the same village for 400 years. She decided to sell all her family's ancient artifacts and move to a city where she refuses to speak her native language or follow any old customs. Is Sarah actively preserving her heritage?
options: Yes, because she has lived in the same village her whole life with her large family.
No, because heritage only means the money a family keeps in the bank.
Yes, because selling ancient artifacts helps other people learn about the past.
No, because she is giving up the customs, language, and objects passed down to her.
questions.why: Heritage is the customs, language, and objects handed down from earlier generations.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Old fishing boats and pearl-diving songs are part of the heritage of the Gulf,” the word “heritage” means traditions passed down from the past.
questions.why: Heritage is what earlier generations hand down to us.

questions.stem: Our class chose Huda to ____ us at the student council meeting because she speaks clearly and listens well.
questions.why: To represent a group is to speak or act for it.

questions.stem: The lawyer stood up in court and argued for the innocence of his client. He wore the client's favorite color and spoke exactly the words the client wanted the judge to hear. Does the lawyer represent the client in this situation?
options: No, because the client did not stand up and speak to the judge himself.
Yes, because he wore his client's favorite color to the courtroom that day.
No, because a lawyer can only represent a client by wearing the same clothes.
Yes, because he spoke and argued in court on behalf of his client.
questions.why: To represent someone is to speak or act on that person's behalf.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe a “siege” or not?

rows.text: An army camped around the fortress for months so no food could get in.
Soldiers marched through the town during a festival parade.
Enemy ships blocked the harbor while troops surrounded the walls until the city ran out of water.
Two teams met on a field for a single afternoon match.

questions.why: A siege surrounds a place and cuts off its supplies.

questions.stem: Visitors to Al-Masmak Fort in Riyadh learn about the history and ____ of the Saudi people.
questions.why: Heritage is the history and traditions of a people.

questions.stem: The enemy army surrounded the city walls, cutting off all food and water supplies for three months. However, they left the back gate open and allowed people to come and go as they pleased. Would you say the city is currently under a siege?
options: No, because the army stayed for only three months, which is far too short.
No, because a siege cuts a place off completely, but people could still come and go.
Yes, because the city had less food and water than it did before.
Yes, because any army standing anywhere near a city wall, even for a single day, is a siege.
questions.why: In a siege, the place is surrounded so nothing and no one can freely get in or out.

questions.stem: Which TWO actions would help a family protect its “heritage”? Choose two.
options: The children stop speaking their home language with their grandparents.
Grandmother teaches the children the old songs she learned as a girl.
The family keeps their great-grandfather's handwritten letters safe in a box.
The family throws away old photographs to make more space.
questions.why: Protecting heritage means keeping traditions and family history alive.

questions.stem: A small island nation recently began building fast-food chains, adopted the English legal system, and started broadcasting American Hollywood movies on every channel. Does this shift in culture suggest a move to westernize the nation?
options: No, because building restaurants has nothing at all to do with a nation's culture or way of life.
Yes, because the nation is taking on the food, laws, and movies of Western countries.
No, because a nation can only westernize by moving closer to the west on a map.
Yes, because the nation has decided to keep all of its oldest customs exactly the same.
questions.why: To westernize is to adopt the customs and ways of Western countries.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “During the siege of the castle, the soldiers outside blocked every road. Inside, the people had to share the last sacks of grain.” What does “siege” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “During the siege of the castle, the soldiers outside blocked every road. Inside, the people had to share the last sacks of grain.” What does “siege” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: a long trip across a wide desert

options.label: B
options.text: a celebration held inside a castle

options.label: C
options.text: a peace meeting between two leaders

options.label: D
options.text: surrounding a place so supplies cannot get in

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: “Inside”

options.label: D
options.text: “the people”

questions.why: Blocking every road keeps supplies out, which is what a siege does.

questions.stem: In the 1800s, some leaders wanted to ____ their countries by adopting European clothing, schools, and factories.
questions.why: Adopting European ways is a way to westernize.

questions.stem: True or false: A team captain who speaks to the referee for all the players represents the team.
questions.why: Speaking for a group is representing it.

questions.stem: Sort these forms of “represent” and “westernize” into nouns and verbs.

rows.text: representation
represent
westernization
westernize

questions.why: The suffixes -ation and -ization turn verbs into nouns.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “flogging” correctly?
options: The farmer is flogging water onto his young tomato plants every single morning.
In some old navies, flogging was a common punishment for sailors who broke rules.
The baker is flogging the bread so it will smell sweet and fresh.
Mona was flogging her friend a birthday card through the mail.
questions.why: Flogging is a punishment of whipping or beating.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “represent” to mean “stand for or be a symbol of”? Choose two.
options: On the map, small blue dots represent wells in the desert.
A lawyer represents people who need help in court.
Faisal will represent our school at the national science fair.
On the weather chart, a yellow sun represents a clear day.
questions.why: Represent can mean to stand for something, or to speak for someone.

questions.stem: Some people feel that cities which quickly adopt fast food and foreign styles are becoming ____.
questions.why: After “becoming,” an adjective form such as westernized is needed.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “represent” in it.

pairs.left: Hamad will represent his class in the debate.
These red lines represent rivers on the map.
pairs.right: stand for; be a symbol of

pairs.left: The painting represents a busy market in old Jeddah.

questions.why: Represent has several related meanings.

questions.stem: True or false: A city under siege can easily bring in fresh food and supplies whenever it needs them.
questions.why: A siege cuts off supplies, so the city cannot bring them in easily.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence: “The guide explained that the old city gates were built thick and tall so the town could survive a long ____.”
questions.why: Thick walls and gates help a town survive being surrounded in a siege.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about “heritage” and “siege”: “The town of Diriyah is part of Saudi heritage. Long ago, its mud-brick walls protected people during a siege. Today, visitors come to westernize the old palaces and learn about the past.”
segments: The town of Diriyah is part of Saudi heritage.
Long ago, its mud-brick walls protected people during a siege.
Today, visitors come to westernize the old palaces
questions.correction: Today, visitors come to explore the old palaces
questions.why: Visitors explore historic places; they do not westernize them.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “heritage” correctly.

segments.text: Weaving Sadu rugs is an important part of Bedouin heritage.
Majed ate a heritage for breakfast before school.
The heritage of the car broke on the highway.
Please heritage the window before the dust storm.

questions.why: Sadu weaving is a tradition passed down, so it is part of heritage.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: lawyer is to represent as army is to ____.
questions.why: A lawyer represents a client; an army besieges, or lays siege to, a city.

questions.stem: Is each example part of a country's “heritage” or not?

traditional folk dances taught to children
a brand-new phone released this week
a traffic jam on a busy morning

questions.why: Heritage is what is handed down from the past.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “westernize” most accurately?
options: The sun began to westernize as it slowly set behind the tall golden dunes.
The camel westernized across the desert toward the well.
After the war, the government chose to westernize its schools by copying European teaching methods.
Lina westernized her bicycle tire with a small pump.
questions.why: Westernize describes adopting Western ways, not moving toward the west.

questions.stem: Put these events of a historical “siege” in the order they would most likely happen.
sequence: An army marches toward the walled city.
Soldiers surround the walls and block the roads.
Food and water inside the city slowly run out.
The city's leaders agree to talk about peace.
questions.why: A siege begins with surrounding a place, and the shortages come later.

questions.stem: “Represent” comes from a Latin word meaning “to show again.” Which TWO sentences use a form of “represent” correctly? Choose two.
options: Our representative on the student council shared our ideas with the principal.
The represent of the club spoke at the meeting.
Ali representationed the new rules to his friends.
This drawing is a representation of the old souq as it looked in 1950.
questions.why: Representative names a person who speaks for others; representation is a noun for a picture or likeness.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this sentence about punishments on old ships: “Long ago, some ships used siege as a punishment, and sailors who broke rules were whipped in front of the crew.”
