questions.why: Whipping as a punishment is flogging, not a siege.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: “Since the 1800s, some nations have debated how much to ____ their economies while still protecting their traditional culture.”
questions.why: Changing an economy to follow Western models is to westernize it.

questions.stem: The factory owners ignored the safety regulations for years, and the eventual consequence was a permanent shutdown of the plant. Would you say the shutdown was an unrelated event or a direct result of the owners' actions?
options: It was a direct result, because a consequence is what happens because of an earlier action.
It was unrelated, because factories sometimes close for reasons that nobody can ever explain to anyone.
It was a direct result, because the workers decided they wanted a long holiday.
It was unrelated, because the owners ignored the rules for years before anything happened.
questions.why: A consequence is a result caused by an earlier action.

questions.stem: Match each Concept Vocabulary word from “All Summer in a Day” with its meaning: “consequence,” “immense,” “resilient,” “savagely,” and “vital.”

pairs.right: able to recover quickly from difficulty

questions.why: These meanings help you describe size, strength, and importance.

questions.stem: The astronaut looked out the window of the space station and was overwhelmed by the immense darkness of the universe. Does the word “immense” suggest the darkness felt cramped or vast?
options: Cramped, because darkness always makes a place feel smaller.
Cramped, because the astronaut was inside a small space station.
Vast, because the astronaut could see only a few tiny stars.
questions.why: Immense means huge, so the darkness felt vast.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The Empty Quarter is an immense desert that covers much of southern Arabia,” the word “immense” means very small.
questions.why: Immense means extremely large.

questions.stem: Water is ____ for date palms, so farmers in Al-Ahsa use springs to keep the trees alive.
questions.why: Something vital is necessary for life.

questions.stem: Despite losing her home in the fire, the resilient woman began drawing up plans to rebuild the very next day. Would you describe her as someone who wasn't easily defeated by her circumstances?
options: Yes, because she was the only person in town whose home did not burn.
No, because she should have waited many years before making any plans.
No, because losing her home in the fire means she was defeated.
Yes, because she recovered quickly and started planning to rebuild.
questions.why: A resilient person bounces back quickly after hardship.

questions.stem: Is each person or thing in these sentences “resilient” or not?

rows.text: After losing the first match, Reem trained harder and won the next tournament.
Omar gave up on learning to swim after one cold lesson.
The coral reef grew back slowly after the storm damaged it.
The team stopped trying as soon as the other side scored.

questions.why: Resilient people and things recover after difficulty.

questions.stem: Skipping breakfast every day can have a ____: you may feel tired and hungry by mid-morning.
questions.why: Feeling tired is a result, or consequence, of skipping breakfast.

questions.stem: The hungry wolves attacked the carcass savagely, leaving nothing behind but scattered bones in the snow. Did the wolves eat in a gentle, orderly fashion?
options: Yes, because wolves always wait patiently and take turns at a meal.
No, because they were not hungry and ate only a little.
No, because “savagely” means in a fierce and violent way.
Yes, because they left the bones neatly scattered in the snow.
questions.why: Savagely describes fierce, wild action, not gentle eating.

questions.stem: Which TWO things are “vital” for a camel crossing the desert? Choose two.
questions.why: Vital things are needed to stay alive.

questions.stem: When climbing at high altitudes, carrying extra oxygen is vital because the air is too thin to breathe on its own. Would you say the oxygen was optional for the climbers?
options: Yes, because the air is thin but still easy to breathe up there.
No, because the oxygen tanks were too heavy to leave behind.
Yes, because climbers can choose whether or not they want it.
No, because “vital” means absolutely necessary for life.
questions.why: Vital means necessary, the opposite of optional.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The storm attacked the coast savagely. Huge waves smashed the boats, and the wind tore roofs from the houses.” What does “savagely” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The storm attacked the coast savagely. Huge waves smashed the boats, and the wind tore roofs from the houses.” What does “savagely” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: slowly and quietly

options.label: B
options.text: happily and playfully

options.label: C
options.text: carefully and neatly

options.label: D
options.text: fiercely and violently

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the sentences best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the coast”

options.label: B
options.text: “from the houses”

options.label: C
options.text: “The storm”

options.label: D
options.text: “smashed the boats”

questions.why: Smashing boats shows fierce, violent force.

questions.stem: The spider's web looked delicate, but it was ____ enough to spring back after the strong wind passed.
questions.why: Something resilient springs back into shape.

questions.stem: True or false: A consequence is something that happens before the action that causes it.
questions.why: A consequence comes after the action that causes it.

questions.stem: Sort these forms of “resilient” and “vital” by part of speech.

rows.text: resilience
resilient
vitality
vital
revitalize

questions.why: The suffixes -ence and -ity make nouns; -ize makes verbs.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “immense” correctly?
options: The blue whale is an immense animal, longer than two buses.
Lama whispered in an immense voice so the baby would not wake.
The ant carried an immense crumb that was smaller than a seed.
The tiny kitten curled up in an immense corner of the shoebox.
questions.why: Immense describes something huge, like a blue whale.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe a “consequence” of an action? Choose two.
options: Because Fahad forgot to water the plant, its leaves turned brown.
After practicing every day, Sara's handwriting became much neater.
Ahmad likes both football and basketball.
The sky is blue on most summer days in Riyadh.
questions.why: A consequence is a result that follows an action.

questions.stem: Medical workers do ____ work, because without them many sick people could not get better.
questions.why: Work that people cannot do without is vital.

questions.stem: Match each description with the word “resilient,” “savagely,” or “immense” that it describes.

pairs.left: a mountain so huge it fills the whole sky
a rubber ball that bounces back into shape
a lion tearing fiercely at its meal

questions.why: Each description shows the word's meaning in action.

questions.stem: True or false: If something is vital to a plan, the plan can work just as well without it.
questions.why: A vital part is necessary; the plan fails without it.

questions.stem: Which word best replaces “very big” to show the greatest size: “The Rub' al Khali is a very big sea of sand.”
questions.why: Immense is stronger than large; it means extremely big.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about mangroves: “Mangrove trees along the Red Sea coast are resilient; they survive salty water and strong tides. These trees are vital to many young fish, and one resilient consequence of cutting them down is that the shore washes away more quickly.”
segments: Mangrove trees along the Red Sea coast are resilient;
they survive salty water and strong tides.
These trees are vital to many young fish,
and one resilient consequence of cutting them down
is that the shore washes away more quickly.
questions.correction: and one serious consequence of cutting them down
questions.why: A consequence can be serious, but it cannot be resilient.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “savagely” correctly.

segments.text: The hungry falcon tore savagely at its food.
The grandmother smiled savagely as she hugged her grandson.
The baby slept savagely in her soft, warm crib.
The teacher savagely thanked the class for their kind cards.

questions.why: Savagely fits fierce actions, like a falcon tearing at food.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: tiny is to immense as fragile is to ____.
questions.why: Tiny is the opposite of immense, and fragile is the opposite of resilient.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “vital”?

rows.text: essential
necessary
unimportant
optional

questions.why: Vital means essential, so unimportant is its opposite.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “resilient” to describe a material rather than a person?
options: My resilient grandfather walked again only weeks after his operation.
Even after failing the test, Noor stayed resilient and studied harder for the next one.
The resilient villagers rebuilt their school just one year after the flood.
The new running shoes have resilient soles that spring back with every step.
questions.why: Resilient can describe a material that springs back, as well as a person who recovers.

questions.stem: Put these sizes in order from smallest to largest, showing where “immense” fits.
sequence: tiny
small
large
immense
questions.why: Immense is at the very top of the size scale.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show a “consequence” that is good rather than bad? Choose two.
options: One consequence of eating too many sweets was a painful toothache.
One consequence of the new bike lanes was fewer accidents on the street.
As a consequence of daily reading, Huda's vocabulary grew quickly.
As a consequence of the dust storm, all flights were delayed.
questions.why: Consequences can be good or bad results.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this sentence about the sand cat: “The sand cat hunts savagely at night, but during the day it rests vitally in a cool burrow.”
segments: The sand cat hunts savagely at night,
questions.why: Vitally means in a necessary way; resting is better described as quiet.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: “Doctors explained that sleep is ____ for teenagers, because the brain and body repair themselves during the night.”
questions.why: Sleep is necessary, or vital, for growing bodies.

questions.stem: Even though the two debaters strongly disagreed on every policy, they remained civil throughout the night, shaking hands and refraining from insults. Would you say the debaters treated each other with hostility?
options: Yes, because the debate lasted the whole night without a single break.
No, because being civil means staying polite and respectful during a disagreement.
No, because they agreed with each other on almost every policy.
Yes, because people who disagree strongly on every single policy are always angry enemies.
questions.why: Civil means polite, the opposite of hostile.

questions.stem: Match each Concept Vocabulary word from “Celebrities as Heroes” with its meaning: “civil,” “conservation,” “indulge,” “influence,” and “notoriety.”

pairs.right: to allow yourself something you enjoy

questions.why: These words help you discuss fame and its effects.

questions.stem: The local community started a conservation project to protect the wetlands from being turned into a shopping mall. Is the goal of this project to destroy the natural environment or to preserve it?
options: To destroy it, because the land will become a busy and useful shopping mall.
To preserve it, because conservation means protecting nature from harm.
To destroy it, because wetlands are wasted land that should be filled in.
To preserve it, because the community wants to build the mall faster.
questions.why: Conservation means protecting and preserving nature.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The two team captains stayed civil after the close game and shook hands,” the word “civil” means rude and angry.
questions.why: Civil means polite and respectful.

questions.stem: The Farasan Islands reserve is a ____ area where gazelles and sea turtles are protected.
questions.why: A conservation area protects wildlife.

questions.stem: After finishing her final exams, Maya decided to indulge in a long afternoon of napping and eating her favourite chocolates. Was Maya restricting herself or allowing herself to enjoy a treat?
options: Restricting herself, because chocolates and naps are not very enjoyable.
Allowing herself a treat, because to indulge means to enjoy something you like.
Restricting herself, because she had worked hard and needed to rest quietly at home.
Allowing herself a treat, because her teacher ordered her to rest.
questions.why: To indulge is to let yourself enjoy something pleasant.

questions.stem: Does each sentence show “civil” behavior or not?

rows.text: The neighbors disagreed about parking but talked calmly and found a solution.
Two drivers shouted insults at each other at the traffic light.
Even though she lost the vote, Muna congratulated the winner politely.
A fan threw a bottle at the referee after a bad call.

questions.why: Civil behavior is calm and polite, even in disagreement.

questions.stem: Good friends can have a positive ____ on your habits, such as reading more or exercising.
questions.why: An influence is an effect on how someone thinks or acts.

questions.stem: The legendary artist had a massive influence on the younger generation, leading many of them to copy her unique painting style. Did the artist have an effect on the new painters?
options: Yes, because she painted portraits of each of the younger painters.
No, because the young painters chose their own styles without any help from her.
Yes, because her influence led many young painters to copy her style.
No, because an influence is only a person's age and fame.
questions.why: Influence is the power to affect what others do.

questions.stem: Which TWO actions are examples of “conservation”? Choose two.
options: leaving the lights on in an empty room
throwing plastic bags into the sea
turning off the tap while brushing your teeth
planting mangroves to protect a coastline
questions.why: Conservation saves resources and protects nature.

questions.stem: The outlaw gained notoriety across the Old West for his daring and illegal train robberies. Is the outlaw famous for doing something helpful and kind, or for something negative?
options: Something negative, because nobody in the Old West knew who he was.
Something helpful, because notoriety means being loved and admired by many people.
Something negative, because notoriety means being well known for something bad.
Something helpful, because he was brave enough to stop the moving trains.
questions.why: Notoriety is fame for bad or harmful actions.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The hacker gained notoriety after he broke into a bank's computers. News reports everywhere warned people about his crimes.” What does “notoriety” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The hacker gained notoriety after he broke into a bank's computers. News reports everywhere warned people about his crimes.” What does “notoriety” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: fame for doing something bad

options.label: B
options.text: skill at fixing computers

options.label: C
options.text: a secret that nobody knows

options.label: D
options.text: a reward for helping others

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the sentences best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “a bank's computers”

options.label: B
options.text: “warned people about his crimes”

options.label: C
options.text: “News reports”

options.label: D
options.text: “The hacker”

questions.why: Being known everywhere for crimes is notoriety.

questions.stem: On the first day of the summer holiday, Grandmother lets the children ____ in extra sweets and stay up a little later.
questions.why: To indulge in something is to enjoy a treat.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who wants to influence others is trying to change what they think or do.
questions.why: To influence means to affect others' thoughts or actions.

questions.stem: Sort these forms of “conservation” and “indulge” by part of speech.

rows.text: conservation
conserve
indulgence
indulge
indulgent

questions.why: The suffixes -tion and -ence make nouns; -ent makes an adjective.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “notoriety” correctly?
options: The kind nurse gained notoriety for gently caring for sick children in the hospital.
The pirate's notoriety spread to every port, and sailors feared his ship.
We drank cold notoriety after the long football match outside.
Huda's notoriety was her neat blue notebook for science class.
questions.why: Notoriety fits someone feared for bad deeds, like a pirate.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “indulge” correctly? Choose two.
options: After a week of hard training, the swimmer indulged in a big plate of kabsa.
The farmer indulged the fence to keep goats from escaping.
Grandfather likes to indulge his grandchildren with stories every evening.
Please indulge the trash before the truck arrives.
questions.why: Indulge means to enjoy a treat or to please someone with one.

questions.stem: The movie star used her ____ to raise money for a hospital, so many fans donated.
questions.why: Her power to affect fans is her influence.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “civil” in it.

pairs.left: The two leaders kept a civil tone during the tense meeting.
A civil engineer designs roads and bridges for the public.
Citizens have civil rights that the law protects.
pairs.right: related to the rights of citizens

questions.why: Civil can mean polite, or related to citizens and public life.

questions.stem: True or false: Someone who gains notoriety has usually earned praise for being honest and kind.
questions.why: Notoriety is fame for something bad, not praise.

questions.stem: Which word has the most negative connotation?
questions.why: Notoriety means being famous for something bad.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about a famous diver: “Many young people follow a famous diver online. She uses her influence to teach them about coral conservation. Because of her notoriety for protecting reefs, thousands joined a beach cleanup.”
segments: Many young people follow a famous diver online.
She uses her influence to teach them about coral conservation.
Because of her notoriety for protecting reefs,
questions.correction: Because of her fame for protecting reefs,
questions.why: Notoriety is negative, so good work earns fame instead.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “conservation” correctly.

segments.text: Water conservation is important in dry countries like Saudi Arabia.
Fatima had a long conservation with her aunt on the phone.
The conservation of the cake was chocolate and cream.
He ran to the store in great conservation.

questions.why: Conservation means saving resources; do not confuse it with conversation.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: waste is to conservation as rudeness is to ____.
questions.why: Waste is the opposite of conservation, and rudeness is the opposite of civility.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “indulge”?

rows.text: treat oneself
pamper
deny
restrict

questions.why: Indulge means to treat or pamper; deny and restrict mean the opposite.

questions.stem: “Influence” can be a noun or a verb. In which sentence is “influence” used as a verb?
options: Grandmother has a strong influence on our family meals.
The moon's influence causes the ocean tides to rise.
The coach's calm influence helped the whole team stay focused.
Clever ads can influence what shoppers decide to buy.
questions.why: After “can,” influence is an action, so it is a verb.

questions.stem: Put these words in order from the most positive to the most negative, showing where “notoriety” fits.
sequence: honor
fame
notoriety
questions.why: Honor is admiring, fame is neutral, and notoriety is negative.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe someone who chooses NOT to “indulge”? Choose two.
options: Reem bought three new novels and spent the weekend reading them.
Even though the cake looked delicious, Hassan ate only fruit before his match.
Rana saved her allowance instead of buying another video game.
After the exam, Khalid ate a whole box of his favorite dates.
questions.why: Choosing not to indulge means holding back from a treat.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this sentence about the Arabian oryx: “Thanks to careful conservation, the Arabian oryx, which once nearly disappeared, has indulged in the wild again in protected reserves.”
segments: the Arabian oryx, which once nearly disappeared,
has indulged in the wild again
questions.correction: has returned to the wild again
questions.why: Indulge means to enjoy a treat; the oryx returned to the wild.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: “Even when fans disagreed online about the match, the club asked everyone to keep their comments ____.”
questions.why: Civil comments are polite even during disagreement.

questions.stem: The young child held her favourite stuffed animal tightly against her bosom as she drifted off to sleep. Would you say the child was holding the toy against her chest?
options: Yes, because the bosom is the front of a person's chest.
No, because the bosom is the back of a person's neck and shoulders.
Yes, because the child placed the toy on the pillow beside her.
No, because she was holding the toy tightly in her two hands.
questions.why: The bosom is the front of the chest.

questions.stem: Match each Concept Vocabulary word from “Famous” with its meaning: “bosom,” “briefly,” “inherit,” and “spectacular.”

pairs.right: to receive something from an older family member

questions.why: These words help you describe people, time, and sights.

questions.stem: The CEO walked through the office and spoke briefly to the team before rushing out the door for a flight. Did the CEO have a long, detailed conversation with the team?
options: No, because he did not say a single word to anyone on the team.
No, because “briefly” means for only a short time.
Yes, because he walked through the whole office talking to everyone.
Yes, because a CEO always speaks with each worker for a long time.
questions.why: Briefly means for a short time, not long and detailed.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The teacher spoke briefly, just two sentences, before the test began,” the word “briefly” means for a short time.
questions.why: Two sentences is a brief, short talk.

questions.stem: The view of the city lights from the top of the Kingdom Centre tower was truly ____.
questions.why: A spectacular view is amazing to see.

questions.stem: When the old king passed away, the young prince was told he would inherit the crown and the responsibility of ruling the land. Did the prince buy the crown, or did it pass down to him from his family?
options: It passed down to him, because he found it lying in the palace garden.
He bought it, because he had to pay to take on the responsibility of ruling.
It passed down to him, because to inherit means to receive something from a family member.
He bought it, because a crown is something that can only be sold in a market to the highest buyer.
questions.why: To inherit is to receive something passed down in a family.

questions.stem: Was each thing most likely “inherited” or not?

rows.text: a gold ring passed from a grandmother to her granddaughter
a new jacket Majed bought at the mall
curly hair that Lina got from her father
a trophy Sami won in a race

questions.why: Inherited things or traits come from earlier family members.

questions.stem: Before the game, the coach spoke ____, using just three sentences, then sent us onto the field.
questions.why: Three sentences is a brief talk.

questions.stem: The fireworks display at the end of the festival was so spectacular that the entire crowd gasped and began to cheer at once. Was the display boring and ordinary?
options: Yes, because the crowd gasped, which shows they were feeling bored.
No, because the fireworks ended very quickly before anyone looked.
Yes, because fireworks are seen at many festivals every single year.
No, because “spectacular” means amazing and impressive to watch.
questions.why: Spectacular is the opposite of boring and ordinary.

questions.stem: Which TWO things can a person “inherit”? Choose two.
options: a family house left by a grandfather
a cold caught from a classmate
a prize for winning a spelling bee
questions.why: People inherit property and traits from family members.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The mother held her newborn baby close to her bosom,” where is the baby?
options: inside a cot near the window
questions.why: The bosom is the chest, so the baby is held against it.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The comet was visible only briefly. It flashed across the sky for a few seconds and then disappeared.” What does “briefly” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The comet was visible only briefly. It flashed across the sky for a few seconds and then disappeared.” What does “briefly” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: far away

options.label: B
options.text: very brightly

options.label: C
options.text: many times

options.label: D
options.text: for a short time

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the sentences best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “The comet”

options.label: B
options.text: “across the sky”

options.label: C
options.text: “was visible”

options.label: D
options.text: “for a few seconds”

questions.why: A few seconds is a brief time.

questions.stem: Faisal will ____ his grandfather's old telescope, which has been in the family for sixty years.
questions.why: Receiving a family object passed down is to inherit it.

questions.stem: True or false: A spectacular sunset is plain and easy to forget.
questions.why: A spectacular sunset is striking and memorable.

questions.stem: Sort these forms of “inherit” and “spectacular” by part of speech.

rows.text: inheritance
inherit
spectacle
spectacular
inheritable

questions.why: The suffix -ance makes a noun; -ar and -able make adjectives.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “spectacular” correctly?
options: The tiny grain of sand looked spectacular because nobody could see it.
The quiet, gray morning was spectacular because nothing at all happened.
The waterfall was spectacular, crashing down from high rocky cliffs.
The empty paper bag was spectacular, so we threw it straight in the bin.
questions.why: Spectacular describes an amazing sight, like a crashing waterfall.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “bosom” correctly? Choose two.
options: The bird tucked its head against its feathered bosom to stay warm.
Salem kicked the ball with his bosom.
Mona wore new shoes on her bosom.
The young mother hugged her baby to her bosom.
questions.why: The bosom is the chest, where you can hold or tuck something.

questions.stem: My grandfather kept the old letter close to his ____, tucked inside the front pocket of his thobe.
questions.why: A front pocket lies against the chest, or bosom.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of “bosom” in it.

pairs.left: The child slept against her mother's bosom.
Huda and Amal have been bosom friends since first grade.
The boat rested on the calm bosom of the sea.
pairs.right: the surface, like a resting place

questions.why: Bosom can mean the chest, a very close friend, or a surface that holds something.

questions.stem: True or false: If you inherit a family's bakery, you must have bought it from strangers.
questions.why: To inherit is to receive something from family, not to buy it.

questions.stem: Which word is the strongest way to describe a fireworks show that amazes everyone?
questions.why: Spectacular is much stronger than pleasant or acceptable.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about Rashid's garden: “Rashid inherited his grandmother's garden. He visited it briefly every evening for three long hours. Each spring, the flowers there looked spectacular.”
segments: every evening for three long hours.
Each spring, the flowers there looked spectacular.
questions.why: Three long hours is not brief, so briefly is misused.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “inherit” correctly.

segments.text: Sara will inherit her aunt's collection of old coins.
Faris inherited the ball across the field to score.
Please inherit the door quietly when you leave.
The cat inherited up the tree to catch a bird.

questions.why: A family collection can be inherited.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: long is to brief as dull is to ____.
questions.why: Long is the opposite of brief, and dull is the opposite of spectacular.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “spectacular”?

rows.text: magnificent
dazzling
ordinary
dull

questions.why: Spectacular means magnificent; ordinary and dull mean the opposite.

questions.stem: “Inherit” can describe objects or traits. Which sentence uses “inherit” to describe a trait rather than an object?
options: Bandar will inherit his uncle's old fishing boat.
Many children inherit their parents' talent for drawing.
The two brothers inherited their great-grandfather's mud-brick house in Diriyah.
Noura inherited her grandmother's silver necklace.
questions.why: A talent is a trait, while a boat, house, or necklace is an object.

questions.stem: Put these lengths of time in order from the briefest to the longest.
sequence: a blink
a minute
a school day
a year
questions.why: A blink is the briefest; a year is the longest.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use a form of “brief” correctly? Choose two.
options: Faisal briefly slept for twelve hours straight.
The brief elephant could not fit through the gate.
The rain stopped briefly, then poured again.
Before the trip, the guide gave us a brief talk about safety.
questions.why: Brief and briefly describe a short time, not size or long periods.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this sentence about a meteor shower: “The meteor shower was spectacular, and because it would last only briefly, the children inherited outside to watch it at once.”
segments: and because it would last only briefly,
questions.why: Inherit means to receive from family; the children hurried.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: “When the old fisherman passed away, his sons were proud to ____ not only his boat but also his love of the sea.”
questions.why: The sons received his boat and his love of the sea, so they inherit them.

questions.stem: The state passed a law making it mandatory for every citizen to wear a seatbelt while the vehicle is in motion. Does the word mandatory imply that the law is a suggested guideline or a strict requirement?
options: A suggested guideline, because drivers can decide whether it is really needed.
A strict requirement, because seatbelts are sold in every single car shop.
A suggested guideline, because the law only applies when cars are parked.
A strict requirement, because “mandatory” means something must be done.
questions.why: Mandatory means required, not optional.

questions.stem: Match each Concept Vocabulary word from “Mandatory Volunteer Work for Teenagers” with its meaning: “mandatory,” “propensity,” “extracurricular,” “allocate,” and “grudgingly.”

pairs.right: to give out for a particular purpose

questions.why: These words help you argue about rules, time, and choices.

questions.stem: The young scientist has a propensity for staying up late into the night to observe the stars through her telescope. Does the word propensity describe a one-time event or a habitual behavior?
options: A one-time event, because she looked through the telescope on only one special night of the year.
A habitual behavior, because a propensity is a kind of telescope.
A one-time event, because scientists never stay up late more than once.
A habitual behavior, because a propensity is a natural tendency to do something often.
questions.why: A propensity is a habit or natural tendency.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Wearing a helmet is mandatory at the bike park,” the word “mandatory” means optional.
questions.why: Mandatory means required.

questions.stem: Hessa joined the chess club, which is her favorite ____ activity after school.
questions.why: Clubs after school are extracurricular activities.

questions.stem: The school offers a robotics club and a choir that meet on Saturday mornings, outside of the standard Monday through Friday schedule. Are these activities considered part of the core curriculum or extracurricular?
options: Core curriculum, because they meet on Saturday when all students must attend.
Extracurricular, because they meet outside the regular school schedule.
Extracurricular, because robotics and singing are not useful skills at all.
Core curriculum, because every subject taught at a school is part of it.
questions.why: Activities outside regular class time are extracurricular.

questions.stem: Is each school activity “mandatory” or optional for most students?

rows.text: taking the final math exam
joining the drama club
attending classes on school days
entering the school poetry contest

questions.why: Mandatory activities are required; optional ones are chosen.

questions.stem: The city will ____ more money to build parks in neighborhoods that have none.
questions.why: To allocate money is to set it aside for a purpose.

questions.stem: The principal had twenty new laptops and had to allocate them among the five different grade levels in the school. Would you say the principal gathered the laptops for herself or assigned them to specific groups?
options: She assigned them, because to allocate means to share something out for a purpose.
She gathered them for herself, because the laptops were brand new and very expensive.
She assigned them, because she sold the laptops to the five grade levels.
She gathered them for herself, because principals need many computers.
questions.why: To allocate is to give out shares to different groups.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe someone acting “grudgingly”? Choose two.
options: Laila happily offered her umbrella to a friend in the rain.
Rania frowned as she shared the last piece of cake with her cousin.
Turki sighed loudly and slowly picked up his toys after his mother asked three times.
Omar cheerfully volunteered to clean the classroom board.
questions.why: Doing something grudgingly means doing it unwillingly.

questions.stem: After his brother won the coin toss, Sam grudgingly handed over the front seat of the car, though he scowled and muttered to himself the whole way. Does the word grudgingly suggest that Sam gave up the seat willingly or reluctantly?
options: Willingly, because he handed over the front seat to his brother.
Reluctantly, because he never wanted to ride in the car at all that day.
Willingly, because he was happy that his brother won the coin toss.
Reluctantly, because he scowled and muttered while giving up the seat.
questions.why: Grudgingly means reluctantly, as shown by scowling and muttering.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “Our cat has a propensity for sleeping in sunny spots. Every afternoon, she moves from window to window to follow the sunlight.” What does “propensity” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “Our cat has a propensity for sleeping in sunny spots. Every afternoon, she moves from window to window to follow the sunlight.” What does “propensity” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: a type of bed

options.label: B
options.text: a single surprise

options.label: C
options.text: a fear of something

options.label: D
options.text: a natural habit or tendency

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the sentences best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “sunny spots”

options.label: B
options.text: “Our cat”

options.label: C
options.text: “Every afternoon”

options.label: D
options.text: “the sunlight”

questions.why: Doing something every afternoon shows a habit, or propensity.

questions.stem: The teacher had to ____ the twenty minutes of class time so each group could present its project.
questions.why: Dividing time among groups is allocating it.

questions.stem: True or false: A student who grudgingly does his chores is excited and eager to help.
questions.why: Grudgingly means unwillingly, not eagerly.

questions.stem: Sort “allocation,” “propensity,” “allocate,” “mandatory,” and “extracurricular” by part of speech.

rows.text: allocation
propensity
allocate
mandatory
extracurricular

questions.why: Nouns name things, verbs show actions, and adjectives describe.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “allocate” correctly?
options: Please allocate your shoes neatly by the door before you enter.
The tired camel allocated under a palm tree to rest its long legs.
Majed allocated loudly when his team scored the winning goal.
The club will allocate two hours each week to practicing robotics.
questions.why: Allocate means to set aside time or resources for a purpose.

questions.stem: Which TWO activities are “extracurricular”? Choose two.
options: a weekend football team run by the school
questions.why: Extracurricular activities take place outside regular classes.

questions.stem: Although he wanted to keep playing, Yazan ____ turned off the game when his father called him to dinner.
questions.why: Stopping something you want to keep doing is done grudgingly.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “propensity,” “allocate,” or “mandatory” that best fits it.

pairs.left: Every visitor must wear a hard hat on the building site.
My little brother always tends to lose his pencils.
The coach split the water bottles among the three teams.

questions.why: Each sentence shows the meaning of one word.

questions.stem: True or false: Someone with a propensity for drawing tends to draw often and naturally.
questions.why: A propensity is a natural tendency.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence: “Because swimming lessons are ____ at this school, every sixth grader must pass the pool test.”
questions.why: “Must pass” shows the lessons are required, or mandatory.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about school clubs: “Our school offers many extracurricular clubs. This year, the principal will allocate a new room for the science club. Joining any club is mandatory, so students can choose freely.”
segments: Our school offers many extracurricular clubs.
This year, the principal will allocate a new room
questions.why: If students choose freely, joining is optional, not mandatory.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “grudgingly” correctly.

segments.text: After losing the bet, Hamad grudgingly washed his brother's bike.
The puppy grudgingly wagged its tail when it saw its favorite treat.
Noor grudgingly accepted the prize she had always dreamed of winning.
The children grudgingly cheered as the holiday began.

questions.why: Washing a bike after losing a bet is done unwillingly.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: optional is to mandatory as willingly is to ____.
questions.why: Optional is the opposite of mandatory, and willingly is the opposite of grudgingly.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “mandatory”?

rows.text: required
compulsory
optional
voluntary

questions.why: Mandatory means required; voluntary means freely chosen.

questions.stem: “Extracurricular” is made of “extra-” (outside) + “curricular” (the regular course of study). Which word uses the prefix “extra-” with the same meaning?
options: extremely (to a very great or unusual degree)
questions.why: Extraterrestrial means outside the Earth, just as extracurricular means outside regular classes.

questions.stem: Put these steps in order for how a school would “allocate” money for its clubs.
sequence: Find out how much money the school has.
Decide which clubs need money most.
Allocate a set amount to each club.
Clubs spend the money on supplies.
questions.why: Allocating comes after deciding needs and before spending.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “propensity” correctly? Choose two.
options: Kareem has a propensity to laugh when he is nervous.
We walked to the propensity to buy fresh bread.
The propensity of the box was made of hard cardboard.
Desert foxes have a propensity for hunting at night.
questions.why: A propensity is a tendency to act a certain way.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this sentence about a beach cleanup: “The volunteers grudgingly smiled and sang happy songs as they eagerly collected every bottle on the shore.”
questions.why: Happy songs and eager work do not match grudgingly.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: “Some people argue that community service should be ____ for teenagers, while others believe it only means something when it is freely chosen.”
questions.why: The contrast with “freely chosen” shows the word means required.

questions.stem: The hallway in the old basement was only five feet high, so the tall teacher had to stoop just to get to the other side. If the teacher had kept his back perfectly straight and his head held high, would he still be stooping?
options: Yes, because a tall teacher is always stooping wherever he goes.
Yes, because walking through any basement hallway always counts as stooping.
No, because stooping means walking quickly without stopping.
No, because to stoop means to bend the body forward and down.
questions.why: To stoop is to bend forward and down, not to stand straight.

questions.stem: Match each Concept Vocabulary word from “The Treasure of Lemon Brown” with its meaning: “stoop,” “impromptu,” “tentatively,” “involuntary,” and “commence.”
questions.why: These words help describe how people move and act.

questions.stem: The graduation speaker lost her notes on the way to the stage, so she had to give an impromptu speech using only the ideas in her head. Was this a planned and rehearsed speech?
options: Yes, because she used ideas that were already in her head.
No, because an impromptu speech is given without any preparation.
Yes, because she was the graduation speaker, so she must have practiced it.
No, because she read every single word from her lost notes.
questions.why: Impromptu means done without planning or rehearsal.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Grandfather had to stoop to pick up the dropped date,” the word “stoop” means to bend down.
questions.why: To stoop is to bend the body down.

questions.stem: The school play will ____ at seven o'clock, so please be in your seats by then.
questions.why: Commence means to begin.

questions.stem: The hiker wasn't sure if the fallen log was strong enough to hold his weight, so he tentatively tapped it with his toe before stepping on it. Did the hiker move with full confidence and speed?
options: Yes, because he stepped onto the log right after tapping it.
No, because “tentatively” means in a careful, unsure way.
No, because he was too tired to lift his foot very high.
Yes, because experienced hikers never worry about fallen logs.
questions.why: Tentatively means carefully and without confidence.

questions.stem: Is each action “involuntary” or voluntary?

rows.text: sneezing when dust gets in your nose
raising your hand to answer a question
blinking when a bright light flashes
choosing a book at the library

questions.why: Involuntary actions happen without choosing them.

questions.stem: Laila had not planned to sing, but her friends cheered until she gave an ____ performance of her favorite song.
questions.why: A performance given without planning is impromptu.

questions.stem: When the cold wind blasted into the room, Sarah gave an involuntary shiver that made her shoulders shake. Did Sarah decide to shiver to show people she was cold?
options: Yes, because shaking your shoulders is always something you plan to do.
No, because she was not really cold when the wind blew in.
No, because an involuntary action happens without a person choosing it.
Yes, because she wanted everyone in the room to close the window.
questions.why: Involuntary means not chosen or controlled.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe someone moving “tentatively”? Choose two.
options: The new student peeked into the classroom and slowly stepped inside.
The confident diver leaped straight off the high board.
Fahad sprinted across the field and jumped over the hurdle.
Sara touched the hot pan's handle lightly before picking it up.
questions.why: Moving tentatively means moving carefully and unsurely.

questions.stem: The referee blew the loud silver whistle to signal that the championship game was finally ready to commence. Does this mean the game is about to start?
options: Yes, because the whistle was loud and made of shiny silver.
No, because the referee blew the whistle to stop a player.
No, because “commence” means to end, so the game is over.
questions.why: Commence means to begin or start.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The kitten stepped tentatively onto the ice. It tested each spot with one paw and pulled back at every crack.” What does “tentatively” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The kitten stepped tentatively onto the ice. It tested each spot with one paw and pulled back at every crack.” What does “tentatively” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: quickly and boldly

options.label: B
options.text: carefully and without confidence

options.label: C
options.text: loudly and angrily

options.label: D
options.text: happily and playfully

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the sentences best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “tested each spot with one paw”

options.label: B
options.text: “stepped”

options.label: C
options.text: “onto the ice”

options.label: D
options.text: “The kitten”

questions.why: Testing each spot shows careful, unsure movement.

questions.stem: To fit through the low tent opening, the camper had to ____ and crawl inside.
questions.why: To get through a low opening, you stoop.

questions.stem: True or false: An impromptu party is one that is carefully planned months ahead.
questions.why: Impromptu means unplanned.

questions.stem: Sort these forms of “involuntary,” “commence,” and “tentatively” by part of speech.

rows.text: commencement
commence
involuntarily
tentatively

questions.why: The suffix -ment makes a noun, and -ly often makes an adverb.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “commence” correctly?
options: Please commence the light switch before you leave the room tonight.
The baker commenced the cake into eight equal and tasty slices.
Our teacher commenced the dusty window with a damp cloth.
The swimming race will commence when the starter fires the signal.
questions.why: A race can commence, or begin.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “impromptu” correctly? Choose two.
options: The coach gave an impromptu talk after the surprise victory.
The impromptu speech had been practiced every night for a month.
When the power went out, the family held an impromptu picnic on the roof.
The impromptu exam had been announced three weeks earlier.
questions.why: Impromptu events happen without planning.

questions.stem: Hearing the sudden thunder, the baby gave an ____ jump in her mother's arms.
questions.why: A startled jump happens without choosing, so it is involuntary.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “stoop,” “tentatively,” or “impromptu” that fits it.

pairs.left: Grandmother bent down to pick a flower.
Nora whispered her answer, unsure if it was right.
The boys made up a game on the spot with an empty can.

questions.why: Each sentence shows one word's meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: Yawning when you are tired is often an involuntary action.
questions.why: Yawning usually happens without choosing it.

questions.stem: Which choice is the most formal way to fill the blank: “The graduation ceremony will ____ at nine o'clock.”
questions.why: Commence is a formal word for begin.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about a museum tour: “The museum tour will commence at ten. Visitors must stoop to enter the low doorway of the old mud house. Inside, the guide gives an involuntary talk, made up on the spot, about life long ago.”
segments: The museum tour will commence at ten.
Visitors must stoop to enter the low doorway of the old mud house.
Inside, the guide gives an involuntary talk,
made up on the spot, about life long ago.
questions.correction: Inside, the guide gives an impromptu talk,
questions.why: A talk made up on the spot is impromptu, not involuntary.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “stoop” correctly.

segments.text: The old man had to stoop to tie his shoelace.
The rocket will stoop high into the sky tonight.
Rana stooped the song loudly in music class.
We stooped the car at the gas station.

questions.why: Bending down to tie a shoelace is stooping.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: begin is to commence as unplanned is to ____.
questions.why: Commence means begin, and impromptu means unplanned.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “tentatively”?

rows.text: hesitantly
cautiously
boldly
confidently

questions.why: Tentatively means hesitantly; boldly means the opposite.

questions.stem: The prefix “in-” in “involuntary” means “not.” Which word uses “in-” with the same meaning?
questions.why: Invisible means not visible, just as involuntary means not voluntary.

questions.stem: Put these events of a school show in order, from before it would “commence” to its end.
sequence: The audience takes their seats.
The host announces that the show will commence.
The performers act out the first scene.
The audience claps at the final bow.
questions.why: A show commences after people are seated and ends with the bow.

questions.stem: Which TWO actions are usually “involuntary”? Choose two.
options: hiccuping after drinking water too quickly
your heart beating faster during a race
writing your name on a test
tying your shoes before a run
questions.why: Involuntary actions happen by themselves.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this sentence about Yousef's first swim: “Afraid of the deep water, Yousef stepped impromptu into the pool, holding the rail and testing each step.”
segments: Yousef stepped impromptu into the pool,
questions.correction: Yousef stepped tentatively into the pool,
questions.why: Careful, unsure steps are taken tentatively.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: “Instead of rushing up the dark staircase, Maher climbed ____, stopping on every step to listen for sounds.”
questions.why: Stopping on every step shows he climbed tentatively.

questions.stem: After finishing his homework, the student felt calm and slightly relieved, then quietly went to bed. Would you say the student was ecstatic?
options: No, because he went to bed, and people who sleep cannot feel happy.
No, because “ecstatic” means extremely happy and excited, not just calm.
Yes, because finishing homework always makes every single student feel ecstatic.
Yes, because feeling slightly relieved is the same as being ecstatic.
questions.why: Ecstatic means overjoyed, which is much stronger than calm or relieved.

questions.stem: Match each Concept Vocabulary word from “The Day I Saved a Life” with its meaning: “ecstatic,” “keystone,” “conceded,” “vivisection,” and “lobbying.”

pairs.right: the central part that holds everything together
operating on living animals for research

questions.why: These words help you discuss feelings, science, and laws.

questions.stem: In a stone arch, one central stone at the top supports all the others and keeps the structure from falling apart. Would you describe this stone as the keystone?
options: No, because the stone at the top of the arch supports nothing at all.
Yes, because a keystone is the central stone that holds an arch together.
No, because a keystone is any small stone lying at the bottom of an old wall.
Yes, because a keystone is a stone that is used to make a key.
questions.why: A keystone is the top central stone that locks an arch in place.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Reem was ecstatic when she won first place in the national math competition,” the word “ecstatic” means very disappointed.
questions.why: Ecstatic means extremely happy.

questions.stem: Fans were ____ when their team scored the winning goal in the final minute.
questions.why: A last-minute win makes fans ecstatic.

questions.stem: During an argument, one person stopped talking and walked away without admitting the other person was right. Would you say the person conceded the argument?
options: Yes, because walking away from an argument always means you have lost it.
Yes, because he stopped talking, which is the same as agreeing completely.
No, because to concede means to admit that the other person is right.
No, because he was the one who was right the whole time.
questions.why: Conceding means admitting the other side is right, which he did not do.

questions.stem: Does each sentence show someone who “conceded” or not?

rows.text: After checking the map, Ali admitted his sister had chosen the right road.
Huda kept insisting she was right even after seeing the answer key.
The chess player tipped over his king and admitted the game was lost.
Majed refused to admit the ball had gone out.

questions.why: To concede is to admit something is true or that you have lost.

questions.stem: Bees are a ____ of many farms, because without them, lots of fruit trees could not grow fruit.
questions.why: A keystone is the part everything else depends on.

questions.stem: Scientists study animal behaviour by observing animals in their natural habitat without harming or cutting them. Would this be considered vivisection?
options: Yes, because any kind of scientific animal study is called vivisection.
Yes, because watching animals in their natural habitat always harms them.
No, because vivisection means cutting into living animals for research.
No, because vivisection means studying only plants in a laboratory.
questions.why: Vivisection involves operating on living animals; watching them is not vivisection.

questions.stem: Which TWO activities are examples of “lobbying”? Choose two.
options: A group of doctors meets with government officials to support a new food-safety rule.
A family waits in a hotel lobby for their room key.
Students vote for a class president in their classroom.
Farmers write letters to officials asking for a rule to protect water wells.
questions.why: Lobbying means trying to persuade officials about rules or laws.

questions.stem: A group regularly meets lawmakers and writes formal letters to influence how a new law will be written. Would you describe this activity as lobbying?
options: Yes, because lobbying means meeting friends to talk about the weather.
Yes, because lobbying means trying to influence lawmakers' decisions.
No, because lobbying means waiting in the front hall of a large building.
No, because writing formal letters is not a way to share any opinions.
questions.why: Lobbying is working to influence the people who make laws.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “At first, Sami argued that the Moon makes its own light. After his teacher showed him how sunlight reflects off it, he finally conceded the point.” What does “conceded” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “At first, Sami argued that the Moon makes its own light. After his teacher showed him how sunlight reflects off it, he finally conceded the point.” What does “conceded” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: argued more loudly

options.label: B
options.text: asked a new question

options.label: C
options.text: admitted something was true

options.label: D
options.text: forgot what he said

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the sentences best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the Moon makes its own light”

options.label: B
options.text: “his teacher”

options.label: C
options.text: “At first, Sami argued”

options.label: D
options.text: “After his teacher showed him how sunlight reflects off it”

questions.why: After seeing the evidence, Sami admitted he was wrong.

questions.stem: The environmental group spent months ____ city officials to build more bike lanes.
questions.why: Trying to persuade officials is lobbying.

questions.stem: True or false: A keystone is an unimportant piece that can be removed without any effect.
questions.why: A keystone holds everything together, so removing it causes collapse.

questions.stem: Sort “concession,” “concede,” “ecstatic,” and “vivisection” by part of speech.

rows.text: concession
concede
ecstatic
vivisection

questions.why: The suffixes -sion and -tion make nouns.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “ecstatic” correctly?
options: Bandar felt ecstatic and gloomy when his favorite toy broke into small pieces.
The children were ecstatic when the first rain of the year finally fell.
The ecstatic rock lay quietly at the bottom of the dry riverbed.
Mona was ecstatic because she had to wait three hours at the clinic.
questions.why: Ecstatic fits a moment of great joy.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “keystone” to mean “the most important part that holds something together”? Choose two.
options: The keystone of the cake was a cherry on top.
Faisal lost the keystone to his front door.
The goalkeeper was the keystone of the team's defense.
Honesty is the keystone of a strong friendship.
questions.why: A keystone is the central support that everything depends on.

questions.stem: The two chess players shook hands after one player ____ that the other had played better.
questions.why: Admitting the other played better is conceding.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “ecstatic,” “lobbying,” or “vivisection” that fits it.

pairs.left: Some people question whether operating on living animals for research is right.
Volunteers met officials to ask for a law protecting sea turtles.
Huda jumped and shouted with joy when she heard the news.

questions.why: Each sentence describes one word's meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: Someone who is lobbying is trying to persuade officials to make or change a rule.
questions.why: Lobbying means trying to influence lawmakers or officials.

questions.stem: Which word shows the greatest amount of happiness?
questions.why: Ecstatic means extremely happy, stronger than pleased or content.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this paragraph about sea otters: “Sea otters are a keystone species because they keep sea urchins from eating kelp forests. A conservation group has been lobbying lawmakers to protect them. After many meetings, the lawmakers were ecstatic that the otters needed protection.”
segments: Sea otters are a keystone species
because they keep sea urchins from eating kelp forests.
A conservation group has been lobbying lawmakers to protect them.
After many meetings, the lawmakers were ecstatic
questions.correction: After many meetings, the lawmakers conceded
questions.why: After being persuaded, lawmakers concede, or admit, a point.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses “vivisection” correctly.

segments.text: Many countries have strict rules that limit vivisection on living animals.
We enjoyed a vivisection of fresh oranges at lunch.
The vivisection of the song was loud and cheerful.
Lina painted a colorful vivisection on her bedroom wall.

questions.why: Vivisection is operating on living animals, which is controlled by rules.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: denied is to conceded as miserable is to ____.
questions.why: Denied is the opposite of conceded, and miserable is the opposite of ecstatic.

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “ecstatic”?

rows.text: overjoyed
thrilled
miserable
heartbroken

questions.why: Ecstatic means overjoyed; miserable means the opposite.

questions.stem: “Vivisection” comes from the Latin roots “vivi” (alive) and “sect” (cut). Which word shares the root “sect” with the same meaning?
options: select (to choose carefully from a group)
questions.why: Dissect means to cut apart, just like the “sect” in vivisection.

questions.stem: Put these feelings in order from calmest to most excited, showing where “ecstatic” fits.
sequence: calm
pleased
excited
ecstatic
questions.why: Ecstatic is the strongest feeling of joy.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use a form of “concede” correctly? Choose two.
options: The happy crowd conceded loudly when the fireworks began.
After seeing the evidence, the scientist conceded that her first idea was wrong.
Grandmother conceded the rice for twenty minutes.
The runner conceded that his opponent was faster on the final lap.
questions.why: To concede is to admit that something is true.

questions.stem: Find the misused word in this sentence about a class campaign for a crosswalk: “Our class spent weeks keystone the city council for a crosswalk near the school, and we were ecstatic when it was built.”
segments: for a crosswalk near the school,
and we were ecstatic when it was built.
questions.why: Trying to persuade a council is lobbying.

questions.stem: Choose the best word: “Fresh water is the ____ of life in an oasis; without it, the palms, birds, and travelers would all disappear.”
questions.why: Everything in the oasis depends on water, so water is the keystone.

questions.stem: A soldier carried a long stick made of wood for hiking during training. Would you say the soldier was carrying a bayonet?
options: Yes, because a bayonet is a wooden walking stick that soldiers use on long hikes.
Yes, because anything long that a soldier carries during training is called a bayonet.
No, because soldiers are never allowed to carry anything at all while they train.
No, because a bayonet is a metal blade fixed to the end of a rifle, not a stick.
questions.why: A bayonet is a long blade attached to the end of a rifle.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “bayonet,” “distraught,” “eerie,” “imposing,” and “integration.”

pairs.right: a blade fixed to the end of a rifle
bringing separate groups together as equals

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you understand the word in any sentence.

questions.stem: After losing her dog, the girl cried uncontrollably and could not focus on anything else. Would you say the girl was distraught?
options: No, because a person can only feel distraught about schoolwork and exams, not pets.
Yes, because she was so upset that she could not think about anything else.
Yes, because she was busy and focused on finding a new pet as quickly as possible.
No, because crying that much shows she was calm and had accepted the loss.
questions.why: Distraught means so upset and worried that you cannot think clearly.

questions.stem: Standing before Masmak Fortress in Riyadh, the students looked up at its thick mud walls and huge wooden door. The fortress looked so ____ that they all felt very small.
questions.why: Something imposing is large and impressive and makes people feel small.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The empty market was eerie at night, with only the wind rattling the shutters,” the word “eerie” means strange and a little frightening.
questions.why: Eerie describes a place or feeling that is strange in a frightening way.

questions.stem: The abandoned house was silent, covered in fog, and made everyone feel uneasy. Would you describe the house as eerie?
options: Yes, because the house was large and had been painted in bright colors.
No, because only a person, not a building, can ever be described as eerie.
Yes, because the silence and fog made it feel strange and frightening.
No, because an eerie place must be loud, bright, and full of people.
questions.why: Silence, fog, and an uneasy feeling are signs of an eerie place.

questions.stem: Is each place described in a way that is “eerie” or not eerie?

rows.text: A dark cave where water drips and strange echoes answer every footstep.
A sunny park full of families sharing a picnic.
A silent, foggy harbor where an empty boat drifts with no one aboard.
A busy classroom where students laugh during a group game.

questions.why: Eerie places feel strange, lonely, and a little frightening.

questions.stem: When her little brother went missing at the crowded mall for ten minutes, Mama was ____ until a guard found him near the fountain.
questions.why: A worried mother searching for her child is distraught.

questions.stem: The small, broken fence was easy to step over and did not attract attention. Would you describe the fence as imposing?
options: No, because a fence can be imposing only when it is painted a very dark color.
Yes, because every fence is imposing since it is built to keep people from entering.
Yes, because a broken fence is dangerous and can easily hurt anyone who steps over it.
No, because something imposing is large and impressive, and this fence was small.
questions.why: Imposing describes something big and impressive that gets attention.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “distraught,” “imposing,” or “integration” that it describes.

pairs.left: The lost hiker's family paced and wept all night.
The new tower rose sixty floors above the city.
Students from twelve countries joined one robotics team and worked as equals.

questions.why: Each sentence gives a clue to one word's meaning.

questions.stem: Students from different backgrounds were brought together to learn and work in the same classroom. Would you say this situation shows integration?
options: No, because integration happens only in math class when students solve problems.
No, because integration means keeping each group in its own separate room.
Yes, because the classroom was clean and all of the desks were in neat rows.
Yes, because different groups were brought together to learn as one class.
questions.why: Integration means bringing different groups together as equal members.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show “integration”? Choose two.
options: The club welcomed new members from every neighborhood, and all of them voted on decisions.
The library kept old books and new books on separate shelves.
Each group of fans sat in its own section and never mixed with the others.
After the two schools merged, students who once studied apart now shared classes and teams.
questions.why: Integration joins groups together; keeping them apart is the opposite.

questions.stem: The old ____ in the history museum was a sharp steel blade that soldiers once fixed to the end of their rifles.
questions.why: A bayonet is the blade fixed to the end of a rifle.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who calmly finishes a puzzle while humming a song could be described as distraught.
questions.why: Distraught means extremely upset, not calm and happy.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “imposing” correctly?
options: The imposing kitten curled up inside a small shoebox and fell asleep.
The imposing mountain rose high above the tiny village below it.
The imposing pebble slipped easily into my pocket.
Her imposing whisper was so soft that nobody heard a word.
questions.why: Imposing fits something large and impressive, like a mountain.

questions.stem: Decide whether each person is “distraught” or calm.

rows.text: Khalid paces the hospital hallway, unable to sit still while he waits for news.
Reem reads quietly on the balcony as the sun sets.
After the flood ruined their home, the family wept and could not decide what to do.
The pilot spoke slowly and steadily as she landed the plane.

questions.why: Distraught people are too upset to stay calm or think clearly.

questions.stem: Which word is the closest synonym for “eerie”?
questions.why: Spooky and eerie both mean strange and frightening.

questions.stem: The city's plan for the ____ of the two bus systems will let riders use one card on every route.
questions.why: Integration means combining parts into one whole.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “imposing”? Choose two.
questions.why: Grand and majestic are synonyms; modest and unimpressive are opposites.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Even the brave guards grew quiet in the eerie silence of the empty tomb,” what does “eerie” mean?

partA.stem: In the sentence “Even the brave guards grew quiet in the eerie silence of the empty tomb,” what does “eerie” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: strange and frightening

options.label: B
options.text: short and sudden

options.label: C
options.text: warm and peaceful

options.label: D

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Even brave people became quiet and uneasy.

options.label: D
options.text: The silence lasted for a long time.

questions.why: If even brave guards grow uneasy, the silence must be strange and frightening.

questions.stem: Which word describes the MOST intense feeling of being upset?
questions.why: Distraught is the strongest; the others describe milder feelings.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a history museum, then correct it.
segments: In the history museum, we saw an old rifle with a bayonet fixed to its end.
The guide explained the long struggle for integration in schools.
Then we walked into a dim hall with eerie music and flickering lights.
The tiny, imposing display case held only a single coin.
questions.correction: The tiny, modest display case held only a single coin.
questions.why: Something tiny cannot be imposing; modest fits a small case.

questions.stem: Both “big” and “imposing” can describe a building, but “imposing” also suggests ____.
questions.why: Imposing has a connotation of impressive size and power.

questions.stem: Read: “The newcomers felt more at home once the town's integration program paired each family with a local family.” What does “integration” mean in this sentence?

partA.stem: Read: “The newcomers felt more at home once the town's integration program paired each family with a local family.” What does “integration” mean in this sentence?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: bringing people into a community as full members

partB.stem: Which phrase from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “paired each family with a local family”

options.label: B
options.text: “The newcomers”

options.label: C
options.text: “the town's”

options.label: D
options.text: “program”

questions.why: Pairing newcomers with local families brings them into the community.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “distraught” is used correctly.

segments.text: The distraught farmer smiled as he harvested his best crop ever.
The distraught traveler searched every bag for her missing passport, close to tears.
The distraught breeze cooled the garden on a calm evening.
Ali felt distraught after winning first prize and hugging his friends.

questions.why: A traveler close to tears over a lost passport is distraught.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy. joyful : distraught :: separation : ____
questions.why: Joyful and distraught are opposites, and so are separation and integration.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a desert night, then correct it.
segments: The campfire had burned low, and the dunes were silent.
A strange howl drifted across the sand, making the night feel eerie.
My little cousin grew distraught and grabbed my arm.
Our uncle laughed, lit a bayonet, and said the sound was only a fox.
questions.correction: Our uncle laughed, lit a lantern, and said the sound was only a fox.
questions.why: A bayonet is a blade, so it cannot be lit; a lantern can.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “bayonet,” “eerie,” or “integration” correctly? Choose three.
options: The integration of new students went smoothly thanks to the buddy program.
She spread eerie butter on her warm toast.
The empty stadium felt eerie after the lights went out.
The bayonet sang a lovely song at the festival.
Integration means keeping each team in a separate building.
The soldier attached the bayonet to his rifle before the parade.
questions.why: Each correct sentence matches the word's real meaning.

questions.stem: When the two neighborhood clubs combined, the ____ was so smooth that, after a month, no one remembered which club a player had come from.
questions.why: Integration is the joining of groups into one.

questions.stem: Sort each sentence by the meaning of “imposing” it shows.

rows.text: The imposing palace gates were three times taller than a man.
The council is imposing a fine on drivers who park on sidewalks.
The imposing granite statue towered over the square.
The coach was imposing a strict bedtime before the final match.

questions.why: As an adjective, imposing means grand; as a verb form, it means forcing a rule or cost.

questions.stem: A student walked into a dark room, turned on the light immediately, and picked up the book from the desk. Would you say the student groped for the book?
options: No, because a person can only grope for something outdoors, never inside a room.
No, because the student could see the book and did not have to feel around for it.
Yes, because the student picked up the book by hand, which is exactly what groping means.
Yes, because walking into any dark room always means that a person is groping.
questions.why: To grope is to feel around blindly for something you cannot see.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “groped,” “reveal,” “institution,” “confounding,” and “sentiment.”

pairs.right: a long-lasting organization such as a school or hospital

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you understand the word in any sentence.

questions.stem: The magician slowly lifted the cloth, and the hidden object could finally be seen by the audience. Would you say the magician revealed the object?
options: Yes, because the magician made the hidden object disappear from the stage.
No, because the magician moved the cloth slowly instead of pulling it away fast.
No, because to reveal something means to hide it under a cloth or cover.
Yes, because the magician uncovered the object so the audience could see it.
questions.why: To reveal is to show something that was hidden.

questions.stem: During the power cut, Huda ____ along the wall for the light switch, sliding her hands slowly across the cool paint.
questions.why: Feeling along a wall in the dark is groping.

questions.stem: True or false: King Saud University, which has taught students for many decades, can be called an institution.
questions.why: A university is a long-lasting organization, so it is an institution.

questions.stem: A small group of friends met after school to work on a science project for one week. Would you call this group an institution?
options: No, because a small group that meets for one week is not a long-lasting organization.
Yes, because any group of friends that meets after school is called an institution.
Yes, because the group worked on a science project, and science is an institution.
No, because an institution must always have fewer than three people in it.
questions.why: An institution is an established organization that lasts a long time.

questions.stem: Is each example an “institution” or not?

rows.text: The National Museum in Riyadh
Two cousins playing catch in the yard
A city hospital that has served patients for fifty years
A one-time picnic with neighbors

questions.why: Institutions are established organizations, not short, casual activities.

questions.stem: When the archaeologists brushed away the sand, they ____ an ancient clay pot that had been buried for centuries.
questions.why: Brushing away sand reveals, or uncovers, what was hidden.

questions.stem: The math problem included unclear instructions and extra information that made students unsure how to solve it. Would you describe the problem as confounding?
options: No, because math problems can never be confounding if they include numbers.
Yes, because the problem was printed on the very first page of the math test.
No, because a confounding problem is one that is very short and simple to solve.
Yes, because the unclear and extra details left students confused about what to do.
questions.why: Confounding means confusing or puzzling.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “groped,” “reveal,” or “sentiment” that fits it.

pairs.left: Nora's thank-you card expressed her love for her teacher.
The diver felt along the dark sea floor for his dropped watch.
The scientist will finally show the results of her experiment tomorrow.

questions.why: Each sentence gives a clue to one word's meaning.

questions.stem: The sentence states a fact: “Water freezes at 0°C.” Would you say this sentence expresses a sentiment?
options: Yes, because water is important, so any sentence about it shows a feeling.
No, because a sentiment must always be written as a question, not a statement.
Yes, because every sentence that has a number in it expresses a sentiment.
No, because the sentence states a fact and does not express a feeling.
questions.why: A sentiment is a feeling or opinion, not a fact.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences express a “sentiment”? Choose two.
options: Our class believes that kindness matters more than winning.
I feel proud every time I see our flag raised at school.
The Red Sea lies between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula.
questions.why: Sentiments share feelings or opinions; the others state facts.

questions.stem: The instructions for the new board game were so ____ that even Grandfather, who loves puzzles, scratched his head and gave up.
questions.why: Instructions that confuse even a puzzle lover are confounding.

questions.stem: True or false: A student who keeps a secret locked in her diary and tells no one has revealed it.
questions.why: Keeping a secret hidden is the opposite of revealing it.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “reveal”?
questions.why: To conceal is to hide, the opposite of to reveal.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe someone who “groped” or someone who did not?

rows.text: In the dark tent, Sami felt around the floor for his flashlight.
Under the bright lamp, Lina picked up her pen at once.
With his eyes covered for the game, Fahad reached out blindly for the wall.
Noura spotted her keys on the table and grabbed them.

questions.why: Groping means searching with your hands when you cannot see.

questions.stem: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “Yesterday, the sudden change in plans ____ everyone at the meeting.”
questions.why: “Yesterday” calls for the past tense, confounded.

questions.stem: Grandmother's letters are full of warm ____, like her hope that the family will always stay close.
questions.why: Hopes and loving feelings are sentiments.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms of “confounding”? Choose two.
questions.why: Puzzling and baffling both mean confusing.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Feeling his way through the hall, the firefighter groped for the door handle,” what does “groped” mean?

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: B
