options.label: C
options.text: “the firefighter”

options.label: D
options.text: “through the hall”

questions.why: “Feeling his way” shows he was searching by touch.

questions.stem: Which word best describes a problem that keeps people confused even after they study it for a long time?
questions.why: Confounding stresses confusion; challenging only means hard.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a hospital visit, then correct it.
segments: Our class visited the city hospital, an institution that has cared for patients for eighty years.

She then revealed shelves of old medical tools.
Each tool had a clear label in Arabic, which we found confounding.
questions.correction: Each tool had a clear label in Arabic, which we found helpful.
questions.why: Clear labels are not confusing, so confounding does not fit.

questions.stem: Keeping her grandfather's old watch is ____ for Maha; it reminds her of the stories he told her.
questions.why: Sentimental is the adjective form of sentiment and describes things tied to feelings.

questions.stem: In the sentence “At first the strange symbols on the ancient stone were confounding, but after weeks of study the scholar finally understood them,” what does “confounding” mean?

partA.stem: In the sentence “At first the strange symbols on the ancient stone were confounding, but after weeks of study the scholar finally understood them,” what does “confounding” mean?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.why: Needing weeks to understand the symbols shows they were confusing.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “reveal” is used correctly.

segments.text: The fog began to reveal the city, hiding every tower from view.
Lifting the lid will reveal the cake we baked for Mother.
Please reveal your secret by never telling anyone.
The thick curtain will reveal the stage by covering it.

questions.why: Lifting a lid shows what is underneath, which is revealing.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy. hide : reveal :: clear : ____
questions.why: Hide and reveal are opposites; clear and confounding are opposites.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a school library, then correct it.
segments: The school library is an institution that every student depends on.

Its colorful map of the world was confounding at first, but we soon understood it.
Then the lights went out, and I sentiment along the shelf for my book.
questions.correction: Then the lights went out, and I groped along the shelf for my book.
questions.why: Feeling for a book in the dark is groping, not a sentiment.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “institution,” “sentiment,” or “confounding” correctly? Choose three.
options: The old hospital is an institution that the whole town trusts.
She wore a sentiment around her neck at the party.
The confounding riddle kept us guessing all afternoon.
His words revealed a deep sentiment of gratitude toward his parents.
The bright sun was confounding, so we saw everything clearly.
My two friends and I started an institution for one afternoon.
questions.why: Each correct sentence matches the word's real meaning.

questions.stem: Many people share the ____ that clean neighborhoods make happier communities.
questions.why: A shared opinion or feeling is a sentiment.

questions.stem: Sort each sentence by the meaning of “institution” it shows.

rows.text: The university is a respected institution of learning.

She works at a research institution in Jeddah.
The yearly family trip to the farm has become an institution.

columns.text: an organization such as a school or hospital

questions.why: Institution can name an organization or a custom that has lasted a long time.

questions.stem: The coach shook the player's hand and said, “Good job,” after the game. Would you say the coach anointed the player?
options: No, because a handshake is not a ceremony that blesses or officially chooses someone.
No, because only the players who lose a game can be anointed by their coach.
Yes, because shaking hands after a game is exactly the same thing as anointing a player.
Yes, because to anoint means to praise a person loudly in front of a big crowd.
questions.why: To anoint is to put oil on someone in a ceremony, or to formally choose someone for an honor.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “anoint,” “meticulously,” “pungent,” “react,” and “vow.”

pairs.right: to put oil on in a ceremony or to choose for an honor
with great care for every detail

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you understand the word in any sentence.

questions.stem: Before submitting the project, the student checked every detail carefully, fixing even small mistakes. Would you say the student worked meticulously?
options: Yes, because checking every detail and fixing small mistakes shows great care.
No, because a student can work meticulously only on art, not on projects.
Yes, because the student handed in the project before the teacher asked.
No, because working meticulously means finishing quickly without checking anything.
questions.why: Meticulously means with great attention to every detail.

questions.stem: The smell of the fish market was so ____ that we could notice it from the parking lot.
questions.why: A smell strong enough to notice from far away is pungent.

questions.stem: True or false: When Yousef makes a vow to visit his grandmother every Friday, he is making a serious promise.
questions.why: A vow is a serious promise.

questions.stem: The flower had a very light smell that could barely be noticed. Would you describe the smell as pungent?
options: No, because pungent describes only how something looks, not how it smells.
Yes, because pungent describes any smell that is light, sweet, and pleasant.
Yes, because every flower has a pungent smell, even when it is very hard to notice.
No, because a pungent smell is strong and sharp, and this smell was very light.
questions.why: Pungent smells are strong and sharp, not light.

questions.stem: Is each smell “pungent” or mild?

rows.text: freshly chopped raw onions
a bowl of plain cooked rice
strong vinegar spilled on the counter
a soft cotton towel just out of the cupboard

questions.why: Pungent smells are sharp enough to sting the nose.

questions.stem: Ahmad ____ to the surprising news by jumping up and cheering.
questions.why: Jumping and cheering is how he responded, or reacted.

questions.stem: When the fire alarm rang, the students quickly stood up and followed the teacher outside. Would you say the students reacted to the alarm?
options: No, because students can react only to things they see, not things they hear.
No, because reacting means staying seated and waiting for more information.
Yes, because they responded to the alarm right away by standing up and leaving.
Yes, because the teacher had already told them to stand up long before the alarm rang.
questions.why: To react is to respond to something that happens.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “pungent,” “vow,” or “react” that it shows.

pairs.left: Saeed promised solemnly never to give up on his studies.
The garlic sauce had a sharp smell that filled the kitchen.
The cat jumped back when the balloon popped.

questions.why: Each sentence gives a clue to one word's meaning.

questions.stem: The student casually said, “Maybe I'll try harder next time,” and then laughed. Would you say the student made a vow?
options: No, because a vow must always be written down and signed by a teacher first.
Yes, because saying the word “maybe” about the future always counts as a vow.
No, because a vow is a serious promise, and the student spoke casually and laughed.
Yes, because a vow is any sentence that a person says right before laughing.
questions.why: A vow is serious; a casual “maybe” is not a promise.

questions.stem: Which TWO actions are done “meticulously”? Choose two.
options: Before the flight, the pilot checked every switch and gauge on a list.
The calligrapher shaped each letter slowly, checking every curve.
Badr threw his clothes into the suitcase in two minutes.
The painter splashed paint quickly across the wall, missing several spots.
questions.why: Meticulous work is slow, careful, and checks every detail.

questions.stem: At the graduation ceremony, the students made a ____ to use their knowledge to help their community.
questions.why: A serious promise at a ceremony is a vow.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who glances at a math test for a few seconds and turns it in has checked it meticulously.
questions.why: Checking meticulously takes time and careful attention.

questions.stem: Which word is the best synonym for “pungent”?
questions.why: A pungent smell is sharp and strong.

questions.stem: Does each sentence show a “vow” or a casual remark?

rows.text: “I promise with all my heart to protect this garden for as long as I live.”
“Maybe I'll clean my room later, if I feel like it.”
The new team captain swore to lead the players fairly and honestly.
“I might try the new café sometime,” Lama said with a shrug.

questions.why: A vow is a serious, solemn promise.

questions.stem: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The jeweler is ____; she checks every stone with a magnifying glass.”
questions.why: After “is,” the sentence needs the adjective meticulous.

questions.stem: The judges ____ the young poet as the brightest new voice of the year, giving her the festival's top award.
questions.why: To anoint someone can mean to choose them for a special honor.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms of “vow”? Choose two.
questions.why: A pledge and an oath are serious promises, like a vow.

questions.stem: In the sentence “When the teacher dropped a beaker, the class reacted with a loud gasp,” what does “reacted” mean?

questions.why: The gasp was the class's response to the dropped beaker.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “The spice market's ____ air made Omar's eyes water.”

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about Grandmother's kitchen, then correct it.
segments: Grandmother cooked meticulously, measuring each spice with a tiny spoon.

When my brother tasted the sauce, he reacted with a happy grin.

questions.correction: The faint smell of the plain boiled rice was so light that we hardly noticed it.
questions.why: A smell we hardly notice is faint, not pungent.

questions.stem: “Strong-smelling” is a neutral description, but calling a cheese “pungent” suggests that its smell is ____.
options: sharp enough to sting the nose
too weak to notice at all
questions.why: Pungent suggests a sharp, stinging strength.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Rania worked meticulously on her model of the solar system: she measured every planet twice and repainted any ring that was uneven,” what does “meticulously” mean?

partA.stem: In the sentence “Rania worked meticulously on her model of the solar system: she measured every planet twice and repainted any ring that was uneven,” what does “meticulously” mean?

options.text: “she measured every planet twice”

options.label: C
options.text: “her model of the solar system”

questions.why: Measuring everything twice shows careful attention to detail.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “react” is used correctly.

segments.text: Plants react to sunlight by bending toward it.
The mountain will react tomorrow at noon for the picnic.
Please react the book to the library by Thursday.
My uncle reacts a new car every five years.

questions.why: Plants respond, or react, to sunlight.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy. promise : vow :: careful : ____
questions.why: A vow is a stronger promise; meticulous is a stronger form of careful.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a science lab, then correct it.
segments: Our teacher warned us that some chemicals react quickly with water.

One mixture gave off a pungent smell, so we opened the windows.
At the end, we vowed the beakers with soap and water.
questions.correction: At the end, we washed the beakers with soap and water.
questions.why: A vow is a promise; beakers are washed, not vowed.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “pungent,” “vow,” or “meticulously” correctly? Choose three.
options: The engineer meticulously measured the bridge with a quick guess.
The chef seasoned the soup with a pungent spice.
The kitten was so pungent that it purred all day.
The doctor meticulously cleaned the wound before bandaging it.
I vow that I might help, or maybe not.
The scouts made a vow to always help people in need.
questions.why: Each correct sentence matches the word's real meaning.

questions.stem: Scientists observe how different metals ____ when they are placed in salty water.
questions.why: Metals respond, or react, to salty water.

questions.stem: Sort each sentence: is “anoint” used with its literal meaning or its figurative meaning?

columns.text: Literal: put oil or ointment on

questions.why: Literally, anoint means to put oil on; figuratively, it means to choose someone for an honor.

questions.stem: The dog ran straight toward the open field, leaping with energy and excitement. Would you say the dog bounded across the field?
options: No, because only kangaroos and rabbits can bound, and dogs never can.
Yes, because the field was wide open and had no fences around it at all.
Yes, because the dog moved forward with big, energetic leaps across the field.
No, because bounding means walking slowly and carefully while on a leash.
questions.why: To bound is to move forward with leaps and jumps.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “bound,” “contemplate,” “deliberately,” “retrieve,” and “vigorously.”
questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you understand the word in any sentence.

questions.stem: Sarah sat by the window, staring at the sky and thinking carefully about her decision to join the science club. Would you say Sarah was contemplating her choice?
options: No, because a person can contemplate only while talking aloud with others.
No, because contemplating means looking at the sky to predict the weather.
Yes, because she was thinking deeply and carefully about her decision.
Yes, because she was sitting by a window, and that is all the word means.
questions.why: To contemplate is to think deeply about something.

questions.stem: The hikers rested halfway up the steep ____ before climbing to the top of the hill.
questions.why: A steep slope on a hill is an incline.

questions.stem: True or false: If Nasser breaks a glass on purpose, he broke it deliberately.
questions.why: Deliberately means on purpose.

questions.stem: Tom knocked over the vase accidentally while running through the living room. Would you say he did it deliberately?
options: No, because deliberately describes only things done slowly at night.
No, because he knocked it over by accident, not on purpose.
Yes, because deliberately means that something breaks into pieces.
Yes, because running always makes things happen on purpose.
questions.why: Something done deliberately is done on purpose, not by accident.

questions.stem: Was each action done “deliberately” or by accident?

rows.text: Maha chose the blue paint because it matched the sky in her picture.
Faris tripped on a rock and dropped his water bottle.
The goalkeeper stepped left to block the shot he expected.
A gust of wind blew Huda's homework off the table.

questions.why: Deliberate actions are planned; accidents are not.

questions.stem: Our dog loves to ____ the ball and bring it straight back to us.
questions.why: To retrieve is to fetch something and bring it back.

questions.stem: During the hike, the trail gradually inclined upward, making the climb a bit harder. Would you say the trail inclined?
options: Yes, because the trail sloped upward, which made the climb harder.
No, because an inclined trail is completely flat and easy to walk.
No, because only roofs and ramps can incline, never hiking trails.
Yes, because the hikers felt tired after walking a long way that day.
questions.why: To incline is to slope upward or downward.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “bound,” “incline,” or “vigorously” that fits it.

pairs.left: The deer leaped across the stream in one great jump.
The road sloped gently up toward the village.
Lulwa scrubbed the pot hard until it shone.

questions.why: Each sentence gives a clue to one word's meaning.

questions.stem: The child threw the ball into the yard, and the dog ran to retrieve it. Would you say the dog retrieved the ball?
options: Yes, because the child threw the ball into the yard deliberately.
No, because retrieving means throwing an object as far as possible.
Yes, because the dog went to get the ball and brought it back.
No, because a dog can retrieve only things that belong to the dog.
questions.why: To retrieve is to go and get something back.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe actions done “vigorously”? Choose two.
options: The sleepy cat stretched slowly on the warm rug.
Grandmother tapped the table gently with one finger.
Dad stirred the thick dough with strong, quick strokes.
The swimmer kicked hard and fast to reach the wall first.
questions.why: Vigorous actions are strong and full of energy.

questions.stem: Before choosing a university, Hessa took a week to ____ her options and talk with her family.
questions.why: Thinking carefully about options is contemplating them.

questions.stem: After hearing the news, Maria shook the bottle of paint vigorously until it mixed completely. Would you say Maria mixed it vigorously?
options: No, because vigorously means moving something very gently and slowly.
Yes, because she heard some news right before she picked up the paint.
No, because people can do things vigorously only while playing sports.
Yes, because she shook the paint with strong, energetic force until it mixed.
questions.why: Vigorously means with strength and energy.

questions.stem: True or false: A person who wants to retrieve a lost phone is trying to throw it away.
questions.why: To retrieve something is to get it back, not throw it away.

questions.stem: Is each person “contemplating” something or not?

rows.text: Ibrahim sat quietly, thinking about whether to join the robotics club or the art club.
Lina laughed as she raced her cousins to the beach.
The scientist studied her notes for an hour, considering every possible explanation.
The baby giggled while splashing in the bath.

questions.why: Contemplating means thinking deeply and carefully.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “deliberately”?
questions.why: Accidentally is the opposite of deliberately; the others mean on purpose.

questions.stem: After the race, the coach asked us to ____ all the cones from the field and return them to the storage room.
questions.why: Collecting the cones and bringing them back is retrieving them.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms of “contemplate”? Choose two.
questions.why: Consider and ponder both mean to think carefully.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The path to the museum entrance has a gentle incline, so visitors in wheelchairs can roll up it easily,” what does “incline” mean?

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.why: Rolling up the path shows that it slopes.

questions.stem: In the sentence “I incline to agree with your plan, but let me read it again,” what does “incline” mean?
questions.why: As a verb, incline can mean to lean toward an opinion.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a puppy at the park, then correct it.
segments: At the park, our puppy bounded across the grass.
I deliberately threw the frisbee toward the top of the hill.
He raced up the steep incline and contemplated the frisbee in seconds.
Then he wagged his tail vigorously as he trotted back to me.
questions.correction: He raced up the steep incline and retrieved the frisbee in seconds.
questions.why: The puppy fetched the frisbee, so retrieved fits; contemplated means thought about.

questions.stem: “On purpose” and “deliberately” mean almost the same thing, but “deliberately” can also suggest that the person acted ____.
questions.why: Deliberately can suggest slow, careful, planned action.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Before answering the difficult question, the judge paused to contemplate the evidence, reading each page twice,” what does “contemplate” mean?

partA.stem: In the sentence “Before answering the difficult question, the judge paused to contemplate the evidence, reading each page twice,” what does “contemplate” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: throw away quickly

options.label: B
options.text: read aloud

options.label: C
options.text: think about carefully

options.label: D
options.text: hide from others

partB.stem: Which phrase from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the difficult question”

options.label: B
options.text: “Before answering”

options.label: C
options.text: “reading each page twice”

options.label: D
options.text: “the judge”

questions.why: Reading every page twice shows careful thinking.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “vigorously” is used correctly.

segments.text: The tired runner vigorously sat still on the bench.
The team cheered vigorously when the final whistle blew.
She vigorously whispered so no one would wake.
The snail moved vigorously, barely an inch an hour.

questions.why: Loud, energetic cheering is done vigorously.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy. throw : retrieve :: lose : ____
questions.why: Retrieve means get back what was thrown; recover means get back what was lost.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a gymnastics class, then correct it.
segments: Coach Reem asked us to warm up vigorously before practice.
Lamees bounded onto the mat with a big smile.
She deliberately chose a hard routine to challenge herself.
Before starting, she retrieved each move in her mind for a moment.
questions.correction: Before starting, she contemplated each move in her mind for a moment.
questions.why: Thinking about moves is contemplating, not retrieving.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “retrieve,” “incline,” or “bound” correctly? Choose three.
options: The fisherman retrieved his net from the sea at sunrise.
She retrieved the ball across the field with a strong kick.
The road inclines sharply as it climbs the mountain.
The flat parking lot has a steep incline.
The goat bounded from rock to rock.
Ali deliberately forgot his keys by accident.
questions.why: Each correct sentence matches the word's real meaning.

questions.stem: The doctor told Grandfather to exercise ____ for thirty minutes a day, walking fast enough to raise his heart rate.
questions.why: Exercise that raises the heart rate is done vigorously.

questions.stem: Sort each sentence by the meaning of “bound” it shows.

rows.text: The puppy bounded down the hallway to greet us.
The old books were bound with leather string.
If you keep practicing, you are bound to improve.
The gazelle bounded over the rocks.

questions.why: Bound can mean to leap, to be tied, or to be sure to happen.

questions.stem: The climbers reached the top of the mountain after hours of hiking through strong winds and rocky paths. Would you say the climbers conquered the mountain?
options: Yes, because they overcame the wind and rocky paths to reach the top.
Yes, because the climbers hiked in a group instead of climbing alone.
No, because only armies can conquer, and mountains cannot be conquered.
No, because to conquer means to give up before reaching a goal.
questions.why: To conquer is to overcome something difficult.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “conquer,” “crinkly,” “desert,” “master,” and “pine.”
questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you understand the word in any sentence.

questions.stem: Grandma handed me a letter with crinkly edges that looked like it had been folded many times. Would you say the edges of Grandma's letter are crinkly?
options: Yes, because folding the paper many times left small wrinkles and creases.
Yes, because Grandma handed the letter to me herself, and she wrote it.
No, because only plastic bags can be crinkly, never paper or letters.
No, because crinkly means smooth, flat, and brand new like fresh paper.
questions.why: Crinkly means covered in small wrinkles or creases.

questions.stem: Maryam practiced the oud every day for three years until she could ____ even the hardest songs.
questions.why: To master something is to gain complete skill in it.

questions.stem: True or false: A student who pines for summer vacation is longing for it.
questions.why: To pine for something is to long for it.

questions.stem: During lunch, Leo left his sandwich untouched for a few minutes before taking a bite. Would you say Leo deserted his lunch?
options: Yes, because deserted means eating something very quickly and happily.
No, because deserting means hiding food so that nobody else can find it.
Yes, because leaving food untouched for any amount of time means deserting it.
No, because Leo left his lunch for only a few minutes and did not abandon it.
questions.why: To desert is to abandon something and not come back.

questions.stem: Does each person or animal “desert” something or stay with it?

rows.text: The captain stayed on the ship until every passenger was safe.
The guard left his post and never came back.
Rakan kept helping his team even after they lost three games.
The birds abandoned the nest after the storm destroyed it.

questions.why: To desert is to leave something behind for good.

questions.stem: The old map was so ____ from years of being folded that Father had to smooth it out on the table.
questions.why: A map with many folds and wrinkles is crinkly.

questions.stem: After months of practice, Sofia could play the violin perfectly without looking at the sheet music. Would you say Sofia mastered the violin?
options: No, because months of practice show that she still had not learned it.
No, because to master an instrument a person must teach it to others first.
Yes, because she could play perfectly, which shows she gained full skill.
Yes, because she owned a violin and also had a copy of the sheet music.
questions.why: To master something is to gain complete skill in it.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “conquer,” “merit,” or “pine” that fits it.

pairs.left: Hassan finally overcame his fear of speaking in front of the class.
The judges praised the science project for its real value and quality.
Far from home, the student longed for her mother's cooking.

questions.why: Each sentence gives a clue to one word's meaning.

questions.stem: Jamal received a certificate for being helpful, responsible, and always kind to his classmates. Would you say Jamal earned merit for his actions?
options: No, because merit is a punishment given to students who break the rules.
Yes, because merit means getting a certificate without doing anything.
Yes, because his helpful and kind actions deserved praise and a reward.
No, because a person can earn merit only by winning a sports competition.
questions.why: Merit is the quality of deserving praise or reward.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe someone who “pines” for something? Choose two.
options: Omar enjoys his new school and rarely thinks about the old one.
Every night, the lonely puppy waits by the door for its owner to return.
Since moving to Canada, Majed misses the warm evenings in Jeddah and often dreams of them.
Sara forgot about her old toy as soon as she got a new one.
questions.why: Pining means longing for someone or something that is gone.

questions.stem: Ever since Max's best friend moved to another city, he pined for the days when they played soccer together after school. Would you say Max is pining for his friend?
options: No, because a person can pine only for a place, not for a friend.
Yes, because Max and his friend both enjoyed playing soccer together.
No, because pining means feeling glad that a friend has moved away.
Yes, because he keeps longing for the time he spent with his friend.
questions.why: To pine is to long for someone or something you miss.

questions.stem: With hard work and patience, the team was able to ____ the steep dunes of the Empty Quarter.
questions.why: To conquer a hard climb is to overcome it.

questions.stem: True or false: A smooth sheet of paper straight from a new pack is crinkly.
questions.why: Crinkly paper has wrinkles; new paper is smooth.

questions.stem: Does each person show “merit” or not?

rows.text: Dana volunteered every weekend to tutor younger students.
Waleed copied a classmate's homework and handed it in.
The engineer designed a cheaper way to clean water for villages.
Jumana skipped practice and blamed her teammates for losing.

questions.why: Merit comes from actions that deserve praise.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “desert” when it means “to leave someone behind”?
questions.why: Support is the opposite; abandon, forsake, and leave are synonyms.

questions.stem: Nawaf's essay was chosen for the prize because of its ____: it was clear, well-researched, and original.
questions.why: Being clear, researched, and original gives work merit.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms of “conquer”? Choose two.
questions.why: Overcome and defeat mean the same as conquer.

questions.stem: In the sentence “After weeks in the hospital, the boy pined for the fresh air of his family's farm,” what does “pined” mean?

partA.stem: In the sentence “After weeks in the hospital, the boy pined for the fresh air of his family's farm,” what does “pined” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: complained about

options.label: B
options.text: forgot about

options.label: C
options.text: was allergic to

options.label: D
options.text: longed for

partB.stem: Which phrase from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the fresh air”

options.label: B
options.text: “After weeks in the hospital”

options.label: C
options.text: “his family's”

options.label: D
options.text: “the boy”

questions.why: Being away from the farm for weeks explains why he longed for it.

questions.stem: In which sentence does “desert” mean “to abandon”?
options: The desert sand grows very cold after the sun goes down.
A true friend will never desert you when times are hard.
Camels can travel across the desert for days without water.
Many desert plants store water in their thick leaves.
questions.why: As a verb, desert means to abandon; as a noun, it means a dry land.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about Grandfather's old letter, then correct it.
segments: My grandfather keeps a crinkly old letter in his desk.
He wrote it to his father while learning to master carpentry in another city.
In it, he says he pined for home but would never desert his training.
He promised to merit every challenge until he succeeded.
questions.correction: He promised to conquer every challenge until he succeeded.
questions.why: Challenges are conquered, or overcome; merit means deserved worth.

questions.stem: Both “learn” and “master” describe gaining a skill, but “master” suggests ____.
options: a skill that is quickly lost
questions.why: Master suggests learning something completely.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Although she was the youngest player, Leen was chosen as captain on merit, not because her uncle was the coach,” what does “on merit” mean?

partA.stem: In the sentence “Although she was the youngest player, Leen was chosen as captain on merit, not because her uncle was the coach,” what does “on merit” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: because she deserved it

options.label: B
options.text: because no one else wanted it

options.label: C
options.text: because she was youngest

options.label: D
options.text: because of her family

partB.stem: Which phrase from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “was chosen as captain”

options.label: B
options.text: “Although”

options.label: C
options.text: “not because her uncle was the coach”

options.label: D
options.text: “she was the youngest player”

questions.why: The sentence rules out family help, so she was chosen because she deserved it.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “master” is used as a verb meaning “to learn completely.”

segments.text: The ship's master gave orders to the crew.
It takes years to master Arabic calligraphy.
The master bedroom is at the end of the hall.
This painting is the work of a master.

questions.why: Only “to master Arabic calligraphy” uses master as a verb meaning to learn completely.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy. smooth : crinkly :: stay : ____
questions.why: Smooth and crinkly are opposites; stay and desert are opposites.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about learning to swim, then correct it.
segments: At first, I was afraid of deep water.
I pined for the day I could swim like my older sister.
Every afternoon, I practiced until I began to master the backstroke.
By the end of summer, I had crinkled my fear and swam across the pool.
questions.correction: By the end of summer, I had conquered my fear and swam across the pool.
questions.why: Fears are conquered, not crinkled.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “desert,” “crinkly,” or “merit” correctly? Choose three.
options: Grandmother's crinkly hands kneaded the bread dough.
The lifeguard would never desert her post while children were swimming.
Lina deserted the cake by eating every bite.
She pined the door closed with a key.
The crinkly glass window was perfectly smooth.
His idea has merit, so let's test it.
questions.why: Each correct sentence matches the word's real meaning.

questions.stem: Before she can drive alone, Aunt Noura must ____ the rules of the road.
questions.why: To master rules is to learn them completely.

questions.stem: Sort each sentence by the meaning of “pine” it shows.

rows.text: The pine trees on the mountain stay green all winter.
She began to pine for the sea after moving inland.
The table was made of pine from a northern forest.
The homesick student pined for his family's garden.

questions.why: Pine can name a tree or mean to long for something.

questions.stem: During the class discussion, Sam listened to everyone's opinions, even when he disagreed, and spoke respectfully to all classmates. Would you say Sam was being bigoted?
options: No, because a person can be bigoted only when speaking to adults, not classmates.
Yes, because he disagreed with some classmates, and disagreeing makes a person bigoted.
No, because he respected everyone's opinions instead of unfairly rejecting them.
Yes, because a bigoted person is someone who listens carefully during class.
questions.why: A bigoted person unfairly refuses to accept people or ideas that are different.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “bigoted,” “bond,” “coincide,” “hostile,” and “participate.”

pairs.right: to happen at the same time

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you understand the word in any sentence.

questions.stem: After working together on the science project for weeks, the two students trusted each other and became close friends. Would you say the students formed a bond?
options: No, because working on a project together always makes students dislike each other.
No, because a bond can form only between family members who live together.
Yes, because the science project was due at the end of several weeks.
Yes, because working together built trust and a close connection between them.
questions.why: A bond is a close connection built on trust.

questions.stem: Every student in the class will ____ in the beach cleanup on Saturday.
questions.why: To participate is to take part in an activity.

questions.stem: True or false: If the football final and Ahmad's birthday fall on the same day, the two events coincide.
questions.why: Events that happen at the same time coincide.

questions.stem: The school trip was scheduled for the same day as the math competition, so both events happened at the same time. Would you say the two events coincided?
options: Yes, because both events were planned by the same school for its students.
No, because events coincide only when one happens right after the other.
No, because coincide means two events were canceled for the same reason.
Yes, because the trip and the competition happened on the same day.
questions.why: To coincide is to happen at the same time.

questions.stem: Is each group “hostile” or friendly?

rows.text: The neighbors brought dates and coffee to welcome the new family.
The angry crowd shouted insults at the visiting team's bus.
The guard dog growled and bared its teeth at every stranger.
The shopkeeper smiled and helped the lost child find her parents.

questions.why: Hostile behavior is unfriendly and aggressive.

questions.stem: The two sisters share a strong ____; they tell each other everything and always help one another.
questions.why: A close connection between people is a bond.

questions.stem: When the new student arrived, the class welcomed her with smiles and offered to help her find her classroom. Would you say the class was hostile toward the new student?
options: No, because the class was friendly and welcoming, not unfriendly or angry.
Yes, because any class that meets a new student for the first time is hostile.
Yes, because welcoming a new student with smiles is a hostile action.
No, because only animals, not people, can ever behave in a hostile way.
questions.why: Hostile means unfriendly, the opposite of welcoming.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “bigoted,” “coincide,” or “participate” that fits it.

pairs.left: The man refused to hire anyone from a different town, no matter how skilled.
The solar eclipse happened at the same moment as the school assembly.
Yara joined the debate team and argued in every round.

questions.why: Each sentence gives a clue to one word's meaning.

questions.stem: During the group activity, Amina shared her ideas, helped her teammates, and completed her assigned task. Would you say Amina participated in the activity?
options: No, because participating means watching quietly without helping at all.
Yes, because she took an active part by sharing ideas and doing her task.
No, because a person participates only when they are the group's leader.
Yes, because she was in the same room while the group activity happened.
questions.why: To participate is to take an active part.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe someone who is “bigoted”? Choose two.
options: He enjoys meeting people from many cultures.
She judges people unfairly because of the way they speak.
She changes her mind when someone shows her good evidence.
He refuses to listen to anyone whose family comes from a different country.
questions.why: Bigoted people judge others unfairly for being different.

questions.stem: Because the meeting will ____ with my dentist appointment, I cannot attend both.
questions.why: Two events that happen at the same time coincide.

questions.stem: True or false: Someone who cheers for the other team and shakes their players' hands is being hostile.
questions.why: Cheering and shaking hands are friendly, not hostile.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “hostile”?
questions.why: Friendly is the opposite of hostile; the others are similar in meaning.

questions.stem: Does each student “participate” or not?

rows.text: Majed raised his hand and shared his idea in the discussion.
Reem sat at the back and played with her pencil during the game.
Turki helped carry chairs for the school festival.
Hind stayed home and did not join the class trip.

questions.why: Participating means taking an active part.

questions.stem: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “It was a happy ____ that my cousin and I were born on the same day.”
questions.why: After “a happy,” the sentence needs the noun coincidence.

questions.stem: The two countries signed an agreement to stop being ____ and to trade peacefully with each other.
questions.why: Hostile is the opposite of peaceful.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms of “bigoted”? Choose two.
questions.why: Prejudiced and intolerant mean the same as bigoted.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Camping together in the desert for a week created a strong bond between the scouts, who now call each other brothers,” what does “bond” mean?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: a close connection

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: a sharp argument

options.label: B
options.text: “who now call each other brothers”

options.label: C
options.text: “the scouts”

options.label: D
options.text: “created a strong”

questions.why: Calling each other brothers shows a close connection.

questions.stem: Which word best describes a crowd that is openly unfriendly and ready to fight?
questions.why: Hostile describes open unfriendliness; bigoted describes unfair beliefs.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a school sports day, then correct it.
segments: Our school held a sports day that coincided with the national holiday.
Every class participated, from the youngest to the oldest students.
Students from different classes formed a strong bond as they cheered together.
Even the visiting team was hostile, thanking us for the warm welcome.
questions.correction: Even the visiting team was friendly, thanking us for the warm welcome.
questions.why: A team that thanks its hosts is friendly, not hostile.

questions.stem: Calling someone “bigoted” is much stronger than saying they are “unfamiliar with other cultures,” because “bigoted” suggests that the person ____.
questions.why: Bigoted has a strong negative connotation of unfair intolerance.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The two holidays coincide this year, so families will celebrate both on the same weekend,” what does “coincide” mean?

partA.stem: In the sentence “The two holidays coincide this year, so families will celebrate both on the same weekend,” what does “coincide” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: happen at the same time

options.label: B
options.text: get canceled

options.label: C
options.text: become longer

options.label: D
options.text: happen far apart

partB.stem: Which phrase from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “The two holidays”

options.label: B
options.text: “on the same weekend”

options.label: C
options.text: “this year”

options.label: D
options.text: “families will celebrate”

questions.why: Celebrating both on the same weekend shows they happen together.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “participate” is used correctly.

segments.text: All students may participate in the science fair.
The river participated slowly toward the sea.
Please participate the salt into the soup.
My shoes participate under the bed.

questions.why: To participate is to take part, as in a science fair.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy. friendly : hostile :: open-minded : ____
questions.why: Friendly and hostile are opposites; open-minded and bigoted are opposites.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a debate club, then correct it.
segments: Twenty students participate in the debate club each year.
Members learn to disagree politely and are never bigoted toward others.
Over the year, the team develops a close bond.
This year, the final debate will hostile with the school's anniversary.
questions.correction: This year, the final debate will coincide with the school's anniversary.
questions.why: Events that happen at the same time coincide.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “hostile,” “bond,” or “coincide” correctly? Choose three.
options: The two events coincide because one is in May and one is in June.
Both festivals coincide in the month of March.
The hostile dog barked and growled at the mail carrier.
The bond between the twins grew stronger each year.
The bigoted kitten purred in my lap.
She participated the cake into slices.
questions.why: Each correct sentence matches the word's real meaning.

questions.stem: Even though he was new to the team, Rayan chose to ____ fully in every training session.
questions.why: Taking full part in training is participating.

questions.stem: Sort each sentence by the meaning of “bond” it shows.

rows.text: The bond between the mother camel and her calf is very strong.
This glue forms a bond that can hold fifty kilograms.
Shared hard times created a lifelong bond between the teammates.
Atoms in water are held together by chemical bonds.

columns.text: a force that holds things together

questions.why: Bond can mean a connection between people or a physical hold between things.

questions.stem: A short tale explains one single event without any problems, twists, or actions that move the tale forward. Would you say the tale has a plot?
options: Yes, because every tale automatically has a plot, even when nothing at all happens to anyone in it.
No, because a plot can be found only in very long books, never in short tales.
No, because a plot is a series of events with problems and actions, and this tale has none.
Yes, because a plot is only the title and the name of the person who wrote it.
questions.why: A plot is the series of events, problems, and actions that move a narrative forward.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “plots,” “frowned,” “embarrassed,” “mispronouncing,” and “deaf.”

pairs.right: series of events in stories, or secret plans
wrinkled the forehead to show displeasure
feeling awkward or ashamed in front of others
saying a word the wrong way

questions.why: Knowing each meaning helps you understand the word in any sentence.

questions.stem: When the teacher announced a surprise test, the student's eyebrows pulled together and the corners of his mouth turned down. Would you say the student frowned?
options: No, because a person can frown only when they are sick or very tired.
Yes, because pulling the eyebrows together and turning the mouth down is a frown.
Yes, because the teacher announced a test, and surprise tests are always very difficult.
No, because a frown means smiling widely when someone hears good news.
questions.why: To frown is to pull the eyebrows together and turn the mouth down.

questions.stem: Rawan felt ____ when she tripped on the stage in front of the whole school.
questions.why: Tripping in front of others makes a person feel embarrassed.

questions.stem: True or false: A child who says “pasghetti” instead of “spaghetti” is mispronouncing the word.
questions.why: Mispronouncing means saying a word with the wrong sounds.

questions.stem: The student answered the question correctly, and the class clapped for her. She smiled confidently. Would you say the student felt embarrassed?
options: No, because a person can feel embarrassed only when alone at home.
Yes, because people always feel embarrassed when a class claps for them.
No, because she felt proud and confident, not uncomfortable or ashamed.
Yes, because answering a question correctly is an embarrassing mistake.
questions.why: Embarrassed means uncomfortable or ashamed, not confident.

questions.stem: Would each person most likely feel “embarrassed” or proud?

rows.text: Talal's voice cracked loudly in the middle of his presentation.
Afnan's drawing was chosen for the school's front wall.
Bader called his teacher “Mom” by mistake in front of the class.
Lujain finished the race after months of training.

questions.why: Awkward mistakes in front of others cause embarrassment.

questions.stem: Because her grandfather is ____, the family uses sign language and written notes to talk with him.
questions.why: People who cannot hear may use sign language.

questions.stem: While reading aloud, the student said “libary” instead of “library.” Would you say the student was mispronouncing the word?
options: No, because a student who reads aloud can never mispronounce words.
Yes, because the student was reading aloud to the whole class.
No, because mispronouncing means spelling a word wrong on paper.
Yes, because the student said the word with the wrong sounds.
questions.why: Leaving out a sound when saying a word is mispronouncing it.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word “frowned,” “plots,” or “deaf” that fits it.

pairs.left: The coach's brow wrinkled as the team missed another goal.
Mystery novels are full of surprising twists and turns in their events.
After the illness, the old sailor could no longer hear at all.

questions.why: Each sentence gives a clue to one word's meaning.

questions.stem: A person does not hear someone calling because the music is very loud in the room. Would you say the person is deaf?
options: Yes, because loud music makes every person in a room deaf forever.
Yes, because anyone who does not answer a call even one single time is deaf.
No, because deaf means that a person cannot see what is around them.
No, because the person can hear, but the loud music covered the sound.
questions.why: Deaf means unable to hear, not just unable to hear over loud noise.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe someone “mispronouncing” a word? Choose two.
options: Lina read the word “library” slowly and correctly.
Hamad wrote “freind” instead of “friend” on his test.
questions.why: Mispronouncing is about saying a word, not spelling it.

questions.stem: When Dad saw the muddy shoes on the clean carpet, he ____ in disappointment and asked who had walked in from the garden.
questions.why: A disappointed face is a frown.

questions.stem: True or false: A friend who will not listen to any advice can be described as “deaf to advice,” even though she can hear perfectly.
questions.why: Deaf can be used figuratively to mean unwilling to listen.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “frowned”?
questions.why: Smiled is the opposite; the others are similar to frowned.

questions.stem: Is each speaker saying the word correctly or mispronouncing it?

rows.text: Saud says “li-brar-y” for library.
Mona says “nu-cu-lar” for nuclear.
Fares says “ex-press-o” for espresso.
Jood says “pac-i-fic” for specific.

questions.why: Mispronouncing means adding, dropping, or changing sounds.

questions.stem: Which word means almost the same as “embarrassed”?
questions.why: Ashamed and embarrassed both describe uncomfortable feelings in front of others.

questions.stem: The class worked together to write a ____ with a clear problem, rising action, and a surprising ending.
questions.why: A plot has a problem, rising action, and an ending.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms of “frowned”? Choose two.
questions.why: Scowled and grimaced describe unhappy faces, like frowned.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Amal was so embarrassed by her mistake that her cheeks turned red and she stared at the floor,” what does “embarrassed” mean?

partA.stem: In the sentence “Amal was so embarrassed by her mistake that her cheeks turned red and she stared at the floor,” what does “embarrassed” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: angry and loud

options.label: B
options.text: uncomfortable and ashamed

options.label: C
options.text: sleepy and slow

options.label: D
options.text: calm and happy

partB.stem: Which phrase from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “her cheeks turned red and she stared at the floor”

options.label: B
options.text: “the floor”

options.label: C
options.text: “that her”

options.label: D
options.text: “Amal was so”

questions.why: Red cheeks and looking down are signs of embarrassment.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “deaf” in a figurative way?
options: The stubborn coach was deaf to every suggestion from his players.
The doctor tested the child's ears to see whether she was deaf.
The composer kept writing music even after he became deaf.
Many deaf students use sign language to talk with their friends.
questions.why: “Deaf to suggestions” means unwilling to listen, a figurative use.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a reading club, then correct it.
segments: In reading club, we discussed the plots of three adventure books.
Kareem kept mispronouncing a hard name, so the teacher helped him.
He was not embarrassed; he laughed and tried again.
When Sultan arrived late, the teacher deaf at the clock.
questions.correction: When Sultan arrived late, the teacher frowned at the clock.
questions.why: A teacher frowns at the clock; deaf is not an action.

questions.stem: Being “embarrassed” is milder than being “humiliated”; a person who is embarrassed feels ____.
options: a little uncomfortable in front of others
questions.why: Embarrassed is a milder feeling than humiliated.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The two little brothers whispered their plots for surprising their mother on her birthday,” what does “plots” mean?

partA.stem: In the sentence “The two little brothers whispered their plots for surprising their mother on her birthday,” what does “plots” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: secret plans

options.label: B
options.text: points on a graph

options.label: C
options.text: pieces of land

options.label: D
options.text: events in a book

partB.stem: Which phrase from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “The two little brothers”

options.label: B
options.text: “on her birthday”

options.label: C
options.text: “whispered their plots for surprising”

options.label: D
options.text: “their mother”

questions.why: Whispering about a surprise shows the plots are secret plans.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which “deaf” is used correctly.

segments.text: The dog was deaf to the smell of food.
Born deaf, Rashid learned to communicate using sign language.
The deaf painting hung on the wall.
Her voice was too deaf to sing loudly.

questions.why: Deaf describes a person who cannot hear.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy. smile : frown :: proud : ____
questions.why: Smile and frown are opposites; proud and embarrassed are opposites.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this paragraph about a spelling bee, then correct it.
segments: At the spelling bee, Sara was nervous about mispronouncing the words.
When she misspelled “necessary,” she felt embarrassed.
Her coach plotted at her warmly and told her she had done her best.
Sara smiled and promised to practice harder for next year.
questions.correction: Her coach smiled at her warmly and told her she had done her best.
questions.why: Plotted means planned; a warm look is a smile.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use “plots,” “frowned,” or “embarrassed” correctly? Choose three.
options: Rana frowned happily because she was so pleased.
The detective uncovered the thieves' plots before they could act.
The parrot was mispronouncing the color of its feathers.
Grandmother frowned when she saw the broken vase.
The deaf radio played music loudly all day.
Musa felt embarrassed when he forgot his lines during the school show.
questions.why: Each correct sentence matches the word's real meaning.

questions.stem: The new student kept ____ my name until I taught him to say it slowly: “Ha-ya.”
questions.why: Saying a name wrongly is mispronouncing it.

questions.stem: Sort each sentence by the meaning of “plot” it shows.

rows.text: The plot of the novel follows a girl who sails across the Red Sea.
The spies' plot was discovered before they could escape.
The farmer planted palm trees on a narrow plot near the well.
Every good mystery has a plot that keeps readers guessing.

questions.why: Plot can mean a story's events, a secret plan, or a small piece of land.

questions.stem: After the heavy rain, the old mud wall began to crack and then ____ into a pile of dirt.
questions.why: To collapse is to fall down suddenly, which is what a cracked wall does.

questions.stem: “Loose rocks on the mountain road are a hazard for drivers.” What is a hazard?
options: a sign that shows drivers the way
a tool used for fixing roads
a thing that can cause harm
a place for travelers to rest
questions.why: A hazard is something dangerous that can hurt people, like falling rocks.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The river will alter its path after the flood,” the word “alter” means the river will stay exactly the same.
questions.why: To alter means to change, so the river's path will be different.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a valley with the meaning of its multiple-meaning word: “bank,” “drop,” and “face.”

pairs.left: Mud covered the river bank after the storm.
pairs.right: the land along the side of a river

pairs.left: The wind will drop the sand in a new place.
Climbers studied the steep face of the cliff.
pairs.right: the front surface of a rock or mountain

questions.why: A multiple-meaning word gets its meaning from the other words around it.

questions.stem: Is each change to the land in a desert valley a slow change or a fast change?

rows.text: Wind wears down a rock over 100 years.
A landslide rushes down a hill in one minute.
A river carries sand toward the sea for centuries.
A volcano erupts and covers a field with lava.

questions.why: Weathering and erosion take many years, but landslides and eruptions happen quickly.

questions.stem: Under which heading would a reader find out how rock pieces are carried away?
questions.why: The “Erosion” section explains how wind and water carry the pieces away.

questions.stem: Reread the section “Deposition” in “How Wind and Water Change Rock.” Which sentence tells what happens when the wind or water slows down?

segments.text: Deposition is the last step.
The wind or water slows down and drops the pieces in a new location.
A powerful river can move sand and pebbles a long distance from the place where they started.
Rain, ice, and plant roots can crack even the hardest stone over many years.

questions.why: Rereading the section shows that slow wind or water drops the pieces in a new place.

questions.stem: Part A: How is weathering different from erosion?

partA.stem: Part A: How is weathering different from erosion?

options.label: A
options.text: Weathering breaks rock into pieces, but erosion moves the pieces away.

options.label: B
options.text: Weathering moves rock pieces away, but erosion breaks the rock apart.

options.label: C
options.text: Weathering happens only in rivers, but erosion happens only in deserts.

options.label: D
options.text: Weathering is very fast, but erosion takes many years to happen.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Over time, the pieces can build a sandy beach or an enormous dune.

options.label: B
options.text: Erosion happens when wind or moving water carries those pieces away.

options.label: C
options.text: Deposition is the last step.

options.label: D
options.text: All three changes are slow.

questions.why: Weathering breaks the rock; erosion carries the broken pieces away.

questions.stem: Put the three changes from “How Wind and Water Change Rock” in the order they happen to a rock.
sequence: Rain and ice crack the rock into pieces.
Wind or a river carries the pieces away.
The pieces are dropped and build a beach or dune.
questions.why: Rock is broken first (weathering), then moved (erosion), then dropped (deposition).

questions.stem: What does the diagram in “How Wind and Water Change Rock” show? Choose two.
options: a volcano erupting near a small town
people building a wall to stop the wind
wind and a river carrying pieces to a beach
a tall rock breaking into small pieces
questions.why: The diagram shows the rock breaking and the pieces being carried to a beach.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “severe” correctly?
options: The severe sandstorm closed the airport for a whole day.
The kitten was so severe that it purred on my lap.
The severe breeze gently cooled the children at the park.
Ali was severe happy to see his cousins after school.
questions.why: Severe means very strong or serious, like a sandstorm that closes an airport.

questions.stem: Scientists watch volcanoes closely because eruptions can be ____; they sometimes happen with very little warning.
questions.why: Unpredictable means no one can know ahead of time when it will happen.

questions.stem: In each sentence about water in the land, does “spring” mean a place where water comes out of the ground or a season of the year?

rows.text: Travelers filled their bottles at the cool spring.
Wildflowers bloom in the desert in spring.
The oasis gets its water from an underground spring.
Heavy rain sometimes falls in early spring.

questions.why: The other words in the sentence show which meaning of “spring” is used.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about an earthquake drill has an error with a key word?
segments: the students learned that a building can collapsed
so they practiced hiding under their desks.
questions.correction: the students learned that a building can collapse
questions.why: After “can,” use the base form of the verb: “can collapse.”

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe a crisis? Choose two.
options: A flood cuts off the only road to a village, and food runs low.
A family plants new palm trees in their garden after school.
A fire spreads through a market, and hundreds of people must leave fast.
The class plans a trip to the science museum next week.
questions.why: A crisis is a time of great danger or trouble that needs action right away.

questions.stem: Match each key word from a news report about a flood with a detail that shows it: “destruction,” “substantial,” “crisis,” “hazard.”

pairs.right: Houses and roads are broken and ruined.
The water rose by almost two meters.
Families need help right away to stay safe.
A fallen power line lies in the water.

questions.why: Each detail is an example of what the key word means.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences. “The weather in the mountains is unpredictable. A sunny morning can turn into a storm by noon.” What does “unpredictable” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences. “The weather in the mountains is unpredictable. A sunny morning can turn into a storm by noon.” What does “unpredictable” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: very hot and dry all the time

options.label: B
options.text: always the same from day to day

options.label: C
options.text: easy to see from far away

options.label: D
options.text: not able to be known ahead of time

partB.stem: Part B: Which words best help the reader understand “unpredictable”?

options.label: A
options.text: in the mountains

options.label: B
options.text: can turn into a storm by noon

options.label: C
options.text: A sunny morning

options.label: D
options.text: The weather

questions.why: A sunny morning that suddenly becomes a storm shows the weather cannot be known ahead of time.

questions.stem: Which word is the closest synonym of “alter”?
questions.why: To alter something is to change it.

questions.stem: The earthquake caused ____ damage; more than half of the buildings in the town had to be rebuilt.
questions.why: Substantial means large in amount, like damage to half of a town.

questions.stem: Put the steps a town follows to prepare for a flood hazard in a sensible order.
sequence: Scientists measure how fast the river is rising.
Leaders warn families that a flood may come.
Families move to higher ground with emergency bags.
Workers clean up after the water goes down.
questions.why: Monitoring comes first, then warnings, then moving to safety, then cleanup.

questions.stem: Part A: How is creep different from a landslide?

partA.stem: Part A: How is creep different from a landslide?

options.label: A
options.text: Creep is caused by gravity, but a landslide is caused by strong wind.

options.label: B
options.text: Creep happens on flat land, but a landslide happens on steep hills.

options.label: C
options.text: Creep moves soil slowly over years, but a landslide moves it in minutes.

options.label: D
options.text: Creep destroys homes quickly, but a landslide only makes posts lean.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Scientists call this slow movement creep.

options.label: B
options.text: Roads may collapse, and homes can be buried.

options.label: C
options.text: Suddenly, an entire hillside can slide down in less than a minute.

options.label: D
options.text: Both creep and landslides are caused by gravity pulling soil and rock downhill.

questions.why: The landslide happens in less than a minute, while creep takes years.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Two Kinds of Change on a Mountain” that tell how creep and landslides are alike.

segments.text: Both creep and landslides are caused by gravity pulling soil and rock downhill.
A landslide is very different.
Both are more likely on steep slopes with few plants to hold the ground in place.
Families have years to notice the problem and repair their land.

questions.why: Words like “both” signal how two things are alike.

questions.stem: Why did the author include the heading “How They Are Alike”?
options: to introduce a list of ways that families can repair their land
to explain how scientists chose the name for slow movement
to signal that the section explains what the two changes share
to show that the section tells which change is more dangerous
questions.why: Headings tell readers what a section is about, here the ways creep and landslides are alike.

questions.stem: In “Two Kinds of Change on a Mountain,” does each detail describe creep, a landslide, or both?

rows.text: Fence posts begin to lean.
A hillside slides down in less than a minute.
Gravity pulls soil downhill.
Roads may collapse.

questions.why: Sorting details by topic helps readers compare and contrast.

questions.stem: What information does the diagram add to the passage?
options: It explains why plants help hold the soil in place.
It lists the steps for repairing a leaning wall.
It shows the time each change takes, side by side.
It tells where in Saudi Arabia creep usually happens.
questions.why: The labels “years” and “minutes” compare how long each change takes.

questions.stem: The word “rock” has more than one meaning. Which TWO sentences use “rock” as a verb meaning to move back and forth? Choose two.
options: A huge rock rolled onto the mountain road.
Strong waves rock the fishing boats in the harbor.
The small earthquake made the lamps rock on the tables.
Weathering slowly breaks the rock into sand.
questions.why: When “rock” is an action, it means to move back and forth; as a noun it means stone.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short report about a sandstorm.
segments: A severe sandstorm swept across the city.
Strong winds caused substantial damage to signs.
Drivers faced a hazard because they could not see.
The storm was so unpredictable that everyone knew exactly when it would arrive.
questions.correction: The storm was so unpredictable that no one knew when it would arrive.
questions.why: Something unpredictable cannot be known ahead of time, so no one knew when it would come.

questions.stem: The city's quick emergency plan turned a possible ____ into a small problem, and no one was hurt when the dam began to leak.
questions.why: A crisis is a dangerous situation; good planning kept it small.

questions.stem: True or false: “Destruction” and “collapse” both describe things breaking down, but “destruction” is a noun and “collapse” can be used as a verb.
questions.why: Destruction names the damage (noun); collapse can name the action of falling (verb).

questions.stem: Which sentence best contrasts weathering with a volcanic eruption?
options: Weathering and eruptions both happen deep inside the Earth and slowly turn rock into lava.
An eruption is a kind of weathering that happens only near the ocean shore.
Weathering changes rock little by little, while an eruption can alter land in hours.
Weathering is caused by lava cooling, while an eruption is caused by wind and rain.
questions.why: A contrast shows a difference: weathering is slow, but an eruption is fast.

questions.stem: “Sara hesitated before she raised her hand to answer.” What did Sara do?
options: She raised her hand quickly without thinking.
She shouted the answer across the room.
She waited a moment because she was unsure.
She left the classroom to find her teacher.
questions.why: To hesitate is to pause because you are not sure.

questions.stem: When Ahmad saw his sister working hard on her science project, it gave him the ____ to start his own.
questions.why: Inspiration is something that makes you want to do or create something.

questions.stem: Match each idiom about friends and feelings with its meaning: “break the ice,” “butterflies in my stomach,” “see eye to eye.”

pairs.right: start talking in a friendly way

questions.why: An idiom has a meaning different from its exact words.

questions.stem: True or false: If Noor's mother advises her about the talent show, she gives Noor ideas about what to do.
questions.why: To advise someone is to give them helpful ideas or suggestions.

questions.stem: Is each problem a character might face in a school story an internal conflict or an external conflict?

rows.text: Huda cannot decide whether to tell her friend the truth.
A storm cancels the school trip.
Two brothers argue over who gets the bike.
Faris is afraid to sing in front of the class.

questions.why: An internal conflict happens inside a character's mind; an external conflict is with someone or something else.

questions.stem: What is Sara's main conflict in “Lina's Plan”?
options: She cannot find the clay she needs for her camel.
She is angry that Ms. Huda cancelled the art exhibition.
She and Lina disagree about which colors to use.
She wants her own project but is afraid to tell Lina.
questions.why: Sara's problem is inside her: she wants something different but fears hurting Lina.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Lina's Plan” shows that Sara is worried about her friend's feelings?

segments.text: At home, she stared at the lump of clay sitting on her desk, and her stomach felt tight.
If she told Lina the truth, would her friend feel disappointed?
Sara opened her mouth, then closed it again.
The next morning, Lina proudly waved a sketch of the picture in the air.

questions.why: Sara's question shows she is afraid Lina will be disappointed.

questions.stem: Part A: What will Sara most likely do next?

partA.stem: Part A: What will Sara most likely do next?

options.label: A
options.text: show Lina the clay camel and explain her idea

options.label: B
options.text: throw the clay camel away and forget about it

options.label: C
options.text: ask Ms. Huda to choose a project for her

options.label: D
options.text: paint the sky in Lina's picture without a word

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: When Ms. Huda announced the school art exhibition, Lina immediately clapped her hands.

options.label: B
options.text: Lina and Sara had been best friends since the first day of first grade.

options.label: C
options.text: She held her clay camel behind her back and took a deep breath.

options.label: D
options.text: “You can paint the sky,” she announced.

questions.why: Taking a deep breath while holding the camel suggests Sara is getting ready to speak up.

questions.stem: Put these events from “Lina's Plan” in order.
sequence: Ms. Huda announces the school art exhibition.
Lina says they will paint one picture together.
Sara stares at her clay at home and feels worried.
Lina tells Sara she can paint the sky.
questions.why: Following the order of events helps readers understand the plot.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from “Lina's Plan” show that Lina makes decisions for both girls? Choose two.
options: Lina tells Sara that she can paint the sky.
Lina says she has already chosen the colors.
Lina claps her hands at the news.
Lina has been Sara's friend since first grade.
questions.why: Choosing the colors and Sara's part shows Lina deciding for both of them.

questions.stem: Majed felt ____ when he tripped on the stage and everyone laughed, but his friends helped him up and he finished his poem.
questions.why: Humiliated means very embarrassed in front of others.

questions.stem: Which idiom means “to feel too nervous to do something you planned”?
questions.why: To get cold feet is to become too nervous to go ahead with a plan.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about Khalid's costume in the school play has an error?
segments: The new costume was too tight,
questions.why: An adverb like “uncomfortably” describes how someone moves.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences show a character being accountable? Choose two.
options: Bilal promised to bring snacks, so he packed them the night before.
Rana admits she broke the vase and offers to pay for it.
Tala blames her little brother for the mess she made.
Omar forgets his homework and says the dog ate it.
questions.why: Being accountable means taking responsibility for what you do.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences. “Basma desperately wanted to join the art club. She asked the teacher three times and even made a poster to show her skill.” What does “desperately” mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences. “Basma desperately wanted to join the art club. She asked the teacher three times and even made a poster to show her skill.” What does “desperately” mean?

options.label: A
options.text: in a calm and quiet way

options.label: B
options.text: without any interest

options.label: C
options.text: with a very strong need

options.label: D
options.text: in a slow, careful way

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail best helps the reader understand “desperately”?

options.label: A
options.text: She asked the teacher three times.

options.label: B
options.text: She made something.

options.label: C
options.text: She talked to the teacher.

options.label: D
options.text: She wanted to join the art club.

questions.why: Asking three times shows how strongly Basma wanted to join.

questions.stem: Match each clue from a story about a school contest with the most likely prediction.

pairs.left: Nasser practices his speech every night in front of a mirror.
pairs.right: He will speak well at the contest.

pairs.left: Reem hesitated when her friend asked to share the stage.
pairs.right: She feels unsure and may say no.

pairs.left: Hamad forgot to fix his broken guitar string.
pairs.right: He will have trouble during his song.

questions.why: Good predictions use clues about what characters say and do.

questions.stem: Does each sentence about a talent show use an idiom or only literal words?

rows.text: Dana was over the moon when she won.
Dana smiled when she won first place.
Yasir told his friend to break a leg before the show.
Yasir wished his friend good luck before the show.

questions.why: Idioms like “over the moon” do not mean exactly what the words say.

questions.stem: After his grandmother praised his drawings, Tamer's ____ grew, and he finally entered the art contest.
questions.why: Self-esteem is how much you believe in yourself.

questions.stem: Put these plot events about Zain and the poetry contest in order.
sequence: Zain writes a poem for the school poetry contest.
His friend Ali keeps telling him to change every line.
Zain decides to read the poem the way he wrote it.
The judges smile, and Zain and Ali shake hands after the show.
questions.why: A plot moves from the beginning to the conflict, the turning point, and the resolution.

questions.stem: True or false: A character who feels humiliated after a mistake on stage feels proud and happy about what happened.
questions.why: Humiliated means deeply embarrassed, not proud.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the idiom “caught between a rock and a hard place” mean as it is used in the story?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the idiom “caught between a rock and a hard place” mean as it is used in the story?

options.label: A
options.text: stuck under a pile of heavy stones

options.label: B
options.text: facing two choices that both seem difficult

options.label: C
options.text: very excited about a new game

options.label: D
options.text: angry at a friend for a long time

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Then he read the date again.

options.label: B
options.text: Finally, he knocked quietly on his grandfather's door.

options.label: C
options.text: The next morning, Yousef found Majed beside the school gate.

options.label: D
options.text: He loved chess, but playing football for the school had always been his dream.

questions.why: Yousef loves both chess and football, so either choice is hard.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences describe Yousef's internal conflict? Choose two.
options: Coach Adel will not let him join the football team.
He worries that telling the truth will hurt his friendship.
Majed refuses to play chess with anyone else.
He wants to try out for football but does not want to let Majed down.
questions.why: An internal conflict is a struggle inside a character's own mind.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Same Saturday” best helps the reader predict that Yousef will tell Majed the truth?

segments.text: “Tell Majed honestly how you feel,” Grandfather said gently.
The tryouts were on the same Saturday as the city chess tournament.
Majed, his partner on the chess team, was already making confident plans.
That night he could not sleep a wink.

questions.why: Grandfather's advice is a clue that Yousef will speak honestly.

questions.stem: What does the idiom “could not sleep a wink” show about Yousef?
options: He had a cold and kept coughing.
He was excited about the gold cup.
He was too worried to rest.
questions.why: Not sleeping a wink means not sleeping at all, which shows worry.

questions.stem: How does Grandfather's advice affect the plot?
options: It shows that Yousef is angry with his grandfather.
It makes Yousef give up football and stay with chess.
It causes Majed to change the date of the tournament.
It helps Yousef choose to face the problem honestly.
questions.why: The advice leads Yousef to the turning point: speaking from the heart.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about a spelling bee.
segments: Mariam hesitated before spelling the last word.
She remembered her teacher's advise to go slowly.
She spelled it correctly and won the trophy.
questions.correction: She remembered her teacher's advice to go slowly.
questions.why: “Advise” is the verb; “advice” is the noun that names the helpful idea.

questions.stem: Even though Nawaf felt nervous, he refused to let one mistake ruin his ____; he reminded himself of all the songs he had performed well.
questions.why: Remembering past successes protects a person's self-esteem.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an idiom to show that a character is being honest about her feelings?
options: “I need to get this off my chest,” Huda told her friend.
