“The show starts at four o'clock,” Huda told her friend.
“I will paint the sky blue,” Huda told her friend.
“We should practice after school,” Huda told her friend.
questions.why: To get something off your chest means to finally say what you have been feeling.

questions.stem: Which part of speech is each key word from a talent-show story: “inspiration,” “hesitated,” “desperately,” “uncomfortably,” “advise”?

rows.text: inspiration
hesitated
desperately
uncomfortably
advise

questions.why: Many adverbs end in -ly, and many nouns end in -tion.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Faisal was accountable for the team's lost ball, so he searched the field until he found it,” Faisal takes responsibility for the problem.
questions.why: An accountable person accepts responsibility and fixes the problem.

questions.stem: The students sold homemade cookies to raise ____ for a new water cooler at school.
questions.why: Funds are money collected for a purpose.

questions.stem: Match each word with a suffix to its meaning: “helpful,” “careless,” “seller.”
questions.why: The suffix -ful means full of, -less means without, and -er can mean a person who.

questions.stem: True or false: A compassionate shop owner who gives free meals to hungry workers cares about other people.
questions.why: Compassionate means caring about others and wanting to help them.

questions.stem: Which word has a suffix that means “able to be”?
questions.why: The suffix -able means able to be, so washable means able to be washed.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about a juice shop the central idea or a supporting detail?

rows.text: The juice shop helps its neighborhood in many ways.
It gives free juice to hospital workers on Fridays.
It pays students to work during the summer.

questions.why: The central idea is the big point; details are examples that support it.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Businesses Can Be Good Neighbors”?
options: Customers should only shop at big stores.
Older people need to learn to use computers.
Bakeries should give all their bread away.
Helping others can make a business stronger.
questions.why: The author says helping others makes a business stronger, and every section supports that.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Businesses Can Be Good Neighbors” best supports the idea that kindness helps a business earn customers?

segments.text: When customers see a shop helping others, they want to shop there again.
A computer shop offers free weekend classes for older people.
Many grandparents have learned to video call their families.
A business needs to earn money, but it can also help the people around it.

questions.why: This sentence links helping others to customers coming back.

questions.stem: Match each heading in “Businesses Can Be Good Neighbors” with the detail found under it.

pairs.right: A bakery gives extra bread to a food bank.
A computer shop offers free classes.
Customers want to shop there again.

questions.why: Headings tell what each section is about, so they help readers find details.

questions.stem: Part A: Which detail supports the claim that helping others is good for a community?

partA.stem: Part A: Which detail supports the claim that helping others is good for a community?

options.label: A
options.text: Families in need get fresh bread from a bakery.

options.label: B
options.text: A business needs to earn money to survive.

options.label: C
options.text: Customers shop at the same store each week.

options.label: D
options.text: A computer shop sells many new laptops.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Kindness brings in new customers.

options.label: B
options.text: Families in need get fresh bread, and nothing goes to waste.

options.label: C
options.text: A business needs to earn money, but it can also help the people around it.

options.label: D
options.text: When customers see a shop helping others, they want to shop there again.

questions.why: The bread helps families in the community, which supports the claim.

questions.stem: In “Businesses Can Be Good Neighbors,” the author's opinion is that every business should ____.
options: find one way to give back
questions.why: The conclusion states the author's opinion: every business should give back.

questions.stem: The new app that turns old phones into weather stations is an ____ idea that no one had tried before.
questions.why: Innovative means new and creative.

questions.stem: Which TWO words end with a suffix that turns a verb into a noun? Choose two.
questions.why: The suffixes -tion and -ment turn verbs (donate, pay) into nouns.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a bakery's morning routine has an error?
segments: the bakers follow the same routine:
they mix the dough, shape the loaves,
questions.why: Verbs in a list should match: mix, shape, and bake.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Collecting old clothes for every family in the village was a huge undertaking,” the word “undertaking” means a big job that takes a lot of work.
questions.why: An undertaking is a large task or project someone takes on.

questions.stem: Which word uses the suffix -al to mean “having the quality of”?
questions.why: Exceptional means having the quality of an exception, or being unusually good.

questions.stem: Match each word built from “compassion,” “exception,” and “innovate” with its part of speech.
questions.why: Suffixes like -ate, -ly, and -ion change a word's part of speech.

questions.stem: Opening a small food truck that also trains young cooks was an ____ that made money and helped the community.
questions.why: An enterprise is a business or project.

questions.stem: Put the steps in the process a toy company used to donate toys to a children's hospital in order.
sequence: The company asked the hospital what toys the children needed.
Workers set aside one toy from every box sold.
Volunteers packed the toys into gift bags.
Nurses gave the gift bags to the children.
questions.why: A process is a series of steps done in order.

questions.stem: Which choice would be the best heading for a section about how a business raised money for charity?
options: Raising Funds for a Good Cause
Colors of the New Shop Logo
questions.why: A good heading names the main topic of the section.

questions.stem: A paragraph's central idea is “The Riyadh book shop's weekly routine helps both readers and the community.” Which TWO details best support this central idea? Choose two.
options: The walls of the shop are painted a bright green color.
The shop owner was born in a small town by the sea.
Each morning, staff read stories to young children before school.
Every Tuesday, the shop gives free books to a children's library.
questions.why: Supporting details must connect to the central idea, not just describe the shop.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the central idea of “Why Giving Can Be Good Business”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the central idea of “Why Giving Can Be Good Business”?

options.label: A
options.text: Children should buy their shoes from companies in Jeddah.

options.label: B
options.text: Companies must keep all of their money to succeed.

options.label: C
options.text: Big brands always sell more shoes than small companies.

options.label: D
options.text: A business can be successful and kind at the same time.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Some people believe a company must keep every riyal it earns to be successful.

options.label: B
options.text: The company also donated thousands of pairs to schools.

options.label: C
options.text: However, the story of a small sports shoe company in Jeddah shows another path.

options.label: D
options.text: This example proves that a business does not have to choose between profit and kindness.

questions.why: The author's conclusion states the central idea directly.

questions.stem: According to the bar graph, how many more pairs of shoes were sold in 2023 than in 2021?
Select two sentences from “Why Giving Can Be Good Business” that support the idea that customers liked the company's promise.

segments.text: Some people believe a company must keep every riyal it earns to be successful.
Many shoppers liked this idea and chose the company over larger brands.
As the graph shows, sales grew every year after the promise began.
The company also donated thousands of pairs to schools.

questions.why: Shoppers choosing the company and rising sales show customers liked the promise.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the section with the heading “The Numbers Tell the Story”?
options: to describe how the shoes are made in factories
to explain why some people disagree with the author
to give evidence that sales grew after the promise
to compare the prices of shoes at different stores
questions.why: The graph and its section give number evidence for the author's claim.

questions.stem: In “Why Giving Can Be Good Business,” is each statement the author's claim or evidence that supports it?

rows.text: A business does not have to choose between profit and kindness.
The company sold 9,000 pairs in 2023.
The company gave thousands of pairs to schools.
When companies help people, customers reward them.

questions.why: A claim is what the author wants you to believe; evidence is the facts that back it up.

questions.stem: Find the error in this sentence about an exceptional young business owner.
questions.why: The adjective “innovative” describes the business; “innovation” is a noun.

questions.stem: Adding the suffix -ly to “routine” makes “routinely,” so “The shop routinely gives away bread” means the shop gives it away ____.
questions.why: Something done routinely is done regularly as part of a habit.

questions.stem: Which word BEST replaces “very good” in this sentence? “Hessa's plan to sell plants and give the money to a hospital was very good, better than any other plan in the contest.”
questions.why: Exceptional means much better than usual.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The factory will process the dates and pack them into boxes,” the word “process” is a noun that names a series of steps.
questions.why: Here “process” is a verb meaning to prepare or treat something.

questions.stem: Which THREE details would best support the central idea “Compassionate businesses make their communities stronger”? Choose three.
options: A restaurant trains young people who need jobs.
A pharmacy delivers free medicine to elderly neighbors.
A café adds a new flavor of juice.
A clothing store moves to a bigger building.
A market gives its unsold fruit to a shelter.
A toy shop changes the color of its sign.
questions.why: Each supporting detail shows a business helping its community.

questions.stem: The owl sat still on the branch, waiting to ____ on the mouse below.
questions.why: To pounce is to jump suddenly to catch something.

questions.stem: What does the prefix un- mean in the word “unsafe”?
questions.why: The prefix un- means not, so unsafe means not safe.

questions.stem: True or false: A rabbit is the prey of a hawk because the hawk hunts and eats it.
questions.why: Prey is an animal that is hunted by another animal.

questions.stem: Match each animal with the adaptation that helps it survive: polar bear, chameleon, hedgehog.
questions.why: Adaptations are body parts or behaviors that help animals survive.

questions.stem: Does the prefix in each word mean “not” or “again”?

rows.text: unhappy
refill
unable
rebuild

questions.why: The prefix un- means not; re- means again.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Built for the Desert”?
options: Camels are the only desert animals strong enough to walk far across soft, deep sand dunes.
The Arabian desert is hotter than any other place in the world.
The sand cat sleeps in a burrow when the sun is strong.
Desert animals have adaptations that help them live with heat and little water.
questions.why: Every section shows an adaptation that helps an animal survive desert heat or dryness.

questions.stem: Which sentence in “Built for the Desert” explains how the sand cat's large ears help it survive?

segments.text: The sand cat's large ears help it hear prey moving under the sand.
Many animals, such as the sand cat, rest in underground burrows when the sun is strong.
They come out to hunt at night, when the air is much cooler.
These special features are called adaptations.

questions.why: The photo caption tells exactly what the ears do.

questions.stem: Match each heading in “Built for the Desert” with the animal described in that section.
questions.why: Headings help readers find information about each adaptation.

questions.stem: Part A: Which is the best summary of the section “Finding Water”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which is the best summary of the section “Finding Water”?

options.label: A
options.text: Water is easy to find in the desert if animals know where to look.

options.label: B
options.text: The oryx drinks from desert rivers every morning before the heat begins.

options.label: C
options.text: The oryx can live for weeks without drinking because its food gives it water.

options.label: D
options.text: The oryx eats only dry plants and never needs any water at all.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Soft sand is hard to walk on.

options.label: B
options.text: It gets the water it needs from the plants it eats.

options.label: C
options.text: They come out to hunt at night, when the air is much cooler.

options.label: D
options.text: Water is difficult to find in the desert.

questions.why: A summary tells the most important ideas of a section in a few words.

questions.stem: Put the sections of “Built for the Desert” in the order they appear.
sequence: Staying Cool
Finding Water
Moving on Sand
questions.why: Headings show how the article is organized.

questions.stem: The bright colors on some frogs warn birds that the frogs are ____ and will make them sick.
questions.why: Poisonous animals can make others sick, and bright colors warn predators.

questions.stem: Which TWO words have a prefix that means “not”? Choose two.
questions.why: The prefixes un- and non- both mean not.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a spider's web has an error?
segments: When an insect lands in the web,
questions.why: A singular subject like “the spider” needs a verb ending in -s.

questions.stem: Which sentence best summarizes these sentences? “Snowshoe hares have brown fur in summer. In winter, their fur turns white. The white fur matches the snow, so foxes have trouble seeing them.”
options: Snowshoe hares have brown fur during the warm summer months.
Snowshoe hares like snow more than they like summer weather.
Foxes cannot see very well when heavy snow falls on the ground in winter.
The hare's fur changes color with the seasons to hide it from predators.
questions.why: A summary combines the key ideas: the fur changes so predators cannot see the hare.

questions.stem: True or false: The word “extraordinary” uses the prefix extra-, so it means “beyond ordinary,” or very unusual.
questions.why: Extra- means beyond, so extraordinary means beyond the ordinary.

questions.stem: Match each key word from an article about animal survival with an example: “camouflaged,” “vibrations,” “dribbles.”

pairs.right: A green insect sits still on a green leaf.
A snake feels the ground shake as a mouse runs.
Water slowly drips from a thirsty camel's mouth.

questions.why: Each example shows what the key word means.

questions.stem: A cheetah can run 100 kilometers an hour, an ____ speed that no other land animal can match.
questions.why: Extraordinary means far beyond what is usual.

questions.stem: Put the steps of how a camouflaged crab spider catches a bee in order.
sequence: The white spider sits still on a white flower.
A bee lands on the flower to drink nectar.
The bee does not notice the spider.
The spider pounces and catches the bee.
questions.why: The spider's camouflage lets it wait unseen until it can pounce.

questions.stem: Which caption would best go with a photo of a hedgehog rolled into a ball?
options: This photo was taken in a garden on a sunny afternoon last May.
Hedgehogs are small animals that live in many parts of the world.
When it senses danger, a hedgehog rolls up so its spines face out.
Hedgehogs eat beetles, worms, and other small creatures at night.
questions.why: A useful caption explains what the photo shows and why it matters.

questions.stem: True or false: A predator that hunts at night may use its sense of hearing to find prey in the dark.
questions.why: Many night predators, like owls, use hearing to find prey.

questions.stem: Part A: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?

partA.stem: Part A: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?

options.label: A
options.text: Stonefish change color to match the sand on the sea floor.

options.label: B
options.text: Sharks are the most dangerous animals in the Red Sea.

options.label: C
options.text: The octopus is the fastest swimmer on the coral reef.

options.label: D
options.text: Camouflage helps reef animals hide from danger or catch food.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The coral reefs of the Red Sea are full of color, but they are also full of danger.

options.label: B
options.text: The octopus can change the color and pattern of its skin in less than a second.

options.label: C
options.text: When a shark swims near, the octopus can look exactly like a rock or a patch of sand.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether they are hiding from predators or waiting for prey, these animals show how camouflage helps them stay alive.

questions.why: The last sentence pulls together both examples into the central idea.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Masters of Disguise in the Red Sea” that explain how the stonefish uses camouflage to catch prey.

segments.text: The octopus can change the color and pattern of its skin in less than a second.
The stonefish does not change color, but its lumpy body looks like a rock covered with algae.
When a shark swims near, the octopus can look exactly like a rock or a patch of sand.
Small fish swim right up to it, and the stonefish swallows them in a flash.

questions.why: The stonefish looks like a rock, so small fish come close enough to be caught.

questions.stem: What do the photo and caption add to the article?
options: They let the reader see how well the stonefish blends with rocks.
They show how quickly the octopus can change its skin color and pattern.
They explain why sharks swim near the coral reefs.
They show where stonefish lay their eggs.
questions.why: The photo and caption help readers see the camouflage described in the text.

questions.stem: In “Masters of Disguise in the Red Sea,” does each detail describe the octopus, the stonefish, or both?

rows.text: changes the color of its skin
has a lumpy body that looks like a rock
uses camouflage to survive
swallows small fish in a flash

questions.why: Sorting details helps readers see how the two animals are alike and different.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences belong in a summary of “Masters of Disguise in the Red Sea”? Choose two.
options: The stonefish's shape helps it hide and catch fish.
A shark is a large fish with sharp teeth.
The Red Sea reefs are full of bright colors.
The octopus changes color to look like rocks or sand.
questions.why: A summary keeps the important ideas and leaves out small details.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in this short paragraph about a desert snake.
segments: The horned viper hides under the sand.
Only its eyes show, so it is camouflaged.
When a lizard walks by, the snake feels its vibrations.
Then the viper pounces and becomes the prey.
questions.correction: Then the viper pounces and catches its prey.
questions.why: The viper is the predator; the lizard it catches is the prey.

questions.stem: When the camel finally reaches the water trough, it drinks so fast that water ____ from its lips onto the sand.
questions.why: Dribbles means falls in small drops.

questions.stem: The prefix pre- means “before.” Which word means “to tell what will happen before it happens”?
questions.why: Predict combines pre- (before) and dict (say).

questions.stem: Is each detail about the fennec fox important enough for a summary or only a minor detail?

rows.text: Its huge ears let heat escape and help it hear prey.
Its thick fur keeps it warm on cold desert nights.
One fennec fox at a zoo was named Sunny.
Some people think fennec foxes look like cartoons.

questions.why: A summary includes details about adaptations, not fun facts that do not matter.

questions.stem: Part A: “The young gazelle is extraordinary at sensing danger. Its large ears pick up tiny vibrations, and it runs before a predator can pounce.” What is the central idea of these sentences?

partA.stem: Part A: “The young gazelle is extraordinary at sensing danger. Its large ears pick up tiny vibrations, and it runs before a predator can pounce.” What is the central idea of these sentences?

options.label: A
options.text: Gazelles have the largest ears of any animal.

options.label: B
options.text: The gazelle's senses help it escape predators.

options.label: C
options.text: Gazelles like running more than resting.

options.label: D
options.text: Predators can never catch young gazelles.

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The gazelle is young.

options.label: B
options.text: Predators pounce on animals.

options.label: C
options.text: Its large ears pick up tiny vibrations.

options.label: D
options.text: Gazelles have ears.

questions.why: The ears sense vibrations, which lets the gazelle escape in time.

questions.stem: Which word is an antonym of “annoyed”?
questions.why: Annoyed means bothered; pleased means the opposite.

questions.stem: Match each part of a play with what it does: cast of characters, stage directions, dialogue.

pairs.right: lists the people or animals who appear
tell actors how to move or speak

questions.why: Plays use special parts to tell actors what to do and say.

questions.stem: The puppy was ____ after a long day, so it growled when the children tried to play with it.
questions.why: Cranky means grumpy and easily annoyed, often when tired.

questions.stem: True or false: “Hot” and “cold” are antonyms because they have opposite meanings.
questions.why: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings.

questions.stem: In a play about a lazy grasshopper, is each line dialogue or a stage direction?

rows.text: GRASSHOPPER: Let's sing all day!
(The ant carries a heavy seed.)
ANT: I must work while the sun shines.
(Wind blows, and leaves fall.)

questions.why: Stage directions are usually in parentheses; dialogue follows a character's name.

questions.stem: What is the theme of “The Bee and the Butterfly”?
options: Working ahead helps you get ready for hard times.
Butterflies are more beautiful and graceful than bees.
It is always fun to rest in the warm spring sunshine.
Gardens are full of flowers in the spring.
questions.why: Bee's hard work saves both friends when the cold comes.

questions.stem: Which stage direction in “The Bee and the Butterfly” shows that Butterfly is cold?

segments.text: (stretching her wings)
(laughing)
(shivering)
(opening the door of her hive)

questions.why: Shivering is what a body does when it is cold.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does Bee keep working instead of resting?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does Bee keep working instead of resting?

options.label: A
options.text: She wants to win a flying race.

options.label: B
options.text: She wants to store honey before the cold days.

options.label: C
options.text: She is lost and cannot find her hive.

options.label: D
options.text: She does not like Butterfly very much.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Come and relax in the sunshine with me!

options.label: B
options.text: I cannot rest yet, because I must store honey before the cold days come.

options.label: C
options.text: Next spring, we will work together.

options.label: D
options.text: The cold days are far away, and there is plenty of time.

questions.why: Bee says she must store honey before the cold days.

questions.stem: Put these events from “The Bee and the Butterfly” in order.
sequence: Bee carries nectar back to her hive.
Butterfly asks Bee to rest in the sunshine.
The flowers fade, and a chilly wind blows.
Bee shares her saved honey with Butterfly.
questions.why: The narrator's lines help show how time passes in a play.

questions.stem: Which TWO questions can be answered by reading the setting of “The Bee and the Butterfly”? Choose two.
options: Where does the play take place?
What season is it at the start?
How does Butterfly feel at the end?
Why does Bee share her honey?
questions.why: The setting tells where and when a play takes place.

questions.stem: The ____ in the stadium grew louder as the fans cheered the winning goal.
questions.why: A commotion is a noisy, excited disturbance.

questions.stem: Which pair of words are antonyms?
questions.why: Frustrated and satisfied have opposite meanings; the others are synonyms.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about Uncle Fahad's cooking has an error?
segments: asks him to cook it on holidays.
questions.why: The singular subject “specialty” needs the singular verb “is.”

questions.stem: Is each word a synonym or an antonym of “frustrated”?

rows.text: upset
calm
discouraged
satisfied

questions.why: Synonyms have similar meanings; antonyms have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: True or false: In a play, a narrator may speak to the audience to explain what is happening.
questions.why: A narrator in a play often tells the audience about events or time passing.

questions.stem: Match each short fable with its theme.

pairs.left: A crow drops pebbles into a jug until the water rises and it can drink.
A selfish dog drops its bone while trying to grab another dog's bone.
pairs.right: Greed can make you lose what you have.

pairs.left: A tiny mouse frees a trapped lion by chewing the net.
pairs.right: Even small friends can be a big help.

questions.why: A theme is the lesson the characters' actions teach.

questions.stem: Grasshopper's lazy ____ changed after the dry season; he began waking early to help gather seeds.
questions.why: An attitude is the way someone thinks and acts about something.

questions.stem: A student reads a play and wants to ask questions about its theme. Which TWO questions would help? Choose two.
options: What lesson does the main character learn by the end?
How many actors are in the cast?
How do the characters' choices lead to good or bad results?
What color is the stage curtain?
questions.why: Questions about lessons and results of choices lead readers to the theme.

questions.stem: Put these lines from a short play about two camels in order.
sequence: NARRATOR: Two camels prepare for a long trip across the desert.
FIRST CAMEL: I will drink plenty of water before we leave.
SECOND CAMEL (annoyed): Why waste time? Let's go now!
NARRATOR: Days later, only the first camel still has strength to walk.
questions.why: The plan, the argument, and then the result make the play's order clear.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym of “familiar” in this sentence? “The road to Grandmother's house was familiar to Badr.”
questions.why: Familiar means well known; strange means not known.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the theme of “The Well in the Oasis”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the theme of “The Well in the Oasis”?

options.label: A
options.text: Planning ahead and working hard prepare you for hard times.

options.label: B
options.text: It is better to rest in the shade than to dig in the sun.

options.label: C
options.text: Wells in an oasis never run dry, even in the summer.

options.label: D
options.text: Neighbors should always share their tea with each other.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Come and join me for a cup of tea.

options.label: B
options.text: I am saving water now, because the hot summer always brings a terrible drought.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the cool season, and the well is full of water.

options.label: D
options.text: The sun burns, and the water in the well sinks lower every day.

questions.why: Sami plans ahead, and his saved water helps both farmers in summer.

questions.stem: Which line from “The Well in the Oasis” shows that Raed's attitude has changed?

segments.text: Why worry, Sami?
The well has never run dry.
My trees are dying, and I do not know what to do!
I will never laugh at hard work again.

questions.why: Raed now respects hard work instead of laughing at it.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of words in parentheses, such as “(lying in the shade of a palm tree)”?
options: to name the setting of each scene
to list all the characters in order
to tell what a character is doing
to show the words a character says aloud
questions.why: Stage directions in parentheses tell actors how to move or act.

questions.stem: In “The Well in the Oasis,” the word “careful” in the cast list is an antonym of ____, which describes Raed early in the play.
questions.why: Careful and careless are opposites; Raed does not plan at first.

questions.stem: Which question would a reader most likely ask after the narrator says, “The sun burns, and the water in the well sinks lower every day”?
options: How many palm trees are on each farm?
What will happen to Raed's trees without water?
Why does Sami grow dates on his farm instead of oranges?
Who dug the well between the two farms?
questions.why: Good readers ask questions about what may happen next in the plot.

questions.stem: Find the misused key word in these lines from a play about a falcon show.
segments: TRAINER: Our falcon's specialty is diving fast.
CHILD (frustrated): Hooray, it caught the lure on the first try!
questions.correction: CHILD (excited): Hooray, it caught the lure on the first try!
questions.why: A child cheering “Hooray” is excited, not frustrated.

questions.stem: Huda was not only annoyed by the broken printer; after trying to fix it for an hour, she felt completely ____.
questions.why: Frustrated is a stronger feeling than annoyed, after trying and failing.

questions.stem: Which line from a play best shows the theme “Being selfish can leave you alone”?
options: FOX (yawning): I am so sleepy after this long and busy day of searching.
FOX (sitting by himself): I kept all the dates, but now no one will eat with me.
FOX (running): I must hurry home before the sun goes down behind the dunes.
FOX (smiling): I found a big basket of dates near the old palm tree today.
questions.why: Fox kept everything for himself and ended up alone, which shows the theme.

questions.stem: True or false: “Cranky” and “cheerful” are antonyms, so a cranky character would probably speak in a happy, friendly way.
questions.why: A cranky character is grumpy, the opposite of cheerful.

questions.stem: Are the words in each pair from a fable about a fox antonyms or synonyms?

rows.text: selfish – giving
annoyed – irritated
familiar – unknown
cranky – grouchy

questions.why: Antonyms are opposites; synonyms mean nearly the same thing.

questions.stem: Match each key word from the animal poems unit to its meaning.

pairs.right: hard but easily broken or cracked
full of details that help you picture something
reached out as far as possible
using imagination to make something new

questions.why: These words help readers talk about how poets describe animals.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The dry autumn leaf was so ____ that it cracked when Huda stepped on it.
questions.why: Something brittle breaks or cracks easily.

questions.stem: True or false: A simile compares two things by using the word like or as.
questions.why: “As fast as the wind” is a simile because it uses as.

questions.stem: Which sentence about a kitten contains a simile?
options: The kitten was as soft as a cloud.
The soft kitten slept beside the window.
The kitten slept on a soft cloud-shaped pillow.
The kitten was a soft cloud of fur.
questions.why: Only the first sentence compares using as.

questions.stem: Decide whether each line about an animal is a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: The cheetah ran like the wind.
The owl is a night watchman.
The turtle's shell is as hard as stone.
The bee is a busy little worker.

questions.why: Similes use like or as; metaphors say one thing is another.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term to what it describes.

pairs.right: words that end with the same sound
the pattern of strong and weak beats in a line
a comparison that uses like or as
a comparison that says one thing is another

questions.why: Poets use these tools to create sound and pictures.

questions.stem: Which two words rhyme with the word flight? Choose two.
questions.why: Bright and night end with the same -ight sound as flight.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The poet used ____ words such as glittering, rough, and enormous so readers could picture the eagle.
questions.why: Descriptive words help readers picture something.

questions.stem: Find the word used incorrectly in the sentence about Salem's eagle poem.
questions.why: A poem full of new ideas is creative, not brittle.

questions.stem: Which line from a poem about an eagle uses a metaphor?
options: The eagle flies as high as the clouds.
The eagle looks like a dark kite in the sky.
The eagle builds its nest on a high cliff.
The eagle is a king of the mountain air.
questions.why: Calling the eagle a king is a metaphor; it does not use like or as.

questions.stem: Part A: Which idea does the poet express about the falcon's wings in “The Desert Falcon”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which idea does the poet express about the falcon's wings in “The Desert Falcon”?

options.label: A
options.text: She is tired after flying over the sea.

options.label: B
options.text: She has small wings that cannot lift her.

options.label: C
options.text: She uses the wind to glide with great ease.

options.label: D
options.text: She shines because her wings are metal.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I watch her from my window, and I hold my breathing still,

options.label: B
options.text: Then suddenly she tumbles down, an arrow from the sky,

options.label: C
options.text: Her outstretched wings are silver sails that catch the winds below.

options.label: D
options.text: The frightened lizards scatter as the hunter rushes by.

questions.why: Sails catch the wind, so the metaphor shows the falcon gliding easily.

questions.stem: Select the line from “The Desert Falcon” that contains a simile.

segments.text: Above the golden dunes the falcon circles, calm and slow,
Her eyes are polished lanterns, searching every rocky ledge,
She hovers like a question mark beside the canyon's edge.
Then suddenly she tumbles down, an arrow from the sky,

questions.why: The falcon is compared to a question mark using like.

questions.stem: For “The Desert Falcon,” decide whether each phrase is a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: her eyes are polished lanterns
hovers like a question mark
an arrow from the sky

questions.why: Only the question-mark phrase uses like.

questions.stem: Which pair of words from “The Desert Falcon” shows the poem's rhyme pattern?
questions.why: Each pair of lines ends in rhyming words, such as slow and below.

questions.stem: How does the speaker of “The Desert Falcon” feel about the falcon?
options: The speaker admires her and wishes to be as brave.
The speaker pities her because she must hunt to eat.
The speaker is bored and would rather watch lizards.
The speaker fears her and wants her to fly away.
questions.why: The speaker wishes for the falcon's courage and skill.

questions.stem: Put the lines of this haiku about a sea turtle in a sensible 5-7-5 order: “to the sandy shore,” “Slow turtle swims on,” “through the warm and silver waves.”
sequence: Slow turtle swims on
through the warm and silver waves
to the sandy shore
questions.why: A haiku has three lines of five, seven, and five syllables.

questions.stem: True or false: A haiku is a short poem of three lines that usually has five, seven, and five syllables.
questions.why: That syllable pattern is the usual structure of a haiku.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: When Ali read his poem aloud, he tapped his desk to keep the steady ____ of each line.
questions.why: Meter is the steady pattern of beats in a line of poetry.

questions.stem: Which two features would most likely appear in a lyric poem about a chimpanzee? Choose two.
options: the speaker's feelings about the chimpanzee
characters speaking lines on a stage
a list of facts with headings and a chart
descriptive words that create a picture
questions.why: Lyric poems share feelings and use descriptive language.

questions.stem: Read the line: “The young chimp was a little acrobat in the treetops.” What does the metaphor tell the reader?
options: The chimp performed tricks for visitors in a show.
The chimp was smaller than the other chimps.
The chimp moved with quick and skillful jumps.
The chimp liked to sleep high in the treetops.
questions.why: An acrobat jumps and swings with skill, so the chimp moves the same way.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the camel's perspective in “The Camel's Song”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the camel's perspective in “The Camel's Song”?

options.label: A
options.text: It is tired of the desert and wants to ride in trucks.

options.label: B
options.text: It is proud of its strength and thinks people misjudge it.

options.label: C
options.text: It is afraid of the stars and the long, dark nights.

options.label: D
options.text: It is angry that the caravans travel too slowly.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: You hurry in your noisy trucks and grumble at the heat,

options.label: B
options.text: The desert is my library, the stars are my old friends,

options.label: C
options.text: But I can cross the empty miles that you will never understand.

options.label: D
options.text: My lashes are like curtains that protect me from the haze.

questions.why: The camel answers people who call it slow by boasting of what it can do.

questions.stem: Select two lines from “The Camel's Song” that use metaphors.

segments.text: My humps are patient storehouses that keep me strong for days,
My lashes are like curtains that protect me from the haze.
The desert is my library, the stars are my old friends,
While I go gently forward on my wide and padded feet.

questions.why: These lines say one thing is another without like or as.

questions.stem: Decide whether each detail in “The Camel's Song” describes the camel or the people.

rows.text: hurry in noisy trucks
go gently forward on padded feet
grumble at the heat
carry every caravan

questions.why: The poem contrasts the calm camel with the hurried people.

questions.stem: Which two statements about the structure of “The Camel's Song” are correct? Choose two.
options: The lines do not rhyme, so it is free verse.
The poem is divided into two stanzas of four lines.
Each line has exactly five syllables like a haiku.
Each pair of lines ends with rhyming words.
questions.why: The poem has two four-line stanzas made of rhyming pairs.

questions.stem: Why does the poet most likely use the camel as the speaker instead of a person?
options: to make the poem shorter and easier to memorize
to show that people and camels never travel together
to let readers see the desert through the camel's eyes
to explain scientific facts about how camels store water
questions.why: A camel speaker shares the animal's own perspective.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence that explains what a metaphor is.
segments: by using the word like or as,
such as “the moon is a lamp.”
questions.correction: without using the word like or as,
questions.why: A metaphor does not use like or as; a simile does.

questions.stem: Read each line from a poem about a desert fox and decide whether it uses a simile, a metaphor, or neither.

rows.text: Its ears are radar dishes turning in the dark.
It slips across the sand as quietly as smoke.
It hunts for beetles when the evening cools.
Its tail is a soft brush sweeping its tracks away.

questions.why: Look for like or as (simile) or a direct comparison (metaphor).

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The eagle landed with its wings ____, then slowly folded them against its body.
questions.why: Outstretched wings are spread wide open.

questions.stem: True or false: Two lines of poetry that have the same meter must also rhyme.
questions.why: Meter is the beat pattern; lines can share a beat without rhyming.

questions.stem: A poem is spoken by a hungry eagle looking down at a field. Which line best shows the eagle's perspective?
options: The field is warm and quiet under the afternoon sun.
The farmer counts his sheep and hopes the eagle stays away.
Below me, tiny dinners run and hide in golden grass.
The eagle looks so fierce and proud that children stop to stare.
questions.why: Only the first line shows how the eagle itself sees the field.

questions.stem: Match each key word about helping after a storm to its meaning.

pairs.right: people who live in a place
the quality of giving freely to others

questions.why: These words describe a community helping after a disaster.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: After the strong wind, broken branches were ____ all over the schoolyard.
questions.why: Scattered means spread out in many places.

questions.stem: True or false: Context clues are nearby words that can help a reader figure out the meaning of an unknown word.
questions.why: Clues in the sentence often explain a hard word.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Nora stepped gingerly over the broken glass so she would not cut her feet.” Which words are the best clue to the meaning of gingerly?
options: Nora stepped over the broken glass
so she would not cut her feet
questions.why: Not wanting to get hurt shows that gingerly means carefully.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about flood helpers is told in first-person or third-person point of view.

rows.text: I packed the blankets into the van.
Sara helped her mother carry water.
We waved as the truck drove away.
The residents thanked the volunteers.

questions.why: First person uses I and we; third person uses names and he, she, or they.

questions.stem: Which two sentences show generosity? Choose two.
options: The bakery donated bread to families whose homes flooded.
Omar sold his old bicycle for a very high price.
Khalid gave half of his lunch to a classmate who forgot his.
Laila kept all of the new markers for herself.
questions.why: Generosity means giving freely to others.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The coach was ____ when choosing players, picking only those who came to every practice.
questions.why: A selective person chooses very carefully.

questions.stem: Find the word used incorrectly in the sentence about Hana's little brother.
questions.why: Crying and throwing toys is not mature, grown-up behavior.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Several organizations, such as the Red Crescent and local food banks, sent trucks of supplies.” What does organizations mean?
options: people who live in houses near the coast
boxes that hold supplies for a long trip
groups of people who work together for a purpose
trucks that carry food from one city to another
questions.why: The example clue “such as the Red Crescent” names groups that work together.

questions.stem: Put the events of Yusuf's memory about the sandstorm in the order they really happened.
sequence: Yusuf's family hears a warning on the radio.
The sandstorm covers the road with sand.
Neighbors help dig out the family's car.
Years later, Yusuf tells his cousin about that day.
questions.why: A flashback is told later, but the events happened in this order.

questions.stem: What does the word gingerly most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 2?
options: quickly, as if late for something
carefully, as if afraid of slipping
angrily, as if the water were a pest
happily, as if playing in a pool
questions.why: Later the narrator remembers Mr. Fahad's careful steps.

questions.stem: Part A: Which part of “The Box of Pencils” is a flashback?

partA.stem: Part A: Which part of “The Box of Pencils” is a flashback?

options.label: A
options.text: the teacher giving out classroom jobs

options.label: B
options.text: the narrator sorting pencils in class

options.label: C
options.text: the narrator's memory of the flooded streets

options.label: D
options.text: the narrator adding an extra eraser

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Two years ago, the rain fell for an entire night.

options.label: B
options.text: Now I am ten, and our class is collecting supplies for families who lost their homes in a storm far away.

options.label: C
options.text: As I pack each box, I remember Mr. Fahad's careful steps, and I add an extra eraser, just in case.

options.label: D
options.text: My teacher assigned me to sort the pencils and notebooks.

questions.why: “Two years ago” takes the reader back to an earlier time.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Box of Pencils” that best helps the reader visualize the flood.

segments.text: By sunrise, brown water was rushing through the streets, and furniture was scattered across the road like broken toys.
I was eight years old then.
My teacher assigned me to sort the pencils and notebooks.
Now I am ten, and our class is collecting supplies for families who lost their homes in a storm far away.

questions.why: Brown rushing water and scattered furniture create a clear picture.

questions.stem: Decide whether each event in “The Box of Pencils” happens in the past memory or in the present.

rows.text: Mr. Fahad wades through the water.
The teacher gives the narrator a job.
Furniture lies across the road.
The narrator packs boxes of supplies.

questions.why: The flood is remembered; the supply drive is happening now.

questions.stem: Which two details show that “The Box of Pencils” is told in the first-person point of view? Choose two.
options: The narrator knows what Mr. Fahad is thinking.
The narrator is never part of the events.
The narrator uses the words I and my.
Readers learn the narrator's own memories and thoughts.
questions.why: A first-person narrator is a character in the story who shares personal thoughts.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The ____ of the old neighborhood met at the park to plan a cleanup day.
questions.why: Residents are the people who live in a place.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a storm shelter to the type of context clue it uses.

pairs.left: The shelter was spacious, or large, enough for fifty families.
Unlike the timid kitten, the puppy was bold.
Debris, such as broken boards and glass, covered the road.
A volunteer is a person who works without pay.

questions.why: Clues can give a synonym, an opposite, examples, or a definition.

questions.stem: True or false: A flashback interrupts a story to show an event that happened earlier.
questions.why: Flashbacks take readers back in time.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “Mama said the shelter was crowded and noisy. To me, it felt like a giant sleepover with new friends.” What do these sentences show?
options: The narrator wants to leave the shelter quickly.
Mama is happy that the shelter is so crowded.
The narrator and Mama both think the shelter is unpleasant.
The narrator and Mama see the shelter differently.
questions.why: Two characters can have different perspectives on the same place.

questions.stem: Find the part that does not fit the meaning of selective in the sentence about the fruit seller.
segments: Because the fruit seller was very selective,
she sold any fruit she found
questions.correction: she sold only the freshest fruit
questions.why: A selective seller chooses carefully, not just any fruit.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Reem's point of view change in “Two Views of the Drive”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Reem's point of view change in “Two Views of the Drive”?

options.label: A
options.text: She first ignores the storm but then visits Al-Bahar.

options.label: B
options.text: She first wants to give books but then decides to give money.

options.label: C
options.text: She first doubts that books can help but then decides to give some.

options.label: D
options.text: She first agrees with Majid but then argues with him.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Majid did not answer at first.

options.label: B
options.text: Instead, he showed her a photograph from the newspaper.

options.label: C
options.text: His sister Reem frowned.

options.label: D
options.text: Then she walked to her room and returned with her favorite atlas and a box of colored pencils.

questions.why: Reem questions the books at first but later gives her own atlas.

questions.stem: What does the word residents mean as it is used in paragraph 1?
options: people who live in a certain place
teachers who give lessons in towns
visitors who stay for one short night
questions.why: Residents of nearby towns are the people who live there.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Two Views of the Drive” that best helps the reader picture the newspaper photograph.

segments.text: A small boy was sitting on a pile of broken bricks, reading a damaged magazine as if it were a precious treasure.
Majid did not answer at first.
Reem studied the picture for a long time.
His sister Reem frowned.

questions.why: Details like broken bricks and a damaged magazine create the picture.

questions.stem: In “Two Views of the Drive,” decide which character holds each view at the start.

rows.text: Books are a useful gift.
Families need roofs and water more than books.
A picture can explain a feeling better than words.

questions.why: Majid believes in the books; Reem doubts them until she sees the photograph.

questions.stem: Which two words best describe Majid's actions in “Two Views of the Drive”? Choose two.
questions.why: He shows generosity by giving his books and patience by answering with a picture instead of arguing.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Unlike his impatient younger brother, Tariq was mature enough to wait calmly for his turn.” Which meaning of mature fits the sentence?
options: older than everyone else in the line
tired after waiting for a long time
fully ripe and ready to be eaten
behaving in a sensible, grown-up way
questions.why: The antonym clue impatient shows that mature means sensible and calm.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: Because the shelter had little space, the volunteers had to be ____ and accept only the most needed items.
questions.why: Little space forces careful, selective choices.

questions.stem: For each sentence, decide whether the clue for the capitalized word is a synonym clue or an antonym clue.

rows.text: The road was HAZARDOUS, or dangerous, after the flood.
The first shelter was CRAMPED, but the new one was roomy.
Her voice was FAINT, or very quiet, after the long trip.
Instead of being SCATTERED, the boxes were stacked neatly.

questions.why: Or signals a synonym; but and instead of signal opposites.

questions.stem: Which two sentences would best begin a flashback in a story about a flood? Choose two.
options: I still remember the night the river rose over its banks.
Right now, the sun is shining on our clean street.
Tomorrow we will deliver the boxes to the shelter.
Three years earlier, our street had looked very different.
questions.why: Flashbacks use words that move back in time, such as remember and earlier.

questions.stem: True or false: In a story told in third-person point of view, the narrator is a character who calls himself I.
questions.why: A third-person narrator is outside the story and uses he, she, and they.

questions.stem: Match each word about standing up for fairness to its meaning.

pairs.right: to show strongly that you disagree
to refuse to buy or use something
officially signed up on a list

questions.why: These words describe ways people work for fairness.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The rescued horse was nervous because it had been ____ by its old owner.
questions.why: Mistreated means treated badly or cruelly.

questions.stem: Decide whether each pair of words are synonyms or antonyms.

rows.text: fair – just
protect – harm
brave – courageous
injustice – fairness

questions.why: Synonyms mean the same; antonyms mean the opposite.

questions.stem: True or false: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings, such as clean and polluted.
questions.why: Clean and polluted have opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Which word is a synonym of encouragement?
questions.why: Encouragement is support that gives someone hope or confidence.

questions.stem: Put the events from Huda's timeline of the beach cleanup in time order.
sequence: March 2: Huda notices plastic on the beach.
March 9: She registers twenty volunteers.
March 16: The volunteers clean the shore.
April 1: The city adds new trash bins.
questions.why: A timeline lists events from earliest to latest.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: Paying some workers less than others for the same job is an example of ____.
questions.why: Unequal pay for equal work is unfair, an injustice.

questions.stem: Which two words are antonyms of encouragement? Choose two.
questions.why: Support and praise are synonyms; the others are opposites.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Mona felt qualified for the job because she had trained as a nurse for three years.” Which word is a synonym of qualified?
questions.why: Three years of training made Mona skilled.

questions.stem: Find the word used incorrectly in the sentence about the new library.
questions.why: People who cheer are not refusing to use the library.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's perspective on Wangari Maathai in “The Woman Who Planted Forests”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the author's perspective on Wangari Maathai in “The Woman Who Planted Forests”?

options.label: A
options.text: The author feels her prize was given too late in life.

options.label: B
options.text: The author believes the officials were right to stop her.

options.label: C
options.text: The author admires her courage and the change she made.

options.label: D
options.text: The author thinks her plan was too costly for Kenya.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: In 1977 she started the Green Belt Movement, which paid village women a small amount to plant trees.

options.label: B
options.text: Her life shows that one determined person can help heal an entire land.

options.label: C
options.text: Many forests had been cut down, the streams were muddy, and families had to walk far to find firewood.

options.label: D
options.text: Wangari Maathai grew up in the green hills of Kenya, where clear streams ran past fig trees.

questions.why: Calling her determined and able to heal a land shows admiration.

questions.stem: Put the events of Wangari Maathai's life in the order shown on her timeline.
sequence: She is born in Kenya.
She earns a doctorate.
She starts the Green Belt Movement.
She wins the Nobel Peace Prize.
questions.why: The timeline runs 1940, 1971, 1977, 2004.

questions.stem: Why did Wangari think the loss of forests was an injustice?
options: Poor families suffered the most from it.
Officials planted trees only in cities.
Women were not allowed to study abroad.
The streams were too far from schools.
questions.why: She saw that the people with the least were hurt the most.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Woman Who Planted Forests” that a reader should reread to learn how officials reacted to Wangari.

segments.text: Some officials disliked her ideas and even had her arrested, but she refused to quit.
Over the years, the women she trained planted millions of trees.
When she returned home in the 1960s after studying in the United States, she was shocked.
In 2004, Wangari became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.why: This sentence tells what the officials did.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the word refused (“she refused to quit”) is an antonym of ____.
questions.why: Rejected, declined, and denied are synonyms of refused; accepted is the opposite.

questions.stem: Match each word about fairness to its antonym.
questions.why: Each pair has opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: Jamal worked extra hours at the shop so he could ____ his promise to buy his sister a new bicycle.
questions.why: To fulfill a promise is to do what you said you would do.

questions.stem: True or false: A timeline shows important events in the order they happened, so it helps a reader reread a biography and check dates.
questions.why: Timelines organize events by time.

questions.stem: Which two sentences about Ibn Sina show an author's perspective rather than only a fact? Choose two.
options: His medical book was later translated into Latin.
It is amazing that his medical book was studied for centuries.
Ibn Sina was the most brilliant doctor of his age.
Ibn Sina was born near Bukhara around the year 980.
questions.why: Words like brilliant and amazing show the author's opinion.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The students decided to boycott the snack shop until it stopped using plastic bags.” What does boycott mean?
options: refuse to buy from as a protest
visit every day to show their strong support
questions.why: A boycott means not buying something to show disagreement.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's perspective on Rachel Carson in “The Scientist Who Heard the Silence”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the author's perspective on Rachel Carson in “The Scientist Who Heard the Silence”?

options.label: A
options.text: The author believes chemical companies were mostly right.

options.label: B
options.text: The author feels her book was less important than protests.

options.label: C
options.text: The author thinks she was too emotional to be trusted.

options.label: D
options.text: The author greatly respects her calm, careful courage.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Some chemical companies attacked her.

options.label: B
options.text: In my view, her quiet courage was more powerful than any loud protest, because her careful evidence changed how a whole nation thought about nature.

options.label: C
options.text: In 1962 she published Silent Spring, a book that warned readers about this danger.

options.label: D
options.text: Rachel Carson loved the ocean long before she ever saw it.

questions.why: “In my view” signals the author's own respectful opinion.

questions.stem: For “The Scientist Who Heard the Silence,” decide whether each statement is a fact or the author's opinion.

rows.text: Carson was born in 1907.
Her quiet courage was more powerful than any loud protest.
Silent Spring was published in 1962.
Her courage mattered more than her critics' attacks.

options.label: D
options.text: The men are resting in the shade.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: In the summer of 1925, the town of Darin sat quietly beside the warm waters of the Gulf.

options.label: B
options.text: Most of the men had sailed away months earlier to dive for pearls.

options.label: C
options.text: People rushed down to the beach, shouting and waving.

options.label: D
options.text: Her father's boat had been gone since spring.

questions.why: The setting is a pearl-diving town whose men are away at sea.

questions.stem: Which details from “Waiting on the Pearl Coast” help the reader picture the setting? Choose two.
options: the narrow lanes between the coral-stone houses
Mariam ran faster than she had ever run
the smell of salt and seaweed
she held his hand and would not let it go
questions.why: Setting details describe the place, not the characters' actions.

questions.stem: How does the setting affect Mariam in “Waiting on the Pearl Coast”?
options: Because the day is very hot, she sleeps in the shade with the cats all afternoon.
Because it is summer, she sails away with the other divers to look for pearls.
Because the lanes are narrow, she cannot run down to the beach to meet the boats.
Because the town is by the sea, she can watch each evening for her father's boat.
questions.why: Living beside the sea lets Mariam watch for her father every evening.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2 of “Waiting on the Pearl Coast,” the daytime heat has great intensity. This means the heat is ____.
questions.why: Intensity means great strength; the heat was so strong even cats hid.

questions.stem: In “Waiting on the Pearl Coast,” is each statement a theme of the story or a detail from the story?

rows.text: Love for family helps people endure long separations.
The men sailed away in the spring.
Patient waiting can bring a joyful reward.
Mariam climbs onto the roof every evening.

questions.why: A theme is a message about life; a detail is a fact from the story.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to the meaning of the key word it uses: forfeit, honor, retreated, intensity.

pairs.left: She will forfeit her turn if she is late.
We honor our ancestors by keeping their traditions.
The scouts retreated before the storm arrived.
The intensity of the sun made the sand too hot to touch.

questions.why: Context in each sentence shows the meaning of the key word.

questions.stem: Choose the word with a positive connotation that best completes the sentence: “The guide was ____ as he led the travelers calmly through the dangerous mountain pass.”
questions.why: Courageous praises the guide; reckless and careless suggest he was foolish.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses despised correctly?
options: The travelers despised the cool water after their long, thirsty walk.
The villagers despised the thieves who stole their horses.
The children despised their grandmother's warm, delicious bread.
The chief despised his sister and hugged her with great joy.
questions.why: Despised means strongly disliked, which fits feelings about thieves.

questions.stem: For each statement about the words endurance and irritating, choose whether it describes denotation or connotation.

rows.text: Endurance means the ability to last through something difficult.
Endurance makes a reader admire a character's strength.
Irritating means causing someone to feel annoyed.
Irritating makes a reader feel that something is unpleasant.

questions.why: Denotation is the exact meaning; connotation is the feeling the word adds.

questions.stem: True or false: Calling a person “stubborn” instead of “determined” gives the description a more positive connotation.
questions.why: Stubborn sounds negative; determined sounds positive.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the theme of “Many Voices”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the theme of “Many Voices”?

options.label: A
options.text: Learning a second language is easy for young children.

options.label: B
options.text: Maps of the world never include small harbors.

options.label: C
options.text: Old sailors always tell the most exciting stories.

options.label: D
options.text: Great achievements often depend on many people working together.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Travelers from many lands came to his workshop to describe the rivers, mountains, and cities they had seen.

options.label: B
options.text: Many sailors spoke too quickly, and some argued about distances.

options.label: C
options.text: “A map is made by many voices,” he said.

options.label: D
options.text: At first he found the work dull.

questions.why: Al-Idrisi says the map needs many voices, including Yusuf's.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Many Voices” that show how Yusuf's feelings about his work change.

segments.text: Yusuf despised the long afternoons of copying numbers.
From then on, Yusuf listened to every traveler with patience, proud to be one of those voices.
The geographer thanked him warmly.
Yusuf, a boy who spoke both Arabic and Greek, was hired to help.

questions.why: Yusuf first despises the work and later feels proud of it.

questions.stem: Why does the author use the word despised instead of disliked in paragraph 2 of “Many Voices”?
options: to show that Yusuf secretly enjoyed copying the numbers
to show how strongly Yusuf hated the dull work at first
to suggest that Yusuf was angry with al-Idrisi himself
to explain why the sailors argued about the distances
questions.why: Despised has a stronger negative connotation than disliked.

questions.stem: How does the setting of al-Idrisi's workshop in Palermo help develop the theme of “Many Voices”?
options: Palermo is far from the sea, so sailors rarely visit and the map stays unfinished.
The year is 1150, so there are no maps of the world and no one knows about harbors.
Travelers from many lands meet there, so knowledge from many people comes together.
The workshop is quiet and empty, so Yusuf can do his work alone without any help.
questions.why: The busy workshop brings many voices together, which is the theme.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Many Voices” in order.
sequence: Yusuf is hired to help in the workshop.
Yusuf grows bored with copying numbers.
An old sailor describes an unknown harbor.
Al-Idrisi adds the harbor and thanks Yusuf.
Yusuf listens to every traveler with patience.
questions.why: Yusuf's attitude changes after al-Idrisi thanks him.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term to its meaning: metaphor, personification, imagery, free verse.

pairs.right: a comparison of two things without using like or as
giving human actions or feelings to something that is not human
words that help readers see, hear, smell, taste, or feel
poetry with no regular rhyme or rhythm

questions.why: Poets use these tools to make their writing vivid.

questions.stem: Early in the morning, a thin ____ covered the valley, so we could barely see the trees.
questions.why: Mist is a cloud of tiny water drops near the ground that makes things hard to see.

questions.stem: In the sentence “My little brother gobbled his breakfast before the hike,” what does gobbled mean?
questions.why: To gobble is to eat very fast.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The roots of our family go back to a small village in the mountains,” the word roots means the parts of a plant under the ground.
questions.why: Here roots means where a family comes from, its origins.

questions.stem: Is each line from a hiking poem a simile or a metaphor?

rows.text: The trail was a ribbon tied around the hill.
My legs felt as heavy as stones.
The sun is a golden coin in the sky.
The wind whistled like a teapot.

questions.why: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.

questions.stem: Select the line from “Up the Green Mountain” that uses personification.

segments.text: The old juniper trees lean over the trail and whisper secrets to the wind.
My little sister skips ahead, then stops to pick tiny yellow flowers.
Early in the morning, my whole family climbs the mountain path near Abha.
My grandmother opens a basket, and we gobble warm bread with honey.

questions.why: Trees cannot really whisper secrets; that is a human action.

questions.stem: In “Up the Green Mountain,” the mist wraps around the family “like a soft gray blanket.” What does this simile help the reader understand?
options: The mist feels gentle and covers them closely.
The weather is warm and bright and sunny.
The family carries blankets up the mountain.
The mist is cold, wet, and very dangerous.
questions.why: A blanket is soft and wraps around you, like the mist.

questions.stem: Which kind of figurative language is used in each phrase from “Up the Green Mountain”?

rows.text: my father ... a camel who never tires
the clouds lie below us like a sleeping sea
the old juniper trees ... whisper secrets to the wind

questions.why: Like signals a simile; calling the father a camel is a metaphor; whispering trees are personified.

questions.stem: True or false: “Up the Green Mountain” is written in free verse because its lines do not follow a regular rhyme pattern.
questions.why: Free verse does not need rhyme or a steady beat.

questions.stem: The speaker of “Up the Green Mountain” feels ____ about the family hike.
options: bored and eager to go home
happy and close to the family
questions.why: The speaker laughs with the family and treasures the mountain.

questions.stem: Which sentences contain personification? Choose two.
options: The moon peeked shyly from behind the clouds.
The kitten was as quiet as a soft feather.
My brother is a walking dictionary.
The old door groaned when Grandfather pushed it open.
questions.why: Peeking shyly and groaning are human actions given to things.

questions.stem: In the line “Morning mist is a curtain hiding the valley,” the poet uses a ____ to compare mist to a curtain.
questions.why: The line says the mist is a curtain without using like or as.

questions.stem: Match each family idiom to its meaning.

pairs.left: a chip off the old block
pairs.right: a child who is like a parent
settle in one place to live

questions.why: An idiom means something different from its separate words.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence names the wrong poetry term? “In my poem, the line ‘The wind sang a lullaby’ is an example of a simile because the wind does something only a person can do.”
segments: the line ‘The wind sang a lullaby’
is an example of a simile
because the wind does something only a person can do.
questions.why: Giving a human action to the wind is personification, not a simile.

questions.stem: True or false: Writing about individuality means writing about the things that make a person different from everyone else.
questions.why: Individuality is what makes someone unique.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the speaker's feeling about her name change in “My Name Is Yasmin”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the speaker's feeling about her name change in “My Name Is Yasmin”?

options.label: A
options.text: She first wants a flower name but later chooses her cousin's name.

options.label: B
options.text: She first loves her name but later wishes it came from a story.

options.label: C
options.text: She first feels angry with her grandmother but later forgives her.

options.label: D
options.text: She first wishes for a grander name but later feels proud of her own.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: My cousins all have names from old family stories, but mine came from a flower.

options.label: B
options.text: My name is not a story from the past; it is a promise still growing.

options.label: C
options.text: At first, I wished my name were as grand and famous as theirs.

options.label: D
options.text: Grandmother named me Yasmin after the jasmine vine on our garden wall.

questions.why: The later line shows her new pride; the “At first” line shows only her early feeling.

questions.stem: Select the line from “My Name Is Yasmin” that uses personification to describe the jasmine vine.

segments.text: Each spring, it climbs higher, reaching for the sun with tiny green fingers.
Grandmother named me Yasmin after the jasmine vine on our garden wall.
and its white blossoms fill the evening air with sweetness.
It is my own, and it belongs to no one else.

questions.why: The vine is given fingers and reaches like a person.

questions.stem: Which senses does the imagery in the line “and its white blossoms fill the evening air with sweetness” from “My Name Is Yasmin” appeal to? Choose two.
questions.why: White blossoms can be seen, and sweetness in the air can be smelled.

questions.stem: In “My Name Is Yasmin,” what does the metaphor “it is a promise still growing” suggest about the speaker's name?
options: Her name will change into a new one when she is older.
Her name points to a future that she is still shaping.
Her name came from an old and well-known family story.
Her name was promised to her by her grandmother's mother.
questions.why: A promise still growing looks toward the future, like a climbing vine.

questions.stem: The speaker's comparison of herself to the jasmine in “My Name Is Yasmin” shows that she values her ____.
questions.why: She is proud that her name is her own and belongs to no one else.

questions.stem: Which line uses imagery that appeals mainly to the sense of hearing?
options: Dry leaves crackle and snap beneath our hiking boots.
Golden light spills across the tops of the far hills.
The cold stream water numbs my fingers in a moment.
The scent of wild mint drifts up from the valley floor.
questions.why: Crackle and snap are sounds.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence using roots or mist is literal or figurative.

rows.text: The roots of the old olive tree push deep into the ground.
Our family's roots are planted in the village where Grandfather was born.
A light mist hung over the lake at sunrise.
My memories of that summer are a mist that is slowly fading.

questions.why: Literal words mean exactly what they say; figurative words compare or suggest.

questions.stem: Read the lines: “My brother is a hungry wolf at dinner; / he can ____ a whole plate of rice in two minutes.” Which word best fits the metaphor?
questions.why: A hungry wolf eats fast, so gobble fits the metaphor.

questions.stem: Which statements about free verse are true? Choose two.
options: Line breaks can be used to slow down or stress certain words.
It does not need to follow a regular rhyme scheme.
It must always be divided into four-line stanzas that rhyme.
Every line must have exactly the same number of syllables.
questions.why: Free verse is open in form, but poets still choose line breaks carefully.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “Grandfather says I have his dark eyes / and his loud, happy laugh. / I am a page from his old book.” What is the speaker's perspective about her family?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “Grandfather says I have his dark eyes / and his loud, happy laugh. / I am a page from his old book.” What is the speaker's perspective about her family?

options.label: A
options.text: She wishes she looked more like her grandfather.

options.label: B
options.text: She thinks her grandfather's stories are boring.

options.label: C
options.text: She sees herself as part of her grandfather's family story.

options.label: D
options.text: She wants to write a book about her grandfather.

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the lines contains the metaphor that supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I have his dark eyes

options.label: B
options.text: his loud, happy laugh

options.label: C
options.text: I am a page from his old book

options.label: D
options.text: Grandfather says

questions.why: Calling herself a page from his book shows she belongs to his story.

questions.stem: In “Two Views from the Dune,” whose perspective does each detail show?

rows.text: misses the city lights
sees the stars as an audience
wants the night to last forever
counts the hours until leaving

questions.why: Each speaker describes the same desert in a different way.

questions.stem: Part A: How is the sister's perspective different from the brother's in “Two Views from the Dune”?

partA.stem: Part A: How is the sister's perspective different from the brother's in “Two Views from the Dune”?

options.label: A
options.text: She finds the desert night beautiful, while he finds it unpleasant.

options.label: B
options.text: She is afraid of the dark, while he enjoys the quiet desert.

options.label: C
options.text: She wants to go home early, while he wants to stay longer.

options.label: D
options.text: She dislikes the cold wind, while he likes the blowing sand.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I hope this night stretches on forever, like the dunes around our tent.

options.label: B
options.text: I count the long hours until we pack the tent and drive back home.

options.label: C
options.text: The wind hums an old song that my grandfather once taught me.

options.label: D
options.text: The cold wind bites my ears, and the sand creeps into everything I own.

questions.why: The sister wants the night to last, which shows she loves it.

questions.stem: Select two lines from “Two Views from the Dune” that use personification.

segments.text: The cold wind bites my ears, and the sand creeps into everything I own.
The wind hums an old song that my grandfather once taught me.
I count the long hours until we pack the tent and drive back home.
I hope this night stretches on forever, like the dunes around our tent.

questions.why: Biting, creeping, and humming are actions given to wind and sand.

questions.stem: Which metaphor in “Two Views from the Dune” shows the sister's sense of wonder?
options: like the dunes around our tent
the sand creeps into everything I own
The desert at night is empty and silent
The desert at night is a giant theater
questions.why: Calling the desert a theater is a metaphor full of wonder.

questions.stem: In “Two Views from the Dune,” both speakers begin with the same words to show that they see the same place with ____ feelings.
questions.why: The same opening makes the contrast between their perspectives clear.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning: naturalist, debris, encounter, generations.

pairs.right: a person who studies plants and animals
scattered pieces of broken or leftover material
a meeting, often an unexpected one
groups of people born around the same time

questions.why: These words often appear in writing about nature and history.

questions.stem: After the storm, the beach was covered with ____ such as broken branches and torn fishing nets.
questions.why: Debris is scattered broken material.

questions.stem: Which word best completes the sentence? “The view of the canyon at sunset was so ____ that everyone stopped talking to look.”
questions.why: Spectacular means amazing to see.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentences “The wind blew hard” and “Please wind the clock,” the word wind is pronounced the same way.
