options.text: It can coat the feathers of seabirds and wash onto beaches where turtles lay their eggs.

questions.why: The boom is pulled around the oil to trap it, which keeps the oil in one place.

questions.stem: Put the steps for cleaning up the spill in “Fences on the Water” in order.
sequence: A ship leaks oil near the coast.
Crews pull a boom around the oil.
Skimmers lift the oil off the water.
The oil is pumped into tanks.
questions.why: The passage uses signal words such as “first” and “next” to show the order of the solution.

questions.stem: Which sentence in “Fences on the Water” answers the question “How do workers remove the oil from the water?”

segments.text: A skimmer glides across the surface and lifts the oil off the water, the way a spoon lifts cream from the top of milk.
A boom is a long, floating tube that works like a fence on the water.
Workers must act quickly to stop the oil from spreading.
Booms and skimmers do not solve every problem, but they give workers valuable time to protect the shore and the animals living there.

questions.why: The skimmer is the tool that actually lifts the oil off the water.

questions.stem: Which two details from “Fences on the Water” describe techniques that workers use? Choose two.
options: Turtles lay their eggs on sandy beaches.
Oil coats the feathers of many seabirds.
Skimmers lift oil off the surface of the water.
Crews pull a floating boom around the oil.
questions.why: Techniques are the methods workers use; the wrong choices describe harm, not methods.

questions.stem: Match each Latin root found in collaborate, function, flexible, and artificial to its meaning.
questions.why: Latin roots give clues: flexible means able to bend, and collaborate means work together.

questions.stem: The Latin root flex means “bend.” A diver's wetsuit is ____, so it bends easily every time she moves.
questions.why: Flexible contains the root flex, “bend,” so a flexible suit bends easily.

questions.stem: Sort these words by the Latin root they share with flexible (flex, “bend”) or collaborate (labor, “work”).

rows.text: reflex
collaborate
laboratory
flexible
laborious

questions.why: Words that share a root share part of their meaning: a laboratory is a place where people work.

questions.stem: Collaborate contains co-, meaning “together,” and labor, meaning “work.” Which sentence uses collaborate correctly?
options: Engineers and divers collaborate to seal the broken pipe.
The thick oil collaborates slowly across the calm water.
The tired pelican collaborated its wings to dry them off.
She collaborated alone in her room all through the night.
questions.why: To collaborate, people must work together, as the engineers and divers do.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about how a pelican stays dry uses a word incorrectly?
questions.why: Feathers function, or work, to keep the bird dry; an obstacle is something in the way.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “Engineers built a robot arm that could mimic the movements of a human hand. Divers could not reach the broken pipe a mile below the surface, so the robot did the work for them.” What does mimic mean in these sentences?

partA.stem: Read the sentences: “Engineers built a robot arm that could mimic the movements of a human hand. Divers could not reach the broken pipe a mile below the surface, so the robot did the work for them.” What does mimic mean in these sentences?

options.label: A
options.text: copy

options.label: B
options.text: measure

options.label: C
options.text: stop

options.label: D
options.text: repair

partB.stem: Which phrase best helps the reader understand the meaning of mimic?

options.label: A
options.text: a mile below the surface

options.label: B
options.text: did the work for them

options.label: C
options.text: a robot arm that could

options.label: D
options.text: the movements of a human hand

questions.why: The robot arm does what a human hand does, so it copies, or mimics, the hand's movements.

questions.stem: For each sentence about a marsh cleanup, decide whether it describes a problem or a solution.

rows.text: Thick oil blocked sunlight from reaching the sea grass.
Volunteers washed oily birds with gentle soap.
A storm was an obstacle that kept boats in the harbor.
Crews placed floating booms in front of the marsh.

questions.why: A problem is something that goes wrong; a solution is an action taken to fix it.

questions.stem: A student reading an article about rescued sea turtles asks, “Why did the turtles need to rest in warm pools?” Which detail would best answer this question?
options: The rescue center was built close to a beach with soft, white sand.
Oil had made the turtles cold and weak, so warm water helped them heal.
Volunteers counted the turtles each day and wrote the numbers down.
Turtles swim thousands of miles across the open ocean every single year.
questions.why: Only this detail gives the reason the turtles needed warm water.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “The cleanup workers were dedicated to saving the marsh. They worked twelve-hour shifts in the heat. Some slept in tents near the beach so they could start before sunrise. The marsh is home to crabs, herons, and small fish.” Which two details best support the central idea? Choose two.
options: The marsh is home to crabs, herons, and small fish.
The cleanup workers were dedicated to saving the marsh.
They worked twelve-hour shifts in the heat.
Some slept in tents near the beach so they could start before sunrise.
questions.why: Relevant details prove the central idea; the first sentence is the central idea itself, not a supporting detail.

questions.stem: Before reading an article about oil spills, Maha wrote this question to guide her reading: “What ____ do scientists use to remove oil from feathers?”
questions.why: Maha wants to learn the methods, or techniques, that scientists use.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “Borrowing Ideas from Nature”?

partA.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “Borrowing Ideas from Nature”?

options.label: A
options.text: Scientists solved a cleanup problem by copying a feature of a plant.

options.label: B
options.text: Oil spills harm the ocean more than any other kind of pollution.

options.label: C
options.text: Ordinary sponges are still the best tool for cleaning the ocean.

options.label: D
options.text: Lotus leaves are covered with tiny bumps and a waxy coating.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Workers can squeeze the oil out, collect it in a container, and use the same sponge again many times.

options.label: B
options.text: Oil and water do not mix, yet separating them after a spill is surprisingly difficult.

options.label: C
options.text: Water rolls off a lotus leaf in round drops because the leaf is covered with tiny bumps and a waxy coating.

options.label: D
options.text: Scientists designed an artificial sponge that mimics this surface.

questions.why: The central idea connects the problem (removing oil) with the nature-based solution (a sponge that mimics a lotus leaf).

questions.stem: Which sentence in “Borrowing Ideas from Nature” explains the problem that the lotus-inspired sponge was designed to solve?

segments.text: Ordinary sponges soak up both liquids, so they quickly fill with seawater and stop working.
Its fibers push water away but grab oil and hold it inside.
The new sponges are also flexible.
Inventors call this approach biomimicry.

questions.why: The problem was that ordinary sponges filled with seawater instead of only oil.

questions.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, what does the word artificial tell the reader about the sponge?
options: It was built to soak up seawater along with the oil.
It was too weak to use again after just one spill.
It was made by people rather than grown in nature.
It was taken straight from a lotus plant in a pond.
questions.why: Artificial means made by people; the sponge copies the plant but is not part of it.

questions.stem: Which two details from “Borrowing Ideas from Nature” best support the idea that the new sponges create less waste? Choose two.
options: The same sponge can be used again many times.
Water rolls off lotus leaves in round drops.
Workers can squeeze the oil out of the sponges.
Ordinary sponges fill quickly with seawater.
Inventors study how animals solve problems.
questions.why: A sponge that can be emptied and reused does not have to be thrown away.

questions.stem: Match each question a reader might ask about “Borrowing Ideas from Nature” to the paragraph that answers it.

pairs.left: Where did scientists get their idea?
How can one sponge be used many times?

questions.why: Asking and answering questions while reading helps you find where key information is located.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about boats waiting out a storm uses a key word incorrectly?
questions.why: A storm that stops the work is an obstacle; to mimic means to copy.

questions.stem: Decide whether each word has the Latin root fac / fic (“make, do”) or the root funct (“perform”).

rows.text: artificial
factory
function
malfunction
efficient

questions.why: Artificial (made by skill) and factory (a place where things are made) share the root that means “make.”

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word flexible to mean “willing to change plans”?
options: The rescue leader stayed flexible and moved the team when the wind changed.
The diver's flexible fins bent easily with each strong kick through the water.
The flexible rubber tube bent around the sharp rocks without breaking apart.
A flexible plastic straw let the sick pelican drink while it was lying down.
questions.why: Flexible can describe objects that bend or people who adapt; only the leader adapts a plan.

questions.stem: Engineers studied how a shark's rough skin keeps tiny sea creatures from sticking to it so that they could ____ that skin on the hull of a cleanup ship.
questions.why: To mimic is to copy, and engineers often copy useful features of animals.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The valve did not function after the explosion, so oil kept leaking,” the word function means “to work as designed.”
questions.why: The valve did not work as it was designed to, so the oil leaked.

questions.stem: Which word names a person who learns about the past by digging up and studying old objects?
questions.why: An archaeologist digs up and studies objects that people left behind long ago.

questions.stem: The old clay pot came out of the ground still ____, with no cracks or missing pieces.
questions.why: Intact means whole and undamaged.

questions.stem: Match each word about studying ancient objects to its meaning.

pairs.right: a long period of time in history
kept safe from damage or decay
a person who studies and writes about the past

questions.why: These words often appear together in articles about history and archaeology.

questions.stem: True or false: If a museum has only remnants of an ancient rug, it has the whole rug in perfect condition.
questions.why: Remnants are the small parts that remain, not the whole object.

questions.stem: Using old drawings and a few broken stones, the team tried to ____ what the ancient wall once looked like.
questions.why: To reconstruct is to build or picture something again from the parts that remain.

questions.stem: What is the author's claim in “Small Tokens, Big Ideas”?
options: Clay tokens were mostly toys that children played with long ago.
Farmers in Mesopotamia owned more sheep than they owned grain.
Clay tokens were one of the earliest ways people kept records.
Writing was invented before people needed to keep any records.
questions.why: The author states the claim in paragraph 1 with the words “I believe.”

questions.stem: Which sentence in “Small Tokens, Big Ideas” states the author's claim?

segments.text: I believe that small clay tokens found in ancient Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, were one of the earliest record systems in the world.
Archaeologists have found thousands of these tokens.
Some tokens were sealed inside hollow clay balls.
Long before people wrote words, they still needed to keep records.

questions.why: A claim is the position the author argues for; the other sentences give background or evidence.

questions.stem: What does the word hollow most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 3?

partA.stem: What does the word hollow most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 3?

options.label: A
options.text: empty inside

options.label: B
options.text: brightly painted

options.label: C
options.text: cracked into pieces

options.label: D
options.text: very heavy

partB.stem: Which phrase from paragraph 3 best helps the reader understand hollow?

options.label: A
options.text: the tokens inside

options.label: B
options.text: There is more evidence

options.label: C
options.text: check the count

options.label: D
options.text: Marks pressed on the outside

questions.why: Tokens could be sealed inside the balls, so the balls must have been empty inside.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement from “Small Tokens, Big Ideas” is evidence for the author's claim or a background detail.

rows.text: Each token shape seems to stand for a different good.
Mesopotamia was in what is now Iraq.
Marks on the clay balls matched the tokens inside.
People did not yet write words.

questions.why: Evidence shows that the tokens were used as records; background only sets the scene.

questions.stem: Put the ideas in “Small Tokens, Big Ideas” in the order the author presents them.
sequence: Clay tokens were an early record system.
Each token shape stood for a different good.
Tokens were sealed in clay balls with matching marks.
The tokens may have led to writing.
questions.why: Arguments often move from the claim, to reasons and evidence, to a strong conclusion.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The archaeologist found only fragments of the bowl—dozens of small, sharp pieces scattered in the sand.” What does fragments mean?

partA.stem: Read the sentence: “The archaeologist found only fragments of the bowl—dozens of small, sharp pieces scattered in the sand.” What does fragments mean?

options.label: A
options.text: small broken pieces

options.label: B
options.text: large heavy stones

options.label: C
options.text: colorful paintings

options.label: D
options.text: ancient metal tools

partB.stem: Which words in the sentence are the best context clue for fragments?

options.label: A
options.text: small, sharp pieces

options.label: B
options.text: The archaeologist found

options.label: C
options.text: of the bowl

options.label: D
options.text: in the sand

questions.why: The words after the dash restate what fragments are.

questions.stem: The ancient boat was ____ in the cold, airless mud, so its wood did not rot for two thousand years.
questions.why: The clue “did not rot” shows that the boat was kept safe, or preserved.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence uses the word intact correctly or incorrectly.

rows.text: The jar was found intact, with its lid still in place.
The vase was intact after it shattered on the floor.
Even after the long journey, the old map arrived intact.
The intact wall had crumbled into a pile of stones.

questions.why: Intact means whole, so it cannot describe something shattered or crumbled.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Unlike historians, who mostly study written records, archaeologists learn about the past from objects buried in the ground.” Which word signals a contrast?
questions.why: Unlike is a signal word that shows how two things are different.

questions.stem: Which two sentences include a context clue that explains the meaning of era? Choose two.
options: Historians wrote a long book about that famous era.
The Inca era, a period of about one hundred years, ended in the 1500s.
The era was an exciting one for many people in the city.
During the era of sailing ships, which lasted for centuries, trips took months.
questions.why: Good context clues tell the reader that an era is a long period of time.

questions.stem: Compare a historian and an archaeologist. Decide whom each description fits best.

rows.text: reads old letters and diaries
digs carefully at ancient sites
studies people of an earlier era
brushes dirt off remnants of pottery

questions.why: Both study the past, but historians focus on writings and archaeologists on objects.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “Researchers found remnants of a stone road high in the Andes Mountains. By measuring the pieces and comparing them with old maps, they were able to reconstruct the road's path. They learned that runners once used the road to carry messages across the empire.” Which sentence is the best summary?
options: Old maps are the best way to learn about mountain roads and the people who built them.
By studying road remnants, researchers rebuilt its path and learned how messages traveled.
Researchers found pieces of an old stone road high in the Andes Mountains of South America.
Runners in the Andes were faster than messengers who lived in other parts of the world.
questions.why: A summary includes all the key ideas in a few words and leaves out opinions and extra details.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about rebuilding an ancient wall uses the wrong word?
questions.why: To show how something once looked, a team reconstructs it; to preserve is to keep it safe.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “Quipus used knots on strings to record numbers.” “Clay tablets used marks pressed into clay to record numbers.” Which two statements correctly compare these record systems? Choose two.
options: Both were used to record numbers.
Neither could be used to keep records.
They were made from different materials.
Both used knots to show amounts.
questions.why: Comparing means finding likenesses (both record numbers) and differences (strings versus clay).

questions.stem: True or false: A good summary of a historian's article includes the most important ideas and leaves out small details and personal opinions.
questions.why: Summaries are short and objective, so they keep only the key ideas.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the author's claim in “Save the Past in Pixels”?

partA.stem: Which statement best describes the author's claim in “Save the Past in Pixels”?

options.label: A
options.text: Museums should stop letting visitors see real ancient objects.

options.label: B
options.text: Museums should make digital copies of their oldest objects.

options.label: C
options.text: Ancient objects in museums cannot be protected from damage.

options.label: D
options.text: Digital copies are more valuable than the original objects.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Every year, ancient objects in museums become a little weaker.

options.label: B
options.text: Standing in front of an intact object from a distant era is a powerful experience.

options.label: C
options.text: Cloth fades, wood cracks, and paper crumbles into fragments.

options.label: D
options.text: In my view, every museum should create detailed digital copies of its oldest treasures before more of them are lost.

questions.why: The words “In my view” and “should” signal the author's claim.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Save the Past in Pixels” that give reasons supporting the author's claim.

segments.text: First, digital copies protect the originals.
Second, scans allow people everywhere to learn.
Every year, ancient objects in museums become a little weaker.
Some people argue that a copy can never replace the real thing, and they are partly right.

questions.why: The words “First” and “Second” introduce the author's two reasons.

questions.stem: How does the author respond to people who say that a copy can never replace the real thing?
options: The author ignores the idea and changes the subject to lighting in museums.
The author agrees completely and decides that scanning objects is a waste of money.
The author argues that real objects are far more boring than digital scans.
The author agrees in part but explains that a scan helps the original survive.
questions.why: Strong arguments admit what is true in a counterclaim and then answer it.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word intact most likely means ____.
questions.why: Seeing a complete, undamaged object in person is the powerful experience the author describes.

questions.stem: In “Save the Past in Pixels,” does the author connect each statement with a digital scan or with the original object?

rows.text: can be studied by people far away
should be kept in a dark, cool room
gives a powerful experience when seen in person
can be studied on a screen by students and researchers

questions.why: Comparing and contrasting shows how the author weighs the two ways of studying the past.

questions.stem: Match each key word about the Inca to the context clue that best signals its meaning.

pairs.right: only a few leftover threads remained
rebuilt the bridge using the original plan
kept safe from rot in the dry desert air

questions.why: Context clues may give a definition, an example, or a restatement of a word.

questions.stem: Which sentence states a claim rather than a fact?
options: Some quipus that survive have more than one hundred strings.
Quipus deserve more study than any other Inca object.
Archaeologists have found hundreds of quipus in dry areas of Peru.
Quipus were made from cotton thread or from the soft hair of llamas.
questions.why: A claim is a position that someone argues for; facts can be checked and proved.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about an ancient shipwreck contains an incorrect word?
questions.why: Cold, deep water kept the hull safe, so it was preserved.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The historian, a writer who studies records from the past, described the Inca era,” the words set off by commas are a context clue for historian.
questions.why: Words set off by commas often restate or define the word just before them.

questions.stem: Although the outer strings of the quipu had rotted away, the inner cords were ____, so researchers could still count every knot.
questions.why: The signal word although shows a contrast: rotted outer strings, but whole inner cords.

questions.stem: Which word describes a person who speaks openly and boldly about what he or she believes?
questions.why: An outspoken person says what he or she thinks, even when it is not popular.

questions.stem: Rania was too ____ to raise her hand in class, even though she knew the answer.
questions.why: A reserved person is quiet and keeps thoughts and feelings private.

questions.stem: Match each word from the Frederick Douglass review to its meaning.

pairs.right: looked for or tried to get
the excited feeling of waiting for something

questions.why: These words describe how people act when they work for fairness.

questions.stem: True or false: If two teams are given unequal amounts of practice time, one team gets more time than the other.
questions.why: Unequal means not the same in amount or value.

questions.stem: Every child is ____ to a safe place to learn and play.
questions.why: Entitled means having a right to something.

questions.stem: What does the caption in “A Voice for Readers Who Could Not See” add to the biography?
options: It shows that Braille's code is still used by many people today.
It describes why some teachers did not want to use the new books.
It tells the exact year that Louis Braille started school in Paris.
It explains how Louis Braille hurt his eye in the family workshop.
questions.why: The caption tells about readers today, which the paragraphs do not mention.

questions.stem: Put the events from Louis Braille's life in “A Voice for Readers Who Could Not See” in order.
sequence: He hurt his eye in his father's workshop.
He became blind in both eyes.
He won a place at a school in Paris.
He created a code of raised dots.
questions.why: Biographies usually tell the events of a person's life in time order.

questions.stem: Which sentence in “A Voice for Readers Who Could Not See” best shows the author's perspective about Louis Braille?

segments.text: Louis Braille gave blind readers something they had always deserved: the freedom to read on their own.
Louis Braille was born in a small French village in 1809.
The school owned only a few books, and each one used huge raised letters that were slow to read.
At age fifteen, he created a code of raised dots that fingers could read quickly.

questions.why: Words like “deserved” and “freedom” show that the author admires what Braille did.

questions.stem: What does the word sought mean as it is used in paragraph 3?

partA.stem: What does the word sought mean as it is used in paragraph 3?

options.label: A
options.text: searched for

options.label: B
options.text: gave away

options.label: C
options.text: forgot about

options.label: D
options.text: taught to others

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: At age fifteen, he created a code of raised dots that fingers could read quickly.

options.label: B
options.text: An infection spread, and by age five he was blind in both eyes.

options.label: C
options.text: At that time, blind children rarely went to school.

options.label: D
options.text: Louis was lucky.

questions.why: Louis looked for a better way and then created one, so sought means “searched for.”

questions.stem: Which two sentences belong in a summary of “A Voice for Readers Who Could Not See”? Choose two.
options: The old books at his school had huge letters.
He invented a raised-dot code that blind people still use.
His father owned a workshop full of tools.
Louis Braille became blind as a young child.
questions.why: A summary keeps the most important events and leaves out small details.

questions.stem: Sort the words unequal, rebuild, unfair, dishonest, and reread by their prefix.

rows.text: unequal
rebuild
unfair
dishonest
reread

questions.why: A prefix comes at the beginning of a word and changes its meaning.

questions.stem: Adding the prefix un- to equal makes the word ____, which means “not the same in amount or value.”
questions.why: The prefix un- means “not,” so unequal means “not equal.”

questions.stem: Match each suffix in anticipation, hopeful, fearless, and boldly to its meaning.
questions.why: Suffixes come at the end of words and often change the part of speech.

questions.stem: Anticipation is made of anticipate + -tion. What does anticipation mean in the sentence “The crowd waited in anticipation for the speaker to arrive”?
questions.why: The suffix -tion turns the verb anticipate (look forward to) into a noun.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a debate club has a word with an incorrect prefix?
questions.why: A judge who favors neither team is neutral; “unneutral” is not a correct word.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence from a biography of Marie Curie shows the author's perspective or only states a fact.

rows.text: She was born in 1867 in Warsaw, Poland.
Her bravery in the laboratory still inspires young scientists.
She won two Nobel Prizes.
Few people have ever shown such remarkable determination.

questions.why: Words that judge or praise, such as “remarkable,” reveal the author's perspective.

questions.stem: A biography includes a photograph of a crowded hall with this caption: “People packed the hall in 1847, eager to hear the outspoken speaker.” What does the caption help readers understand?
options: Many people wanted to hear the speaker talk.
The hall was built in the year of the speech.
The speaker was too shy to talk to anyone.
Few people cared about the speaker's ideas.
questions.why: Captions explain what a photograph shows and add facts to the main text.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “People warned Amna to stay quiet, but she chose to defy them and asked for a new library at the meeting.” What does defy mean?

partA.stem: Read the sentence: “People warned Amna to stay quiet, but she chose to defy them and asked for a new library at the meeting.” What does defy mean?

options.label: A
options.text: forget about

options.label: B
options.text: agree with

options.label: C
options.text: wait for

options.label: D
options.text: refuse to obey

partB.stem: Which words from the sentence best help the reader understand defy?

options.label: A
options.text: asked for a new library

options.label: B
options.text: she chose

options.label: C
options.text: warned Amna to stay quiet, but

options.label: D
options.text: at the meeting

questions.why: The word but shows that Amna did the opposite of what she was told.

questions.stem: Which two words describe a person who would probably NOT speak up at a large public meeting? Choose two.
questions.why: Reserved and shy people tend to keep their thoughts to themselves.

questions.stem: For years, she ____ a way to bring clean water to her village, and at last she found one.
questions.why: Sought is the past tense of seek, which means “to look for.”

questions.stem: What is the author's perspective on Helen Keller?

partA.stem: What is the author's perspective on Helen Keller?

options.label: A
options.text: The author admires her courage and achievements.

options.label: B
options.text: The author feels she should have stayed quiet.

options.label: C
options.text: The author thinks her life was mostly unhappy.

options.label: D
options.text: The author believes she relied too much on her teacher.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: For several years she lived in a silent, dark world, and she often became angry because no one could understand her.

options.label: B
options.text: Her life proves that courage can open doors that seem permanently locked.

options.label: C
options.text: Anne spelled words into Helen's hand with her fingers.

options.label: D
options.text: Everything changed in 1887, when a teacher named Anne Sullivan arrived.

questions.why: The final sentence shows the author's admiration by praising Keller's courage.

questions.stem: What information does the caption in “Helen Keller: Speaking for Others” add that the paragraphs do not state?
options: Keller traveled to more than thirty countries to speak.
Keller believed all children had a right to be educated.
Keller learned the word water from her teacher Anne Sullivan.
Keller became very ill before she was two years old.
questions.why: Only the caption tells what Keller believed about every child's education.

questions.stem: Identify the prefix or suffix in each word from “Helen Keller: Speaking for Others.”

rows.text: unable
achievement
suddenly
permanently

questions.why: Un- means “not,” -ment makes a noun, and -ly makes an adverb.

questions.stem: Which three ideas belong in a summary of “Helen Keller: Speaking for Others”? Choose three.
options: Cool water poured over one of Helen's hands.
Helen spoke out for the rights of people with disabilities.
An illness left Helen unable to see or hear.
Helen often became angry as a small child.
Anne Sullivan taught Helen that objects have names.
questions.why: A summary tells the most important events from the beginning, middle, and end.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in “Helen Keller: Speaking for Others” that shows Helen was not reserved about her beliefs.

segments.text: She did not stay quiet about what she had learned.
Anne spelled words into Helen's hand with her fingers.
Helen went on to graduate from college, a remarkable achievement for anyone at that time.
Suddenly Helen understood that every object had a name, and she was eager to learn them all.

questions.why: Someone who does not stay quiet is the opposite of reserved.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about the school election results contains an error in word choice?
segments: and did not reveal any names.
questions.why: A teacher who reveals nothing stays silent; an outspoken person says what he or she thinks.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows that a biographer has a positive perspective on the subject?
options: She worked at the children's hospital from 1990 until 2015.
Her tireless work changed the lives of thousands of families.
She moved with her family to the city of Jeddah at age nineteen.
She sometimes made small mistakes that cost her extra time.
questions.why: Words such as “tireless” show that the author admires the subject.

questions.stem: When the referee was accused of favoring one team, he insisted that he had stayed completely ____.
questions.why: A neutral referee does not take either team's side.

questions.stem: Match each prefixed word (unequal, disagree, misjudge, rewrite) to its meaning.
questions.why: Un- means not, dis- means opposite, mis- means wrongly, and re- means again.

questions.stem: True or false: In the word outspoken, the part out- adds the idea of speaking openly, so an outspoken person rarely shares opinions.
questions.why: Out- in outspoken means openly, so an outspoken person shares opinions often.

questions.stem: Which word describes a person who is always asking questions and wants to learn new things?
questions.why: An inquisitive person is curious and asks many questions.

questions.stem: Bilal was ____ when his little sister solved the difficult puzzle in only two minutes.
questions.why: Astounded means very surprised.

questions.stem: Match each word from the “Where's Brownie?” review to its meaning.
questions.why: These words help describe how characters act while solving a mystery.

questions.stem: True or false: A suspicious person believes that something may be wrong or that someone may not be telling the truth.
questions.why: Being suspicious means having doubts about someone or something.

questions.stem: The scientist made a ____ measurement of the lizard's tail, exact to the millimeter.
questions.why: A precise measurement is exact.

questions.stem: What does the adage “Haste makes waste” mean as Grandfather uses it?
options: Working quickly is always the best way to finish.
Saving things for later is usually a smart choice.
Rushing often causes mistakes and wasted effort.
Small problems tend to solve themselves in time.
questions.why: An adage is a short, wise saying; this one warns against rushing.

questions.stem: Which part of “The Missing Compass” best helps the reader visualize where the scene takes place?

segments.text: A lantern hangs from the center pole, and sleeping bags cover the floor.
(calmly)
(entering with a smile)
(laughing)

questions.why: Stage directions about the setting help readers picture the place.

questions.stem: Label each part of “The Missing Compass” as dialogue or a stage direction.

rows.text: Don't panic, Sami.
pointing at the sand near the door
Haste makes waste, children.
entering with a smile

questions.why: Dialogue is spoken by characters; stage directions in parentheses tell how they act.

questions.stem: How does Huda's perspective on the missing compass differ from Sami's?

partA.stem: How does Huda's perspective on the missing compass differ from Sami's?

options.label: A
options.text: Huda blames Grandfather, while Sami blames Huda.

options.label: B
options.text: Huda stays calm and thinks, while Sami is upset.

options.label: C
options.text: Huda is angry, while Sami thinks it is funny.

options.label: D
options.text: Huda wants to stop, while Sami wants to search.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Don't panic, Sami.

options.label: B
options.text: Do you think a camel carried my compass away?

options.label: C
options.text: We climbed the enormous dune, we fed the camels, and then we helped Grandfather build the evening fire.

options.label: D
options.text: Look at those wide, padded tracks leading directly toward the camels!

questions.why: Huda tells Sami not to panic, which shows her calm, thoughtful perspective.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Missing Compass” in order.
sequence: Sami discovers that the compass is missing.
Sami lists the places he visited.
Grandfather warns that haste makes waste.
Huda notices tracks near the door.
Grandfather explains what a curious camel likes to do.
questions.why: Following the order of the dialogue helps you see how the mystery is solved.

questions.stem: Match each proverb, such as “Two heads are better than one,” to its meaning.

pairs.left: Two heads are better than one.

pairs.right: What you do matters more than what you say.
Doing something often helps you improve.

questions.why: Proverbs are short sayings that share a lesson about life.

questions.stem: When the inquisitive twins finally found the missing key by sharing their ideas, their father smiled and said, “____”
options: Every cloud has a silver lining.
The early bird catches the worm.
Two heads are better than one.
questions.why: The twins succeeded by working together, which fits “Two heads are better than one.”

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a classroom mystery is a proverb that teaches a lesson or a literal statement.

rows.text: Slow and steady wins the race.
The inquisitive students searched the classroom for an hour.
Where there's a will, there's a way.
The chameleon was hiding behind the plant.

questions.why: A proverb gives general advice; a literal statement simply tells what happened.

questions.stem: Nora was suspicious of the new student until she saw him help a younger child carry her books. Which proverb best fits what Nora learned?
options: The early bird catches the worm.
Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
Don't judge a book by its cover.
questions.why: Nora learned not to judge someone before knowing what he is really like.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about the hidden chameleon uses a key word incorrectly?
segments: changed its color to match the leaf,
questions.why: A chameleon that matches a leaf is concealed, or hidden; inquisitive means curious.

questions.stem: Identify each part of a script about a lost kitten.

rows.text: LAYLA, a curious girl of ten
A quiet kitchen late at night
(peeking under the table)
MR. FARIS, a kind neighbor

questions.why: A script lists the cast, describes the setting, and uses stage directions for actions.

questions.stem: Read the stage direction: “(Rain taps against the dark window as Yusuf tiptoes toward the creaking closet, holding a flashlight.)” Which two details help a reader picture that moment? Choose two.
options: Rain taps against the dark window
questions.why: Sensory details in stage directions help readers see and hear the scene.

questions.stem: Read the lines: “REEM: (frowning) I think someone took the chameleon on purpose. ADAM: Maybe, but we shouldn't be suspicious of our friends without proof.” How is Adam's perspective different from Reem's?

partA.stem: Read the lines: “REEM: (frowning) I think someone took the chameleon on purpose. ADAM: Maybe, but we shouldn't be suspicious of our friends without proof.” How is Adam's perspective different from Reem's?

options.label: A
options.text: Adam thinks the pet ran out the door.

options.label: B
options.text: Adam wants proof before blaming anyone.

options.label: C
options.text: Adam is sure that a friend took the pet.

options.label: D
options.text: Adam does not care about the lost pet.

partB.stem: Which words from Adam's line best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Maybe, but

options.label: B
options.text: on purpose

options.label: C
options.text: shouldn't be suspicious of our friends without proof

options.label: D
options.text: I think someone took

questions.why: Adam asks for proof, while Reem already thinks someone took the pet.

questions.stem: In a script, the lines that the characters speak are called the ____.
questions.why: Dialogue is the words characters say to each other.

questions.stem: Why do playwrights include stage directions such as “(astounded, dropping her book)”?
options: to tell audience members when to clap
to list every character in the cast
to give the title of the next scene
to show how a character feels and moves
questions.why: Stage directions tell actors and readers how characters feel and what they do.

questions.stem: How does Omar's perspective change during “The Tortoise Who Disappeared”?

partA.stem: How does Omar's perspective change during “The Tortoise Who Disappeared”?

options.label: A
options.text: He first suspects Khalid but later sees that he was wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: He first wants to search but later decides to go home.

options.label: C
options.text: He first feels calm but later becomes angry at Khalid.

options.label: D
options.text: He first blames Maryam but later blames the hot weather.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I suppose I should reconsider what I said.

options.label: B
options.text: I heard my name!

options.label: C
options.text: I saw Khalid standing near the garden after school.

options.label: D
options.text: Look at this freshly dug soil under the lettuce.

questions.why: When Omar says he should reconsider, he shows that he has changed his mind.

questions.stem: What does Omar mean when he says, “Appearances can be deceiving”?
options: Things are not always what they first seem to be.
People should always trust the first thing they see.
Looking neat matters more than being kind to others.
Clues are useless when trying to solve a mystery.
questions.why: Omar learns that the situation looked bad for Khalid, but it was not what it seemed.

questions.stem: Which line from “The Tortoise Who Disappeared” shows that Maryam wants to use evidence before deciding what happened?

segments.text: We should interpret the clues before we blame anyone.
Our tortoise, Qamar, was inside this fence yesterday afternoon.
Here she is, concealed beneath the leaves and perfectly safe!
Maybe he took her home without asking.

questions.why: To interpret clues means to figure out what they show.

questions.stem: In the stage directions, the word perplexed shows that Maryam feels ____.
questions.why: Maryam cannot understand how the tortoise escaped, so she is perplexed.

questions.stem: Which two details from “The Tortoise Who Disappeared” help the reader visualize the setting? Choose two.
options: a low wooden fence surrounds a patch of grass
a pile of leafy lettuce that nobody has touched
I locked the gate when I left
Maybe he took her home without asking
questions.why: The setting description at the start of a scene paints a picture of the place.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about the detective club contains an error in word choice?
segments: Jana asked her brother to precise
questions.correction: Jana asked her brother to interpret
questions.why: To interpret is to explain the meaning of something; precise means exact.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word reconsider correctly?
options: After hearing new evidence, the judge agreed to reconsider her decision.
He reconsidered the heavy ball all the way across the field to his teammate.
We reconsidered our sandwiches at noon in the busy school cafeteria.
The frightened cat reconsidered under the bed until the loud storm ended.
questions.why: To reconsider means to think again about a decision or opinion.

questions.stem: True or false: The proverb “Still waters run deep” suggests that a quiet person may have deep thoughts and feelings.
questions.why: The proverb compares a quiet person to calm water that is deeper than it looks.

questions.stem: The young detectives were ____ by the empty terrarium: the lid was locked, the glass was unbroken, and yet the lizard was gone.
questions.why: The clues do not make sense together, so the detectives are confused, or perplexed.

questions.stem: Which three words could describe a character who studies every clue carefully and asks many questions? Choose three.
questions.why: A careful, curious detective is inquisitive, precise, and observant.

questions.stem: Which word names a group of lines that forms one section of a poem?
questions.why: A stanza is like a paragraph in a poem.

questions.stem: Match each poetry term from “How Do I Hold the Summer?” to its meaning.

pairs.right: repeating the same beginning sound in nearby words
a regular pattern of strong and weak beats
a short poem that expresses personal feelings
a way of showing a thought or feeling

questions.why: Knowing poetry terms helps you talk about how a poem is built.

questions.stem: The peacock spread its bright blue ____ to show off its beautiful tail feathers.
questions.why: Plumes are large, showy feathers.

questions.stem: True or false: Barren land is covered with thick, green plants and tall trees.
questions.why: Barren land has few or no plants growing on it.

questions.stem: Grandmother's old photograph is ____ to me because it reminds me of our happy trip to Abha.
questions.why: Something meaningful is important because of the feelings or memories it holds.

questions.stem: In the first stanza of “Keeping the Sea,” what does the poet compare the waves to?
questions.why: The line “The waves are silver ribbons” is a metaphor that compares waves to ribbons.

questions.stem: Decide whether each line from “Keeping the Sea” uses a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: I hold the warm and golden afternoon like water in my hand.
The waves are silver ribbons that unravel on the sand;
and all the fishing boats are sleepy whales that drift nearby.

questions.why: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.

questions.stem: Which line from “Keeping the Sea” best shows the theme that we can hold on to happy memories?

segments.text: I fill a jar with memories, with laughter, salt, and light,
The seagulls are writing messages in circles on the sky,
collecting every shining shell the tide delivered here before.
and all the fishing boats are sleepy whales that drift nearby.

questions.why: Filling a jar with memories shows the speaker saving the joy of summer.

questions.stem: True or false: “Keeping the Sea” has two stanzas, and each stanza has four lines.
questions.why: A blank line separates the two four-line stanzas.

questions.stem: “Keeping the Sea” is a lyric poem because it ____.
questions.why: A lyric poem shares a speaker's own thoughts and emotions.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a summer day uses a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: The sun was a golden coin in the sky.
The sand felt as hot as an oven.
Summer is a book I never want to close.
The waves ran like children to the shore.

questions.why: Look for like or as to spot a simile.

questions.stem: Which two lines use alliteration? Choose two.
options: The moon is round and white.
We laughed beneath the palm tree.
questions.why: Alliteration repeats the same first sound in words that are close together.

questions.stem: In the line “My memory is a treasure chest,” the poet uses a ____ to compare memory to a treasure chest without using like or as.
questions.why: A metaphor makes a direct comparison without like or as.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence explaining similes contains an error?
questions.why: A simile always uses like or as; a metaphor does not.

questions.stem: Which sentence best explains the metaphor “Her laugh was music on a sad day”?
options: She liked to sing songs whenever she felt sad.
Her laugh was pleasant and made a sad day feel better.
She played music on the radio every afternoon.
Her laugh was loud and hurt other people's ears.
questions.why: The metaphor compares the laugh to music to show that it was pleasant and comforting.

questions.stem: Read the lines: “The SUN is UP, the DAY is BRIGHT, / The BIRDS are SINGing IN the LIGHT.” Which statement best describes the meter of these lines?

partA.stem: Read the lines: “The SUN is UP, the DAY is BRIGHT, / The BIRDS are SINGing IN the LIGHT.” Which statement best describes the meter of these lines?

options.label: A
options.text: Each line has a steady pattern of four strong beats.

options.label: B
options.text: Each line has exactly two strong beats.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the first line has strong beats.

options.label: D
options.text: The lines have no pattern of beats at all.

partB.stem: Which feature of the lines best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The lines describe a bright morning.

options.label: B
options.text: Weak and strong syllables take turns in a regular pattern.

options.label: C
options.text: The second line begins with the word The.

options.label: D
options.text: Both lines describe things found in nature.

questions.why: Meter is the regular pattern of strong and weak beats in a line of poetry.

questions.stem: Sort each feature: does it describe a rhymed poem with regular meter or a poem written in free verse?

rows.text: Lines follow a steady beat.
Lines can be any length.
Ending sounds repeat in a pattern.
Lines sound like natural speech.

questions.why: Free verse has no set rhyme or meter, so it often sounds like everyday speech.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states a theme a reader might find in a lyric poem about saving seashells at the end of summer?
options: Seashells are found on many beaches in the world.
Summer is the hottest season of the whole year.
Collecting seashells can be dangerous for children.
Small objects can keep precious memories alive.
questions.why: A theme is a message about life, not a fact about the topic.

questions.stem: Put these steps for finding the theme of a lyric poem in a logical order.
sequence: Read the poem and notice the speaker's feelings.
Look for images and words that repeat.
Ask what the speaker learns or realizes.
State the lesson in a complete sentence.
questions.why: Finding a theme starts with noticing details and ends with stating a message.

questions.stem: A poet's choice of strong, colorful words is a form of personal ____, a way of showing feelings to readers.
questions.why: Expression is the way a person shows thoughts and feelings.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “After the Rain in the Desert”?

partA.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “After the Rain in the Desert”?

options.label: A
options.text: Something that seems empty may be quietly waiting to grow.

options.label: B
options.text: Wind is the most powerful force found in the desert.

options.label: C
options.text: Bees travel long distances to find flowers in spring.

options.label: D
options.text: Desert storms are dangerous and should be avoided.

partB.stem: Which line from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Then one evening the heavy clouds arrived,

options.label: B
options.text: The land had not been empty after all.

options.label: C
options.text: and the bees were humming, busy as merchants in a crowded market.

options.label: D
options.text: For months the valley was barren and brown,

questions.why: The speaker realizes that the barren land was only waiting, which reveals the theme.

questions.stem: Classify each line from “After the Rain in the Desert” as a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: a dusty page that nobody wanted to open or read
Purple flowers opened like delicate umbrellas
busy as merchants in a crowded market
tiny green fingers were reaching upward everywhere

questions.why: Similes use like or as; metaphors call one thing another.

questions.stem: Which two features show that “After the Rain in the Desert” is written in free verse? Choose two.
options: Each line ends with a word that rhymes.
The lines do not follow a regular rhyme pattern.
The lines have different lengths and no steady meter.
Every stanza has exactly two short lines.
questions.why: Free verse does not use a fixed rhyme scheme or meter.

questions.stem: In the second stanza, what does the phrase “gray plumes of feathers” suggest about the clouds?
options: They are birds flying together in a large flock.
They are sharp, hard, and about to break apart.
They are thin lines of smoke from a small fire.
They are soft and light, drifting like feathers.
questions.why: Plumes are soft feathers, so the image makes the clouds seem light and soft.

questions.stem: The word barren in the first stanza most likely means ____.
options: empty and unable to grow plants
wet and full of rich soil
questions.why: Before the rain, the valley is brown and dusty, so it is barren.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a poetry lesson uses a key word incorrectly?
questions.why: A group of lines followed by a blank space is a stanza; alliteration is a sound device.

questions.stem: Match each line of poetry to the device it uses: alliteration, simile, metaphor, or personification.

pairs.left: The moon is a lantern in the night.
The river ran like a racing horse.
The old door groaned and complained.

questions.why: Each device creates a different effect: sound, comparison, or human qualities.

questions.stem: Which line uses a metaphor to describe a barren place?
options: The empty field was a forgotten page.
The empty field was quiet like a library.
The empty field stretched far and wide.
The empty field felt as dry as old bread.
questions.why: Only the first line says the field is something else without using like or as.

questions.stem: True or false: In free verse, a poet must keep exactly the same meter in every line.
questions.why: Free verse does not follow a set meter.

questions.stem: A poem describes a barren tree that blooms again every spring. Which two statements could be its theme? Choose two.
options: Hope can return after a difficult period.
Spring is the shortest season of the year.
Hard times do not last forever.
Trees need water in order to grow tall.
questions.why: A theme is a lesson about life that the poem's images suggest.

questions.stem: Match each word about space science with its meaning: orbit, diameter, spheres, approximately.

pairs.right: the curved path one object follows around another in space
the distance straight across a circle through its center
close to an exact amount, but not exact

questions.why: Knowing these words helps you read about planets and their movements.

questions.stem: The Moon takes ____ 27 days to travel once around Earth, so the number is close but not exact.
questions.why: Approximately means about or nearly, which fits a number that is close but not exact.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Earth's orbit around the Sun takes one year,” the word orbit means a curved path around an object in space.
questions.why: An orbit is the path a planet or moon follows around another body.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word spheres correctly?
options: The spheres of the box had four sharp, pointed corners.
Sara folded the paper into two flat, square spheres.
The Sun, the Moon, and Earth are all huge spheres.
Ahmed drew a straight spheres from one side to the other.
questions.why: A sphere is round like a ball, so planets and moons are spheres.

questions.stem: Each word below comes from a Greek root. Tell which root meaning each word uses: astronomical, geology, thermometer, asteroid, diameter.

rows.text: astronomical
geology
thermometer
asteroid
diameter

questions.why: Greek roots such as astro, geo, and meter give clues to the meanings of many science words.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “Al-Biruni Measures Earth”?
options: Al-Biruni climbed mountains because he enjoyed the view of the horizon.
Al-Biruni used a mountain, an angle, and math to find Earth's size.
Al-Biruni proved that earlier thinkers were wrong about the shape of Earth.
Al-Biruni traveled across many deserts to measure the distance between towns.
questions.why: The central idea tells what the whole passage is mostly about: how Al-Biruni measured Earth.

questions.stem: Part A: According to the diagram, what did Al-Biruni measure from the mountaintop?

partA.stem: Part A: According to the diagram, what did Al-Biruni measure from the mountaintop?

options.label: A
options.text: the distance back to the town

options.label: B
options.text: the angle of dip toward the horizon

options.label: C
options.text: the length of the mountain's shadow

options.label: D
options.text: the height of the clouds above him

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Al-Biruni found a simpler way.

options.label: B
options.text: Other thinkers had tried before, but their methods needed long trips across deserts.

options.label: C
options.text: First, he measured the height of a mountain near the town of Nandana.

options.label: D
options.text: He measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line.

questions.why: The diagram's label “angle of dip” matches the sentence about how far the horizon dipped.

questions.stem: Put the steps Al-Biruni followed to measure Earth in order.
sequence: He measured the height of a mountain near Nandana.
He climbed to the top and looked at the horizon.
He measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line.
He used a calculation to work out the size of Earth.
questions.why: Signal words such as first, next, and with these two numbers show the order of the steps.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Al-Biruni Measures Earth” answers the question “How close was Al-Biruni's answer to the answer used today?”

segments.text: Al-Biruni found a simpler way.
He measured how far the horizon dipped below a level line.
His answer was approximately the same as the one scientists use today.
He showed that a clever idea can be as useful as a long and difficult journey.

questions.why: The sentence with approximately the same answers the question directly.

questions.stem: Which two details support the idea that Al-Biruni's method was simpler than earlier methods? Choose two.
options: He asked other scholars to travel for him.
He did not need to make long trips across deserts.
He measured the height of clouds over Nandana.
He needed only a mountain height and one angle.
questions.why: Relevant details explain why his method was simpler: no long trips and only two numbers.

questions.stem: Which two words share a Greek root meaning “star”? Choose two.
questions.why: Astro and aster both mean star, as in astronomical and asterisk (a star-shaped mark).

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “The astronomers set clear criteria to evaluation which comet photos were the sharpest.”
questions.why: After to, use the verb evaluate, which means to judge carefully.

questions.stem: Before choosing a telescope, the astronomy club listed its ____: it had to be light, sturdy, and affordable.
questions.why: Criteria are the rules or standards used to make a choice.

questions.stem: The Greek root photo means “light” and graph means “write” or “record.” What does photograph most likely mean?
options: a letter written about the sky
a map of light in the stars
a drawing made with a pencil
questions.why: Putting the roots together gives an image recorded with light.

questions.stem: Match each Greek root found in astronomy words with its meaning: tele, scope, meter, geo.
questions.why: A telescope lets you look at far things; a meter measures; geo means earth.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does a weather balloon burst high in the sky?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does a weather balloon burst high in the sky?

options.label: A
options.text: The radiosonde becomes too heavy for the string to hold.

options.label: B
options.text: The air pressure around it drops, so it swells too much.

options.label: C
options.text: The helium freezes into ice once it is very cold.

options.label: D
options.text: The parachute opens and tears the side of the balloon.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The air pressure gets lower as the balloon climbs higher.

options.label: B
options.text: Forecasters use the data to predict storms and plan safe flights.

options.label: C
options.text: It sends this data back to the ground by radio every few seconds.

options.label: D
options.text: Each balloon carries a small box of instruments called a radiosonde.

questions.why: Lower pressure lets the balloon swell until it bursts.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Weather Balloons” answers the question “What does a radiosonde measure?”

segments.text: Each balloon carries a small box of instruments called a radiosonde.
As the balloon rises, the radiosonde measures temperature, air pressure, and moisture.
The parachute then opens, and the radiosonde drifts gently back to Earth.

questions.stem: Tell whether each fact about weather balloons is shown in the diagram of “Weather Balloons” or is stated only in the paragraphs.

rows.text: The balloon is filled with helium.
A parachute hangs below the balloon.
The balloon bursts about 30 kilometers up.
Data is sent by radio every few seconds.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Weather Balloons”?
options: Weather balloons carry instruments that collect data used for forecasts.
Weather stations around the world are built in hundreds of places.
Weather balloons are filled with helium and tied to small parachutes.
Weather balloons burst at about thirty kilometers above the ground.
questions.why: The central idea covers the whole passage: balloons collect data that forecasters use.

questions.stem: Which two details are most relevant to the central idea of “Weather Balloons”? Choose two.
options: Forecasters use the data to predict storms.
The radiosonde measures temperature, air pressure, and moisture.
The parachute drifts gently back to Earth.
The balloon is filled with helium.
questions.why: Relevant details support the idea that balloons collect useful weather data.

questions.stem: Tell whether each word contains the Greek root sphere (“ball”) or meter (“measure”): atmosphere, hemisphere, perimeter, diameter, spheres.

hemisphere
perimeter
diameter
spheres

questions.why: A singular subject such as each planet needs the verb follows.

questions.stem: Which two sentences use the word evaluate correctly? Choose two.
options: The rocket will evaluate into space at noon.
Please evaluate the cookies on the top shelf.
The judges will evaluate each science project using a checklist.
Scientists evaluate new data before they publish their results.
questions.why: Evaluate means to judge or check the value of something carefully.

questions.stem: Put the steps a student follows to find the diameter of a ball by calculation in order.
sequence: Wrap a string once around the widest part of the ball.
Measure the length of the string with a ruler.
Divide that length by approximately 3.14.
Record the answer as the ball's diameter.
questions.why: A calculation follows clear steps: measure, then divide, then record.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “Watching Earth from Space”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “Watching Earth from Space”?

options.label: A
options.text: The first satellite was small, but it carried many instruments.

options.label: B
options.text: Satellites let scientists study Earth as one whole, connected system.

options.label: C
options.text: Thermometers on rooftops were the best tools for studying weather.

options.label: D
options.text: Dust storms travel across oceans for thousands of kilometers.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Today, satellites give scientists a view of Earth as one connected system rather than a collection of separate places.

options.label: B
options.text: Satellites changed that.

options.label: C
options.text: A thermometer on a rooftop recorded the temperature of one city, and a ship could measure the waves of one patch of sea.

options.label: D
options.text: The first satellite, launched in 1957, was about the size of a beach ball.

questions.why: The final paragraph sums up the central idea: satellites show Earth as one system.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Watching Earth from Space” that are relevant details showing what satellites help scientists observe.

segments.text: Before the space age, scientists could study only small pieces of Earth at a time.
Circling high above the surface, these machines photograph clouds, oceans, forests, and ice every day.
The first satellite, launched in 1957, was about the size of a beach ball.
Researchers have watched sea ice shrink, deserts spread, and enormous dust storms travel thousands of kilometers across oceans.

questions.why: These two sentences give details about what satellites let scientists see.

questions.stem: The Greek root atmos means “vapor,” and sphaira means “ball.” What does atmosphere most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 2?
options: the hot rock found deep inside Earth
the deep water that covers most of Earth
the round metal body of a satellite
the layer of air that surrounds the planet
questions.why: Atmos plus sphere suggests a ball of gas: the air around Earth.

questions.stem: Decide whether each detail from “Watching Earth from Space” is important to the central idea or is interesting but less important.

rows.text: Satellites photograph clouds, oceans, and ice every day.
The first satellite was about the size of a beach ball.
Satellite data revealed patterns that were once invisible.
A ship could measure the waves of one patch of sea.

questions.why: Important details support the central idea; others are interesting facts that do not.

questions.stem: Put the ideas of “Watching Earth from Space” in the order the author presents them.
sequence: Scientists once studied only small pieces of Earth.
Satellites began photographing the whole planet every day.
Satellite data revealed patterns such as shrinking sea ice.
Scientists now see Earth as one connected system.
questions.why: The author moves from the past, to satellites, to discoveries, to a conclusion.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: rely, nominate, sympathy, weakling.

pairs.right: to depend on someone or something
to suggest someone for a job or honor
a feeling of sorrow for another person's trouble
a person who is not strong

questions.why: Learning exact meanings helps you use each word correctly.

questions.stem: The coach could ____ on Hamad to arrive early, because he was never late to practice.
questions.why: Only rely is used with on to mean depend on.

questions.stem: True or false: A supportive friend is someone who encourages you when you are having a hard time.
questions.why: Supportive means giving help and encouragement.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Our class decided to nominated Sara as team captain.”
questions.why: After to, use the base form of the verb: nominate.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word obviously correctly?
options: We obviously hid the gift where nobody would ever be able to find it.
The floor was wet and muddy, so obviously someone had come in from the rain.
The teacher whispered obviously so that no one in the room could hear.
Obviously, I have no idea at all where my sister went this afternoon.
questions.why: Obviously means in a way that is easy to see or understand.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Ruth's action at the end of “The Soup Pot, 1932” show about her?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Ruth's action at the end of “The Soup Pot, 1932” show about her?

options.label: A
options.text: She wants to leave home and find work.

options.label: B
options.text: She does not like the taste of the soup.

options.label: C
options.text: She is angry that Mama said no to her.

options.label: D
options.text: She is generous even when she has little.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: She simply poured half of her own bowl into a glass jar and wrapped it carefully in a towel to keep it warm.

options.label: B
options.text: In the winter of 1932, Papa lost his job at the shoe factory, and the family's small savings disappeared within a few months.

options.label: C
options.text: Ruth did not argue.

options.label: D
options.text: Mama started making soup from whatever was left in the cupboard.

questions.why: Giving away half of her own food shows Ruth is generous.

questions.stem: Based on the end of “The Soup Pot, 1932,” what will Ruth most likely do next?
options: Eat the soup in the hallway so Mama will not see her.
Ask her little brother to carry the jar to the factory.
Pour the soup back into the pot because Mama said no.
Take the jar of soup to Mr. Kaplan's door.
questions.why: Ruth wrapped her food and stepped into the hallway toward her neighbor's home.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Soup Pot, 1932” best helps the reader predict where Ruth is going?

segments.text: Some nights it was only potatoes and water with a little salt.
One evening, Ruth noticed that old Mr. Kaplan next door had not lit his stove for several days.
Mama sighed and rubbed her tired eyes.
Ruth did not argue.

questions.why: Ruth noticed her neighbor had no fire, a clue that she will bring him food.

questions.stem: Tell whether each detail about the family in “The Soup Pot, 1932” shows a problem or a character's response to the problem.

rows.text: Papa lost his job at the shoe factory.
Some nights the soup was only potatoes and water.
Mama made soup from whatever was left.
Ruth poured half of her bowl into a jar.

questions.why: Characters show who they are by how they respond to problems.

questions.stem: Which two words best describe Mama in “The Soup Pot, 1932”? Choose two.
questions.why: Mama sighs, looks tired, and thinks carefully about how much food the family has.

questions.stem: Match each idiom about hard times with its meaning: in the same boat, tighten our belts, keep your chin up, make ends meet.

pairs.right: have just enough money for needs

questions.why: An idiom means something different from its exact words.

questions.stem: Obviously worried, Uncle Faisal told us, “The shop has closed, so we will have to ____ until I find new work.”
questions.why: Tighten our belts means spend less money, which fits losing a job.

questions.stem: Tell whether the key word in each sentence is used correctly or incorrectly: assume, sympathy, weakling, nominate.

rows.text: I assume the bus is late because it has not arrived yet.
Her sympathy for the lost kitten made her search for its owner.
The weakling lifted the heavy piano all by himself.
We nominate the weather to be sunny tomorrow.

questions.why: A weakling is not strong, and people, not weather, are nominated.

questions.stem: Which two sentences contain an idiom? Choose two.
options: Let's not beat around the bush; just tell me the news.
The clouds moved slowly across the evening sky.
My little sister was on cloud nine after the school show.
We walked around the bush in my uncle's garden.
questions.why: On cloud nine means very happy; beat around the bush means avoid the main point.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Grandpa said the old radio cost an arm and a leg,” the idiom means the radio was very expensive.
questions.why: Cost an arm and a leg is an idiom meaning very expensive.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main conflict in “Leo's Plan”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main conflict in “Leo's Plan”?

options.label: A
options.text: Leo wants to quit arithmetic, but his teacher will not allow it.

options.label: B
options.text: Leo and Pa argue about who should sell newspapers on the corner.

options.label: C
options.text: Leo cannot find a corner where he is allowed to sell newspapers.

options.label: D
options.text: Leo wants to earn money, but Pa wants him to stay in school.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: In the morning, he explained his plan carefully.

options.label: B
options.text: He felt caught between two things he cared about.

options.label: C
options.text: Each morning Pa left before sunrise, and each evening he came home with empty hands and a tired smile.

options.label: D
options.text: Leo pushed his beans around his plate.

questions.why: Leo is caught between helping his family and staying in school.

questions.stem: What does the idiom “drive a hard bargain” mean as it is used in the last paragraph of “Leo's Plan”?
options: travel a long way to buy something
argue well to get what you want
work at a job that is very difficult
refuse to listen to anyone's advice
questions.why: Pa means Leo made a strong case and won the deal.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Leo's Plan” in order.
sequence: Leo offers to sell newspapers on the corner.
Pa says that Leo's job is school.
Leo lies awake until he thinks of a plan.
Pa agrees if Leo keeps his grades up.
questions.why: Following the plot shows how the conflict builds and is resolved.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Leo's Plan” shows how Leo solves his problem?

segments.text: Each morning Pa left before sunrise, and each evening he came home with empty hands and a tired smile.
Pa shook his head.
He loved his lessons, especially arithmetic, but he hated seeing his family worry about every penny.
He would sell papers for one hour before school and still be in his seat when the bell rang.

questions.why: Leo's plan lets him work and still go to school, which resolves the conflict.

questions.stem: Tell what each detail from “Leo's Plan” reveals about Leo's character.

rows.text: He hated seeing his family worry about every penny.
He would work one hour before school and still be on time.
He was tired of watching his father search for work.
He found a way to keep both his job and his lessons.

questions.why: Characters' thoughts and actions reveal their traits.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Obviously, the injured runner was no weakling; he finished the race on a sore ankle.” What does weakling mean?

options.label: B

questions.stem: Which three sentences use a key word correctly? Choose three.

Don't assume you know the answer before you read the question.

The neighbors showed sympathy by bringing meals to the family.
We rely the bus every day to get to school.
questions.why: Supportive means helpful, and rely needs on.

questions.stem: Match each idiom about effort and choices with its meaning: a blessing in disguise, bite off more than you can chew, the ball is in your court.

pairs.right: something good that first seemed bad

pairs.left: bite off more than you can chew
the ball is in your court
pairs.right: it is your turn to decide

questions.why: Idioms must be understood as whole phrases.

questions.stem: Part A: Which type of conflict is most important in “Black Sunday”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which type of conflict is most important in “Black Sunday”?

options.label: A
options.text: a struggle between two neighbors

options.label: B
options.text: a struggle inside Mae about school

options.label: C
options.text: a struggle between Mae and Grandpa

options.label: D

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Black Sunday” that help the reader predict that a dangerous storm is coming.

segments.text: Mae's family had stayed on their farm through three hard years, but every storm tested their patience.
On a quiet Sunday afternoon, Mae was hanging laundry when the birds suddenly went silent.

Mae ran toward the chickens with her heart pounding.

questions.why: The silent birds and the wall of dust are clues that a storm is about to hit.

questions.stem: Based on Grandpa's orders, what will the family most likely do next in “Black Sunday”?

finish hanging the laundry before the wind arrives
walk to town to warn the neighbors about the storm
load the wagon and drive toward the dust cloud
questions.why: Wetting cloths for the windows shows they plan to keep the dust out and stay inside.

questions.stem: Tell which trait each detail from “Black Sunday” reveals.

rows.text: Grandpa studied the sky and wasted no time.
Grandpa gave clear orders about the animals and windows.
Mae froze when she saw the dust.
Mae ran to the chickens with her heart pounding.

questions.why: Actions and reactions reveal characters' traits.

questions.stem: Which two details show that the family's struggle with nature had lasted a long time? Choose two.
options: Fences were already buried and crops ruined.
They had stayed on the farm through three hard years.
Mae was hanging laundry on a Sunday.
questions.why: Details about years of storms show a long conflict with nature.

questions.stem: Match each word about plants and animals with its meaning: thrive, widespread, declined, probable.

questions.stem: Date palms ____ in hot, dry places where many other trees would struggle to survive.

unexpected
widespread
orderly

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Lionfish Do Not Belong Here” explains why lionfish numbers grow so fast in the Atlantic?

segments.text: Lionfish are beautiful fish with striped fins and long spines.
In the Atlantic, lionfish have no natural enemies.
Some restaurants now serve lionfish, which gives people another good reason to hunt them.

questions.stem: According to the chart in “Lionfish Do Not Belong Here,” what happened to the young reef fish after lionfish arrived?

questions.stem: Tell under which heading of “Lionfish Do Not Belong Here” each detail appears.

rows.text: Lionfish have no natural enemies in the Atlantic.
Each female can lay thousands of eggs.
Divers and fishers should catch lionfish.
Restaurants now serve lionfish.

questions.stem: Which two statements would the author of “Lionfish Do Not Belong Here” most likely agree with? Choose two.
options: Lionfish are a danger to Atlantic reef fish.
Reef fish do not need any protection.
Lionfish should be brought to more oceans.

questions.stem: Which two words have the same root as identify? Choose two.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Visitors to the park declined after the bridge closed,” the word declined means ____.

questions.stem: Match each word with its Latin root and the root's meaning: dictionary, transport, construct, spectator.

questions.why: After to, use the base form decline.

questions.stem: Tell whether the prefix in each word means “not / opposite of” or “again”: unexpected, disorder, regrow, reintroduce.

disorder
regrow
reintroduce

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's perspective on honeybees in “A Welcome Newcomer”?

questions.stem: Which two questions are answered in the section “How Do Honeybees Help Farmers?” Choose two.

Where did honeybees first come from?

questions.stem: Tell whether each statement from “A Welcome Newcomer” is a fact or the author's opinion.

rows.text: Honeybees carry pollen as they collect nectar.

questions.stem: Put the steps a scientist might follow to identify an invasive plant in order.

Report the plant if it is not native.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “After the unexpected frost, the number of orange trees have declined across the valley.”

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's perspective in “A Tree That Went Too Far”?

options.label: A
