questions.stem: Tell whether each detail in “A Tree That Went Too Far” was a reason planners chose mesquite or a result they did not plan.

It could grow with very little rain.
Thorny forests covered grazing land.
Native trees lost their water.

questions.stem: Which two words best describe the author's attitude toward quick fixes in “A Tree That Went Too Far”? Choose two.
questions.why: The author warns that quick fixes can cause costly problems.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: bulletin, enlisted, recruits, survival.

questions.why: These words often appear in stories about wartime.

questions.stem: True or false: If a goalkeeper can intercept a pass, he stops the ball before it reaches the other player.

The contributions ran quickly across the field toward the fence.
She painted her contributions bright blue during the art class.
The bus made contributions at every stop along the main road.
questions.why: Contributions are things given to help a cause.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Victory Garden” shows where the flashback begins?

segments.text: Nora knelt in the dirt and pulled a fat orange carrot from the ground.
Back in the spring of 1943, Nora had felt useless.
All summer, Nora watered and weeded under the hot sun.
Now, as she filled her basket, she finally understood.

questions.why: Back in and had felt signal a move to an earlier time.

questions.stem: Part A: Which sentence best states a theme of “The Victory Garden”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which sentence best states a theme of “The Victory Garden”?

options.label: A
options.text: Families should always live close to farms.

options.label: B
options.text: Gardening is easier than working in a factory.

options.label: C
options.text: Even small efforts can make a real difference.

options.label: D
options.text: Young people should not try to do adult jobs.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Some days her back ached, and she wanted to quit.

options.label: B
options.text: Even a girl with a shovel could make a difference.

options.label: C
options.text: She smiled, remembering the day the garden began.

options.label: D
options.text: Her brother had joined the navy, and her mother worked long hours at the factory.

questions.why: The last sentence states the lesson Nora learns.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Victory Garden” in the order they actually happened.
sequence: Nora felt useless after her brother joined the navy.
Grandpa handed Nora a shovel.
Nora watered and weeded all summer.
Nora pulled a carrot and filled her basket.
questions.why: A flashback tells events out of order; this is the time order.

questions.stem: Which is the best summary of “The Victory Garden”?
options: Nora's back aches all summer, and she almost quits her garden.
Grandpa gives Nora a shovel and points at the empty backyard.
Nora grows a garden in wartime and learns she can help.
Nora's brother joins the navy and her mother works at a factory.
questions.why: A summary tells the most important events and the main lesson briefly.

questions.stem: Tell whether each event from “The Victory Garden” happens in the present or in the flashback.

rows.text: Nora pulls a carrot from the ground.
Grandpa hands Nora a shovel.
Nora feels useless in the spring of 1943.
Nora fills her basket with vegetables.

questions.why: The flashback shows what happened before the present scene.

questions.stem: Choose the correct homophone, flour or flower, for each sentence about a wartime bakery.

rows.text: Aunt Huda sifted the ____ for the bread.
A red ____ grew beside the bakery door.
Everyone's contributions included a bag of ____ for the ovens.
Libby pinned a paper ____ to the bulletin board.

questions.why: Flour is for baking; a flower is a plant.

questions.stem: Which two sentences use the homophones correctly? Choose two.
options: Their contributions helped the club buy new books.
There survival depended on clean water.
The pilots new the operations plan well.
The recruits knew the new rules by heart.
questions.why: Their shows ownership; knew is the past of know.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “The bulletin said that it's to late to enlist this year.”
questions.why: Too means more than enough; to shows direction.

questions.stem: The city is proud of the ____ of its people, who come from many different countries.
questions.why: Diversity means variety, such as people from many places.

questions.stem: Match each homophone in the pairs peace / piece and whole / hole with its meaning.
questions.why: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.

questions.stem: Part A: Which sentence best states the theme of “The Scrap Drive”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which sentence best states the theme of “The Scrap Drive”?

options.label: A
options.text: Old things should always be thrown away.

options.label: B
options.text: Neighbors rarely help one another.

options.label: C
options.text: Children should not work during a war.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep trying even when others doubt you.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: He had learned that patience could turn a closed door into an open one.

options.label: B
options.text: The truck pulled away, piled high with old pots, broken bicycles, and rusty tools.

options.label: C
options.text: One man even laughed and said a boy could not help win a war.

options.label: D
options.text: Tom waved until it turned the corner, and then he looked down at his empty wagon and grinned proudly.

questions.why: Tom keeps trying, and patience brings success.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Scrap Drive” signals that the story is moving back in time?

segments.text: Gradually, doors began to open.
Three weeks earlier, he had stood in the same spot feeling foolish.
That evening, Tom almost gave up.
By the end of the month, Tom's wagon had made forty trips across town.

questions.why: Three weeks earlier tells the reader a flashback is starting.

questions.stem: Which two details are most important to include in a summary of “The Scrap Drive”? Choose two.
options: Mrs. Lee gave him a dented kettle.
Tom collected scrap metal to help build ships.
Tom made a sign and kept asking until neighbors helped.
questions.why: A summary includes main events, not small details.

questions.stem: In “The Scrap Drive,” Tom's neighbors were slow to help, but ____ gifts filled the truck in the end.
questions.why: Their shows that the gifts belong to the neighbors.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Scrap Drive” in the order they happened in time.
sequence: The town bulletin asked for scrap metal.
Most neighbors shook their heads at Tom.
Tom painted a sign for his wagon.
The truck pulled away piled high with metal.
questions.why: The story starts at the end, so the time order differs from the telling order.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The ship's radio team worked day and night to intercept enemy messages before they reached their target.” What does intercept mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The ship's radio team worked day and night to intercept enemy messages before they reached their target.” What does intercept mean?

options.label: A
options.text: catch something before it arrives

options.label: B
options.text: read something aloud

options.label: C
options.text: send something far away

options.label: D
options.text: write something in code

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the sentence best helps the reader understand intercept?

options.label: A
options.text: before they reached their target

options.label: B
options.text: The ship's radio team

options.label: C
options.text: worked day and night

options.label: D
options.text: enemy messages

questions.why: Catching messages before they arrive is what intercept means.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to summarize how the town bulletin led to a food drive.
sequence: The town bulletin asked families for help.
Families made contributions of canned food.
Volunteers packed the food into boxes.
Trucks carried the boxes to the soldiers.
questions.why: A good summary keeps the main events in order.

questions.stem: Which three sentences use a key word correctly? Choose three.
options: The survival of the garden depended on daily watering.
Her brother enlisted in the navy when he turned eighteen.
The cat tried to intercept a nap on the sofa.
The diversity of the team was all one single color.
The factory ran its operations day and night.
questions.why: Diversity means variety, and intercept means stop on the way.

questions.stem: The new recruits had to ____ outside the office for their orders.
questions.why: Wait means stay until something happens; weight is how heavy something is.

questions.stem: Read: “Omar was too young to enlist, so he collected scrap metal and wrote letters to soldiers.” Which theme does this sentence suggest?
options: Young people should wait until they are older to help.
Writing letters is always better than other kinds of work.
Everyone can help in some way.
Collecting metal is a fun weekend hobby for children.
questions.why: Omar finds his own way to help, which suggests everyone can contribute.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the theme of “The Night Shift”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the theme of “The Night Shift”?

options.label: A
options.text: Hard work always brings quick rewards.

options.label: B
options.text: Quiet, unseen work can be very important.

options.label: C
options.text: Young people should never do dull jobs.

options.label: D
options.text: Radios are the best way to learn history.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: She never learned what most of them said.

options.label: B
options.text: The work was dull and exhausting.

options.label: C
options.text: Grandmother Ellen turned the old radio dial slowly, as if it might still carry secrets.

options.label: D
options.text: Years later, she discovered that her careful notes had helped others crack the codes and protect ships at sea.

questions.why: Her unseen notes protected ships, which shows the theme.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Night Shift” that describe events from the flashback.

segments.text: Grandmother Ellen turned the old radio dial slowly, as if it might still carry secrets.
In 1942, she had joined hundreds of young women at a quiet station by the sea.
Night after night, she sat with headphones pressed to her ears, writing down strings of letters that meant nothing to her.

questions.why: The flashback tells about Ellen's work in 1942.

questions.stem: Why does the author most likely use a flashback in “The Night Shift”?
options: to compare Ellen's life with the lives of sailors
to explain how secret codes are written and read
to show how Ellen's past explains her words now
to describe how a modern radio is built and used
questions.why: The flashback shows the experience behind Ellen's final words.

questions.stem: Tell whether each statement about “The Night Shift” belongs in a summary or is a minor detail.

rows.text: Ellen copied coded messages during the war.
Ellen turned the radio dial slowly.
Her notes helped protect ships at sea.
She wore headphones on her ears.

questions.why: A summary keeps key events and leaves out small details.

questions.stem: In “The Night Shift,” Ellen wrote down every letter, but she never ____ what most of the messages meant.
questions.why: Knew is the past of know; new means not old.

questions.stem: Match each word about animal survival with its meaning: frigid, agile, forage, cache.

pairs.right: able to move quickly and easily

questions.why: These words describe how animals live in harsh places.

questions.stem: Thick blubber ____ a seal's body from the icy water.
questions.why: Insulates means keeps heat in and cold out.

questions.stem: True or false: An animal that is dormant is very active and moves around all day.
questions.why: Dormant means resting or inactive for a time.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Some bears hibernates through the long winter.”
questions.why: The plural subject bears needs hibernate.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of an adaptation?
options: a fish's glowing light that helps it find food in the dark
a diver's flashlight that helps her see deep under the water
a boat's strong motor that pushes it through rough waves
a scientist's camera that takes photos of the sea floor
questions.why: An adaptation is a body part or behavior that helps a living thing survive.

questions.stem: Part A: Why do many deep-sea animals make their own light?

partA.stem: Part A: Why do many deep-sea animals make their own light?

options.label: A
options.text: Their food glows in the dark.

options.label: B
options.text: No sunlight reaches that deep.

options.label: C
options.text: The water there is very warm.

options.label: D
options.text: They want to scare away divers.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Animals use their light in different ways.

options.label: B
options.text: Because there is no light, many deep-sea animals make their own.

options.label: C
options.text: The anglerfish has a glowing lure that hangs above its mouth.

options.label: D
options.text: This glow is called bioluminescence.

questions.why: The signal word because shows the cause.

questions.stem: Match each cause from “Lights in the Deep” with its effect.

pairs.left: Small fish swim toward the anglerfish's lure.
A shrimp sprays a glowing cloud.
Sunlight cannot reach the deep ocean.
pairs.right: The water below 1,000 meters is dark.

questions.why: A cause is why something happens; an effect is what happens.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Lights in the Deep” is a context clue that helps explain the word lure?

segments.text: Below about 1,000 meters, the water is completely dark.
Small fish swim toward the light, and the anglerfish quickly snaps them up.
Some shrimp spray a cloud of glowing liquid when a predator comes near.
Light can also help animals find each other in the endless dark.

questions.why: Fish swim toward the lure and get caught, so a lure is something that attracts prey.

questions.stem: Which question is answered in paragraph 2 of “Lights in the Deep”?
options: How do fish find each other in the dark?
How deep can sunlight travel in the sea?
How does the anglerfish catch its food?
How cold is the water in the deep sea?
questions.why: Paragraph 2 explains the anglerfish's glowing lure.

questions.stem: Which two animals in “Lights in the Deep” use light to hunt or to escape? Choose two.
questions.why: The anglerfish hunts with light, and the shrimp escapes with it.

questions.stem: The ____ squirrel leaped from branch to branch without ever slipping.
questions.why: The clue leaped without slipping shows the squirrel moves quickly and easily.

questions.stem: Read: “The volcano had been dormant for centuries; it was quiet, and no lava had flowed.” Which two clues help explain dormant? Choose two.
questions.why: The clues after the semicolon describe something inactive.

questions.stem: Tell which type of context clue explains the key word in each sentence about animals.

rows.text: The jay hid a cache, or secret store, of acorns.
Some animals hibernate, such as bears, bats, and groundhogs.
Unlike the frigid north, the tropics are warm all year.
Seals forage, or search for food, under the ice.

questions.why: Clue words such as or, such as, and unlike signal different kinds of context clues.

questions.stem: Match each ocean science word with its meaning: pressure, predator, prey, current.

pairs.right: the force of something pressing down

questions.why: These words help you read about life in the ocean.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Fur insulates the fox, so it stays warm in the snow,” the clue “stays warm” helps explain insulates.
questions.why: Stays warm tells what insulating fur does.

questions.stem: Part A: According to the map in “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor,” where are the vent sites found?

partA.stem: Part A: According to the map in “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor,” where are the vent sites found?

options.label: A
options.text: near the surface of the ocean

options.label: B
options.text: in the middle of a calm bay

options.label: C
options.text: along a ridge on the sea floor

options.label: D
options.text: on the beaches of the islands

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: As a result, tubeworms, crabs, and clams live near the vents even though sunlight never reaches them.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the water carries chemicals, tiny bacteria can turn them into food.

options.label: C
options.text: Vents form where the plates of Earth's crust slowly pull apart.

options.label: D
options.text: These openings are called hydrothermal vents.

questions.why: Plates pull apart at ridges, which is where the map shows the stars.

questions.stem: Put the steps that create a hydrothermal vent, as described in “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor,” in order.
sequence: Plates of Earth's crust pull apart and form cracks.
Seawater sinks into the cracks.
Melted rock below heats the water.
Hot water shoots back up through the vent.
questions.why: Cause-and-effect steps follow one another in order.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor” explains why animals can live near the vents without sunlight?

segments.text: In 1977, scientists in a small submarine called Alvin made a surprising discovery near the Galápagos Islands.
These openings are called hydrothermal vents.
Because the water carries chemicals, tiny bacteria can turn them into food.
Seawater sinks into the cracks, is heated by melted rock below, and then shoots back up.

questions.why: Bacteria make food from chemicals, so animals can eat without sunlight.

questions.stem: Tell whether each question about hydrothermal vents can be answered with the map or with the paragraphs of “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor.”

rows.text: Where are the vent sites located?
Which islands are near a vent site?
In what year were the vents discovered?
Which animals live near the vents?

questions.why: Maps show where things are; paragraphs explain when, how, and why.

questions.stem: What does the word vents most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 1 of “Hot Springs on the Ocean Floor”?
options: deep holes that fill with sand
small animals that live in cracks
large rocks on the ocean floor
questions.why: The clue These openings are called hydrothermal vents defines the word.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Arctic foxes cache extra food in summer; they bury lemmings and eggs to eat when the frigid winter arrives.” What does cache mean in this sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Arctic foxes cache extra food in summer; they bury lemmings and eggs to eat when the frigid winter arrives.” What does cache mean in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: share something with others

options.label: B
options.text: cook something over a fire

options.label: C
options.text: store something in a hidden place

options.label: D
options.text: catch something very quickly

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the sentence best helps the reader understand cache?

options.label: A
options.text: Arctic foxes

options.label: B
options.text: extra food in summer

options.label: C
options.text: they bury lemmings and eggs to eat

options.label: D
options.text: when the frigid winter arrives

questions.why: Burying food to eat later shows that cache means hide and store.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Because the water is so frigid, the walrus rely on thick blubber, which insulates its body.”
questions.why: The walrus is singular, so the verb is relies.

questions.stem: Put the events in the cause-and-effect chain of a ground squirrel's winter in order.
sequence: The days grow short and cold.
Food becomes hard to find.
The squirrel enters its burrow to hibernate.
Its body stays dormant until spring.
questions.why: Each event causes the next one.

questions.stem: Which three sentences describe an animal adaptation? Choose three.
options: An agile octopus squeezes through tiny cracks to escape.
A boat carries a lamp to see underwater.
A deep-sea fish has huge eyes that collect faint light.
A diver wears a wetsuit in cold water.
A polar bear's thick fur insulates it from the cold.
questions.why: Adaptations are features of living things, not tools people use.

questions.stem: Tell whether the first part of each sentence about animals in harsh places is a cause or an effect.

rows.text: Because food is scarce in the deep sea, fish forage over long distances.
Whales grow thick blubber since the water is frigid.
The squid is agile, so it escapes most hunters.
The seeds stayed dormant because the soil was dry.

questions.why: Because, since, and so signal cause-and-effect relationships.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main cause of the Red Sea's warm deep water?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main cause of the Red Sea's warm deep water?

options.label: A
options.text: Deep-sea animals warm the water as they swim.

options.label: B
options.text: Rivers bring warm water from the deserts.

options.label: C
options.text: A shallow entrance blocks cold deep currents.

options.label: D
options.text: Hot springs on the sea floor heat the water.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: This unusual warmth has consequences.

options.label: B
options.text: The Red Sea is a remarkable exception.

options.label: C
options.text: Most of the deep ocean is frigid, with temperatures barely above freezing.

options.label: D
options.text: Bab el-Mandeb is shallow, so the icy deep currents of the Indian Ocean cannot flow over it.

questions.why: Cold currents cannot enter, so the deep water stays warm.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Warm Deep of the Red Sea” that describe effects of the deep water's warmth.

segments.text: Most of the deep ocean is frigid, with temperatures barely above freezing.
The answer lies at the southern entrance.
Many deep-sea animals from the Indian Ocean need cold water, so they cannot survive in the Red Sea's depths.
As a result, its deep waters hold fewer species, yet several of them are found nowhere else.

questions.why: These sentences tell what happens because the water is warm.

questions.stem: What does the word basin most likely mean as it is used in the paragraph that begins “Why is the deep water so warm?”
options: a strong current that moves quickly
a narrow passage between two seas
a large, low area that holds water
a layer of salt on the ocean floor
questions.why: The water sinks and fills the basin, so a basin is a low area that holds water.

questions.stem: Tell whether each fact about the Red Sea is shown on the map in “The Warm Deep of the Red Sea” or is given only in the paragraphs.

rows.text: Bab el-Mandeb is at the southern end of the sea.
The Red Sea lies between Africa and Arabia.
The deep water is about 21 degrees Celsius.
Fewer species live in the deep water.

questions.why: Maps show places and connections; paragraphs give facts and explanations.

questions.stem: Which two questions are answered in “The Warm Deep of the Red Sea”? Choose two.
options: When was the Red Sea first explored by submarine?
What connects the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean?
How do Red Sea fish find food in the dark?
Why does surface water in the Red Sea sink?
questions.why: Asking questions and finding answers helps check understanding.

questions.stem: Match each word about travel and meeting people with its meaning: blares, errand, exchange, connection.

pairs.right: makes a very loud, harsh sound
a short trip to do a small job
giving one thing and getting another back
a link or friendship between people or things

questions.why: These words help you talk about journeys, trades, and friendships.

questions.stem: Every morning the old bus horn ____ outside our school gate, and everyone covers their ears.
questions.why: Blares means makes a loud, harsh sound, which is why everyone covers their ears.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Mom sent me on an errand to buy bread,” an errand is a short trip to do a small job.
questions.why: An errand is a small task, such as buying something from a shop.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses personification?
options: The tired kettle sighed on the stove.
The kettle boiled water for the family's tea.
The kettle on the stove was made of steel.
The kettle was as hot as the desert sun.
questions.why: Personification gives a human action, like sighing, to a thing that is not human.

questions.stem: Tell whether each sentence about packing for a trip uses personification or not.

rows.text: The suitcase yawned open on the bed.
The train left the station at noon.
The waves waved goodbye to our boat.
We packed water and dates for the road.

questions.why: A suitcase cannot yawn and waves cannot wave goodbye, so those sentences use personification.

questions.stem: Tell whether each line repeats a vowel sound (assonance) or a consonant sound (consonance).

rows.text: Blue moons glow over the dunes.
Tick, tock, the black clock clicks.
The rain stayed away all day.
The dog dug deep under the red sand.

questions.why: Assonance repeats vowel sounds (oo, long a); consonance repeats consonant sounds (k, d).

questions.stem: A poem that tells a story with characters, a setting, and events is called a ____ poem.
questions.why: A narrative poem tells a story; a lyric poem shares feelings.

questions.stem: True or false: A lyric poem mainly shares the speaker's thoughts and feelings instead of telling a long story.
questions.why: Lyric poems focus on emotions and personal thoughts.

questions.stem: Which two lines use assonance, the repeating of a vowel sound? Choose two.
options: Go slow on the road back home.
The light of the white kite climbs high.
Pick up the cookie and the cup.
questions.why: The long i in light, white, kite and the long o in go, slow, road, home are repeated vowel sounds.

questions.stem: In the line “The radio blares a song across the busy market,” what does blares mean?
options: shines with a bright, sudden light
questions.why: Something that blares is very loud, like a radio turned all the way up.

questions.stem: Which line from “The Library Door” uses personification to describe the library door?

segments.text: Every afternoon the library door opens its patient arms and invites me inside,
I choose a heavy atlas, and the pages flutter like eager birds beneath my fingers.
Suddenly I am standing in a crowded market in Morocco, where copper lanterns glow,
When the clock on the wall announces closing time, I return the atlas to its shelf,

questions.why: A door does not have arms and cannot invite anyone, so the poet gives it human traits.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the speaker's point of view about reading?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the speaker's point of view about reading?

options.label: A
options.text: Reading is much less exciting than taking a real journey.

options.label: B
options.text: Reading an atlas is useful only for finishing school projects.

options.label: C
options.text: Reading in a library is difficult because it is so noisy.

options.label: D
options.text: Reading lets a person explore the world without leaving home.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I choose a heavy atlas, and the pages flutter like eager birds beneath my fingers.

options.label: B
options.text: Then I am sailing across the cold green sea toward the islands of Norway,

options.label: C
options.text: I have never needed a ticket or a suitcase to discover the wonderful world.

options.label: D
options.text: When the clock on the wall announces closing time, I return the atlas to its shelf,

questions.why: The speaker says books let her discover the world without a ticket or suitcase.

questions.stem: Which two phrases from “The Library Door” use imagery that appeals to the sense of hearing? Choose two.
options: the wind sings a long, low song
the waves slap the sides of the wooden boat
questions.why: Singing wind and slapping waves are sounds; glowing lanterns are sight and tea is taste.

questions.stem: In the line “a merchant offers me sweet mint tea in exchange for a friendly conversation,” the word exchange means ____.
options: a long and tiring journey to a distant city
a gift given without expecting anything back
a loud argument between two busy sellers
giving one thing and receiving another in return
questions.why: In an exchange, each person gives something and gets something back.

questions.stem: Why is “The Library Door” best described as a lyric poem?
options: It follows several characters through a dangerous adventure.
It tells a long story about a sailor's trip to Norway.
It explains the rules for borrowing books from a library.
It shares the speaker's feelings about the joy of reading.
questions.why: A lyric poem expresses a speaker's emotions, like the delight of traveling through books.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a busy street.
questions.why: The singular subject siren needs the verb blares.

questions.stem: Match each line about a desert journey with the device it shows: personification, metaphor, assonance, simile.

pairs.left: The lazy river yawned beneath the bridge.
The road was a gray ribbon across the sand.
I sleep deep and dream of green streets.
The sand was as hot as an oven.

questions.why: Each device works differently: human actions, direct comparison, repeated vowels, or a comparison with like/as.

questions.stem: These lines come from a short narrative poem about an errand to the market. Put them in story order.
sequence: Grandma handed me a coin and a list for the market.
I raced past the bakery as the street horn blared.
The fruit seller wrapped six oranges in paper.
I hurried home and placed the oranges in Grandma's hands.
questions.why: A narrative poem follows events from beginning to end, like a story.

questions.stem: Which sentence about a desert trip is written from a first-person point of view?
options: They watched the camels cross the dunes at sunset.
The guides watched camels cross the dunes at sunset.
I watched the camels cross the dunes at sunset.
She watched the camels cross the dunes at sunset.
questions.why: First-person point of view uses words like I, me, and my.

questions.stem: True or false: The phrase “a cool, smooth pool of blue” is an example of imagery because it helps the reader picture and feel a scene.
questions.why: Imagery uses words that appeal to the senses, such as sight and touch.

questions.stem: The line “Spices sting my nose, drums thunder in my chest, and silk slides cool across my hand” uses imagery. Which three senses does it appeal to? Choose three.
questions.why: Spices are smelled, drums are heard, and silk is felt.

questions.stem: The poet repeats the s and l sounds in “silk slides slowly” to create ____, a sound device that makes the line feel smooth.
questions.why: Consonance is the repeating of consonant sounds, such as s and l.

questions.stem: Tell whether each description fits a lyric poem or a narrative poem.

rows.text: It follows a boy's errand from start to finish.
It expresses the speaker's joy at seeing the sea.
It has characters, a setting, and a plot.
It focuses on one feeling or one moment.

questions.why: Narrative poems tell stories; lyric poems focus on feelings.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “My cousin from Jakarta taught me a song, / and I taught her a game from Riyadh; / now each of us carries a piece of the other's home.” What is the speaker's perspective on this cultural exchange?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “My cousin from Jakarta taught me a song, / and I taught her a game from Riyadh; / now each of us carries a piece of the other's home.” What is the speaker's perspective on this cultural exchange?

options.label: A
options.text: Visiting relatives is tiring and not very useful.

options.label: B
options.text: Learning a new game is harder than learning a song.

options.label: C
options.text: Sharing traditions brings people closer together.

options.label: D
options.text: People should keep their own traditions to themselves.

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the lines best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: My cousin from Jakarta

options.label: B
options.text: a game from Riyadh

options.label: C
options.text: taught me a song

options.label: D
options.text: carries a piece of the other's home

questions.why: Carrying a piece of each other's home shows the speaker values what they shared.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Through letters, the two pen pals built a strong connection across three oceans.” What does connection mean?
options: a long road that joins two cities
a quarrel that keeps people apart
a bond that links people together
a fee paid for sending a letter
questions.why: A connection is a link or relationship between people.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Grandfather believe about the meeting between Layla and the sailor?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Grandfather believe about the meeting between Layla and the sailor?

options.label: A
options.text: Strangers at the harbor should never be offered gifts.

options.label: B
options.text: Seashells are worth much more than a basket of dates.

options.label: C
options.text: A small trade can connect people from different places.

options.label: D
options.text: Layla should not have stayed so long on the busy dock.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: She carries the seashells home, and Grandfather listens as she describes the stranger.

options.label: B
options.text: Grandfather hands Layla a basket of dates and sends her on an errand to the harbor.

options.label: C
options.text: On the crowded dock, a tired sailor from a distant island rests beside his heavy bag.

options.label: D
options.text: “Sometimes,” he says, “a simple exchange becomes a bridge between two different worlds.”

questions.why: Grandfather calls the exchange a bridge between two worlds, which shows his perspective.

questions.stem: Select two lines from “The Errand to the Harbor” that use personification.

segments.text: Grandfather hands Layla a basket of dates and sends her on an errand to the harbor.
The morning sun stretches its golden fingers across the sleepy rooftops of the town,
Layla offers him the sweetest dates, and he smiles and opens a small wooden box.
Layla places the shells on her windowsill, where they whisper of the open ocean every evening.

questions.why: The sun cannot stretch fingers and shells cannot whisper; these are human actions.

questions.stem: Why is “The Errand to the Harbor” a narrative poem rather than a lyric poem?
options: It shares only the speaker's private feelings about the sea.
It tells a story with characters, events, and an ending.
It describes one single moment without any characters at all.
It repeats the same vowel sound at the end of every line.
questions.why: A narrative poem tells a story with characters and events.

questions.stem: In the line “far away the ferry horn blares twice,” the verb blares is imagery that helps the reader ____.
options: hear a loud, sudden sound at the harbor
taste the sweet dates in the basket
see the bright colors of the busy dock
feel the smooth shells in Layla's hand
questions.why: Blares describes a loud sound, so it appeals to hearing.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Errand to the Harbor” in order.
sequence: Grandfather sends Layla to the harbor with dates.
Layla gives the sailor some of the sweetest dates.
The sailor shares seashells from a wooden box.
Grandfather explains the meaning of the exchange.
questions.why: The narrative poem moves from the errand, to the trade, to Grandfather's lesson.

questions.stem: Match each word about two friends who must compete with its meaning: bout, clarify, improvise, emerge.

pairs.right: a single match or contest between two opponents
to make something easier to understand
to make or do something without planning ahead
to come out from a hidden place into view

questions.why: These words help you describe a contest and the people in it.

questions.stem: When the coach's game plan fell apart in the second half, the players had to ____ new moves on the spot.
questions.why: To improvise is to make something up on the spot, without a plan.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Grandfather sat pensively by the window after the long phone call,” pensively means in a cheerful, careless way.
questions.why: Pensively means in a quiet, deeply thoughtful way.

questions.stem: Which sentence about sports day uses bout with its correct meaning?
options: The wrestler won his first bout in one minute.
Sara gently opened the bout to let the cat inside.
The bout of the house was painted a pale shade of green.
Majid drank a cold bout of juice after the long game.
questions.why: A bout is a single match or contest, such as one round of wrestling.

questions.stem: Tell whether the key word in each sentence about a school sports day is used correctly or incorrectly.

rows.text: The referee stopped the bout when one boxer slipped.
The coach asked us to clarify the ball into the net.
The swimmers emerged from the pool, dripping and smiling.
Hamad improvised his lunch slowly so it would last.

questions.why: A bout is a match and to emerge is to come out; clarify and improvise do not fit the other two sentences.

questions.stem: Which two statements are themes rather than topics? Choose two.
options: Doing your best matters more than winning.
True friends stay loyal even when they must compete.
a boxing match between two friends
questions.why: A theme is a complete message about life; a topic is just a subject.

questions.stem: A theme is ____ that a story expresses about life or people.
questions.why: Theme is the big idea or lesson the reader takes away.

questions.stem: True or false: An author usually states the theme of a realistic fiction story directly in the first sentence.
questions.why: Readers usually infer the theme from what characters do, say, and learn.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Even after losing the final bout, Samir cheered for his friend and walked home with him as usual.” Which theme does this detail most support?
options: Losing makes people forget their friends.
Teams should always change their players.
Practice is the only way to win a final.
questions.why: Samir stays close to his friend after losing, which shows friendship lasting through disappointment.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a runner before a race.
questions.why: The sentence is in the past tense, so think must be thought.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states a theme of “The Final Round”?
options: Winning a trophy is the best way to prove you are smart.
Strong friends can compete hard and still respect each other.
Chess is a game that only patient players can ever master.
Friends should never enter the same tournament together.
questions.why: The boys play their best and stay friends, which shows respect in competition.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does Karim decide to play his best against Yusuf?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does Karim decide to play his best against Yusuf?

options.label: A
options.text: He was told to win by the tournament judges.

options.label: B
options.text: He believes Yusuf is a much weaker player.

options.label: C
options.text: He thinks holding back would disrespect his friend.

options.label: D
options.text: He wants to end his friendship with Yusuf.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: He worried that beating Karim might damage their friendship.

options.label: B
options.text: Karim felt the same way, but he also knew that holding back would be a kind of insult.

options.label: C
options.text: After two exhausting hours, Yusuf won by a single pawn.

options.label: D
options.text: Now both boys had reached the final round of the city tournament, and only one of them could win the trophy.

questions.why: Karim sees holding back as an insult, so playing his best is a sign of respect.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Final Round” best shows that the friendship survives the competition?

segments.text: The night before the match, Yusuf sat at his desk, pensive and silent.
Karim launched a barrage of attacks, and Yusuf defended calmly, move after move.
After two exhausting hours, Yusuf won by a single pawn.
Both boys laughed, and they walked home together, just as they always had.

questions.why: Walking home together as always shows the friendship is unchanged.

questions.stem: The author ends “The Final Round” with the boys walking home together to show that ____.
options: Karim was still angry about losing the match
their friendship is stronger than the contest
the tournament hall was close to their homes
the boys had nowhere else to go that night
questions.why: Walking home together as always shows the competition did not break the friendship.

questions.stem: Which two details from “The Final Round” show that Yusuf was worried before the match? Choose two.
options: He sat at his desk, pensive and silent.
He won by a single pawn.
He defended calmly, move after move.
He feared beating Karim could harm their friendship.
questions.why: Being pensive and fearing for the friendship show worry before the game.

questions.stem: Read the claim “Lina is a loyal friend.” Tell whether each detail about Lina supports the claim or does not support it.

rows.text: She defended her friend when others teased him.
She likes to read adventure books.
She visited her sick friend every day.
She lives near the school gate.

questions.why: Strong evidence must connect directly to loyalty.

questions.stem: Put the steps for answering a theme question about a realistic fiction story with text evidence in order.
sequence: Read the question and decide what it asks.
Reread to find details about what characters do and learn.
Choose the detail that best supports your answer.
Explain how the detail shows the theme.
questions.why: Good answers move from understanding the question to explaining the evidence.

questions.stem: Match each key word with the everyday situation it describes: affect, clarify, emerge, improvise.

pairs.right: The long heat wave changed how well the crops grew.
The teacher drew a diagram so the rule was easier to understand.
A turtle's head slowly came out of its shell.
With no ball, the boys made one from rolled-up socks.

questions.why: Each sentence describes the meaning of the word without using it.

questions.stem: Which sentence would be the strongest evidence that Huda is a hardworking athlete?
options: Huda once watched a race on television with friends.
Huda has two older brothers who also enjoy sports.
Huda owns a pair of bright blue running shoes.
Huda trains on the track every morning before school.
questions.why: Training every morning shows hard work; the others are unrelated details.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Losing the first bout did not affect Yasir's confidence,” affect means to change or influence.
questions.why: To affect something is to change or influence it.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a noisy match.
questions.why: The subject cheering is singular, so the verb must be was.

questions.stem: After two weeks of training, a clear leader began to ____ from the quiet group of new players.
questions.why: To emerge is to come out or become noticeable.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “Omar and Bilal were rivals on the track, but every evening they trained together. When Bilal twisted his ankle, Omar walked him home and carried his bag.” Which two themes are best supported by these sentences? Choose two.
options: Winning a race is the most important goal.
Real friends show kindness even to their rivals.
People should avoid sports that cause injuries.
Competition does not have to destroy friendship.
questions.why: Omar competes with Bilal yet helps him, showing kindness and friendship.

questions.stem: Read: “Before the final bout, the referee asked both coaches to clarify which gloves their boxers would wear.” Which word is closest in meaning to clarify?
questions.why: To clarify something is to explain it so it is clear.

questions.stem: True or false: The best text evidence for a theme is any sentence that mentions the main character's name.
questions.why: Evidence must show what the character does, says, or learns that connects to the theme.

questions.stem: Part A: Which theme does the author develop through Dana's choice during tryouts?

partA.stem: Part A: Which theme does the author develop through Dana's choice during tryouts?

options.label: A
options.text: Loyalty to a friend matters more than an easy win.

options.label: B
options.text: Friends should never try out for the same team.

options.label: C
options.text: Coaches always choose the most talented player.

options.label: D
options.text: Injuries are a normal part of every sport.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “You chose my health over an easy victory, and I won't forget that.”

options.label: B
options.text: Then the coach announced that the school team needed only one goalkeeper, and the two friends became rivals overnight.

options.label: C
options.text: Eventually, the coach selected Dana for the position, explaining that her reflexes were remarkably quick.

options.label: D
options.text: Finally, Reem knocked on Dana's door holding two pairs of gloves.

questions.why: Reem's words show that Dana put her friend before winning.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Two Gloves, One Goal” shows that Dana faced a difficult choice?

segments.text: Dana could have stayed silent, since an injured rival would make her own victory almost certain.
Eventually, the coach selected Dana for the position, explaining that her reflexes were remarkably quick.
Reem was disappointed, and for a few days the silence between them felt devastating.
Then she grinned and offered to help her friend practice every afternoon before the championship season.

questions.why: Dana had to choose between an easy victory and helping her friend.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Two Gloves, One Goal” in order.
sequence: The coach says the team needs only one goalkeeper.
Dana tells the coach about Reem's wrist.
The coach chooses Dana for the position.
Reem visits Dana with two pairs of gloves.
questions.why: The events move from the competition, to Dana's choice, to the friends making peace.

questions.stem: Tell whether each statement about Reem and Dana in “Two Gloves, One Goal” is stated directly or must be inferred.

rows.text: The team needed only one goalkeeper.
Dana values her friend more than an easy win.
Reem brought two pairs of gloves to Dana's door.
Reem has accepted the result and values Dana's friendship.

questions.why: Inferences combine text evidence with what the reader already knows.

questions.stem: Why does Reem bring two pairs of gloves to Dana's door?
options: to return gloves that Dana had lent her the week before
to ask Dana to give her the goalkeeper position instead
to show Dana that she has joined a different team
to show she wants to stay friends and help Dana train
questions.why: Reem offers to help her friend practice, which shows the friendship continues.

questions.stem: Match each word about young changemakers with its meaning: activist, advocate, initiative, impact.

pairs.right: a person who works hard for social or environmental change
a person who speaks up in support of a cause
the energy to start something without being told
a strong effect on someone or something

questions.why: These words describe people who make a difference and the results of their work.

questions.stem: Nora showed ____ when she started a recycling club without waiting for a teacher to ask.
questions.why: Initiative means taking action on your own.

questions.stem: True or false: To persevere means to give up quickly when a task becomes difficult.
questions.why: To persevere is to keep trying even when something is hard.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word contribute correctly?
options: Faisal decided to contribute his bike in the garage.
Every student can contribute an idea to the class garden.
The tired puppy wanted to contribute on the soft rug.
The heavy rain will contribute the roads very slippery.
questions.why: To contribute is to give or add something to help a shared goal.

questions.stem: Tell whether advocate, impact, or inspire in each sentence is used as a noun or a verb.

rows.text: She is an advocate for clean water.
He advocates for safer bike lanes.
The new park had a big impact on the town.
Her speech will inspire many students.

questions.why: A noun names a person or thing; a verb shows an action.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “Mariam wanted children in hospitals to have books. She collected donations from neighbors, sorted hundreds of books, and delivered them herself. She also wrote to local shops asking them to help.” Which two details support the idea that Mariam took action for others? Choose two.
options: She asked local shops to help.
She lives in a large city.
She sorted and delivered hundreds of books.
questions.why: Supporting details must connect to the central idea of taking action.

questions.stem: The ____ of a biography is the most important point the author makes about the person's life.
questions.why: The central idea is what the whole text is mostly about.

questions.stem: Put the sentences of a short biography of a young activist named Sami in a logical order.
sequence: At age twelve, Sami noticed plastic bags piling up on the beach near his home.
He started a weekend cleanup club and invited his classmates.
Within a year, more than two hundred volunteers had joined him.
Today, the city credits his initiative with cleaner beaches.
questions.why: Biographies often use time order, from the problem to the results.

questions.stem: True or false: A central idea is usually supported by several key details, not just one.
questions.why: Authors build a central idea with many details and examples.

questions.stem: Read: “Young people around the world are solving real problems. One teen built a low-cost water filter. Another designed an app that helps farmers.” Which sentence best states the central idea?
options: Teenagers enjoy designing new apps in their free time.
Young people are finding ways to solve real problems.
Water filters are cheaper than they used to be.
Farmers use many different apps on their phones.
questions.why: The first sentence is the central idea; the others are examples.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “The Boy Who Gave Books Fingertips”?
options: As a teenager, Louis Braille created a reading system that still helps people.
Louis Braille injured his eye while playing in his father's workshop.
Charles Barbier was a soldier who invented a way to read at night.
Schools in Paris used very large books with heavy raised letters.
questions.why: The whole biography explains how young Louis created braille and why it matters.

questions.stem: Part A: What problem did Louis Braille's code solve?

partA.stem: Part A: What problem did Louis Braille's code solve?

options.label: A
options.text: Soldiers could not send messages during the night.

options.label: B
options.text: Books for blind children were too expensive to print.

options.label: C
options.text: Teachers in Paris did not have enough classrooms.

options.label: D
options.text: Blind readers had no quick, easy way to read by touch.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Louis later became a teacher and continued improving his code.

options.label: B
options.text: Louis Braille was born in a small French village in 1809.

options.label: C
options.text: At ten, Louis entered a school for blind children in Paris.

options.label: D
options.text: The school's few books used huge raised letters that were slow and difficult to read by touch.

questions.why: The raised-letter books were slow and difficult, which is the problem braille solved.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Boy Who Gave Books Fingertips” shows the impact Braille's work still has today?

segments.text: Barbier's system was complicated, but Louis recognized its possibilities.
By 1824, when he was only fifteen, his new alphabet was ready.
Louis later became a teacher and continued improving his code.
Today, braille is used around the world, and millions of blind readers can enjoy books independently because of a teenager's persistence.

questions.why: The last sentence tells the effect of his work on millions of readers today.

questions.stem: Put the events of Louis Braille's life in order.
sequence: Louis is injured in his father's workshop.
Louis enters a school for blind children in Paris.
Charles Barbier shares his night-reading code.
Louis completes his six-dot alphabet at fifteen.
questions.why: Biographies are often told in time order.

questions.stem: Which two details best support the idea that Louis showed determination? Choose two.
options: He simplified a complicated code into six dots.
He kept improving his code as a teacher.
A soldier visited his school in Paris.
He was born in a small French village.
questions.why: Simplifying and continually improving the code show he did not give up.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about young changemakers.
questions.why: The plural subject activists needs the verb have.

questions.stem: Match each claim about a young inventor named Rana with the evidence that best supports it.

pairs.right: She tested her design forty times before it worked.
Her water filter now serves three villages.
She started the project without waiting for help.
Dozens of students later began projects of their own.

questions.why: Good evidence matches the exact idea in each claim.

questions.stem: For the claim “Hana is a dedicated advocate for animals,” tell whether each detail is strong evidence or weak evidence.

rows.text: She volunteers at the animal shelter every Saturday.
She likes the color blue.
She wrote letters asking the city for a dog park.
Her brother is older than she is.

questions.why: Strong evidence connects directly to the claim about helping animals.

questions.stem: Although his first three designs failed, Daniel continued to ____ until his solar oven finally worked.
questions.why: To persevere is to keep going despite failure.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best support the claim “Young people can contribute to their communities”?
options: A group of teens repaired benches in the town park.
Some students prefer science classes to art classes.
A new phone model was released for young buyers.
Many teenagers enjoy listening to music after school.
questions.why: Repairing benches is a clear example of contributing to a community.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The teacher's story inspired Khalid to start a reading club,” inspired means filled someone with the desire to do something.
questions.why: To inspire is to give someone the wish and energy to act.

questions.stem: Which three words or phrases are synonyms for persevere? Choose three.
questions.why: Persist, keep going, and endure all mean continuing despite difficulty.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about planting trees.
questions.why: The subject initiative is singular, so the verb is has had.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “(1) Amal began a tutoring program for younger students. (2) She trained ten volunteers to help. (3) Her school has a red front door. (4) Test scores rose the next year.” Which sentence is least relevant to the central idea?
questions.why: The color of the door does not support the idea of Amal's tutoring program.

questions.stem: An ____ often gives speeches, writes letters, and organizes events to support a cause such as protecting coral reefs.
questions.why: An activist works actively for a cause.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “The Windmill Builder”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “The Windmill Builder”?

options.label: A
options.text: Building a windmill requires costly tools and expert training.

options.label: B
options.text: Malawi suffered a terrible drought at the start of the century.

options.label: C
options.text: Curiosity and hard work helped a teenager solve a serious problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Libraries in small villages often have very few science books.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: There he discovered a science book with a picture of windmills on its cover.

options.label: B
options.text: His story shows that curiosity and persistence can contribute more to success than expensive equipment.

options.label: C
options.text: Neighbors laughed as William collected scrap metal, an old bicycle frame, and plastic pipes from a junkyard.

options.label: D
options.text: In 2001, a severe drought struck Malawi, and William Kamkwamba's family, like many farming families, could barely find enough food.

questions.why: The last sentence sums up the central idea of the biography.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Windmill Builder” that show how William persevered despite obstacles.

segments.text: Unable to pay school fees, fourteen-year-old William had to leave school.
Instead of giving up on learning, he visited a small village library.
Although his English was limited, he studied the diagrams carefully and imagined building one himself.
Later, he built a larger windmill to pump water for crops.

questions.why: He kept learning after leaving school and studied hard despite limited English.

questions.stem: Tell whether each detail from “The Windmill Builder” is an obstacle William faced or an action William took.

rows.text: A drought left his family short of food.
He studied diagrams in a library book.
His neighbors laughed at him.
He collected scrap from a junkyard.

questions.why: Sorting obstacles and actions shows how William overcame challenges.

questions.stem: The author includes the detail that neighbors laughed at William in order to ____.
options: prove that his neighbors were scientists
show the doubts he had to overcome
questions.why: The detail shows that William kept going even when others doubted him.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the impact of William's windmills?
options: They brought light to his home and water to crops.
They made his neighbors stop farming completely.
They allowed his family to move to a large city.
They replaced the library that had closed in 2001.
questions.why: The windmills powered lights and later pumped water for crops.

questions.stem: Tell which meaning of the word contrary is used in each sentence.

rows.text: Contrary to the forecast, the day stayed dry.
The contrary goat refused to walk through the gate.
Her answer was contrary to what we expected.
The contrary toddler said no to every snack.

questions.why: Contrary can mean opposite, or it can describe someone who stubbornly does the opposite.

questions.stem: After a week of camping with only canned food, Faris began to ____ his mother's fresh bread.
questions.why: To crave something is to want it very strongly.

questions.stem: Match each key word from “Cocoon” with the situation that best shows it: chrysalis, compulsion, crave, thrill.

pairs.right: a hard green case hanging under a leaf while a caterpillar changes
Hani cannot stop himself from checking the clock every minute.
After the long hike, Sara can think only of a cold drink.
Omar's heart races as his kite climbs higher and higher.

questions.why: Each situation acts out the meaning of one word.

questions.stem: True or false: A chrysalis is the hard case that protects a caterpillar while it changes into a butterfly.
questions.why: The chrysalis is the stage between caterpillar and butterfly.

questions.stem: Read: “Contrary to what Noor expected, the shy new girl turned out to be very funny.” Which phrase means almost the same as contrary to?
questions.why: Contrary to means the opposite of what was expected.

questions.stem: Tell whether each word used to describe a person's body or behavior has a positive or a negative connotation.

rows.text: slender
scrawny
curious
nosy

questions.why: Words with similar denotations can carry very different feelings.

questions.stem: Which two words have nearly the same denotation as the noun thrill? Choose two.
questions.why: A thrill is a sudden feeling of excitement or delight.

questions.stem: The word thrifty has a positive connotation, while the word ____ has nearly the same denotation but a negative connotation.
questions.why: Thrifty and stingy both mean careful with money, but stingy sounds unkind.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a butterfly.
questions.why: The singular subject caterpillar needs the verb changes.

questions.stem: What is the denotation of compulsion in the sentence “Tamer felt a compulsion to tap his pencil, even though he tried to stop”?
options: a feeling of calm and quiet rest
a plan made carefully ahead of time
an urge that is very hard to resist
a rule that a teacher writes down
questions.why: The words even though he tried to stop show that a compulsion is hard to resist.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3 of “The Lemon Tree,” Noura checks the chrysalis every morning because she ____.
options: is eager to see what will happen to it
is afraid it will harm the lemon tree
wants to move it into her bedroom
has been asked to guard the lemons
questions.why: Her daily checking shows she is eagerly waiting for the change.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the tone of the final paragraph of “The Lemon Tree”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the tone of the final paragraph of “The Lemon Tree”?

options.label: A
options.text: confident and hopeful

options.label: B
options.text: silly and playful

options.label: C
options.text: lonely and sad

options.label: D
options.text: angry and impatient

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Every morning before school, Noura checked the chrysalis.

options.label: B
options.text: Her voice trembled, and her hands felt cold and clumsy.

options.label: C
options.text: That afternoon, Noura stepped onto the stage, took a deep breath, and began to speak in a clear, steady voice.

options.label: D
options.text: Noura found the chrysalis hanging beneath a leaf of her grandmother's lemon tree.

questions.why: Words like clear and steady create a confident tone.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Lemon Tree” uses word choice to show Noura's nervousness?

segments.text: Every morning before school, Noura checked the chrysalis.
Her voice trembled, and her hands felt cold and clumsy.
On the day of the speech, Noura woke early and hurried to the tree.
After a few quiet minutes, it lifted gracefully into the air.

questions.why: Trembled, cold, and clumsy show how anxious Noura feels.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare the chrysalis to “a tiny green lantern” in paragraph 1?
options: to show that Noura is afraid of the dark
to explain how the butterfly finds its food
to show that the chrysalis gives off bright light
to suggest something hidden and special is inside
questions.why: The comparison creates a mysterious, hopeful tone about what is hidden inside.

questions.stem: Which two words from “The Lemon Tree” help create a gentle, calm tone? Choose two.
questions.why: Delicate and gracefully suggest softness and calm; trembled and clumsy suggest nerves.

questions.stem: Tell whether each word used to describe a quiet classmate has a positive or a negative connotation.

rows.text: reserved
sullen
peaceful
cowardly

questions.why: Reserved and peaceful sound respectful; sullen and cowardly sound critical.

questions.stem: True or false: The words chuckle and cackle have the same basic denotation (to laugh) but different connotations.
questions.why: A chuckle sounds friendly, while a cackle often sounds unkind or strange.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the idea that its key word expresses.

pairs.left: Ali felt a thrill as the plane lifted off.
After the race, Lama craved a long rest.
Nadia felt a compulsion to recheck the locked door.
pairs.right: an urge that is hard to control

pairs.left: Contrary to his fears, the test was easy.
pairs.right: the opposite of what was expected

questions.why: Each key word carries its own shade of meaning.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a short paragraph about a girl watching a chrysalis.
sequence: Huda found a chrysalis on the jasmine bush.
Each day she checked it before school.
One morning, the case split open.
A butterfly dried its wings and flew away.
questions.why: The paragraph follows the change in time order.

questions.stem: The verb ____ in “The storm ____ the quiet village” creates a frightening tone.
questions.why: Attacked has a violent connotation that makes the storm sound dangerous.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The old house, with its peeling paint and creaking stairs, seemed to hide a hundred secrets.” Which two phrases most help create a mysterious tone? Choose two.
questions.why: Creaking sounds and hidden secrets build a feeling of mystery.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a speech contest.
questions.why: The sentence is in the past tense, so walk must be walked.

questions.stem: Which word best replaces walked to give the sentence “Tariq walked into the hall after winning the award” a proud, confident tone?
questions.why: Strode suggests long, confident steps; the others suggest fear, aimlessness, or clumsiness.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Contrary to the rumors, the museum will stay open all summer,” the phrase contrary to means in agreement with.
questions.why: Contrary to means the opposite of; the rumors said something different.

questions.stem: Tell whether the word crave or craving in each sentence describes a desire for food or a desire for something else.

rows.text: Fasting all day made Saeed crave dates.
The lonely boy craved a friend to talk to.
By noon, Reem was craving a bowl of soup.
The team craved another chance to win.

questions.why: Crave can describe hunger for food or a strong wish for anything.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the tone of “The Borrowed Shell” change from paragraph 1 to paragraph 3?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the tone of “The Borrowed Shell” change from paragraph 1 to paragraph 3?

options.label: A
options.text: from lonely to hopeful

options.label: B
options.text: from cheerful to sad

options.label: C
options.text: from curious to bored

options.label: D
options.text: from angry to calm

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best shows the tone at the end?

options.label: A
options.text: For a few seconds it was soft and completely unprotected.

options.label: B
options.text: His old friends were a thousand kilometers away, and the new school felt enormous.

options.label: C
options.text: Ali watched for a long time.

options.label: D
options.text: His voice shook, but the boy grinned and invited him to the meeting.

questions.why: The boy's grin and invitation make the ending hopeful.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Borrowed Shell” best shows how vulnerable the crab is while it changes shells?

segments.text: One afternoon he spotted a hermit crab dragging a cracked, cramped shell across the sand.
For a few seconds it was soft and completely unprotected.
Then it slipped into the larger shell and marched away, almost proudly.
Ali watched for a long time.

questions.why: Soft and unprotected show the danger of the moment of change.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what connotation does the word cramped add to the description of the old shell?
options: The shell had become too tight and uncomfortable.
The shell was bright and beautifully decorated.
The shell was larger than the crab really needed.
The shell was new and had never been used.
questions.why: Cramped suggests too little space, explaining why the crab must change.

questions.stem: The author ends paragraph 2 with the word ____ to suggest that the crab now feels confident in its new home.
questions.why: Proudly has a positive connotation that shows confidence.

questions.stem: Tell whether each word from “The Borrowed Shell” has a positive or a negative connotation in the story.

rows.text: lonely
cramped
grinned
proudly

questions.why: The negative words show Ali's struggle; the positive words show the change.

questions.stem: Match each word with the sentence that shows its meaning: oblong, taut, somber, ripen.

pairs.right: The tablecloth was twice as long as it was wide.
The tent ropes were pulled so tight they hummed in the wind.
Everyone at the gathering spoke quietly and seriously.
The green figs turned soft and sweet in the summer heat.

questions.why: Each sentence describes the meaning of one word.

questions.stem: Mother sewed a new hem onto my favorite scarf because its ends had become ____ and were losing threads.
questions.why: Frayed cloth is worn, with loose threads at the edges.

questions.stem: True or false: A somber color, such as dark gray, would suit a poem about a sad farewell better than bright yellow would.
questions.why: Somber means dark and serious, which fits a sad poem.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word oblong correctly?
options: The oblong song made the whole room cry.
Grandmother cut an oblong patch for the quilt.
We heard the oblong of the birds at dawn.
Ali felt very oblong after the long, hot race.
questions.why: Oblong describes a shape that is longer than it is wide.

questions.stem: Tell whether plunge is used as a noun or as a verb in each sentence.

rows.text: The hawk will plunge toward the field.
Her plunge into the pool made a big splash.
Prices took a sudden plunge in March.
We plunge our hands into the warm dough.

questions.why: The same word can name a thing or show an action.

questions.stem: Tell whether each sentence about a grandmother's quilt has a warm tone or a cold tone.

rows.text: She folded the quilt around me like a hug.
The quilt lay forgotten in a dark cupboard.
Its bright squares glowed like little suns.
No one had touched the quilt for years.

questions.why: Word choice such as hug and glowed creates warmth; forgotten and dark create coldness.

questions.stem: An author's ____ is the special way a writer uses words, sentence length, and figurative language.
questions.why: Style is how an author writes, not what happens.

questions.stem: Which two words would best create a tender, loving tone in a poem about a mother's sewing? Choose two.
questions.why: Gently and tenderly carry soft, loving connotations.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a patchwork quilt.
questions.why: The subject patch is singular, so the verb must be was.

questions.stem: Which word best describes the tone of the line “She pressed the soft quilt into my hands as if it were gold”?
questions.why: Treating the quilt like gold shows love and care.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the speaker's tone toward the grandmother's weaving in “Sadu”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the speaker's tone toward the grandmother's weaving in “Sadu”?

options.label: A
options.text: worried and fearful

options.label: B
options.text: amused and careless

options.label: C
options.text: admiring and grateful

options.label: D
options.text: bored and impatient

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the poem best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: When I ask her to teach me, she laughs and places my clumsy hands upon the threads,

options.label: B
options.text: My grandmother sits beside the tent with her loom stretched across the sand,

options.label: C
options.text: but the memories inside the weaving will remain as brilliant as the morning.

options.label: D
options.text: Someday the radiant colors will gradually fade and the edges will grow frayed and soft,

questions.why: Saying the memories will stay as brilliant as the morning shows admiration for the weaving.

questions.stem: Which line from “Sadu” best shows that the weaving skill is passed down through generations?

segments.text: pulling crimson and black threads through her experienced fingers as patiently as the desert waits for rain.
She weaves triangles like mountains and diamonds like distant stars,
and together we tie the knots that her mother tied, and her mother's mother before her.
Someday the radiant colors will gradually fade and the edges will grow frayed and soft,

questions.why: The knots are passed down through generations of mothers.

questions.stem: Which two similes does the poet of “Sadu” use to describe the shapes in the weaving? Choose two.
options: her loom stretched across the sand
questions.why: Both similes compare woven shapes to things in nature.

questions.stem: The poet's description of edges that will “grow frayed and soft” suggests that ____.
options: the weaving will age, but its meaning will last
the colors of the desert are always changing
the grandmother wove the threads too loosely
the speaker wants to throw the weaving away
questions.why: The next line says the memories inside will remain bright.

questions.stem: Which feature of the poet's style is most noticeable in “Sadu”?
options: a list of facts written in plain, scientific words
short rhyming lines with a strong, steady beat
long lines filled with detailed images and comparisons
a conversation between two speakers with stage directions
questions.why: The poem uses long, flowing lines full of imagery and similes.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a family quilt with the tone its word choice creates.

pairs.left: The quilt hugged me like an old friend.
The torn quilt lay forgotten in the dusty attic.
Hooray, Grandma finished the quilt at last!
Do not touch the quilt until it dries.

questions.why: Word choice and punctuation signal the tone of each sentence.

questions.stem: Put the steps for making a patchwork quilt in order.
sequence: Cut fabric scraps into oblong pieces.
Arrange the pieces into a pattern.
Stitch the pieces together in rows.
Add a backing and a border.
questions.why: A quilt is built from small pieces, then joined and finished.

questions.stem: True or false: Writing “The needle danced through the cloth” instead of “The needle went through the cloth” makes a writer's style more lively.
questions.why: Vivid verbs and personification add energy to a writer's style.

questions.stem: As the sad news spread through the village, the mood at the evening gathering became quiet and ____.
questions.why: Somber means dark and serious in mood.

questions.stem: Which revision of “My grandmother made a quilt” best shows a poet's descriptive style?
options: Grandmother's hands sewed squares of sunset orange and sea blue.
My grandmother made a quilt, and it was a very nice quilt.
Grandmother made one quilt, and then she made another one.
A quilt was made by my grandmother some time last year.
questions.why: Specific colors and images make writing more descriptive.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about an old instrument.
questions.why: The plural subject strings needs the verb sound.

questions.stem: Read the lines: “Thread by thread, she stitched the scraps together, / thread by thread, she stitched our family's past.” Which two features of style do these lines show? Choose two.
questions.why: Thread by thread is repeated, and stitching the past is figurative.

questions.stem: Tell whether each sentence about a desert town creates a somber tone or a cheerful tone.

rows.text: The old artillery stood silent beside the soldiers' graves.
The ripening dates glowed gold in the morning sun.
Gray clouds hung low over the empty, frayed tents.
Children laughed as they plunged into the cool pool.

questions.why: Silent guns, graves, and gray clouds feel somber; glowing dates and laughter feel cheerful.

questions.stem: True or false: The phrase “a frayed and faded flag” repeats the f sound, which slows the line and gives it a tired tone.
questions.why: Repeated sounds are part of a poet's style and help create tone.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word taut to describe a person's feelings rather than an object?
options: The tent's taut ropes held firm in the strong wind.
The fisherman pulled the net until it was taut.
Before the final exam, Nasser's nerves felt taut.
The drum's skin was stretched taut across its frame.
questions.why: Taut nerves are tense with worry; the other sentences describe tight objects.

questions.stem: Part A: What new understanding of the net does the speaker reach by the end of “Grandfather's Net”?

partA.stem: Part A: What new understanding of the net does the speaker reach by the end of “Grandfather's Net”?

options.label: A
options.text: It holds his grandfather's memories and wisdom.

options.label: B
options.text: It is too old and broken to be repaired.

options.label: C
options.text: It belongs in a museum for visitors to see.

options.label: D
options.text: It is only a simple tool for catching fish.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the poem best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I used to imagine the net was ordinary rope, a simple instrument for catching silver fish,

options.label: B
options.text: while the sunset pours its copper light across the patient water.

options.label: C
options.text: but now I understand that it is also a library of his decisions,

options.label: D
options.text: Each evening on the harbor wall, my grandfather repairs his fishing net,

questions.why: Calling the net a library shows it holds knowledge and memories.

questions.stem: Select two lines from “Grandfather's Net” that compare the net to something that records or stores knowledge.

segments.text: knotting broken cords with fingers that are cracked and brown as driftwood.
The net spreads across his knees like a map of every voyage he remembers,
He never hurries, never complains; he simply hums an ancient sailors' melody
but now I understand that it is also a library of his decisions,

questions.why: A map and a library both hold information, like the net holds memories.

questions.stem: The poet describes the grandfather's fingers as “cracked and brown as driftwood” to create a tone of ____.
options: fear of the dangerous ocean waves
anger about how hard fishing is
