quiet respect for his long working life
questions.why: The image honors the many years of work the grandfather has done.

questions.stem: Tell whether each phrase from “Grandfather's Net” mainly appeals to sight or to sound.

rows.text: hums an ancient sailors' melody
copper light across the patient water
cracked and brown as driftwood
its torn places marking storms

questions.why: Sensory word choice helps create the calm, respectful tone of the poem.

questions.stem: What does the speaker of “Grandfather's Net” most likely mean by calling every knot “a sentence I will someday read to my children”?
options: He thinks knots are too difficult to teach to young children.
He will pass on his grandfather's lessons to his children.
He wants his children to learn to read before they can fish.
He plans to write a book about fishing for young children.
questions.why: The knots stand for knowledge he will hand down to the next generation.

questions.stem: The farm workers followed a yearly ____, moving from the strawberry fields in spring to the grape farms in autumn and back again.
questions.why: A circuit is a regular route that ends where it began and then repeats.

questions.stem: Match each key word from “The Circuit” with the sentence that shows its meaning: acquire, detect, foreman, savor.

pairs.right: Through daily practice, Reem gained a new skill: sewing.
The dog's nose picked up the smell of smoke in the barn.
Mr. Saleh led the farm crew and gave each worker a task.
Grandmother ate the first ripe fig slowly, enjoying each bite.

questions.why: Each sentence acts out the meaning of one word.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The foreman paid the workers at the end of each week,” the foreman is the person in charge of a group of workers.
questions.why: A foreman leads and directs a crew of workers.

questions.stem: Is each detail from a short story about a farm worker's son part of the setting or part of the plot?

rows.text: a dusty farm road in late summer
The boy loses his favorite book and searches for it.
a crowded school hallway at eight in the morning
The boy finds the book under a crate in the barn.

questions.why: Setting is where and when; plot is what happens.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows a character acting hesitantly?
options: Yasir ran straight to his seat and opened his book.
Yasir shouted hello to everyone as he walked in.
Yasir paused at the door, then stepped slowly inside.
Yasir quickly answered the teacher's first question.
questions.why: Acting hesitantly means pausing and moving slowly because you are unsure.

questions.stem: Where and when does “The Last Crate” mainly take place?
options: in a busy city school during the winter
in a large market on the night of a holiday
on a fishing boat during a spring storm
on a date farm during the summer harvest
questions.why: Details such as the date farm, June, and the harvest show the setting.

questions.stem: Put these events from “The Last Crate” in the order they happen.
sequence: Tariq carries crates of dates to the truck.
The farmer hands Tariq a small box of dates.
Tariq eats the dates slowly that night.
questions.why: The plot moves from the work days, to the last day, to that night.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Tariq feel at the end of the harvest?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Tariq feel at the end of the harvest?

options.label: A
options.text: angry and ready to quit

options.label: B
options.text: afraid of the farmer

options.label: C
options.text: proud but also a little sad

options.label: D
options.text: bored and very sleepy

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The work began before sunrise, while the air was still cool and the palm leaves rustled in the breeze.

options.label: B
options.text: By noon his arms ached and the fierce sun burned the back of his neck, yet he still enjoyed the quiet rows of palm trees and the sweet smell of the ripening fruit.

options.label: C
options.text: Tariq felt proud, but he also felt a little sad.

options.label: D
options.text: Every June, Tariq's family followed the harvest to a different farm, and this year it was a date farm near the edge of the desert.

questions.why: The narrator tells us directly that Tariq felt proud and sad.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Last Crate” shows that Tariq wants to savor his last evening on the farm?

segments.text: The work began before sunrise, while the air was still cool and the palm leaves rustled in the breeze.
On the last day of the harvest, the farmer handed Tariq a small box of dates.
Tomorrow the family would load the old truck and drive to another town, where he would have to find a new school, a new seat, and new friends all over again.
That night, he ate the dates slowly, one by one, trying to make the precious moment last as long as possible.

questions.why: Eating slowly to make the moment last is what it means to savor something.

questions.stem: Which two details show that Tariq's family moves often for work? Choose two.
options: He enjoyed the quiet rows of palm trees and the smell of the fruit.
Tariq's job was to carry heavy crates of dates to the truck.
Tariq would have to find a new school and new friends all over again.
Every June, the family followed the harvest to a different farm.
questions.why: A family that follows the harvest moves often, so the child keeps changing schools.

questions.stem: Faris was ____ to raise his hand on his first day; he lowered it twice before finally asking his question.
questions.why: Lowering his hand twice shows he was unsure, or hesitant.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Last week, the foreman hire three new workers so the harvest would finish on time.”
questions.why: Last week shows the past, so hire must be hired.

questions.stem: Which two sentences show a character changing over time, a sign of character development? Choose two.
options: Kareem used to avoid reading aloud; by June he volunteered to read first.
Kareem's school was a long white building near the main road.
Lina wore a blue scarf and carried a green backpack every day.
At first Lina hid in the library at lunch, but by spring she sat with three friends.
questions.why: Character development shows how a character grows or changes.

questions.stem: “Saad had moved so many times that he never unpacked his box of books. When his teacher offered to lend him a dictionary, he smiled for the first time all week.” What does the unpacked box reveal about Saad?
options: He wants his teacher to buy him a new set of books.
He has lost the key that opens his book box.
He does not enjoy reading books of any kind.
He does not expect to stay in one place long.
questions.why: Never unpacking suggests he expects to move again soon.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about the new student Hamza an example of direct characterization (the writer states the trait) or indirect characterization (the reader infers the trait)?

rows.text: Hamza was a shy boy.
Hamza stared at his shoes when the teacher said his name.
Hamza was kind to everyone he met.
Hamza gave half of his sandwich to a boy who had forgotten his lunch.

questions.why: Direct characterization names the trait; indirect shows it through actions.

questions.stem: Match each stage of a short-story plot with an example from a tale about a boy who moves to a farming town.

pairs.right: Omar's family arrives in a small farming town in August.
Omar struggles in class and hides his poor grades.
Omar's teacher asks him to read aloud in front of everyone.
Omar joins the reading club and finally feels at home.

questions.why: A plot moves from exposition through rising action to the climax and resolution.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The nurse used a thermometer to detect Ahmad's fever,” detect means to hide something so that no one finds it.
questions.why: To detect is to discover or notice something.

questions.stem: By listening to the radio every evening, Musa began to ____ new English words and phrases.
questions.why: To acquire is to gain or get something, such as new words.

questions.stem: “The bus rattled past dry fields and empty sheds. A cold wind blew dust against the windows, and the last farm workers were leaving for the season.” What mood does this setting create?
questions.why: Empty sheds, cold wind, and people leaving create a lonely mood.

questions.stem: Which three details help build the setting of a tale about a farm worker's family? Choose three.
options: an old tent beside a row of trucks
the sound of a rooster before dawn
the main character's age and name
the boy's wish to acquire a trumpet
the smell of ripe tomatoes in the morning heat
questions.why: Setting details describe the place, time, and atmosphere.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Nadia change from the beginning to the end of “The Borrowed Notebook”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Nadia change from the beginning to the end of “The Borrowed Notebook”?

options.label: A
options.text: She moves from enjoying travel to fearing every journey.

options.label: B
options.text: She moves from guarding her feelings to hoping she can stay.

options.label: C
options.text: She moves from loving science to wishing she studied art.

options.label: D
options.text: She moves from trusting teachers to doubting all of them.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: For the first time in two years, she found herself hoping the moving truck would be late.

options.label: B
options.text: “You can return it whenever you finish,” Ms. Huda said quietly.

options.label: C
options.text: Nadia had attended four different schools in two years, following her father from one construction project to the next.

options.label: D
options.text: At her newest school in Dammam, the corridor smelled of fresh paint, and the classroom windows overlooked enormous cranes along the harbor.

questions.why: Hoping the truck is late shows she now wants to stay.

questions.stem: What is the main conflict Nadia faces in “The Borrowed Notebook”?
options: She cannot find the library in her large new school.
She has missed a month of work after another move.
She wants to move but her father wants to stay put.
She disagrees with her teacher about a science grade.
questions.why: Having no notes from the first month is the problem she must solve.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Borrowed Notebook” is the turning point, where Nadia's situation begins to change?

segments.text: At each school she had learned the same painful lesson: never become too attached, because the moving truck always arrives.
Her science teacher, Ms. Huda, quickly noticed that Nadia had no notes from the first month of the term.
Without a word, she placed a thick notebook on Nadia's desk, its pages filled with careful diagrams in neat blue ink.
Nadia copied every page that week, staying in the library long after the final bell.

questions.why: The teacher's kind action is the moment that changes things for Nadia.

questions.stem: In “The Borrowed Notebook,” does each detail mainly build the setting or develop Nadia's character?

rows.text: the corridor smelled of fresh paint
the classroom windows overlooked cranes along the harbor
staying in the library long after the final bell
she slipped a thank-you card inside it

questions.why: Place details build setting; actions reveal character.

questions.stem: Which two inferences about Ms. Huda are supported by her actions in “The Borrowed Notebook”? Choose two.
options: She notices students who need help.
She plans to move to another school soon.
She thinks Nadia is careless about school.
questions.why: She sees the missing notes and helps quietly, without a word.

questions.stem: Although the brothers had dreaded the move, they decided to ____ every small pleasure of their final week in the village: the evening breeze, the call of the doves, and Grandmother's bread.
questions.why: To savor is to enjoy something slowly and fully.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about a new worker: “Rami spoke so hesitant that the foreman asked him to repeat his question.”
questions.why: An adverb (hesitantly) is needed to describe how Rami spoke.

questions.stem: Put the plot stages of a tale about a migrant worker's son in the correct order.
sequence: Exposition: Ali's family arrives at a grape farm for the harvest.
Rising action: Ali hides that he cannot read well at his new school.
Climax: Ali is asked to read the class announcements aloud.
Falling action: A classmate quietly offers to practice with him at lunch.
Resolution: Ali reads the announcements with confidence before the family moves on.
questions.why: Plot builds to the climax, then the tension eases toward the resolution.

questions.stem: True or false: A family that follows the harvest circuit and must start at a new school every few weeks faces an outside problem, or external conflict, that can shape a plot.
questions.why: An external conflict comes from forces outside the character, such as constant moving.

questions.stem: “Every time Musa grew used to a classroom, the trucks came back. By October he had stopped telling teachers his name until they asked twice.” Which trait do these details develop most?
questions.why: Holding back his name shows he guards himself because he expects to leave.

questions.stem: Match each word with the sentence that shows its meaning: diverge, sundry, vehemently, attribute.

pairs.right: At the fork, one road turned east and the other turned west.
The drawer held buttons, keys, coins, and string.
Faisal shouted, “That is not true!” and slammed his book shut.
The coach said the win was due to the team's practice.

questions.why: Each sentence acts out one word's meaning.

questions.stem: The twins' interests began to ____ in sixth grade: Nora chose robotics, and Lina chose painting.
questions.why: To diverge is to go in different directions.

questions.stem: True or false: A writer who uses the pronouns “I,” “me,” and “my” to tell about her own life is writing in the first-person point of view.
questions.why: First-person narrators tell about themselves using I, me, and my.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about twins written in the first-person or third-person point of view?

rows.text: I have always shared a bedroom with my twin brother.
She wanted people to see her as an individual.
My sister and I chose different clubs this year.
He finally felt independent at his new school.

questions.why: I and my signal first person; he and she signal third person.

questions.stem: “Everyone calls us ‘the twins,’ but I have my own name, and I want people to use it.” How does the writer feel about being called “the twins”?
options: annoyed, because she wants her own identity
pleased, because the nickname is very funny
proud, because she loves sharing everything
confused, because she forgets her own name
questions.why: Wanting people to use her own name shows she wants her own identity.

questions.stem: From whose point of view is “Two Chairs, Two Choices” told?
options: a neighbor who has known the family for years
Fahad, who describes his twin brother's choices
Faisal, who tells about his own life
a coach who watches both twins play games
questions.why: The narrator says “I” and is called Faisal by the coach.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's perspective on being a twin?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the author's perspective on being a twin?

options.label: A
options.text: Twins should always do the same activities together.

options.label: B
options.text: Twins are happier when they live in separate homes.

options.label: C
options.text: Twins can stay close and still be different people.

options.label: D
options.text: Being a twin is a problem that cannot be solved.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: At first it felt strange and uncomfortable to walk into a room without him beside me.

options.label: B
options.text: Last year, I finally decided that I wanted to change that situation.

options.label: C
options.text: But now I understand that sharing a birthday does not mean sharing an entire life.

options.label: D
options.text: After a few weeks of practice, I won my first match against an experienced opponent.

questions.why: He still loves his brother but knows they lead separate lives.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Two Chairs, Two Choices” shows that the narrator was finally seen as an individual?

segments.text: Teachers gave us the same seat, relatives bought us the same gifts, and neighbors called us both “Fahad-and-Faisal” as if it were one long name.
When the school offered new clubs, Fahad signed up for football right away, but I waited, thought carefully, and chose the chess club instead.
After a few weeks of practice, I won my first match against an experienced opponent.
It was the first time anyone had praised just me.

questions.why: Being praised “just me” shows he was seen as his own person.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Two Chairs, Two Choices” in the order they happen.
sequence: Fahad signs up for football.
Faisal chooses the chess club.
Faisal wins his first match.
The coach says, “Well played, Faisal.”
questions.why: The events follow the school year from choosing clubs to the first win.

questions.stem: Which two details from “Two Chairs, Two Choices” show that people did not tell the twins apart? Choose two.
options: Neighbors called them by one long name.
Faisal won his first chess match.
Fahad signed up for football right away.
Teachers gave the twins the same seat.
questions.why: Treating them the same shows people did not tell them apart.

questions.stem: Some students tried to ____ the new library rule by hiding books under their jackets instead of signing them out.
questions.why: To subvert a rule is to secretly work against it.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Our teacher attribute the twins' high grades to their hard work and daily reading.”
questions.why: The singular subject teacher needs the verb attributes.

questions.stem: Does each sentence about Lama's calligraphy hobby show the author's perspective (her feelings and beliefs) or only state a fact?

rows.text: I believe every letter I draw shows a piece of who I am.
Arabic calligraphy is often written with pens cut from reeds.
Practicing alone has made me more independent.
The art club meets on Tuesdays after school.

questions.why: Perspective shows beliefs and feelings; facts can be checked.

questions.stem: A writer says, “Being the youngest of five has taught me to speak up, because no one waits for the quiet one.” Which two words best describe the writer's perspective? Choose two.
questions.why: She has learned a practical lesson and now speaks up with confidence.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word merit correctly?
options: The merit of the river flooded the nearby farms.
The judges agreed that both essays had real merit.
Huda wore a new merit to the wedding last night.
We heard a loud merit coming from the kitchen.
questions.why: Merit is worth or value that deserves praise.

questions.stem: Match each phrase with its meaning: sundry items, diverging opinions, a plan to subvert, of great merit.

pairs.right: a secret effort to weaken something

questions.why: Reading a key word inside a phrase helps pin down its meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Teachers often attribute the twins' different tastes to their separate friends,” attribute means to say that one thing is caused by another.
questions.why: To attribute a result to something is to name it as the cause.

questions.stem: During the debate, Majed ____ insisted that the twins should be placed in separate classes, raising his voice and pounding the desk.
questions.why: Vehemently means with strong, forceful feeling, like shouting and pounding.

questions.stem: “People think twins must be best friends. My sister and I are close, but our opinions diverge on everything from music to dinner.” Why does the writer include the second sentence?
options: to describe the kinds of music twins enjoy
to challenge a common belief about twins
to explain how to settle family arguments
to show that twins always agree on meals
questions.why: The second sentence shows her own experience differs from what people think.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a short personal narrative about learning to be independent.
sequence: When I turned twelve, my father said I could walk to school alone.
On the first morning, my hands shook as I crossed the busy street.
By the end of the month, I walked confidently and even helped a younger boy cross.
Now I know that being independent starts with one brave step.
questions.why: A personal narrative moves through events and ends with what the writer learned.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes how the narrator's perspective on being a twin changes?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes how the narrator's perspective on being a twin changes?

options.label: A
options.text: She first wants to be different, then chooses to dress exactly like Dana.

options.label: B
options.text: She first feels safe as half of a pair, then sees herself as a separate person.

options.label: C
options.text: She first trusts her teacher completely, then refuses to write more essays.

options.label: D
options.text: She first feels angry about being a twin, then decides to copy her sister.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Our grandmother sewed us identical dresses for every Eid, and our teachers sat us side by side, assuming that whatever one of us knew, the other knew too.

options.label: B
options.text: Today, when someone confuses us, I smile and patiently explain the difference, because I have learned that my identity is something I build, not something I inherit.

options.label: C
options.text: Dana's handwriting leaned forward, quick and confident, while mine stood upright, slow and careful.

options.label: D
options.text: That evening, I compared our notebooks and noticed something surprising.

questions.why: The final sentence shows her new view of herself as her own person.

questions.stem: What does the phrase “a matched set” in paragraph 1 suggest about how others saw the twins?
options: as girls who enjoyed collecting matching dresses
as two parts of one unit, not as individuals
as students who always earned the same high grades
as sisters who argued constantly about their clothes
questions.why: A matched set is a group of things meant to go together as one.

questions.stem: In “Two Handwritings,” which two sentences show the narrator's own interpretation rather than events alone? Select two sentences.

segments.text: Our grandmother sewed us identical dresses for every Eid, and our teachers sat us side by side, assuming that whatever one of us knew, the other knew too.
That evening, I compared our notebooks and noticed something surprising.
Those two handwritings became a symbol for me.
We share a face, but we do not share a mind.

questions.why: These sentences explain what the events mean to her, showing her perspective.

questions.stem: In “Two Handwritings,” does each detail show how others treated the twins or how the narrator came to see herself?

rows.text: identical dresses for every Eid
teachers sat us side by side
my identity is something I build
we do not share a mind

questions.why: Some details show outside treatment; others show her inner view.

questions.stem: Why does the author most likely describe the two handwritings in detail? Choose two.
options: to give a clear example of how the twins differ
to explain why the teacher disliked the essay
to teach readers how to improve their handwriting
to prove that Dana was the better student
to set up a symbol for her separate identity
questions.why: The handwritings are concrete proof and a symbol of being different.

questions.stem: Grandmother's old trunk was full of ____ treasures: letters, coins, photographs, and a broken watch.
questions.why: Sundry means of many different kinds.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Although the two brothers look alike, their opinions diverges on almost every topic.”
questions.why: The plural subject opinions takes the verb diverge.

questions.stem: Does each word contain the Latin root vert, meaning “turn,” as in subvert?

rows.text: convert
divert
version
verb
very

columns.text: Does not have the root vert

questions.why: Vert or vers means turn; in verb and very, the letters ver are not that root.

questions.stem: True or false: An author who writes “Some people think twins have no individual personalities, but my life proves otherwise” is showing a perspective that disagrees with a common view.
questions.why: The author names a common belief and then disagrees with it.

questions.stem: Which sentence best shows an author's perspective rather than a neutral point of view?
options: Identical twins develop from a single cell that splits in two.
Many schools place twins in separate classes after grade one.
I vehemently believe every person deserves to be known by name.
Twins can be identical or fraternal, depending on how they form.
questions.why: Words like “vehemently believe” and “deserves” show a personal belief.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a new stadium with the key word it describes: capacity, rigid, scenario, coalesce.

pairs.left: The steel beams do not bend under the crowd.
Engineers imagine what would happen if every fan jumped at once.
Small groups of fans join into one huge cheering crowd.

questions.why: Each sentence shows one word's meaning in a stadium setting.

questions.stem: Before buying the game, Ali checked that it was ____ with his old computer.
questions.why: Compatible means able to work well together.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The bridge has a capacity of forty tons,” capacity means the most weight the bridge can safely hold.
questions.why: Capacity is the greatest amount something can hold or carry.

questions.stem: Which text structure does each signal word or phrase most often point to in a science article?

rows.text: as a result
first
because
after that
therefore

questions.why: Signal words help readers spot how a text is organized.

questions.stem: “Earthquakes shake the ground. They can crack roads, break windows, and knock down weak buildings.” What is the central idea of these sentences?
options: Weak buildings are found in old towns.
Windows break more easily than roads.
Roads are built with strong materials.
questions.why: The details about roads, windows, and buildings all show damage.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “When Fans Make the Ground Shake”?
options: Many fans jumping together can make the ground shake.
Fans should not jump in stadiums because it is unsafe.
Scientists prefer studying sports to studying earthquakes.
Engineers build stadiums only in cities without earthquakes.
questions.why: Every paragraph explains how crowd jumps shake the ground.

questions.stem: Put the steps that cause the ground near a stadium to shake in order.
sequence: A team scores a goal.
Thousands of fans jump at the same moment.
Their pushes add together in the stands.
The stadium passes the energy into the ground.
questions.why: The passage explains the steps as a chain of causes and effects.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does one fan's jump make almost no difference, while a crowd's jump does?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does one fan's jump make almost no difference, while a crowd's jump does?

options.label: A
options.text: Scientists only measure jumps made in large stadiums.

options.label: B
options.text: A single fan cannot jump as high as a large crowd can.

options.label: C
options.text: The stands are built to stop one person from jumping.

options.label: D
options.text: The small forces add together when everyone jumps at once.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Engineers now study crowd jumps carefully when they design new stadiums, because they want the stands to be strong enough to handle the excitement of a winning goal.

options.label: B
options.text: But when a whole crowd jumps at the same moment, all of those separate pushes add together.

options.label: C
options.text: Nobody was injured, and the buildings remained safe, but the data demonstrated how powerful a crowd's teamwork can be.

options.label: D
options.text: Sports fans love to jump and cheer when their team scores.

questions.why: Many small pushes at the same moment add up to a big one.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “When Fans Make the Ground Shake” explains how scientists measured the vibration?

segments.text: Each fan pushes down on the stands with a small force, and one person's jump makes almost no difference.
Scientists have measured this shaking with the same instruments they use to study earthquakes.
In several cities, the readings resembled a very small earthquake.
The stadium transfers the energy into the ground, which begins to vibrate.

questions.why: This sentence names the tools used to measure the shaking.

questions.stem: In “When Fans Make the Ground Shake,” is each statement a cause or an effect?

rows.text: Thousands of fans jump at once.
The ground begins to shake.
The readings look like a very small quake.
Fans want to celebrate a goal.

questions.why: A cause makes something happen; an effect is what happens.

questions.stem: The school bus was filled to ____, so the last three students had to wait for the next one.
questions.why: Filled to capacity means completely full.

questions.stem: A city is planning its new stadium. Which two sentences describe a scenario the planners might imagine? Choose two.
options: The stadium opened in the year 2019.
The stadium seats are painted blue.
What if every fan jumps at the same moment?
What if a sandstorm hits during a match?
questions.why: A scenario is an imagined situation that might happen.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “Stadiums with a larger capacity needs stronger supports under the stands.”
questions.why: The plural subject stadiums takes the verb need.

questions.stem: A science article has two headings: “The Problem: Cracked Bridges” and “The Solution: Flexible Joints.” Which text structure does it use?
questions.why: The headings name a problem and then a solution.

questions.stem: True or false: An article that asks what would happen if everyone on Earth jumped at once is describing an imagined scenario, not a real event.
questions.why: A scenario is an imagined situation, not one that has really happened.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a bouncing ball with its text structure.

pairs.left: First, the ball is lifted; then it is dropped; finally it bounces.
Because the ball has more mass, it hits the floor with greater impact.
A rubber ball bounces higher than a clay ball, but both fall at the same speed.
Rigid plastic balls kept cracking in the cold, so the company added a softer coating.

questions.why: Each sentence uses a different way of organizing ideas.

questions.stem: Engineers made the stadium roof ____ so that it would not bend, even in a heavy wind.
questions.why: Rigid means stiff and not able to bend.

questions.stem: Is each sentence from an article about the Moon's gravity the central idea or a supporting detail?

rows.text: Gravity on the Moon is much weaker than on Earth.
An astronaut can jump about six times higher there.
A heavy toolbox feels light when lifted on the Moon.

questions.why: The central idea is the main point; details give examples of it.

questions.stem: Which three words or phrases would most likely appear in an article with a cause-and-effect structure? Choose three.
questions.why: These signal words connect causes to their effects.

questions.stem: “The two scientists had compatible ideas, so their project moved quickly.” What does compatible mean in this sentence?
questions.why: Compatible ideas fit together and work well.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “What If Everyone Jumped?”

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “What If Everyone Jumped?”

options.label: A
options.text: Jumping from chairs is a dangerous activity for most people.

options.label: B
options.text: People should organize a world jump to test an important theory.

options.label: C
options.text: Human jumps are far too small to move a planet as massive as Earth.

options.label: D
options.text: Time zones make it hard for scientists to share their results.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Would the planet move?

options.label: B
options.text: The surprising answer is that Earth would barely notice.

options.label: C
options.text: There is also a practical problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Imagine that every person on Earth climbed onto a chair and, at exactly the same second, jumped to the ground.

questions.why: The answer to the question, that Earth would barely notice, is the central idea.

questions.stem: How is paragraph 3 of “What If Everyone Jumped?” organized?
options: It describes the history of an old science experiment.
It explains a problem and why it is hard to solve.
It compares the mass of Earth with the mass of the Moon.
It lists in order the steps for planning a giant jump.
questions.why: Paragraph 3 names a practical problem and explains why it cannot easily be fixed.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “What If Everyone Jumped?” states the lesson the author wants readers to remember?

segments.text: Scientists enjoy hypothetical questions like this one because the answers reveal how physical forces actually work.
Although eight billion people sounds enormous, their combined mass is tiny compared with the mass of the planet.
Even a delay of a few seconds would spread the pushes out, so their effects would fade.
The thought experiment teaches an important lesson: gravity ties every object to every other object, but size determines who moves whom.

questions.why: The final sentence names the lesson directly.

questions.stem: Which two details support the idea that Earth would barely move? Choose two.
options: People in different time zones would be asleep or working.
Scientists enjoy hypothetical questions like this one.
The motion of Earth itself would be negligible.
Their combined mass is tiny compared with the mass of the planet.
questions.why: Both details explain why the planet's motion would be too small to matter.

questions.stem: In “What If Everyone Jumped?”, what is the main job of each paragraph?

rows.text: Paragraph 1
Paragraph 2
Paragraph 3

questions.why: The article moves from a question, to an answer, to a problem with the idea.

questions.stem: Several small rain clouds began to ____, forming one huge storm cloud over the city.
questions.why: To coalesce is to come together into one.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “The rigid steel frame of the stadium were built to handle large crowds.”
questions.why: The singular subject frame takes the verb was.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to form a cause-and-effect paragraph about a dropped glass.
sequence: Gravity pulls the falling glass toward the floor.
The glass strikes the tiles with a sharp impact.
The force of the impact sends cracks through the glass.
As a result, the glass shatters into pieces.
questions.why: Each event causes the next, ending with the final effect.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The new charger is compatible with every tablet in the classroom,” compatible means the charger cannot be used with them.
questions.why: Compatible means able to work together, so the charger works with every tablet.

questions.stem: A writer wants readers to understand how heavy objects and light objects are alike and different when they fall. Which text structure would best suit the writer's purpose?
questions.why: Showing likenesses and differences calls for compare and contrast.

questions.stem: Match each word about school behavior with its synonym: civility, persist, perceive, severe.
questions.why: Synonyms have nearly the same meaning.

questions.stem: Complete the analogy: Wheel is to bicycle as page is to ____.
questions.why: A wheel is part of a bicycle, and a page is part of a book (part to whole).

questions.stem: Is each word pair an example of a part-whole relationship or an item-category relationship?

rows.text: leaf : tree
apple : fruit
finger : hand
falcon : bird

questions.why: A part belongs to a whole; an item belongs to a group or category.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Our school has zero tolerance for bullying,” the phrase zero tolerance means that bullying will not be accepted at all.
questions.why: Zero tolerance means no amount of something is allowed.

questions.stem: “Hind perceived that she was being left out of every game at recess. As a result, she began eating lunch alone in the library.” What is the effect of being left out?
options: Hind joined every game at recess.
Hind became the team's new captain.
questions.why: The signal phrase “as a result” introduces the effect.

questions.stem: What is the author's main claim in “Bystanders Can Make a Difference”?
options: Bullying only happens when teachers are away.
Students who see bullying can help stop it.
Students should avoid anyone who is a bully.
Researchers do not agree about what bullying is.
questions.why: The title and the evidence both point to the power of bystanders.

questions.stem: Part A: Which evidence does the author give to support the claim that bystanders can help?

partA.stem: Part A: Which evidence does the author give to support the claim that bystanders can help?

options.label: A
options.text: Most students are afraid of being bullied at school.

options.label: B
options.text: Bullying often stops quickly when a bystander speaks up.

options.label: C
options.text: Teachers always notice bullying when it happens.

options.label: D
options.text: Bullies usually have trouble with their schoolwork.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Schools can help by teaching students safe and practical ways to respond.

options.label: B
options.text: Many fear that the bully will turn on them next, while others assume that someone else will act.

options.label: C
options.text: Researchers who study schools have found that when a bystander speaks up, bullying often stops in less than a minute.

options.label: D
options.text: Most bullying happens when other students are nearby, watching but not taking part.

questions.why: Research findings are the evidence that supports the claim.

questions.stem: In “Bystanders Can Make a Difference,” is each idea a reason students do not step in or a way they can help?

rows.text: fear that the bully will turn on them
thinking someone else will act
inviting the targeted student to a game
telling a teacher

columns.text: Reason they do not step in

questions.why: The passage gives both causes of silence and ways to help.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Bystanders Can Make a Difference” explains a cause of bystanders choosing not to step in?

segments.text: These students are called bystanders, and although they are not the ones doing the bullying, what they do next matters a great deal.
A simple sentence such as “That's not okay” can change what happens.
Many fear that the bully will turn on them next, while others assume that someone else will act.
Every student can choose to be part of the solution, because kindness from even one classmate can help a hurt student feel less alone.

questions.why: Fear of becoming the next target is a reason students stay silent.

questions.stem: Which two actions does the author list as quieter ways to help? Choose two.
options: shouting at the bully in front of others
walking with the student who was targeted
inviting that student to join a game
questions.why: Quieter ways support the targeted student without a public argument.

questions.stem: The flood caused ____ damage: roads were washed away and hundreds of homes were destroyed.
questions.why: Severe means very serious or harsh.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “When the teacher saw the argument, she asked both students to speak with more civil toward each other.”
questions.why: After more, a noun is needed: civility, not the adjective civil.

questions.stem: Match each item with the category it belongs to: hammer, cucumber, cello, sparrow.
questions.why: In an item-category relationship, the item is one member of a larger group.

questions.stem: Which two sentences show a cause-and-effect relationship? Choose two.
options: Because Ziad showed tolerance, the new student felt welcome.
The school library opens at seven every morning.
Ziad and Maryam both enjoy their science class.
Maryam ignored the warning, so she faced a serious repercussion.
questions.why: Because and so link a cause to its effect.

questions.stem: Which pair shows the same relationship as “chapter : novel”?
questions.why: A chapter is part of a novel, just as a verse is part of a poem.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Breaking the window had serious repercussions for the boys,” repercussions means rewards that someone earns.
questions.why: Repercussions are results of an action, usually unpleasant ones.

questions.stem: Is each statement about school bullying a fact that can be checked or an opinion?

rows.text: Our school held an anti-bullying assembly in March.
Every student should treat classmates with civility.
The survey asked 400 students about recess.
Bystanders are the most important people in solving bullying.

questions.why: Facts can be proven; opinions show beliefs.

questions.stem: Although the other team laughed at her ideas, Rawan continued to ____ until the club agreed to try her plan.
questions.why: To persist is to keep going despite difficulty.

questions.stem: Put this chain of events about a student named Rakan in cause-and-effect order.
sequence: Rakan's classmates leave him out of their football game.
Rakan begins to feel lonely and sad.
Rakan stops wanting to come to school.
His teacher perceives the problem and talks with the class about tolerance.
questions.why: Each event leads to the next one.

questions.stem: “School uniforms prevent all bullying, because everyone looks the same.” Why is this claim weak?
options: It includes too many examples and statistics.
It is too absolute and gives no evidence.
It is supported by a survey of many schools.
It uses a fact that can easily be checked.
questions.why: Words like “all” make a claim too broad, and it offers no proof.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's central claim in “Cyberbullying: Why Schools Must Respond”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the author's central claim in “Cyberbullying: Why Schools Must Respond”?

options.label: A
options.text: Schools should teach students how to respond to cyberbullying.

options.label: B
options.text: Students should never post messages late at night.

options.label: C
options.text: Families should take away phones from all their children.

options.label: D
options.text: Cyberbullying is less harmful than bullying on the playground.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Schools should therefore teach digital citizenship as seriously as they teach mathematics.

options.label: B
options.text: A screen does not make cruelty acceptable, and silence does not make it disappear.

options.label: C
options.text: A cruel message posted at midnight can be read by dozens of classmates before breakfast.

options.label: D
options.text: Some people argue that what happens online is the responsibility of families, not schools.

questions.why: The word therefore signals the author's main claim.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Cyberbullying: Why Schools Must Respond” presents a counterclaim, an opposing view that the author answers?

segments.text: Cyberbullying, or bullying through phones and the internet, differs from bullying on the playground in one important way: it can follow a student home.
Some people argue that what happens online is the responsibility of families, not schools.
However, this view ignores an important fact.
Students need to learn how to report harmful posts, how to support a classmate who is being isolated, and why empathy matters even behind a screen.

questions.why: “Some people argue” introduces a view the author then disagrees with.

questions.stem: Which two reasons does the author give to support the idea that schools should respond to online bullying? Choose two.
options: Families do not care about cyberbullying.
Mathematics matters more than online safety.
Its consequences return to school the next morning.
Phones are expensive and easy to lose.
Online cruelty often begins with conflicts at school.
questions.why: Both reasons connect online bullying back to school life.

questions.stem: In “Cyberbullying: Why Schools Must Respond,” is each statement a cause or an effect of a cruel post?

rows.text: A conflict begins at school during the day.
A student posts a cruel message at midnight.
Dozens of classmates read it before breakfast.
The targeted student feels there is no safe place.

questions.why: The conflict and the post cause the harm that follows.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the argument in “Cyberbullying: Why Schools Must Respond”?
options: It relies mostly on research studies from several different countries.
It agrees with the counterclaim and so does not need any evidence.
It uses sound reasoning but gives no statistics or research as evidence.
It uses many statistics but never states a clear claim about schools.
questions.why: The reasoning is logical, but the essay offers no data or studies.

questions.stem: The coach praised the players' ____: even after the bad call, they shook hands with the referee politely.
questions.why: Civility is polite, respectful behavior.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “The severe comments in the group chat was reported to the principal by two brave students.”
questions.why: The plural subject comments takes the verb were.

questions.stem: Match each word pair with the relationship it shows: keyboard : computer, ruby : gemstone, perceive : notice, civility : rudeness.
questions.why: Analogies can show parts, categories, synonyms, or antonyms.

questions.stem: True or false: A claim supported only by the sentence “Everyone knows bullies are just jealous” has strong, relevant evidence.
questions.why: “Everyone knows” is an opinion, not evidence that can be checked.

questions.stem: “Our school reduced bullying by half after starting a peer-mentor program, so every school in the country should start one immediately.” What is the main weakness in this reasoning?
options: It draws a broad conclusion from a single example.
It uses a counterclaim that the writer never answers.
It does not explain what bullying is or why it hurts.
It gives no information about any school at all.
questions.why: One school's result is not enough to prove what every school should do.

questions.stem: Match each word with the sentence that shows its meaning: heritage, represent, siege, westernize.

pairs.right: The village still performs the dances its grandparents taught.
Rami spoke at the city meeting on behalf of his whole class.
An army surrounded the fort and blocked every road for months.
The town replaced its old market with malls copied from America.

questions.why: Each sentence shows one word's meaning.

questions.stem: Each spring, our family cooks the same dishes that our great-grandparents cooked, because these recipes are part of our ____.
questions.why: Heritage is the traditions handed down from earlier generations.

questions.stem: True or false: A memoir is a true account that an author writes about events from his or her own life.
questions.why: Memoirs are true and told by the person who lived them.

questions.stem: Is the purpose of each piece of writing described below mainly to inform, to persuade, or to entertain?

rows.text: a guide that explains how desert plants store water
a speech asking leaders to protect the town's heritage sites
a funny tale about a goat that eats homework
an article describing the life of sea turtles

questions.why: Authors write to inform, persuade, or entertain.

questions.stem: “I was only ten, but I knew that every girl in my village deserved a school.” From which point of view is this sentence written?
questions.why: The pronoun I shows the first-person point of view.

questions.stem: What is the author's main purpose in “The Reading Corner”?
options: to describe the books stored in her grandfather's cupboard
to explain how libraries in large cities are organized
to share how she worked to bring books to her village
to persuade families to buy books instead of toys
questions.why: The memoir tells how the author built a reading corner.

questions.stem: Part A: Which word best describes the narrator of “The Reading Corner”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which word best describes the narrator of “The Reading Corner”?

options.label: A
options.text: determined

options.label: B
options.text: careless

options.label: C
options.text: impatient

options.label: D
options.text: jealous

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Today, our reading corner holds more than four hundred books.

options.label: B
options.text: I wrote letters to every family I knew and asked each of them to donate one book they had finished reading.

options.label: C
options.text: He explained that there was no money for one.

options.label: D
options.text: When I was an eleven-year-old girl, the only books in our village were the ones in my grandfather's wooden cupboard, and I had read each of them so many times that I could recite whole pages from memory.

questions.why: Writing to every family shows she worked hard toward her goal.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Reading Corner” shows that the narrator saw something unfair?

segments.text: One evening, I asked my father why our school had no library.
He explained that there was no money for one.
That answer bothered me for weeks, because it did not seem fair that children in the city could borrow books every day while we had none.
Every time I see a child carry one home, I remember that small ideas can grow into something remarkable.

questions.why: The narrator says it did not seem fair that city children had books while her village had none.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Reading Corner” in the order they happen.
sequence: The narrator asks her father why the school has no library.
She writes letters asking families for books.
Only three books arrive at first.
Her teacher reads her letter aloud at a school meeting.
The reading corner grows to over four hundred books.
questions.why: The memoir is told in time order.

questions.stem: Which two details are the best evidence that the narrator kept going despite setbacks? Choose two.
options: She almost gave up on the plan.
I could recite whole pages from memory.
He explained that there was no money for one.
Only three books arrived at first.
questions.why: She had to keep going after a slow start.

questions.stem: The old city held out for six months during the ____, even though its people had little food left.
questions.why: A siege is when an army surrounds a place and cuts off its supplies.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “The two students who represents our school at the science fair are both in sixth grade.”
questions.why: Who refers to the plural students, so the verb is represent.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about the scientist Ibn al-Haytham a fact or the writer's opinion?

rows.text: Ibn al-Haytham studied how light enters the eye.
He was the most inspiring scientist who ever lived.
He wrote the Book of Optics.
Every student should admire his patience.

questions.why: Facts can be checked; opinions show what a writer believes.

questions.stem: A memoir writer says, “I will never stop speaking out to represent the girls who cannot speak for themselves.” Which two words best describe the writer's point of view? Choose two.
questions.why: Never stopping and speaking out show a determined, outspoken view.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The blue stripe on the flag represents the sea,” what does represents mean?
questions.why: Here represent means to be a symbol of something.

questions.stem: Match each word from a history lesson with the word or phrase closest in meaning: heritage, siege, represent, westernize.
questions.why: Synonyms and close meanings help you remember new words.

questions.stem: True or false: In some countries long ago, flogging was used as a harsh punishment for breaking the law.
questions.why: Flogging is beating someone with a whip or stick as a punishment.

questions.stem: To support her claim that the program helped students, the writer included ____: test scores rose by twenty points in one year.
questions.why: Facts and numbers are evidence that support a claim.

questions.stem: A memoir writer claims, “Our heritage museum changed my town.” Does each sentence give strong or weak evidence for that claim?

rows.text: Visitor numbers tripled in the first year after it opened.
I think museums are nice places.
Twelve local craftspeople now teach weaving classes there.
My cousin likes the color of the building.

questions.why: Strong evidence is specific and directly connected to the claim.

questions.stem: “I tell my life's events not because they are unusual, but because they belong to many girls who were never heard.” What is the author's main purpose in this sentence?
options: to explain why she enjoys writing her memoir
to speak for others who share her experience
to describe the girls who live in her town
to prove that her own life is more unusual
questions.why: She writes to give a voice to others like her.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's main purpose in “Learning to Speak Up”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the author's main purpose in “Learning to Speak Up”?

options.label: A
options.text: to persuade readers to enter speech competitions at their schools

options.label: B
options.text: to describe the rules that a school speech competition must follow

options.label: C
options.text: to show how he found the courage to use his voice despite a challenge

options.label: D
options.text: to explain the best methods for cleaning plastic from a beach

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I read my speech to the mirror, to my little sister, and finally to my uncle, who listened without interrupting once.

options.label: B
options.text: I had discovered that a voice does not need to be perfect to be powerful.

options.label: C
options.text: When classmates laughed, I learned to stay silent, and silence slowly became a habit.

options.label: D
options.text: I spent weekends collecting bottles with my uncle, and I grew angry that no one seemed to care.

questions.why: The closing lesson shows the memoir is about finding his voice.

questions.stem: Which two sentences from “Learning to Speak Up” are the best evidence that the narrator kept working toward his goal? Select two sentences.

segments.text: I practiced for six weeks.
On the day of the competition, my voice shook and I stumbled twice, but I finished every sentence.
For most of my childhood, I avoided speaking in class.
When classmates laughed, I learned to stay silent, and silence slowly became a habit.
That changed the year our coastal town's beach became covered with plastic.

questions.why: Long practice and finishing despite stumbling show he kept going.

questions.stem: What does the simile “like a door that would not open” in paragraph 1 suggest about the narrator's stutter?
options: He was afraid of rooms with closed doors.
Words felt blocked and hard to release.
His voice was too loud for the classroom.
Speaking felt as easy as walking outside.
questions.why: A door that will not open suggests words that are stuck.

questions.stem: Which two inferences about the narrator's perspective are supported by the text? Choose two.
options: He believes his uncle should have entered the competition.
He thinks the principal should cancel speech competitions.
He thinks a speech can succeed without winning first place.
He believes caring about a cause can matter more than fear.
questions.why: He spoke despite fear, and his speech brought forty students to the beach.

questions.stem: In “Learning to Speak Up,” does each detail show the narrator's challenge or his determination?

rows.text: certain sounds caught in my throat
when classmates laughed, I learned to stay silent
I practiced for six weeks
I finished every sentence

questions.why: Some details show the obstacle; others show how he pushed through it.

questions.stem: Some young people in the city began to ____ their clothing, trading traditional thobes for jeans and baseball caps.
questions.why: To westernize is to adopt the customs and styles of Western countries.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error: “During the siege last spring, the defenders become heroes to the whole region.”
questions.why: Last spring shows a finished past event, so the verb must be became.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a paragraph in which a writer states a claim about being resilient and supports it with evidence.
sequence: Resilient people treat failure as a step, not an ending.
For example, the inventor Abbas ibn Firnas is remembered for daring to try to fly, even though his landing was painful.
His bold attempt is still admired by people who study the history of flight.
His example shows that every setback can teach something new.
questions.why: A strong paragraph moves from claim, to evidence, to explanation, to conclusion.

questions.stem: True or false: When an author writes “I” and describes her own feelings about an unfair event she lived through, such as the siege of her city, she is writing from a first-person point of view that shows her personal perspective.
questions.why: First-person writing shares the author's own view and feelings.

questions.stem: A student claims, “The author of the memoir was very determined.” Which quotation would best support this claim?
options: “My brother and I often argued about which game we should play.”
“My favorite food has always been my mother's rice with lentils.”
“I returned to the clinic each day for a year until I could walk.”
“Our house had two windows that faced the mountains to the east.”
questions.why: Returning every day for a year is clear evidence of determination.

questions.stem: Match each science fiction review word with a word close in meaning: “immense,” “vital,” “resilient,” and “savagely.”
questions.why: Synonyms are words with nearly the same meaning.

questions.stem: The colony's greenhouse was ____ to the settlers, because it grew every bit of food they ate.
questions.why: Something the settlers cannot live without is vital to them.

questions.stem: True or false: A resilient desert plant can turn green again after a long, dry summer.
questions.why: Resilient means able to recover after hard times.

questions.stem: Laila forgot her sunscreen on a trip to the beach. Which sentence describes a consequence of that choice?
options: She packed a cold drink in her bag that morning.
Her shoulders were red and sore that evening.
Her brother wore a wide straw hat during the trip.
She chose a shady spot near the water to sit.
questions.why: A consequence is a result that follows an action.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about a storm on a rainy planet a cause or a consequence?

rows.text: The rain fell for seven years without stopping.
The children had never seen the sun.
The wind tore savagely at the colony's roof.
Workers spent the morning repairing the roof.

questions.why: A cause makes something happen; a consequence is what happens as a result.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences are told from the first-person point of view? Choose two.
options: She pressed her face against the window and waited.
The children ran outside when the rain stopped.
We ran outside the moment the rain finally stopped.
I pressed my face against the window and waited for the sun.
questions.why: First-person narrators use I, me, we, and us.

questions.stem: In a story's plot, the ____ is the problem the main character must face.
questions.why: The conflict is the central problem that drives the plot.

questions.stem: Put the events of a story about Omar on a frozen moon base in plot order, from exposition to resolution.
sequence: Omar's family moves to a frozen moon base.
Omar feels lonely in the immense, silent base because he knows no one there.
During a power failure, Omar helps the other children find the emergency lights.
The children invite Omar to join their games.
questions.why: A plot moves from setup to problem to climax to resolution.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about an old robot does not make sense with the word “resilient”? Fix it.
segments: Because the old robot was resilient,
it broke apart after one small fall
questions.correction: it kept working after many hard falls
questions.why: Something resilient recovers from hard knocks instead of breaking.

questions.stem: Which sentence states a theme rather than a topic?
options: Children waiting a long time for the weather.
A tale about children living on a rainy planet.
Being cruel to others can leave a lasting regret.
Space travel and daily life in distant colonies.
questions.why: A theme is a message about life, not just a subject.

questions.stem: Part A: From which point of view is “The Viewing Window” told?

partA.stem: Part A: From which point of view is “The Viewing Window” told?

options.label: A
options.text: third person, by an outside narrator who knows everyone's thoughts

options.label: B
options.text: first person, by a child who lives on the station

options.label: C
options.text: second person, speaking directly to the reader

options.label: D
options.text: first person, by Noor after she arrives from Earth

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: She was quiet and frail after the long journey, and she walked slowly with a cane while her legs adjusted to the low gravity.

options.label: B
options.text: Every few days, when the ice storms clear, the giant planet appears, glowing with bands of orange and cream.

options.label: C
options.text: Then Noor arrived from Earth, and everything changed.

options.label: D
options.text: I always won, because I was the fastest runner on the station, and I was proud of my unbroken record.

questions.why: The narrator uses I to tell about himself or herself, so the story is in first person.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Viewing Window” that shows the turning point (climax) of the story.

segments.text: Then Noor arrived from Earth, and everything changed.
On viewing day, she reached the window last and saw nothing but our backs.
That night I could not sleep, because I kept picturing her face, patient and disappointed.
The next time Jupiter appeared, I ran as fast as ever, but I stopped at the window and saved the center spot until she arrived.

questions.why: The climax is the moment the narrator acts differently and the conflict turns.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of “The Viewing Window”?
options: Winning a race is the best way to make friends.
Real strength includes making room for others.
Living far from Earth makes all children unkind.
New students should always arrive early to class.
questions.why: The fastest child chooses to share the best spot, showing kindness is true strength.

questions.stem: Which TWO details show how the narrator changes from the beginning to the end of “The Viewing Window”? Choose two.
options: Later, the narrator stops running to the window.
At first, the narrator is afraid of seeing Jupiter.
At first, the narrator is proud of always winning.
Later, the narrator saves the best spot for Noor.
questions.why: The narrator moves from pride in winning to thinking of Noor.

questions.stem: In “The Viewing Window,” which part of the plot does each detail belong to?

rows.text: The station has only one window facing the sky.
Noor reaches the window last and sees nothing.
The narrator cannot sleep, picturing Noor's face.
The narrator saves the center spot for Noor.

questions.why: Exposition sets the scene, rising action builds the problem, and the climax is the turning point.

questions.stem: The new rocket was so ____ that it towered over every building in the colony.
questions.why: Something that towers over buildings is immense, or extremely large.

questions.stem: Match each situation on a space station with the word it shows: “consequence,” “resilient,” and “vital.”

pairs.left: losing your turn at the telescope because you arrived late
a crew that rebuilds the garden right after a fire
oxygen tanks that the astronauts cannot live without

questions.why: A consequence is a result, resilient means bouncing back, and vital means necessary.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Huda said that skipping practice had a serious consequence for the team,” the word “consequence” refers to something that happened as a result.
questions.why: A consequence is what follows from an earlier action.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about a stranded astronaut uses the wrong form of “vital”? Fix it.
segments: during her long stay on the station.
questions.why: After the verb was, the adjective vital is needed, not the adverb vitally.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about the Venus colony told in first-person or third-person point of view?

rows.text: My view of the immense gray sky never changed.
Her view of the immense gray sky never changed.
We stayed resilient through seven years of rain.
The colonists learned that sunlight was vital to their mood.

questions.why: My and we signal first person; her and the colonists signal third person.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main conflict in “Dust Season”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main conflict in “Dust Season”?

options.label: A
options.text: The colony may lose power because the storm has blocked the solar panels.

options.label: B
options.text: Tariq argues with his mother about whether he may visit the greenhouse.

options.label: C
options.text: The engineers cannot agree on who should lead the Mars colony next year.

options.label: D
options.text: Tariq is afraid that the tomato plants will never grow ripe again.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: That evening, the greenhouse lamps glowed again.

options.label: B
options.text: When the main battery warning finally flashed red, the adults gathered in the control room, arguing about whether anyone could repair the panels before the power failed entirely.

options.label: C
options.text: His mother hesitated for a long moment before she agreed.

options.label: D
options.text: Tariq sat among the plants, exhausted, and realized that being young did not mean being useless.

questions.why: The battery warning shows the colony is about to lose power.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Dust Season” that shows the climax of the plot.

segments.text: His mother hesitated for a long moment before she agreed.
Tariq crawled beneath the panel frame while the wind hammered his helmet, and he twisted the connector until a small green light blinked on.
That evening, the greenhouse lamps glowed again.
Tariq had studied the panel diagrams for months, and he knew that his small hands could reach the cracked connector that the engineers' gloves could not.

questions.why: The climax is the moment of greatest tension when the problem is solved.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Dust Season” in the order they happen.
sequence: The storm covers the colony and the panels lose power.
The battery warning flashes red.
Tariq's mother agrees to let him try the repair.
Tariq fixes the connector beneath the panel.
The greenhouse lamps glow again.
questions.why: The plot moves from the problem to the repair to the result.

questions.stem: “Dust Season” uses third-person limited point of view. Which TWO details show that the reader sees mainly through Tariq's eyes? Choose two.
options: The reader learns what every engineer was secretly thinking.
The narrator speaks to the reader using the word “you.”
The reader learns that Tariq knew his small hands could reach the connector.
The reader learns what Tariq realized while sitting among the plants.
questions.why: Third-person limited shares only one character's thoughts.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “Dust Season”?
options: Adults should never allow children to help with any dangerous work.
Dust storms on Mars last longer than anyone expects.
Young people can make real contributions when given a chance.
Greenhouses are the most important buildings in a colony.
questions.why: Tariq's repair shows that being young does not mean being useless.

questions.stem: The desert wind howled ____ all night, ripping the tents from their poles and scattering the supplies across the sand.
questions.why: Ripping and scattering show the wind acted in a fierce, violent way.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use “vital” to mean “necessary” or “full of life and energy”?

rows.text: Sunlight is vital for the plants in the greenhouse.
Even at eighty, Grandfather stayed vital, walking five kilometers every day.
Clean air is vital for the astronauts inside the station.
The market felt vital and lively, with music and voices everywhere.

questions.why: Vital can mean necessary for life, or lively and energetic.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “savagely” in a figurative way rather than to describe an animal's attack? Choose two.
options: The hungry wolf savagely tore at its prey in the snow.
The critic savagely attacked the new film in her review.
The winter wind bit savagely at the travelers' faces.
The lion savagely fought off the hyenas near its cubs.
questions.why: A critic and the wind do not really bite or attack, so savagely is used figuratively.

questions.stem: True or false: A story in which a character makes a cruel choice and later faces its consequence may be suggesting a theme about responsibility.
questions.why: Authors often show consequences to teach a lesson about choices.

questions.stem: A story ends: “Years later, Sami still remembered the day he left his friend behind, and the memory stung each time.” What does this ending most likely suggest about the theme?
options: Leaving early is the best way to stay safe.
Memories of school grow weaker every year.
Hurtful choices can stay with us long after.
Friends always forget the mistakes we make.
questions.why: The lasting sting shows that unkind choices leave lasting regret.

questions.stem: Match each word about fame and heroes with the example that shows it: “notoriety,” “indulge,” “civil,” and “conservation.”

pairs.right: a driver who becomes well known for racing dangerously on public roads
enjoying an extra piece of kunafa on a holiday
thanking an opponent politely after a hard debate
protecting the mangrove forests along the coast

questions.why: Linking each word to an example helps you judge claims about fame.

questions.stem: Many teenagers began reading poetry after a popular singer shared her favorite poems online; her ____ on them was clear.
questions.why: Changing what others do shows influence.

questions.stem: True or false: A wildlife conservation project might include guarding the beaches where sea turtles lay their eggs.
questions.why: Conservation means protecting nature and natural resources.

questions.stem: Which sentence states a claim?
options: The team played in Riyadh on Friday night.
The striker scored twice in the second half.
Athletes should visit schools more often.
The stadium can hold sixty thousand fans.
questions.why: A claim is a statement someone argues for, often using should.

questions.stem: Is each statement about a famous football player a fact or an opinion?

rows.text: He scored thirty goals last season.
He is the most civil player in the league.
He spoke at a water conservation event in March.
Every fan should follow his example.

questions.why: Facts can be checked; opinions show beliefs or feelings.

questions.stem: A writer claims, “Famous people have a strong influence on how young people dress.” Which TWO details are relevant evidence for this claim? Choose two.
options: Sales of a sneaker tripled after a star wore it in a match.
Students in a class survey named singers as their main source of style ideas.
Sneakers were first made more than one hundred years ago.
The star grew up in a small town near Tabuk.
questions.why: Relevant evidence connects directly to the claim about clothing choices.

questions.stem: Evidence that comes from a trusted expert, a study, or official numbers makes a claim more ____.
questions.why: Reliable sources make evidence stronger.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about a famous chef uses a word that does not fit? Fix it.
questions.why: Civil means polite, so shouting insults does not fit.

questions.stem: Put the parts of a short argument about a celebrity's influence in a logical order.
sequence: Claim: Celebrities should use their influence to support conservation.
Reason: Millions of people pay attention to what famous people say.
Evidence: After one actor posted about saving water, water use in his city dropped that summer.
Conclusion: Fame is most valuable when it helps others.
questions.why: An argument states a claim, gives reasons and evidence, then concludes.

questions.stem: Which reason best supports the claim “Scientists deserve as much attention as celebrities”?
options: Some scientists prefer to work late at night.
Many scientists wear white coats in their labs.
Their discoveries save lives and improve daily life.
Most scientists study for many long years at school.
questions.why: Only the first reason explains why scientists deserve attention.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's main claim in “Look Closer to Home”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the author's main claim in “Look Closer to Home”?

options.label: A
options.text: Celebrities are never good role models for anyone at all.

options.label: B
options.text: The best role models are often people young people know in daily life.

options.label: C
options.text: Coaches are more talented than most famous football stars.

options.label: D
options.text: Young people should stop watching sports and music shows.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: A boy can see how his coach treats a player from the other team who has been injured.

options.label: B
options.text: This does not mean that celebrities can never be admirable.

options.label: C
options.text: Fame alone does not prove that someone has integrity.

options.label: D
options.text: Many young people idolize singers and football stars, but the most valuable role models are often the people they see every day.

questions.why: The first sentence states the claim that everyday people are the most valuable role models.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Look Closer to Home” that gives research-based evidence for the author's claim.

segments.text: Celebrities are admired for their talent, yet fans rarely know how these stars behave when the cameras are turned off.
Researchers who study character development have found that children learn behavior most easily from adults they interact with regularly.
This does not mean that celebrities can never be admirable.
A student can watch how her science teacher handles a failed experiment, patiently checking each step instead of giving up.

questions.why: Research findings are evidence from experts, not just examples or opinions.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the sentence “This does not mean that celebrities can never be admirable”?
options: to prove that most celebrities behave badly
to change the topic to talented teachers
to tell readers exactly which singers they should admire
to admit a limit and show the argument is fair
questions.why: Admitting a limit makes an argument more balanced and believable.

questions.stem: Which TWO examples does the author of “Look Closer to Home” use as evidence that everyday role models can be observed? Choose two.
options: a football star training before a big match
a coach treating an injured player from the other team
a singer giving money to a hospital
a science teacher handling a failed experiment
questions.why: The author's examples are people young people see every day.

questions.stem: In “Look Closer to Home,” is each statement a claim the author makes or evidence the author gives?

rows.text: Young people should first look for heroes whose daily choices they can witness.
Children learn behavior most easily from adults they interact with regularly.
The most valuable role models are often the people young people see every day.
A student can watch her teacher patiently check each step of an experiment.

questions.why: Claims state what the author believes; evidence supports them.

questions.stem: The website gained ____ when it spread false rumors about a famous athlete.
questions.why: Notoriety is fame for doing something bad.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a famous runner with the word it shows: “influence,” “conservation,” and “civil.”

pairs.left: Hundreds of girls joined running clubs after watching her race.
She raised money to protect the forest where she trained.
She shook hands politely with the rival who had pushed her.

questions.why: Each sentence gives a clue to the word's meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: The statement “This celebrity is the greatest athlete who ever lived” can be proven with evidence alone.
questions.why: Greatest is a judgment, so the statement is an opinion.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about fans who indulge in celebrity gossip has an error? Fix it.
questions.why: The plural subject fans needs the verb indulge.

questions.stem: Is each piece of evidence for the claim “The actor's conservation work is sincere” strong or weak?

rows.text: He has planted trees at the same reserve every month for ten years, often without cameras.
He looked very caring in a photo shared online.
Reserve workers say he quietly paid for a new water pump.
Many people say he is the kindest actor alive.

questions.why: Strong evidence is specific and checkable; weak evidence is vague or based on appearance.

questions.stem: Part A: Which part of the argument in “Fame Can Serve Others” is the weakest?

partA.stem: Part A: Which part of the argument in “Fame Can Serve Others” is the weakest?

options.label: A
options.text: the example of the singer's visit to the village
