options.label: B
options.text: the example of the goalkeeper's blood donation video

options.label: C
options.text: the point that celebrities reach millions of people quickly

options.label: D
options.text: the claim that famous people are smarter than ordinary people

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: A message that might have been ignored on a poster suddenly became impossible to miss.

options.label: B
options.text: When a popular singer visited a village without clean water, cameras followed her.

options.label: C
options.text: According to the regional health office, donations rose by forty percent during the following month.

options.label: D
options.text: Furthermore, everybody knows that famous people are smarter than ordinary people, so their advice is worth following.

questions.why: Everybody knows is not evidence, so this claim is unsupported.

questions.stem: Select TWO sentences from “Fame Can Serve Others” that give specific examples to support the author's claim.

segments.text: Some people complain that celebrities receive too much attention, but fame can be a powerful tool for good.
Consider what happened when a well-known goalkeeper recorded a short video encouraging fans to donate blood.
When a popular singer visited a village without clean water, cameras followed her.
For these reasons, society should encourage celebrities to use their fame for meaningful causes.

questions.why: The goalkeeper and the singer are specific examples; the other sentences state the claim.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best evaluate the evidence in “Fame Can Serve Others”? Choose two.
options: The claim about famous people being smarter is not supported by any facts.
The blood donation figure is strong because it names a source.
The singer example is weak because it mentions cameras.
The argument is weak because it gives no examples at all.
questions.why: Evidence with a named source is stronger than a statement everybody supposedly knows.

questions.stem: Put the parts of the argument in “Fame Can Serve Others” in the order the author presents them.
sequence: Fame reaches millions of people quickly.
A goalkeeper's video increases blood donations.
A singer's visit brings help to a village without clean water.
Society should encourage celebrities to support good causes.
questions.why: The author moves from a reason to examples to a conclusion.

questions.stem: How does the author of “Fame Can Serve Others” respond to people who say celebrities get too much attention?
options: by arguing that the attention can be used to help others
by agreeing that fans should ignore all famous people
by explaining that newspapers are more trusted than stars
by showing that most celebrities avoid cameras and reporters
questions.why: The author turns the complaint into a reason fame can do good.

questions.stem: The singer refused to ____ every fan's request for a photo, because she needed to rest her voice before the show.
questions.why: To indulge a request is to give in to it.

questions.stem: Does each description show fame earned through good work or notoriety?

rows.text: She discovered a new way to purify desert water.
He became famous for insulting other players online.
She led a national campaign for desert conservation.
He is known for breaking the rules of every competition.

questions.why: Notoriety is fame for bad actions; good work earns a better kind of fame.

questions.stem: A writer argues: “Fans should not indulge in following celebrities all day, because doing so leads them to ignore their own goals.” Which TWO statements, if true, would most strengthen this argument? Choose two.
options: Some celebrities began their careers at a young age.
Many celebrities live in large houses in big cities.
Teachers report that some students copy celebrities' habits instead of building their own skills.
A study found that teens who spent hours following stars spent less time on schoolwork.
questions.why: Strong support links following stars to neglecting one's own goals.

questions.stem: True or false: In a civil debate, mocking a celebrity's appearance instead of answering her ideas counts as sound reasoning.
questions.why: Attacking a person instead of the idea is faulty reasoning.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows faulty reasoning?
options: The study included many students, so its results are useful.
She trained for years, so her record was well earned.
He is a celebrity, so his health advice must be correct.
He admitted his mistake, so many fans respect his honesty.
questions.why: Fame does not make someone an expert on health.

questions.stem: Match each sentence from a poem about family life with the review word it shows: “inherit,” “spectacular,” “briefly,” and “bosom.”

pairs.left: A grandson receives his grandfather's old watch.
Fireworks over the Corniche amaze the whole crowd.
The teacher speaks for less than a minute.
A mother holds the sleeping kitten against her chest.

questions.why: Each sentence gives a clue to the word's meaning.

questions.stem: In poetry, lines are grouped together into a ____.
questions.why: A stanza is a group of lines, like a paragraph in prose.

questions.stem: True or false: A poet who writes about an “inherited” lantern is describing a lantern passed down from an older family member.
questions.why: To inherit is to receive something from someone in an earlier generation.

questions.stem: Which line contains a simile?
options: The fireworks were spectacular all night long.
The fireworks are flowers that bloom in the dark.
The proud fireworks danced above the sea.
The fireworks burst like spectacular flowers.
questions.why: A simile compares using like or as.

questions.stem: Does each line from a poem about the seashore use a simile or a metaphor?

rows.text: The spectacular sunset is a painter's spilled paint box.
The comet flashed as briefly as a blink.
The sea's calm bosom is a cradle for the boats.
Her inherited kindness spread like warm light across the room.

questions.why: Similes use like or as; metaphors say one thing is another.

questions.stem: Which TWO lines use personification? Choose two.
options: The bench stands near the old palm tree.
The lonely bench waits patiently for a visitor.
The tired bus groans as it climbs the hill.
The bus is as yellow as a ripe lemon.
questions.why: Personification gives human actions to things.

questions.stem: The words “ground” and “found” at the ends of two lines create a ____.
questions.why: Words with the same ending sound rhyme.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about a fisherman's son uses the wrong form of “inherit”? Fix it.
questions.why: After will, the verb inherit is needed, not the noun inheritance.

questions.stem: Put the lines of a four-line poem about a hardworking shoemaker in order so they follow the AABB rhyme pattern.
sequence: He mends the shoes of all the town,
And never wears a hero's crown.
Yet every step the people take
Is surer for the soles he'll make.
questions.why: AABB means the first two lines rhyme, then the last two.

questions.stem: Which word could best replace “spectacular” in “The view from the top of Jabal Sawda was spectacular”?
questions.why: Spectacular means amazing to see, like breathtaking.

questions.stem: Part A: Which idea about fame does the speaker express in “The Night Baker”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which idea about fame does the speaker express in “The Night Baker”?

options.label: A
options.text: Fame comes only to people who appear in newspapers.

options.label: B
options.text: Fame is something bakers want more than anything.

options.label: C
options.text: Fame should be given only to the hardest workers.

options.label: D
options.text: Fame can mean being important in quiet, everyday ways.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: the baker on our corner is already folding dough with flour-dusted hands.

options.label: B
options.text: His oven hums like a patient camel resting after a long desert journey,

options.label: C
options.text: Nobody photographs him or writes his name in the evening newspaper;

options.label: D
options.text: Perhaps it is a thousand small mornings that people never think to count,

questions.why: The last stanza redefines fame as small, uncounted mornings of work.

questions.stem: Select the TWO lines from “The Night Baker” that use similes.

segments.text: His oven hums like a patient camel resting after a long desert journey,
Nobody photographs him or writes his name in the evening newspaper;
and the warm smell of bread drifts through the windows like a gentle invitation.
Perhaps fame is not a spotlight shining on a single, celebrated stage.

questions.why: Both lines compare using like.

questions.stem: How many stanzas are in “The Night Baker,” and how does the last stanza differ from the first two?
options: two; it repeats the description of the bakery at night
three; it changes from describing the baker to reflecting on fame
four; it lists the people who buy bread every morning
three; it tells the whole story of the baker's childhood in the town
questions.why: The final stanza shifts from description to the speaker's reflection on fame.

questions.stem: Which TWO phrases from “The Night Baker” use metaphor to describe the baker's work or fame? Choose two.
options: a humble light that is famous only to the hungry
writes his name in the evening newspaper
fame is not a spotlight shining on a single, celebrated stage
questions.why: A metaphor describes something as if it were something else.

questions.stem: In “The Night Baker,” which stanza contains each detail?

rows.text: the baker folding dough while the neighborhood sleeps
families eating his bread at breakfast
fame described as a thousand small mornings
nobody writing his name in the newspaper

questions.why: Each stanza develops a different part of the poem's idea.

questions.stem: The famous poet visited our school only ____, reading one short poem before leaving for the airport.
questions.why: One short poem before leaving shows the visit lasted a short time.

questions.stem: Match each line about an old fisherman with the figurative language it uses.

pairs.left: The sea held the boat against its gentle bosom.
His net was a spiderweb of knots and hope.
His boat rocked like a cradle on the waves.
His catch was so spectacular that it could feed the whole country.

questions.why: Each type of figurative language creates meaning in a different way.

questions.stem: True or false: A refrain is a line or group of lines that repeats throughout a poem.
questions.why: A refrain repeats to stress an idea or create rhythm.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about a sunrise over the dunes does not make sense? Fix it.
questions.why: Something spectacular is amazing, so people would stop to look at it.

questions.stem: Is each feature of a poem about an inherited garden part of its structure or its sound?

rows.text: three stanzas of four lines each
the repeated “s” sound in “soft soil sleeps”
a short final line that stands alone
rhyming words at the end of every second line

questions.why: Structure is how lines and stanzas are arranged; sound includes rhyme and repetition.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the effect of the repeated line in “Ordinary Hands”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the effect of the repeated line in “Ordinary Hands”?

options.label: A
options.text: It shows that the workers are tired of their difficult jobs.

options.label: B
options.text: It suggests that the speaker has forgotten the workers' names.

options.label: C
options.text: It stresses that everyday workers deserve to be noticed.

options.label: D
options.text: It explains how the highway lines are painted each night.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Who paints the white lines on the highway after midnight, kneeling in the headlights' glare?

options.label: B
options.text: Not the celebrated ones whose faces shine from enormous billboards above the busy road.

options.label: C
options.text: Ordinary hands, devoted hands, the hands that we must learn to remember.

options.label: D
options.text: not taller than a palm tree, but wider, so that the shade would reach them all.

questions.why: The final, changed refrain asks readers to remember the workers.

questions.stem: Select the line from “Ordinary Hands” in which the speaker shifts from asking questions to stating a wish.

segments.text: Who sweeps the market lanes in Jeddah before the first merchant lifts his shutter?
Not the champions who wave from open buses while the excited crowd celebrates their victories.
I want to build a monument of rough, grateful stone for every one of them,
Let its significance be measured by the quiet work that kept our city breathing.

questions.why: I want marks the shift from questions to the speaker's wish.

questions.stem: Put these features of “Ordinary Hands” in the order they appear.
sequence: a question about painting highway lines
a question about sweeping market lanes
the speaker's wish to build a monument
a changed final refrain asking readers to remember
questions.why: The poem moves from two questions to a wish and a final call.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements describe the structure of “Ordinary Hands”? Choose two.
options: The poem has one long stanza with no breaks.
The first two stanzas each begin with a question.
Each stanza ends with a similar repeated line.
Every line rhymes with the line after it.
questions.why: Repeated questions and a refrain give the poem its pattern.

questions.stem: In “Ordinary Hands,” what does the phrase “the quiet work that kept our city breathing” suggest?
options: The workers clean the city's air using machines.
The workers keep the city healthy and alive.
The city is too noisy for people to rest.
The workers are sick from breathing dust.
questions.why: The city is described as a living thing kept alive by the workers.

questions.stem: In the line “The comet's visit was a single breath in the night,” the metaphor suggests that the comet appeared ____.
questions.why: A single breath is very short, so the comet appeared briefly.

questions.stem: Does each line about a retired teacher use hyperbole or personification?

rows.text: She graded a million papers before breakfast.
The chalk sighed as it crossed the board.
Her patience was taller than any mountain.
The empty desks remembered her kindness.

questions.why: Hyperbole exaggerates; personification gives things human qualities.

questions.stem: Which TWO words have a positive connotation, like “spectacular,” when describing a sunset in a poem? Choose two.
questions.why: Glorious and dazzling praise the sunset; garish and glaring suggest it is unpleasant.

questions.stem: True or false: In a poem, a sudden switch from long lines to one very short line can give that short line extra importance.
questions.why: Changes in line length draw the reader's attention.

questions.stem: A poet writes: “The children inherit the orchard, but not the patience that planted it.” What idea does this line most likely suggest?
options: Receiving a gift is easier than having the qualities that built it.
Orchards should always be divided equally among the children.
Children never enjoy working in their family's orchard.
Patience is a kind of seed that children plant in orchards.
questions.why: The line contrasts receiving the orchard with lacking the patience it took.

questions.stem: Match each hero word with its meaning: “perseverance,” “selfless,” “valiant,” and “distinguish.”

pairs.right: caring more about others than oneself

questions.why: These words help describe and judge heroes.

questions.stem: Mona gave up her own lunch break to help a lost child find his family, a small ____ that the boy never forgot.
questions.why: Giving up something for another person is a sacrifice.

questions.stem: True or false: The word “criteria” refers to the standards used to judge or decide something.
questions.why: Criteria are the standards for a decision.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a claim about heroes?
options: The rescue took place near the coast of Yanbu.
The firefighter arrived at the scene at 3:15.
True heroes put others' safety before their own.
Two people were helped out of the flooded car by divers.
questions.why: A claim is an opinion that can be argued; the others are facts.

questions.stem: Does each action of a hospital volunteer show compassion or perseverance?

rows.text: She held a frightened child's hand during a test.
She kept studying for her nursing exam after failing twice.
She listened kindly to a lonely patient's stories.
She practiced first aid every day for a year.

questions.why: Compassion is caring about others' pain; perseverance is not giving up.

questions.stem: A writer claims, “Ordinary citizens can be heroes too.” Which TWO details best support this claim? Choose two.
options: The national team won its match last week.
A shopkeeper pulled a driver from a burning car before help arrived.
Many movies show heroes with special powers.
A student organized classmates to deliver meals to elderly neighbors during a heat wave.
questions.why: Evidence must show ordinary people acting heroically.

questions.stem: A writer who wants to ____ a hero from a celebrity might compare what each person does for others.
questions.why: To distinguish is to show the difference between two things.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about a valiant lifeguard has an error? Fix it.
questions.why: Verbs in the sentence should stay in the past tense.

questions.stem: Put the parts of an argument about everyday courage in a logical order.
sequence: Claim: Courage is not only shown on battlefields.
Reason: Facing everyday fears also takes bravery.
Evidence: A shy student who speaks up against bullying risks being teased herself.
Conclusion: We should honor small acts of courage, too.
questions.why: An argument moves from claim to reason to evidence to conclusion.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence is most relevant to the claim “Doctors who work in remote villages show selfless service”?
options: Most doctors study science for seven years or longer.
Doctors often wear masks and gloves during surgery.
Some remote villages are located high in the mountains of Asir.
Many give up higher pay to treat patients far from cities.
questions.why: Giving up higher pay shows putting others first.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's claim in “Heroes Without Headlines”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the author's claim in “Heroes Without Headlines”?

options.label: A
options.text: Nurses deserve more money than firefighters and police officers.

options.label: B
options.text: Heroes should always be people who appear on the evening news.

options.label: C
options.text: People who help others patiently over many years are often the most important heroes.

options.label: D
options.text: Firefighters should not be called heroes because their work is too dangerous.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Consider a nurse who works night shifts in a children's hospital.

options.label: B
options.text: That is a fair point.

options.label: C
options.text: However, I believe that the most important heroes are those who show compassion and perseverance over many years, often without anyone noticing.

options.label: D
options.text: Such moments of courage certainly deserve praise.

questions.why: The words I believe signal the author's claim.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which the author of “Heroes Without Headlines” presents a counterclaim.

segments.text: Such moments of courage certainly deserve praise.
Some readers may argue that a single brave act is more heroic because it involves greater danger.
Her sacrifice is quiet, but it changes hundreds of lives.
Nevertheless, danger is not the only measure of heroism.

questions.why: A counterclaim is an opposing view, often introduced with some may argue.

questions.stem: How does the author of “Heroes Without Headlines” respond to the counterclaim?
options: by agreeing it is fair, then arguing danger is not the only measure
by ignoring it and adding a second example about firefighters
by changing the claim so that only brave acts count as heroic
by admitting that the nurse example was not very convincing after all
questions.why: The author grants the point, then answers it with nevertheless.

questions.stem: Which TWO details does the author of “Heroes Without Headlines” use as evidence about the nurse? Choose two.
options: She sometimes misses family dinners and holidays.
She once carried a child from a burning building.
She comforts frightened patients night after night.
She was interviewed on the evening news.
questions.why: These details show the nurse's quiet, lasting sacrifice.

questions.stem: In “Heroes Without Headlines,” is each sentence part of the author's claim, evidence, or counterclaim?

rows.text: Our criteria should include patience and dedication.
The nurse comforts frightened patients night after night.
A single brave act is more heroic because it involves greater danger.
The nurse misses family dinners and holidays.

questions.why: Sorting sentences shows how an argument is built.

questions.stem: Although the climbers were exhausted, their ____ carried them to the summit of the mountain on the third day.
questions.why: Continuing despite exhaustion is perseverance.

questions.stem: Match each hero with the quality the description best shows: “courage,” “compassion,” and “sacrifice.”

pairs.left: A man sells his car to pay for a neighbor's surgery.
A girl jumps into a pool to rescue a drowning toddler.
A boy sits with a classmate who is crying after bad news.

questions.why: Each action matches a different heroic quality.

questions.stem: True or false: Writing “She is valiant because I just feel she is” gives strong evidence for a claim.
questions.why: A feeling is not evidence; strong support uses facts or examples.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence listing criteria for a school hero award has an error? Fix it.
questions.why: Criteria is plural, so it takes the verb were.

questions.stem: Is each reason for calling a coach a selfless hero relevant or irrelevant?

rows.text: He trained a disabled athlete for free for five years.
He drives a new blue car.
He stayed with his team during a dangerous flood and kept them safe.
He has a loud and funny laugh.

questions.why: Relevant reasons connect directly to the claim.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes the reasoning in “Should Heroes Be Perfect?”

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes the reasoning in “Should Heroes Be Perfect?”

options.label: A
options.text: The author argues that inventors are braver than any other kind of hero.

options.label: B
options.text: The author argues that history contains very few real heroes at all.

options.label: C
options.text: The author argues that heroes must have a perfect record of behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: The author argues that mistakes do not prevent someone from being a hero.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Admittedly, serious wrongdoing can outweigh a heroic act.

options.label: B
options.text: His failure did not erase his courage; it demonstrated it.

options.label: C
options.text: Consider Abbas ibn Firnas, the ninth-century inventor from Cordoba who attempted to fly with wings he designed himself.

options.label: D
options.text: First, did the person act to benefit others rather than only themselves?

questions.why: A failure that shows courage proves mistakes do not cancel heroism.

questions.stem: Select the TWO sentences from “Should Heroes Be Perfect?” that state the criteria the author proposes.

segments.text: Every human being makes errors, and if we demanded perfection, history would contain no heroes at all.
First, did the person act to benefit others rather than only themselves?
Second, did they accept risk or hardship to do so?
Admittedly, serious wrongdoing can outweigh a heroic act.

questions.why: First and second introduce the two questions used to judge heroes.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements fairly evaluate the argument in “Should Heroes Be Perfect?” Choose two.
options: The author strengthens the argument by admitting that serious wrongdoing matters.
The author relies only on personal feelings and gives no examples.
The argument is weak because it never states a clear claim.
The Abbas ibn Firnas example supports the idea that failure can show courage.
questions.why: A fair evaluation notes the concession and the relevant example.

questions.stem: Put the parts of “Should Heroes Be Perfect?” in the order the author presents them.
sequence: a question about whether flawed people can be heroes
a historical example of a failed but brave flight
two questions for judging who is a hero
an admission that serious wrongdoing can outweigh heroism
questions.why: The argument moves from question to example to criteria to concession.

questions.stem: Why does the author of “Should Heroes Be Perfect?” say that demanding perfection would leave history with “no heroes at all”?
options: to prove that most famous people in history were dishonest
to argue that heroes from the past matter less than today's heroes
to show that the critics' standard leads to an unreasonable result
to suggest that history books should be written again
questions.why: Showing an extreme result reveals that the critics' standard is unrealistic.

questions.stem: The judges found it hard to ____ between the two finalists, since both had shown remarkable compassion during the flood.
questions.why: To distinguish between two people is to tell which one differs or is better.

questions.stem: Does each sentence about a valiant rescuer contain sound reasoning or faulty reasoning?

rows.text: He risked his life to save strangers, so many call him valiant.
He is tall and strong, so he must be a hero.
Everyone online calls him a hero, so he must be the greatest hero ever.
Three witnesses described how he pulled people from the water.

questions.why: Sound reasoning rests on relevant actions and evidence, not looks or popularity.

questions.stem: A writer argues: “Perseverance is a more important heroic quality than courage.” Which TWO pieces of evidence would best support this claim? Choose two.
options: Most major medical discoveries required years of failed experiments before success.
Courage is a word that comes from an old word for heart.
Rescue teams report that long searches, not single brave moments, save the most lives after earthquakes.
Many people enjoy watching films about brave heroes.
questions.why: Strong evidence shows that long effort produces heroic results.

questions.stem: True or false: A writer who claims “All heroes are selfless” and then gives one example has proven the claim for every hero.
questions.why: One example cannot prove a claim about all heroes.

questions.stem: Which revision makes the claim “Firefighters are heroes” more precise and arguable?
options: Firefighters are heroes who wear helmets and drive red trucks.
Firefighters are heroes, and everybody in the whole world already knows it is true.
Firefighters are heroes because I think firefighters are great.
Firefighters are heroes because they accept daily risk to protect strangers.
questions.why: A precise claim gives a clear, relevant reason.

questions.stem: Match each word about community service with a word close in meaning: “mandatory,” “allocate,” “grudgingly,” and “propensity.”
questions.why: These words often appear in arguments about service.

questions.stem: Attending the fire-safety assembly is ____ for every student, so attendance will be taken at the door.
questions.why: Mandatory means required, so attendance is checked.

questions.stem: True or false: A student who joins the debate club that meets after school is taking part in an extracurricular activity.
questions.why: Extracurricular activities happen outside the regular classes.

questions.stem: Which transition word signals a contrast when comparing two opinions about school service?
questions.why: However shows a difference; the others show likeness.

questions.stem: Does each sentence about school volunteer programs show a similarity or a difference?

rows.text: Both programs help the local hospital.
One program is mandatory, but the other is optional.
Like the city plan, the school plan lasts one year.
The first school gives credits, while the second gives none.

questions.why: Both and like show similarity; but and while show difference.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences state an author's claim about student service? Choose two.
options: Schools should make community service a graduation requirement.
The program began in September and ended in May.
Volunteer work should always remain a free choice.
Last year, two hundred students cleaned the beach.
questions.why: Claims are arguable positions; the others are facts.

questions.stem: Ziad ____ agreed to help at the food bank, but he complained during the whole drive there.
questions.why: Complaining shows he agreed in an unwilling way.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about a volunteer program has an error? Fix it.
segments: before the end of the year.
questions.why: Each student is singular, so it takes is.

questions.stem: Put the sentences of a paragraph comparing two views on mandatory service in a logical order.
sequence: People disagree about whether service should be mandatory.
Supporters say a requirement helps every student learn to give back.
In contrast, critics say forced service is not true volunteering.
Both sides, however, agree that helping the community is valuable.
questions.why: The paragraph introduces the issue, gives each side, then notes common ground.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows that Huda has a propensity for helping others?
options: Huda finished her own homework quickly every night this week.
Huda waited for someone else to clean up the art room.
Huda often stays after class to help classmates with math.
Huda helped a classmate once when her teacher asked her to.
questions.why: A propensity is a natural tendency, so it shows up again and again.

questions.stem: Part A: On which point do the authors of Text 1 and Text 2 agree?

partA.stem: Part A: On which point do the authors of Text 1 and Text 2 agree?

options.label: A
options.text: Students who are forced to help work harder.

options.label: B
options.text: Schools should not reward student volunteers.

options.label: C
options.text: Community service is valuable for students.

options.label: D
options.text: Service should be a graduation requirement.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Volunteering, they point out, means choosing to help.

options.label: B
options.text: A requirement, they say, opens the door.

options.label: C
options.text: Critics agree that service is valuable, but they believe a requirement changes its meaning.

options.label: D
options.text: They argue that many students never volunteer simply because nobody asks them.

questions.why: Text 2 says critics agree service is valuable, which Text 1 also believes.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from Text 2 that gives the critics' alternative to required student service.

segments.text: Volunteering, they point out, means choosing to help.
When students are forced, some count the minutes until they can leave, and the people they serve can feel that lack of interest.
Instead, critics suggest that schools should offer exciting service projects and reward students who join them.
Critics agree that service is valuable, but they believe a requirement changes its meaning.

questions.why: Instead signals the critics' other solution.

questions.stem: Which text about required student service presents each idea?

rows.text: Many students never volunteer because nobody asks them.
Forced helpers may show a lack of interest.
Helping the community has value.
Schools should reward students who join projects.

questions.why: Comparing texts means finding what each says and what they share.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements correctly contrast the two texts about required student service? Choose two.
options: Text 1 uses only statistics; Text 2 uses only personal stories.
Text 1 sees a requirement as a way to open doors; Text 2 sees it as changing the meaning of volunteering.
Text 1 says service has no value; Text 2 says it has great value.
Text 1 focuses on what students discover; Text 2 focuses on how forced helpers act.
questions.why: A correct contrast describes what each text actually says.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of both texts about required student service?
options: to persuade readers about how schools should handle service
to explain the history of volunteer work in many countries
to describe the steps for planting trees in a school garden
to tell an entertaining story about one student's first project
questions.why: Both texts argue for a position on school service.

questions.stem: The principal will ____ the club budget so that the robotics, art, and chess clubs each receive a fair share.
questions.why: To allocate is to divide and give out for a purpose.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a school service day with the word it shows: “mandatory,” “grudgingly,” and “extracurricular.”

pairs.left: Every student must attend the opening assembly.
Saad picked up litter slowly, complaining the whole time.
The photography club, which meets after school, recorded the event.

questions.why: Must, complaining, and after school are the clues.

questions.stem: True or false: A writer who says “Some people believe service should be mandatory, but I disagree” presents both a counterclaim and the writer's own claim.
questions.why: The first part gives the opposing view; I disagree states the writer's claim.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence comparing two service plans has an error? Fix it.
segments: time for students to choose projects.
questions.why: The singular subject it needs the verb allocates.

questions.stem: Is each statement about mandatory volunteer hours a fact or an opinion?

rows.text: The school requires twenty hours of service each year.
Mandatory hours are the best idea the school ever had.
Last year, students served at four local centers.
Every student will love the volunteer program.

questions.why: Facts can be checked; opinions are judgments.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's claim in “Let Service Grow from Choice”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the author's claim in “Let Service Grow from Choice”?

options.label: A
options.text: The city council should require more hours of volunteer work.

options.label: B
options.text: Teenagers are too busy with schoolwork to help their city.

options.label: C
options.text: Making volunteer work mandatory would weaken the spirit of service.

options.label: D
options.text: Charities do not need any help from teenagers in the region.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: It would make volunteer work mandatory for all students aged thirteen to seventeen.

options.label: B
options.text: Small organizations would need to supervise thousands of unwilling helpers.

options.label: C
options.text: Supporters claim that required service teaches responsibility.

options.label: D
options.text: Although the council's goal is admirable, I believe the plan would weaken the very spirit it hopes to build.

questions.why: I believe introduces the author's claim.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Let Service Grow from Choice” that provides the strongest statistical evidence for the author's claim.

segments.text: However, responsibility develops most deeply when people make commitments for themselves.
Teenagers who chose their own projects were twice as likely to keep volunteering a year later.
Furthermore, a mandatory program would place heavy pressure on charities.
Service that grows from initiative lasts far longer than service that grows from obligation.

questions.why: The survey result gives measurable evidence.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements fairly evaluate the reasoning in “Let Service Grow from Choice”? Choose two.
options: The point about charities would be stronger with an example or numbers.
The survey is irrelevant because it is about teenagers.
The author gives no reasons and relies only on insults.
The author addresses the supporters' view before answering it.
questions.why: Good evaluation notes both strengths and places that need more support.

questions.stem: Put the parts of the argument in “Let Service Grow from Choice” in the order they appear.
sequence: the council's plan and the author's claim
the supporters' view and the author's response
the effect of the plan on small charities
the author's alternative approach
questions.why: The author states a claim, answers the other side, adds a reason, then offers a solution.

questions.stem: How does the author's perspective in “Let Service Grow from Choice” differ from the council's?
options: The author wants more hours; the council wants fewer hours.
The author values choice; the council values requiring service.
The author thinks charities need help; the council does not.
The author opposes service; the council opposes all charities.
questions.why: The author prefers chosen service, while the council wants it required.

questions.stem: Researchers found that teenagers who volunteer early often develop a ____ for helping others that lasts into adulthood.
questions.why: A propensity is a natural tendency that keeps showing up.

questions.stem: Does each sentence from an essay on mandatory service compare or contrast?

rows.text: Similarly, both plans ask students to serve at least ten hours.
Whereas the old rule was optional, the new one is a requirement.
Like paid workers, volunteers must arrive on time.
Unlike adults, students must balance service with homework.

questions.why: Similarly and like compare; whereas and unlike contrast.

questions.stem: A writer claims, “Mandatory service would be good for our school.” Which TWO pieces of evidence would best strengthen this claim? Choose two.
options: Our school building was built more than forty years ago.
Some students prefer to spend weekends playing sports.
Schools with service requirements report higher attendance and fewer discipline problems.
Former students say their required projects helped them choose future careers.
questions.why: Strong evidence shows benefits that come from required service.

questions.stem: True or false: Two authors who share the same claim about mandatory volunteering must also use the same evidence.
questions.why: Authors can support the same claim with different evidence.

questions.stem: Which sentence best acknowledges an opposing perspective before restating the writer's claim?
options: Required hours are good, and students who disagree are simply being lazy.
Required hours teach valuable skills, and this fact is perfectly clear to every single person.
Although some feel forced service is unfair, required hours still teach valuable skills.
Some feel forced service is unfair, and they are completely right about that.
questions.why: Although introduces the other view before the writer's claim returns.

questions.stem: Every morning, the old gardener would ____ over each rose bush to check its leaves for insects.
questions.why: To stoop is to bend forward and down.

questions.stem: Which event is impromptu?
options: A teacher prepares a quiz for next Tuesday's lesson.
A family books train tickets three weeks before a trip.
The school holds its graduation on the date set in May.
Friends start a football game on the beach without any plan.
questions.why: Impromptu means done without planning.

questions.stem: True or false: A student who answers tentatively speaks with complete confidence and no doubt.
questions.why: Tentatively means in an unsure, careful way.

questions.stem: Match each word (“tentatively,” “involuntary,” “commence,” “stoop”) with the example that shows it.

pairs.right: raising your hand halfway because you are unsure of the answer
sneezing when dust flies into your nose
the first lesson of a new school year starting on time
bending forward to tie a little brother's shoe

questions.why: Linking a word to a real example helps you remember its meaning.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe a planned event or an impromptu one?

rows.text: The class rehearsed the play for six weeks.
The cousins sang a song on the spot at dinner.
The museum opened its new hall on the announced date.
The neighbors held a quick picnic the moment the rain stopped.

questions.why: Impromptu events happen without planning; planned events are prepared ahead.

questions.stem: What is the main conflict at the beginning of “The Lantern in the Storeroom”?
options: Rami cannot find the lantern his grandfather hid away.
Rami is afraid of the dark, dusty storeroom at home.
Rami and his grandfather argue about the pearl boats.
Rami is upset because he has lost the chess final.
questions.why: The story opens with Rami slamming the door because he lost the chess final.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Lantern in the Storeroom” shows that Rami's feelings have begun to change?

segments.text: Rami slammed the storeroom door behind him, because he had lost the school chess final and did not want to talk to anyone.
I kept the lantern to remember that night.
As Rami turned the lantern over in his hands, his disappointing loss in the chess final suddenly seemed smaller.
Dust covered the crowded shelves, and an old fishing net hung from a rusty hook like an enormous spider web.

questions.why: His loss “seemed smaller” after hearing the story, which shows a change in his feelings.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Lantern in the Storeroom” in order.
sequence: Rami shuts himself in the storeroom after losing.
Rami finds a dented brass lantern.
Grandfather tells the story of the pearl boats.
Rami decides to polish the lantern and keep it.
questions.why: Stories move from a problem to events that change the character to a resolution.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of “The Lantern in the Storeroom”?

partA.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of “The Lantern in the Storeroom”?

options.label: A
options.text: Old objects should be thrown away to make more space.

options.label: B
options.text: Children should never go into storerooms by themselves.

options.label: C
options.text: Hard work always leads to winning every competition.

options.label: D
options.text: Coming home safely matters more than winning a prize.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Just then, his grandfather stepped inside and smiled at him with gentle understanding.

options.label: B
options.text: Dust covered the crowded shelves, and an old fishing net hung from a rusty hook like an enormous spider web.

options.label: C
options.text: In the corner, he noticed a dented brass lantern and lifted it cautiously, because one side was sharp and bent.

options.label: D
options.text: One difficult season, we found no pearls at all, and we returned home with empty hands, but every man came back safe.

questions.why: Grandfather values the safe return over the lost pearls, which helps Rami see his loss differently.

questions.stem: Which two words best describe Rami at the end of “The Lantern in the Storeroom”? Choose two.
questions.why: Rami's anger fades and he thinks about what really matters.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this sentence about Laila on the old stairs.
questions.why: Testing each step shows she moved tentatively, in an unsure and careful way.

questions.stem: When the doctor tapped just below Reem's knee, her leg kicked forward; the movement was ____, so she could not control it.
questions.why: An involuntary movement happens without a person choosing it.

questions.stem: In which sentence is “stoop” a noun meaning the small porch and steps in front of a house, rather than a verb meaning “bend down”?
options: Old age made the farmer stoop as he walked.
Please stoop under the low branch on the trail.
The nurse had to stoop to speak with the small child.
The neighbors sat on the stoop and talked until sunset.
questions.why: After the, stoop names a place where the neighbors sit.

questions.stem: Match each key word (“tentatively,” “impromptu,” “commence,” “involuntary”) with its antonym.
questions.why: An antonym is a word with the opposite meaning.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The meeting will commence as soon as the last guest arrives,” the word “commence” means that the meeting will begin.
questions.why: To commence is to begin.

questions.stem: Why do the old man's hands tremble as he unlocks the door of the tailor shop?
options: He is tired from carrying the heavy tin all the way there.
He is afraid that Noura will report him to the police.
He is cold because the winter wind is blowing so hard.
He feels strong emotion about returning to his old shop.
questions.why: The shop holds forty years of memories, so returning moves him deeply.

questions.stem: How does Noura's view of the tailor shop change during the story?

partA.stem: How does Noura's view of the tailor shop change during the story?

options.label: A
options.text: She first fears the tailor but later learns he is the owner of the building.

options.label: B
options.text: She first wants to buy it but later decides it costs far too much money.

options.label: C
options.text: She first thinks it is new but later learns it was built very long ago.

options.label: D
options.text: She first sees it as sad and empty but later sees it as full of memories.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Now she understood that it held a whole neighborhood's memories.

options.label: B
options.text: Every afternoon, Noura passed the abandoned tailor shop on Al-Souq Street.

options.label: C
options.text: Curious, Noura followed him inside and asked what he was looking for.

options.label: D
options.text: A blue button had come from a teacher's coat, and a gold one from a wedding robe.

questions.why: The word “Now” signals Noura's new understanding of the shop.

questions.stem: Is each detail from “The Tailor's Tin” part of the setting or a character trait of the tailor?

rows.text: a faded sign on Al-Souq Street
keeping one button from every coat for forty years
a notice saying the building will be torn down
naming the owner of each button from memory

questions.why: Setting tells where and when; traits show what a character is like.

questions.stem: Which two themes are developed in “The Tailor's Tin”? Choose two.
options: Old buildings should always be protected by law.
Places matter because of the people connected to them.
Curiosity usually leads people into real danger.
Ordinary objects can hold valuable memories.
questions.why: The buttons and the shop matter because of the people and memories they hold.

questions.stem: What is the most likely reason the tailor gives Noura a green button at the end?
options: to pay her for helping him search under the dusty wooden counter
to ask her politely to sew a brand-new coat for him next week
to show her which of all the buttons was the most expensive one
to pass on part of his memories to someone who now values them
questions.why: The gift shows he trusts her to keep the memories alive.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Yousef tentatively touched the strange machine, ready to pull his hand back.” Which two words could replace “tentatively” without changing the meaning? Choose two.
questions.why: Tentatively suggests acting in an unsure, careful way.

questions.stem: Which word best fits each sentence about the neighborhood market festival?

rows.text: The festival will ____ when the drums sound at sunset.
The baker had to ____ to hand a sweet to the small boy.
Two old friends gave an ____ poetry reading near the fountain.
The final parade will ____ at nine o'clock.

questions.why: Commence means begin, stoop means bend down, and impromptu means unplanned.

questions.stem: Unsure whether the stray cat would let her come close, Hind reached out her hand ____.
questions.why: Being unsure makes a person move tentatively.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows that a character's reaction was involuntary rather than chosen?
options: Omar asked his sister to slice the onion for him.
Omar chose a sharper knife before slicing the onion.
Omar decided to leave the kitchen while the onion was sliced.
Omar's eyes watered at once when the onion was sliced.
questions.why: Watering eyes happen without a choice, so the reaction is involuntary.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about an impromptu celebration that does not make sense.
segments: the fans held an impromptu celebration
that they had planned carefully for months.
questions.why: An impromptu celebration is not planned ahead of time.

questions.stem: Put these parts of the plot of “Karim's Boat” in order.
sequence: Villagers urge Karim to sell his father's boat.
Two boys fail to return as a storm gathers.
Karim starts the old engine and steers into the waves.
The fishermen help Karim repaint the boat.
questions.why: A plot moves from conflict through rising action and climax to resolution.

questions.stem: Which event is the climax of “Karim's Boat”?

partA.stem: Which event is the climax of “Karim's Boat”?

options.label: A
options.text: Karim finds the boys clinging to their overturned rowboat.

options.label: B
options.text: The owners of the modern boats leave for a wedding.

options.label: C
options.text: The fishermen begin calling the boat by a new name.

options.label: D
options.text: A buyer from the city offers Karim a good price for the boat.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: He steered through the rising waves until he spotted the boys clinging to their overturned rowboat.

options.label: B
options.text: Everyone in the village told Karim to sell his father's old wooden boat.

options.label: C
options.text: The modern boats were locked in the harbor, and their owners were away at a wedding in another town.

options.label: D
options.text: Its paint was peeling, its engine coughed black smoke, and a buyer from the city had offered a good price.

questions.why: The climax is the moment of greatest tension, when Karim reaches the boys.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Karim's Boat” that show how the villagers' attitude toward the boat changes.

segments.text: Everyone in the village told Karim to sell his father's old wooden boat.
The next morning, nobody mentioned selling the boat again.
Instead, the fishermen helped Karim scrape and repaint it, and they began to call it by his father's name.
It coughed, sputtered, and finally roared to life.
Two boys from the village had rowed out to fish and had not returned.

questions.why: After the rescue, the villagers stop urging a sale and honor the boat instead.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “Karim's Boat”?
options: Something others consider worthless may prove its value when it is needed.
Modern machines are always less reliable than older ones built by hand.
People who refuse advice from their neighbors will always end up lonely and sorry.
Selling family belongings is the wisest choice when they become old.
questions.why: The old boat everyone wanted sold is the one that saves the boys.

questions.stem: How does the author develop Karim's character in “Karim's Boat”?
options: by explaining how he learns to repair engines from a mechanic in the city
by describing his fear of the sea and how he slowly learns to overcome it
by showing that he deeply regrets refusing the buyer's generous offer
by showing that his stubborn loyalty to his father leads to a brave rescue
questions.why: Karim's refusal to sell, then his rescue, reveal his loyalty and courage.

questions.stem: Hessa was ____ when she read the email saying she had won a place at the summer space camp.
questions.why: Winning a place she wanted would make her extremely happy.

questions.stem: Which person has conceded a point in a debate?
options: Tariq says, “You are right; my numbers were wrong.”
Tariq asks the judges for more time to speak.
Tariq repeats his own argument a little more loudly.
Tariq leaves the room before the debate is finished.
questions.why: To concede is to admit that something is true.

questions.stem: True or false: Vivisection means operating on living animals for scientific research.
questions.why: Vivi- means alive, and -section means cutting.

questions.stem: Match each word (“ecstatic,” “keystone,” “conceded,” “lobbying”) with the example that shows it.

pairs.right: laughing with tears of joy at a brother's safe return
the one player whose passing holds the whole team together
admitted that a rival's science project was better
visiting council members to ask for a new public library

questions.why: Linking each word to an example helps you remember its meaning.

questions.stem: Does each sentence about a family waiting for news of a rescue show someone who is ecstatic or someone who is anxious?

rows.text: Laila shouted with joy when her lost cousin was found.
Laila bit her nails while the search went on.
The family hugged and cheered when the boat reached shore.
The parents paced the beach, watching the dark water.

questions.why: Ecstatic means overjoyed; anxious means worried.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Dana in the Deep End”?
options: Staying calm and remembering training helped the narrator save a child.
The narrator's uncle trained everyone in the family to work as lifeguards.
Swimming at a farm is much more fun than swimming at a city pool.
Little children should never be allowed near any kind of swimming pool.
questions.why: The narrator says that staying calm and listening to the coach made the rescue possible.

questions.stem: How does the narrator of “Dana in the Deep End” feel about being called a hero?

partA.stem: How does the narrator of “Dana in the Deep End” feel about being called a hero?

options.label: A
options.text: confused and angry

options.label: B
options.text: proud and boastful

options.label: C
options.text: modest and thankful

options.label: D
options.text: bored and uninterested

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Suddenly, I saw her small hands splashing desperately above the surface of the water.

options.label: B
options.text: Dana was coughing and frightened, but she was not hurt.

options.label: C
options.text: I did not feel like a hero, though; I simply felt grateful that I had listened carefully to my coach.

options.label: D
options.text: Later, my uncle shook my hand and said I had acted like a professional lifeguard.

questions.why: The narrator rejects the word hero and feels grateful instead.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Dana in the Deep End” shows the narrator's quick response to the emergency?

segments.text: I grabbed the long pool hook from the fence and pushed it toward her.
My cousins and I were swimming in the pool at my uncle's farm in Al-Kharj on a scorching afternoon.
My aunt came running and wrapped Dana in a thick towel.
Dana was coughing and frightened, but she was not hurt.

questions.why: Grabbing the hook is the narrator's action that saves Dana.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Dana in the Deep End” in order.
sequence: Dana slips off her float into the deep end.
The narrator sees small hands splashing.
The narrator pushes the pool hook toward Dana.
The uncle shakes the narrator's hand.
questions.why: Personal narratives usually tell events in time order.

questions.stem: Which two details from “Dana in the Deep End” support the idea that the narrator stayed calm? Choose two.
options: the aunt wrapping Dana in a towel
the swimming trip at the farm
using the pool hook instead of jumping in
questions.why: Clear thinking shows in remembering advice and choosing a safe tool.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly in this sentence about Majed and his sister.
questions.why: To concede is to admit that something is true; lobbying is trying to persuade officials.

questions.stem: Our goalkeeper is the ____ of the team; without her, our whole defense falls apart.
questions.why: A keystone is the central part that holds everything together.

questions.stem: Which phrase is closest in meaning to “conceded” in “After checking the map again, the guide conceded that we had taken the wrong road”?
questions.why: To concede is to admit that something is true.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Many scientists now study animals with computer models instead of vivisection,” the word “vivisection” refers to research that operates on living animals.
questions.why: Vivisection is operating on living animals for research.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use a form of “lobby” to mean “trying to persuade officials” or “the entrance hall of a building”?

rows.text: The fishermen are lobbying the ministry to protect the coral reef.
We waited in the hotel lobby for our taxi.
Parents lobbied the council for a safer crossing.
The museum lobby was filled with school groups.

questions.why: Lobby can be a verb about persuading officials or a noun for an entrance hall.

questions.stem: How does the narrator's point of view about fire drills change in “The Smell of Smoke”?

partA.stem: How does the narrator's point of view about fire drills change in “The Smell of Smoke”?

options.label: A
options.text: from trusting them to doubting that they work at all

options.label: B
options.text: from enjoying them to finding them dull and very tiring

options.label: C
options.text: from fearing them to laughing at them with friends

options.label: D
options.text: from thinking they are pointless to believing they are valuable

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The fire had started in our kitchen, and the firefighters extinguished it before it spread.

options.label: B
options.text: Gray smoke was drifting under my bedroom door, and for a second I felt panic rise in my chest.

options.label: C
options.text: Now, whenever my classmates grumble during a practice evacuation, I describe that terrifying night to them.

options.label: D
options.text: We would line up, march outside, and stand in the blazing sun while the teachers counted us again and again.

questions.why: The narrator now defends drills to classmates who complain.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Smell of Smoke” that show the narrator used what was learned in the drills.

segments.text: I touched the door, and because it felt hot, I did not open it.
Instead, I opened my window, shouted for my father, and woke my younger brother, who was sleeping beside me.
I complained loudly about those drills to anyone who would listen.
Then, one night in January, I woke up to a strange, bitter smell.
Gray smoke was drifting under my bedroom door, and for a second I felt panic rise in my chest.

questions.why: Checking the door and using the window are safety steps learned in drills.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of “The Smell of Smoke”?
options: Kitchens are the most common place in any home for a dangerous fire to begin.
Firefighters visit homes to teach children about fire safety rules.
Practice that seems boring can prepare people to act wisely in danger.
Students should be allowed to skip drills that happen too often.
questions.why: The whole narrative shows boring drills paying off in a real emergency.

questions.stem: In “The Smell of Smoke,” is each statement a fact the narrator reports or an opinion?

rows.text: The fire started in the kitchen.
Fire drills are a waste of time.
A firefighter checked the house.
Every student should take fire drills seriously.

questions.why: Facts can be checked; opinions tell what someone believes.

questions.stem: In “The Smell of Smoke,” the words “I felt panic rise in my chest” show that the narrator's first reaction was ____.
questions.why: Panic is a sudden rush of fear.

questions.stem: Which two sentences show a speaker who has conceded a point? Choose two.
options: “My plan is better, and nothing you say will change that.”
“Let's stop talking about it and ask someone else instead.”
“Fine, I admit that your plan costs less than mine.”
“I still disagree, but you are right that the bus is faster.”
questions.why: Conceding means admitting that part of the other side's argument is true.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word that fits its blank: “ecstatic,” “keystone,” “lobbying,” or “vivisection.”

pairs.left: Trust is the ____ of every strong friendship.
The winners were ____, hugging each other and shouting with joy.
The group spent a year ____ lawmakers to protect the mangrove forests.
Some students wrote reports arguing that ____ should be replaced by computer models.

questions.why: Use the meaning of each sentence and the part of speech needed to choose the word.

questions.stem: Which word best describes how Faisal felt in “When the doctor said his little brother would make a full recovery, Faisal laughed and cried at the same time”?
questions.why: Laughing and crying with joy at good news shows great happiness.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about an ecstatic chess winner that does not make sense.
segments: and hugged her coach with joy.
questions.why: Ecstatic means extremely happy, so she would not frown sadly.

questions.stem: True or false: Calling clean water the “keystone” of a desert town means that the town depends on it more than on anything else.
questions.why: A keystone is the central part that holds everything else together.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's point of view about heroes in “Five Minutes on Platform Two”?

partA.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's point of view about heroes in “Five Minutes on Platform Two”?

options.label: A
options.text: Heroes are people who never feel afraid.

options.label: B
options.text: Heroes act alone without help from others.

options.label: C
options.text: Heroes are mostly trained adults like paramedics.

options.label: D
options.text: Heroes feel fear but act anyway.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Within minutes, paramedics arrived and took over.

options.label: B
options.text: Several passengers stared, unsure what to do.

options.label: C
options.text: Later, the man's son found our family and thanked me.

options.label: D
options.text: It is choosing to act while you are afraid.

questions.why: The author ends by defining courage as acting while afraid.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Five Minutes on Platform Two” most clearly shows the narrator's emotions during the emergency?

segments.text: My hands were shaking, and every instinct told me to step back and let an adult handle it.
I was waiting for the train with my older sister when an elderly man nearby suddenly clutched his chest and sank onto a bench.
The worker placed the pads, and the machine gave clear spoken instructions.
Within minutes, paramedics arrived and took over.

questions.why: Shaking hands and the urge to step back reveal the narrator's fear.

questions.stem: Which three details from “Five Minutes on Platform Two” support the idea that preparation helped the narrator respond? Choose three.
options: passengers staring at the elderly man
telling a worker to bring the defibrillator
the son thanking the family later
questions.why: These actions come from what the narrator learned in the course.

questions.stem: How does the opening sentence of “Five Minutes on Platform Two” contribute to the narrative?
options: It explains the medical reasons why the elderly man fell ill.
It presents a common belief that the narrator's experience will challenge.
It describes the busy setting of the metro station in careful, vivid detail.
It introduces the narrator's sister as the true hero of the event.
questions.why: The narrator states what people believe, then shows it is not true.

questions.stem: Put the narrator's actions in “Five Minutes on Platform Two” in order.
sequence: notices the man sink onto a bench
remembers the first-aid course
asks the sister to call 997
is thanked by the man's son
questions.why: Following the sequence shows how the narrator moved from fear to action.

questions.stem: The ____ new stadium, with its huge steel arches, could be seen from every part of the city.
questions.why: Imposing means large and impressive.

questions.stem: Which place is most likely to feel eerie?
options: a silent, foggy road at midnight
a bright kitchen during family lunch
a sunny playground full of children
a busy classroom on a school morning
questions.why: Eerie means strange in a frightening way.

questions.stem: True or false: A bayonet is a kind of soft hat that soldiers once wore in winter.
questions.why: A bayonet is a blade fixed to the end of a rifle.

questions.stem: Match each word (“distraught,” “integration,” “imposing,” “eerie”) with the example that shows it.

pairs.right: crying and pacing after hearing that a friend was hurt
students from many backgrounds joining one school as equals
a tall stone gate that makes visitors stop and stare
a strange humming sound coming from an empty building

questions.why: These words describe people, places, and events in a memoir.

questions.stem: Is each example a case of integration or separation?

rows.text: Two schools combine so that all students share the same classes.
Students are placed in different buildings according to their background.
A team welcomes players from every neighborhood as equals.
A club allows only members from one street to join.

questions.why: Integration brings separate groups together as equals.

questions.stem: What does the phrase “Hold your head up” most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 2 of “The New Accent”?
questions.why: The mother tells the narrator not to let cruel words decide who they are, so the phrase means stay proud.

questions.stem: What is a theme of “The New Accent”?

partA.stem: What is a theme of “The New Accent”?

options.label: A
options.text: Students should hide their accents to fit in.

options.label: B
options.text: Moving to a new city is always a sad experience.

options.label: C
options.text: Steady kindness can change how others treat you.

options.label: D
options.text: A science club is the best place to make friends.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I learned that patient kindness can change people far more effectively than anger can.

options.label: B
options.text: For days afterward, I seriously considered remaining silent for the rest of the year.

options.label: C
options.text: On the first morning, a group of boys laughed at my accent whenever I answered a question, and one of them whispered that I should return to wherever I had come from.

options.label: D
options.text: I also joined the science club, where nobody cared about my accent and everybody cared about experiments.

questions.why: The narrator states the lesson directly at the end.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The New Accent” shows that the narrator decided not to give up?

segments.text: So I kept raising my hand, even when my voice trembled.
For days afterward, I seriously considered remaining silent for the rest of the year.
But my mother reminded me that our family had always faced difficult times with dignity.
When my family moved from Cairo to a new city, I was the only new student in my sixth-grade class.

questions.why: Raising a hand again shows the narrator kept participating.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The New Accent” in order.
sequence: The boys laugh at the narrator's accent.
The mother tells the narrator to hold up their head.
The narrator joins the science club.
Two of the boys ask the narrator for help.
questions.why: A memoir often moves from a problem to a change in the writer.

questions.stem: Which two words best describe the narrator by the end of “The New Accent”? Choose two.
questions.why: The narrator recovers from the teasing and keeps taking part.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about an old museum hall that does not make sense.
segments: The old museum hall felt eerie,
questions.why: Eerie means strange and frightening, so cheerful music does not fit.

questions.stem: In the history museum, Noor read that soldiers in the 1800s fixed a ____ to the end of their rifles for close fighting.
questions.why: A bayonet is a blade attached to the end of a rifle.

questions.stem: Which phrase is closest in meaning to “distraught” in “The distraught father searched every street after his son failed to come home”?
questions.why: Distraught means extremely upset and worried.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The judge's imposing voice filled the courtroom,” the word “imposing” suggests a voice that is weak and easy to ignore.
questions.why: Imposing means large, strong, and impressive.

questions.stem: Which word best fits each sentence from a history lesson?

rows.text: A rusty ____ lay in the glass case beside the old rifle.
The ____ of the city's schools brought students of all backgrounds together.
The ____ gates of the old fortress were twice as tall as a man.
The soldier's rifle had a sharp ____ attached to its end.

questions.why: Use the meaning of each word and the context of the sentence.

questions.stem: What does the phrase “hiding in the back row like a turtle in its shell” suggest about the narrator in fifth grade?
options: The narrator tried to stay out of sight to feel protected.
The narrator brought a small pet turtle into the classroom.
The narrator moved very slowly and carefully between classes each day.
The narrator preferred a seat far from the board to daydream.
questions.why: A turtle pulls into its shell for protection, just as the narrator hid from others.

questions.stem: What does the simile “the applause felt like a warm wave washing over me” suggest about the narrator's feelings at the end of “Finding My Voice”?

partA.stem: What does the simile “the applause felt like a warm wave washing over me” suggest about the narrator's feelings at the end of “Finding My Voice”?

options.label: A
options.text: The narrator felt cold and frightened.

options.label: B
options.text: The narrator felt embarrassed and ashamed.

options.label: C
options.text: The narrator felt comforted and accepted.

options.label: D
options.text: The narrator felt tired and bored.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: For six weeks, I practiced every evening in front of the mirror.

options.label: B
options.text: Some nights I wanted to quit, but I endured the frustration.

options.label: C
options.text: I did not win first place, but I gained something more valuable: the realization that my voice deserved attention.

options.label: D
options.text: On contest day, I stuttered twice during my speech.

questions.why: A warm wave suggests comfort, and the narrator realizes that the voice deserved attention.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Finding My Voice” best reveals the author's point of view about speaking up?

segments.text: Yet a stubborn voice inside me said that silence was not the same as safety.
Then our teacher announced a public speaking contest for the entire grade.
For as long as I can remember, I have struggled with a stutter.
On contest day, I stuttered twice during my speech.

questions.why: The author believes staying silent is not a real way to be safe.

questions.stem: In “Finding My Voice,” does each phrase show the narrator's fear or the narrator's courage?

rows.text: hiding in the back row
signed up before I could change my mind
avoided speaking whenever I could
practiced every evening in front of the mirror

questions.why: The narrator moves from hiding to acting bravely.

questions.stem: Which two statements express themes of “Finding My Voice”? Choose two.
options: Perseverance can matter more than winning a prize.
Audiences usually judge speakers harshly for mistakes.
Courage means acting even when success is not certain.
People who stutter should avoid speaking contests.
questions.why: The narrator did not win but gained something more important by trying.

questions.stem: Which two words could replace “eerie” in “An eerie silence settled over the empty schoolyard after the storm”? Choose two.
questions.why: Eerie means strange in a way that makes people uneasy.

questions.stem: Although she was ____, the mother forced herself to speak slowly so the rescue team could understand her.
questions.why: Distraught means extremely upset and worried.

questions.stem: Match each word with the context clue that hints at its meaning: “imposing,” “distraught,” “eerie,” and “integration.”

pairs.right: sobbed and could not stop shaking
learned side by side as equals

questions.why: Context clues are nearby words that point to a word's meaning.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The castle's imposing towers seemed to stare down at the small village below.” What is the effect of the word “imposing”?
options: It shows that the towers are old and about to fall.
It makes the towers seem powerful and a little threatening.
It makes the towers seem friendly and easy to visit.
It shows that the village is larger than the castle.
questions.why: Imposing suggests size and power that can make others feel small.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about a distraught traveler that does not make sense.
questions.why: Distraught means extremely upset, so she would not smile calmly.

questions.stem: What does “agonizingly” most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 3 of “Learning to Run Again”?

partA.stem: What does “agonizingly” most likely mean as it is used in paragraph 3 of “Learning to Run Again”?

options.label: A
options.text: in a careless way

options.label: B
options.text: in a calm and easy way

options.label: C
options.text: in a very painful way

options.label: D
options.text: in a surprisingly fast way

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Some days I could barely lift my foot, and the pain made me want to scream.

options.label: B
options.text: Each morning she arrived with a new, seemingly impossible goal: stand for ten seconds, take two steps, climb a single stair.

options.label: C
options.text: Eighteen months after the accident, I crossed the finish line of my school's charity race.

options.label: D
options.text: I was not fast, but I was running.

questions.why: The next sentence describes pain, a context clue for “agonizingly.”

questions.stem: Why does the author describe Ms. Hessa's expectations as “almost hostile at first”?
options: to suggest that the hospital staff in Dammam were often unkind
to explain why the narrator asked the hospital for a different therapist
to prove that Ms. Hessa truly disliked working with young, complaining patients
to show how the narrator misjudged her before understanding her purpose
questions.why: “Only later did I realize” shows that the narrator's first view was wrong.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Learning to Run Again” that best show the author's changed perspective.

segments.text: Only later did I realize that her demands were a form of faith.
However, I gradually discovered that each small victory gave me the strength to attempt the next one.
For weeks, I lay in a hospital bed in Dammam, staring at the ceiling and feeling sorry for myself.
The doctors cautiously warned my parents that I might never run again.
I was eleven, and a car accident had shattered my left leg in three places.

questions.why: “Only later did I realize” and “I gradually discovered” signal new understanding.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “Learning to Run Again”?
options: Strict teachers and therapists are rarely as kind as gentle ones are.
Doctors are usually wrong whenever they try to predict how a young patient will recover.
Small, steady efforts can build the strength needed to overcome setbacks.
Winning a race is the best way to prove that someone has fully healed.
questions.why: Each small victory built the strength for the next until the narrator ran again.

questions.stem: In “Learning to Run Again,” does each detail describe the narrator early or late in recovery?

rows.text: staring at the ceiling and feeling sorry for myself
crossing the finish line of a charity race
trying to stand for ten seconds
using each small victory as strength for the next

questions.why: Tracking details over time shows how the narrator changed.

questions.stem: With his eyes covered for the party game, Saad ____ around the room until he touched his cousin's shoulder.
questions.why: Groped means felt around blindly.

questions.stem: Which word means “to show something that was hidden”?
questions.why: To reveal something is to let it be seen or known.

questions.stem: True or false: A confounding puzzle is one that is very easy to solve.
questions.why: Confounding means very confusing.

questions.stem: Match each word (“institution,” “sentiment,” “confounding,” “groped”) with the example that shows it.

pairs.right: a museum that has served the public for a hundred years
a feeling of gratitude written in a card
a riddle that leaves everyone puzzled
felt around blindly for a dropped key

questions.why: Linking each word to an example helps you remember its meaning.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe something that reveals or something that keeps a thing hidden?

rows.text: The curtain opened to show the new mural.
Sara locked the surprise gift in her drawer.
The test results showed the cause of the illness.
Thick clouds covered the moon all night.

questions.why: To reveal is to uncover or make known.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of “Dots That Speak”?
options: The narrator chose to stop reading books for good after losing sight.
With practice, the narrator learned a new way to read after losing sight.
The narrator learned that “sea” is the most beautiful word in any language.
The narrator's teacher wrote special Braille books for each student in class.
questions.why: The narrative shows the narrator learning Braille and reading again.

questions.stem: How did the narrator of “Dots That Speak” feel when first trying to read Braille?

partA.stem: How did the narrator of “Dots That Speak” feel when first trying to read Braille?

options.label: A
options.text: frustrated

options.label: B
options.text: delighted

options.label: C
options.text: sleepy

options.label: D
