options.text: proud

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I laughed out loud with astonishment, because it was the first word I had read in months.

options.label: B
options.text: My teacher, Mr. Khalid, patiently introduced me to a book written in Braille.

options.label: C
options.text: Each night, I ran my fingertips slowly across the lines, and each night I experienced the same frustration.

options.label: D
options.text: Within a year, I was reading entire chapters independently, and books became my companions once again.

questions.why: The narrator directly names the feeling of frustration.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Dots That Speak” describes the narrator's turning point?

segments.text: Then, one afternoon, the dots suddenly formed a word under my finger: “sea.”
Books had always been my closest companions, and suddenly every page looked like a cloud of gray fog.
At first, the raised dots felt like grains of sand scattered randomly across the paper, and I could not comprehend how anyone could possibly read them.
My teacher, Mr. Khalid, patiently introduced me to a book written in Braille.

questions.why: Reading the first word is the moment everything changes.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Dots That Speak” in order.
sequence: The narrator loses most of their sight.
Mr. Khalid gives the narrator a Braille book.
The narrator reads the word “sea.”
The narrator reads whole chapters alone.
questions.why: Autobiographies usually follow the order of the writer's life.

questions.stem: Which two details from “Dots That Speak” show that the narrator kept trying? Choose two.
options: laughing out loud at the word
practicing even harder after reading one word
thinking the pages looked like fog
questions.why: Persistent people keep practicing even when it is hard.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about the city's old hospital that does not make sense.
segments: and has served the city for eighty years.
questions.why: An institution has lasted a long time, so it could not have opened last Tuesday.

questions.stem: The thank-you letter from the students expressed a warm ____ of gratitude toward the school nurse.
questions.why: A sentiment is a feeling or opinion.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “The rules of the new card game were confounding; even after three rounds, nobody knew who had won.” What does “confounding” mean?
questions.why: Not knowing who won is a clue that the rules were confusing.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The scientist will reveal her findings at tomorrow's meeting,” the word “reveal” means that she will hide her results.
questions.why: To reveal is to show or make known.

questions.stem: Is each item an institution or a sentiment?

rows.text: a national library founded in 1980
a feeling of pride in your hometown
a university that has trained doctors for decades
a belief that every child deserves kindness

questions.why: An institution is a long-lasting organization; a sentiment is a feeling or opinion.

questions.stem: What is the author's perspective on the night the radio arrived in “The Voice in the Desert”?

partA.stem: What is the author's perspective on the night the radio arrived in “The Voice in the Desert”?

options.label: A
options.text: It was a life-changing moment that opened up the world.

options.label: B
options.text: It was the first time the author felt bored in the camp.

options.label: C
options.text: It was a fun evening, but it did not change the author's life.

options.label: D
options.text: It was a frightening night that the family wanted to forget.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: My uncle returned from the city with a battery radio, and that evening our family gathered around it.

options.label: B
options.text: Our nearest neighbors lived a full day's journey away, and for many years I believed the whole world was made of sand and sky.

options.label: C
options.text: I spent my early childhood in a small Bedouin camp in the Empty Quarter.

options.label: D
options.text: The sensation was like a door opening in a wall I had never noticed.

questions.why: The door image shows that the radio opened a new world for the author.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of “The Voice in the Desert”?
options: Bedouin camps in the Empty Quarter are a full day apart from one another.
The author's uncle became a geography teacher after visiting the city.
Hearing about the wider world sparked a lifelong love of learning.
Radios were common in desert camps when the author was a young child.
questions.why: The radio led the author to school, maps, and a career teaching geography.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Voice in the Desert” that show how the radio changed the author's actions.

segments.text: From then on, I was eager to learn about every place the voice mentioned.
My uncle helped me find a school in the nearest town, and I memorized maps the way other children memorized songs.
I spent my early childhood in a small Bedouin camp in the Empty Quarter.
That belief changed when I was eight.
A calm voice described snow falling in a faraway country, rivers wider than our valley, and cities with towers that touched the clouds.

questions.why: After the radio, the author wanted to learn and went to school.

questions.stem: Is each statement about the author of “The Voice in the Desert” supported by the autobiography or not supported?

rows.text: The author lived far from other families as a child.
The author's uncle brought a radio from the city.
The author's parents disapproved of the radio.
The author has since visited every country on the radio.

questions.why: Only choose statements that the text actually gives evidence for.

questions.stem: In “The Voice in the Desert,” the phrase “I memorized maps the way other children memorized songs” shows that the author studied geography ____.
questions.why: Children learn songs because they enjoy them, so the comparison shows enthusiasm.

questions.stem: Which two sentences use a form of “grope” to describe searching blindly or uncertainly? Choose two.
options: Sami groped the answer aloud so that everyone could hear.
The eagle groped across the sky in wide, slow circles.
Half asleep, Rania groped under her pillow for the ringing phone.
Lost in the smoke, the guard groped along the wall for the exit.
questions.why: To grope is to feel around for something you cannot see.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the word that fits its blank: “confounding,” “institution,” “reveal,” or “sentiment.”

pairs.left: The puzzle's ____ clues left even the teacher scratching her head.
A school that has taught children for a century is a respected ____.
Lifting the cloth will ____ the new statue to the crowd.
Her card expressed a kind ____ of thanks.

questions.why: Use the meaning of each sentence and the part of speech needed to choose the word.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “institution” to mean a long-established custom rather than an organization?
options: The bank is a financial institution with many branches.
The university became a famous institution for engineering.
Friday lunch at Grandmother's house is a family institution.
The new hospital is the largest institution in the region.
questions.why: A custom that has lasted for years can also be called an institution.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about a shy student that does not make sense.
segments: Too shy to reveal her feelings,
and shouted it to the whole class.
questions.correction: and slipped it into her friend's bag.
questions.why: A student too shy to reveal her feelings would not shout them to the class.

questions.stem: True or false: A detective who groped for clues was searching in a careful, organized way with a clear plan.
questions.why: Groping for something means searching blindly or uncertainly.

questions.stem: What is the author's perspective on learning sign language in “The Language of Hands”?

partA.stem: What is the author's perspective on learning sign language in “The Language of Hands”?

options.label: A
options.text: It was a burden that took time from other school subjects.

options.label: B
options.text: It was a skill the author learned quickly but rarely used.

options.label: C
options.text: It mattered less to the author than learning to read lips.

options.label: D
options.text: It gave the author a full language that had been missing.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: On the first morning, I watched two teachers talking with their hands, their fingers moving as quickly as birds.

options.label: B
options.text: It was a revelation: language was not something only other people possessed.

options.label: C
options.text: We communicated through pointing, facial expressions, and a few homemade gestures.

options.label: D
options.text: The hardest challenge came later.

questions.why: The author calls learning to sign a revelation that gave language to them too.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “The Language of Hands”?
options: The author's father was too old to learn a new language successfully.
Learning a shared language transformed the author's life and family relationships.
Deaf students in Jeddah always learn sign language faster than children in other cities.
Laughing at jokes is the best way for families to communicate well.
questions.why: Sign language changed school life and, later, the author's bond with the father.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Language of Hands” shows that the author's patient teaching finally succeeded?

segments.text: Two years later, he signed an entire story to me at bedtime.
I wanted my family to learn to sign, but my father insisted he was too old to begin.
We communicated through pointing, facial expressions, and a few homemade gestures.
The hardest challenge came later.

questions.why: The father signing a whole story proves the author's teaching succeeded.

questions.stem: Which three details from “The Language of Hands” support the idea that the author felt left out of family conversations before school? Choose three.
options: enrolling in a school in Jeddah
no one in the family knowing sign language
teaching the father one sign each evening
watching teachers' fingers move like birds
laughing at jokes without understanding them
using only pointing and a few gestures
questions.why: These details show the author could not fully share in family talk.

questions.stem: Put the stages of the author's life in “The Language of Hands” in order.
sequence: communicating with gestures at home
enrolling in a school for deaf students
teaching the father one sign each evening
watching the father sign a bedtime story
questions.why: The autobiography moves forward through the author's life.

questions.stem: The ____ smell of burning rubber made everyone near the race track cover their noses.
questions.why: Pungent describes a strong, sharp smell.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows how Lina reacted to the surprise party?
options: She gasped and then burst out laughing.
She bought the balloons from the market.
She planned the party two weeks earlier.
She wrote the guests' names on cards.
questions.why: To react is to respond to something that happens.

questions.stem: True or false: A pungent smell is so faint that you can barely notice it.
questions.why: A pungent smell is strong and sharp.

questions.stem: Match each word (“meticulously,” “pungent,” “react,” “vow”) with the example that shows it.

pairs.right: checking every stitch of a hand-sewn dress twice
the sharp smell of freshly chopped onions
pulling your hand back from a hot pan
promising solemnly to care for your grandparents

questions.why: Linking each word to an example helps you remember its meaning.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe work done meticulously or carelessly?

rows.text: Hamad measured every angle of the model bridge twice.
Hamad glued the pieces together without checking the plan.
The baker weighed each spoonful of sugar exactly.
The painter splashed paint over the window frames.

questions.why: Meticulously means with great care for every detail.

questions.stem: Which word best describes the tone of the first paragraph of “Fog on the Terraces”?
questions.why: Words like “stuck” and “had not wanted” create a complaining tone.

questions.stem: How does Mira change during “Fog on the Terraces”?

partA.stem: How does Mira change during “Fog on the Terraces”?

options.label: A
options.text: She goes from excited to bored with village life.

options.label: B
options.text: She goes from unwilling to comfortable in the village.

options.label: C
options.text: She goes from happy to homesick for her friends.

options.label: D
options.text: She goes from shy to bossy with her grandmother.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Mira was surprised to find herself humming it before she fell asleep.

options.label: B
options.text: Mira sighed dramatically and followed her reluctantly.

options.label: C
options.text: All her friends were going to the beach in Jeddah, and she was stuck with a family she barely knew.

options.label: D
options.text: On the first morning, the fog was so thick that she could not see the end of the winding road.

questions.why: Humming the family song shows Mira now feels at home.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Fog on the Terraces” uses words that appeal to the sense of smell?

segments.text: The steps were steep, and the air smelled of wet earth and wild herbs.
Her grandmother handed her a basket and pointed toward the terraced fields.
Mira sighed dramatically and followed her reluctantly.
One evening, her grandmother taught her a song that the family's ancestors had sung while harvesting.

questions.why: Sensory words help readers experience the setting.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Fog on the Terraces” in order.
sequence: Mira arrives unhappily in the village.
Grandmother hands Mira a basket.
Mira learns the names of the goats.
Mira hums the harvest song at bedtime.
questions.why: The events show Mira slowly settling into village life.

questions.stem: Which two phrases from “Fog on the Terraces” show that Mira is unwilling at first? Choose two.
options: humming it before she fell asleep
knew the names of the goats
had not wanted to spend the summer
questions.why: Unwilling characters show their feelings through words and actions.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about Faris and his test that does not make sense.
questions.why: A student who vows to study meticulously would review every lesson carefully.

questions.stem: The village elders decided to ____ Khalid as the new leader of the date harvest, an honor his family had never received before.
questions.why: To anoint someone can mean to choose that person for an honor.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Mariam made a vow never to waste food again after visiting the food bank.” What does “vow” mean?
questions.why: Never again shows that Mariam made a serious promise.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The plants react to sunlight by turning their leaves toward the window,” the word “react” means to respond.
questions.why: To react is to respond to something.

questions.stem: Which word best fits each sentence about getting ready for Eid?

rows.text: The ____ smell of frying garlic drifted from the kitchen.
Mother ironed each new dress ____, smoothing every fold.
The children made a ____ to share their Eid money with others.
The ____ scent of strong incense filled the hallway.

questions.why: Pungent describes strong smells, meticulously describes careful work, and a vow is a serious promise.

questions.stem: What does the word “swallowed” suggest about the medina in the first sentence of “The Blue Gate”?

partA.stem: What does the word “swallowed” suggest about the medina in the first sentence of “The Blue Gate”?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a small market that Adam crosses in a minute.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a quiet place that feels empty and peaceful.

options.label: C
options.text: It is so crowded and confusing that Adam feels lost in it.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a dangerous place where visitors often disappear.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: He stopped at a narrow doorway where an old man was stitching a leather slipper.

options.label: B
options.text: His grandfather walked ahead calmly, greeting shopkeepers by name.

options.label: C
options.text: Alleys twisted in every direction, donkeys loaded with copper pots squeezed past him, and merchants called out in a mixture of Arabic and French.

options.label: D
options.text: Adam watched the needle dart in and out of the soft yellow leather.

questions.why: The busy, twisting details explain why Adam feels swallowed up.

questions.stem: How does the tone of “The Blue Gate” change from beginning to end?
options: from overwhelmed to calm and connected
from cheerful to angry and impatient
from peaceful to frightened and tense
from curious to bored and tired
questions.why: Noise and confusion give way to quiet and a sense of belonging.

questions.stem: In “The Blue Gate,” is each phrase an example of a simile or of personification?

rows.text: His hands were as quick as sparrows.
The medina of Fez swallowed Adam
a little less like a maze

questions.why: A simile compares with like or as; personification gives human or animal actions to things.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Blue Gate” shows that Adam begins to feel connected to his family's past?

segments.text: He imagined an ancestor he had never met sitting on that same worn bench.
Adam, who had grown up in quiet Toronto, felt bewildered and slightly dizzy.
His grandfather walked ahead calmly, greeting shopkeepers by name.
Adam watched the needle dart in and out of the soft yellow leather.

questions.why: Picturing his ancestor links Adam to his family's past.

questions.stem: In “The Blue Gate,” the verb “dart” makes the old man's stitching seem ____.
questions.why: Dart describes a fast, sharp, sure movement.

questions.stem: Which two sentences show a character reacting to a surprise? Choose two.
options: Lina rode her old bicycle to school every morning that week.
Lina's mouth fell open when she saw the new bicycle by the door.
Omar jumped back as the toy clown suddenly popped out of its box.
Omar put the toy back in its box on the highest shelf.
questions.why: To react is to respond right away to something that happens.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the tone that its key word helps create.

pairs.left: “The pungent market air stung my nose,” Dalia grumbled.
Grandfather meticulously folded the old letter, as if it were made of glass.
“I vow that I will learn every word,” she said, lifting her chin.

questions.why: An author's word choice helps set the tone of a passage.

questions.stem: Why might an author write that a character “meticulously” arranged the flowers instead of simply “arranged” them?
options: to show the character disliked the task
to show the character was in a hurry
to show the flowers were cheap ones
to show the character's great care
questions.why: Meticulously adds the idea of careful attention to every detail.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence about a power cut at a concert that has a verb error.
segments: and then reacts with nervous laughter.
questions.correction: and then reacted with nervous laughter.
questions.why: Both verbs describe the past, so reacts must be reacted.

questions.stem: True or false: When a story says that a team “anointed” its youngest player as captain, it means that the team chose her for a special honor.
questions.why: Anoint can mean to choose someone for an honor or an important role.

questions.stem: Which word best describes Dalia's attitude in the first paragraph of “Ninety Years of Dates”?
questions.why: She decides to hate the farm before she even arrives.

questions.stem: How does the author develop Dalia's character in the last paragraph of “Ninety Years of Dates”?

partA.stem: How does the author develop Dalia's character in the last paragraph of “Ninety Years of Dates”?

options.label: A
options.text: by showing a shared moment that softens her resistance to the farm

options.label: B
options.text: by showing her refuse to taste the dates from the old palm tree

options.label: C
options.text: by showing her argue with her grandfather about the weak internet

options.label: D
options.text: by showing her decide to fly back home earlier than she planned

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Her grandfather did not seem to notice her sulking.

options.label: B
options.text: Each night she lay awake, homesick for the noisy streets of Chicago.

options.label: C
options.text: That evening, she asked him to teach her the names of the trees.

options.label: D
options.text: One morning, Dalia followed him, mostly from boredom.

questions.why: Asking to learn the trees' names shows Dalia now wants to connect.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Ninety Years of Dates” in which the author's word choice shows the grandfather's love for the palms.

segments.text: Every dawn he walked between the palms, tapping their trunks as if greeting old friends.
“This tree has fed our family for ninety years,” he said, pressing a sticky, amber date into her palm.
Each night she lay awake, homesick for the noisy streets of Chicago.
One morning, Dalia followed him, mostly from boredom.
Dalia bit into it reluctantly, expecting something dry and disappointing.

questions.why: Greeting the trees like friends and honoring the old palm show his love.

questions.stem: In “Ninety Years of Dates,” does each phrase create a tone of frustration or a tone of warmth?

rows.text: the internet signal flickered and died
tapping their trunks as if greeting old friends
she caught only one word in five
for a moment the language between them did not matter

questions.why: Word choice sets the tone, which shifts as Dalia changes.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the grandfather's Arabic as “quick and musical” instead of simply “fast”?
options: to show that Dalia finds it beautiful even though she cannot follow it
to show that Dalia is annoyed by the sound of her grandfather's voice
to show that the grandfather prefers singing to having real conversations
to show that the grandfather speaks slowly so that Dalia can learn
questions.why: “Musical” adds a sense of beauty that the plain word “fast” lacks.

questions.stem: Match each word a stage manager might write in a script note with its meaning: bound, contemplate, retrieve, vigorously.

pairs.right: to leap forward in long, springy jumps
to look at or think about something for a long time
to go and bring something back

questions.why: These words describe actions and thoughts that actors often show on stage.

questions.stem: The puppy dropped Faisal's slipper into the pool, so he used a long net to ____ it before it sank.
questions.why: To retrieve something is to get it back from where it was lost.

questions.stem: True or false: A gazelle that bounds across the sand is moving slowly, one careful step at a time.
questions.why: To bound is to leap forward with energy, not to step slowly.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word deliberately correctly?
options: Without noticing at all, Majid deliberately stepped on his little sister's new drawing.
Sami deliberately left the seat beside him empty so the new student could sit there.
The cup slipped from Huda's wet hand and deliberately fell to the floor by mistake.
The sudden desert wind deliberately blew the papers off the teacher's wooden desk.
questions.why: Deliberately means on purpose, as when Sami planned to save the seat.

questions.stem: Was each action at the school play rehearsal done “vigorously” or gently?

rows.text: Hamza scrubbed the paint off the stage floor with all his strength.
Noura laid the paper flowers on the table so they would not tear.
The drummer pounded the large drum as hard as he could for the opening.
Reem tucked the doll into its tiny cradle without making a sound.

questions.why: Vigorous actions use force and energy; gentle actions are soft and careful.

questions.stem: Which two sentences show someone contemplating a decision? Choose two.
options: Before signing up for the trip, Dana spent the evening thinking over every part of the plan.
Talal grabbed the first book he saw on the shelf without a moment's thought.
Rahaf answered the quiz question instantly by choosing the very first option.
Yasser sat by the window for an hour, weighing whether to join the chess club or the robotics team.
questions.why: To contemplate is to think about something slowly and carefully.

questions.stem: The old man ____ his head toward the speaker so that he could hear the question better.
questions.why: To incline something is to lean or bend it in one direction.

questions.stem: Find the part that contradicts the rest of this sentence about a broken window.
segments: that it was a complete accident.
questions.why: An accident is not done deliberately, or on purpose.

questions.stem: Which word is the best synonym for “vigorously” in “The team rowed vigorously against the strong current”?
questions.why: Vigorously and energetically both mean with great strength and energy.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to tell how Lama's cat got back her lost toy.
sequence: The cat's toy mouse rolled under the heavy bookcase.
The cat stared at the gap and seemed to contemplate her next move.
Lama lay on the floor and stretched her arm to retrieve the toy.
The happy cat bounded across the room to chase it again.
questions.why: The toy is lost, the cat thinks, Lama gets it back, and the cat plays again.

questions.stem: In “The Falcon Lesson,” what is the main purpose of the words in brackets?
options: to explain the lesson the playwright wants every reader to learn
to show the exact words each character says aloud to the others
to tell actors how to move and where the scene takes place
to list the names of the actors who will perform the two roles
questions.why: Stage directions in brackets describe the setting, actions, and tone of voice.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The Falcon Lesson,” why does Uncle Khalid hold out the glove without speaking?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The Falcon Lesson,” why does Uncle Khalid hold out the glove without speaking?

options.label: A
options.text: He wants Reem to decide on her own to keep trying.

options.label: B
options.text: He wants Reem to put the glove away for the day.

options.label: C
options.text: He has forgotten what he planned to teach her next.

options.label: D
options.text: He is too angry with Reem to say anything at all.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I am waiting for you to argue with yourself.

options.label: B
options.text: Forty times is a beginning, not an ending.

options.label: C
options.text: It actually chose me, after everything I said about it.

options.label: D
options.text: Then the falcon can find someone else to train it!

questions.why: Khalid's line shows he wants Reem to talk herself into trying again.

questions.stem: Sort these parts of “The Falcon Lesson” into dialogue and stage directions.

rows.text: Falcons respect patience, not complaints.
A long silence follows.
You are not going to argue with me, are you?
The falcon tilts its head, spreads its wings, and lands gently on her wrist.

questions.why: Dialogue is what characters say; stage directions describe what happens on stage.

questions.stem: Which line from “The Falcon Lesson” shows most clearly that Reem is ready to quit?

segments.text: Then the falcon can find someone else to train it!
It actually chose me, after everything I said about it.
You are not going to argue with me, are you?
Forty times is a beginning, not an ending.

questions.why: Reem's angry line, said as she throws the glove, shows that she wants to give up.

questions.stem: Which two stage directions in “The Falcon Lesson” show a change in Reem's feelings as the scene goes on? Choose two.
questions.why: Reem moves from anger to quiet thought to amazement; the other directions describe Khalid.

questions.stem: In a play script, the list of everyone who appears, printed before the first scene begins, is called the ____.
questions.why: The cast of characters introduces the people in a drama.

questions.stem: Match each drama term with an example of it.

pairs.right: Scene 2: The school courtyard, later that afternoon
Act One, a large section made of three shorter parts

questions.why: Dramas are built from acts and scenes, told through dialogue and stage directions.

questions.stem: True or false: In a drama script, a character's spoken words follow the character's name and a colon instead of appearing inside quotation marks.
questions.why: Scripts use the speaker's name and a colon in place of quotation marks.

questions.stem: Which part of this script line does not match the rest? “MAHA: [bounding vigorously across the stage] I am so tired that I cannot take one more step.”
segments: I am so tired that I cannot
questions.correction: [dragging her feet slowly across the stage]
questions.why: A stage direction should match the dialogue; an exhausted character would not bound vigorously.

questions.stem: A playwright wants to show that a character drops a cup deliberately, not by accident. Which stage direction does this best?
options: [She gasps as the cup tumbles from the high shelf behind her and shatters.]
[She trips over the edge of the old rug, and the cup falls from her tired hand.]
[She looks straight at her brother, then opens her hand and lets the cup fall.]
[The cup slips from her wet fingers as she turns quickly toward the open door.]
questions.why: Looking at someone and then opening her hand shows that the action is done on purpose.

questions.stem: Which moment is the climax of “Faris Reads”?
options: Faris agrees to read one line before he goes home for the day.
Faris realizes the dots he is tracing spell his own name.
Ms. Huda reminds Faris that he identified four letters the day before.
Faris pushes the Braille book away and says the dots feel identical.
questions.why: The climax is the turning point, when Faris discovers he can read.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Faris change from the beginning to the end of “Faris Reads”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Faris change from the beginning to the end of “Faris Reads”?

options.label: A
options.text: He moves from reading quickly to reading very slowly and carefully.

options.label: B
options.text: He moves from enjoying reading to feeling bored by the book.

options.label: C
options.text: He moves from refusing to try to eagerly wanting to read more.

options.label: D
options.text: He moves from trusting Ms. Huda to doubting her patient advice.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Your fingers are still learning an entirely new language, and even expert readers once struggled with the alphabet.

options.label: B
options.text: Yesterday you identified the first four letters, so shall we continue with the fifth character?

options.label: C
options.text: Those dots all feel identical.

options.label: D
options.text: Then tomorrow, I want to read a whole page.

questions.why: His last line shows that the boy who pushed the book away now wants more.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Faris Reads” in order.
sequence: Faris pushes the Braille book away.
Ms. Huda slides the book back and encourages him.
Faris traces the dots slowly with one finger.
Faris discovers that the dots spell his name.
questions.why: The scene builds from refusal to effort to discovery.

questions.stem: Which two stage directions from “Faris Reads” show that Faris is beginning to change? Select two sentences.

segments.text: His expression changes from irritation to concentration.
His voice rises with excitement.
Afternoon light falls across a table holding a thick Braille book.
MS. HUDA, a volunteer instructor, sits patiently beside him.

questions.why: These directions show Faris's feelings shifting toward interest and joy.

questions.stem: In “Faris Reads,” Ms. Huda says she placed Faris's name in the book ____, which shows that she planned his discovery.
questions.why: Ms. Huda put the name there deliberately, or on purpose, so Faris would find it himself.

questions.stem: Which two lines of dialogue reveal that a character is contemplating a hard choice? Choose two.
options: TARIQ: Please pass me the water bottle; practice is about to start.
LAMA: I already told everyone my answer, and I will never change it.
TARIQ: If I tell the coach the truth, I may lose my place... but can I really stay silent?
LAMA: [slowly] Should I accept the scholarship abroad, or stay near my grandmother?
questions.why: Dialogue that weighs two sides of a choice shows a character contemplating it.

questions.stem: In a drama about a stubborn student and a patient tutor, is each event part of the exposition, the rising action, or the climax?

rows.text: A tutor arrives at a family's home and meets a student who refuses all lessons.
The student hides the books, and the tutor calmly finds new ways to teach.
The student suddenly understands a lesson and begs to learn more.
The tutor quarrels with the student's parents about how strict to be.

questions.why: Exposition introduces the situation, rising action builds conflict, and the climax is the turning point.

questions.stem: Which choice best turns this narration into a stage direction: “Yara was so nervous that her hands shook as she reached for the microphone”?
options: YARA: I am reaching for the microphone with my hands.
YARA: [loudly] Everyone, please listen to my speech now!
[Yara reaches for the microphone, her hands trembling.]
[Yara is the main character of the school talent show.]
questions.why: A stage direction shows a feeling through an action the audience can see.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “GRANDFATHER: [inclining his head toward the empty shelf] Someone has moved my old compass. MAJED: [hiding his hands behind his back] I will retrieve it la— I mean, I have not seen it.” What do these lines suggest about Majed?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the lines: “GRANDFATHER: [inclining his head toward the empty shelf] Someone has moved my old compass. MAJED: [hiding his hands behind his back] I will retrieve it la— I mean, I have not seen it.” What do these lines suggest about Majed?

options.label: A
options.text: He is too far from the shelf to see what is missing.

options.label: B
options.text: He has never seen the compass and is truly puzzled.

options.label: C
options.text: He wants Grandfather to buy a brand-new compass.

options.label: D
options.text: He has taken the compass and is trying to hide it.

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “hiding his hands behind his back” and “I will retrieve it la—”

options.label: B
options.text: “Someone has moved my old compass”

options.label: C
options.text: the name “GRANDFATHER” at the start of the line

options.label: D
options.text: “inclining his head toward the empty shelf”

questions.why: Majed's hidden hands and his slip of the tongue reveal that he has the compass.

questions.stem: When a character speaks a short line directly to the audience that the other characters on stage are not supposed to hear, the line is called ____.
questions.why: An aside lets the audience hear a character's private thoughts.

questions.stem: Match each word from a letter of advice with its meaning: conquer, master, merit, pine.

pairs.right: to overcome or defeat something hard
worth or excellence that deserves praise
to long sadly for something that is missing

questions.why: These words often appear when writers give advice about effort and character.

questions.stem: After the rainy season, the pages of Grandfather's old notebook had dried into ____, wavy sheets that rustled when he turned them.
questions.why: Crinkly means full of small wrinkles and folds, like wavy paper.

questions.stem: True or false: A guard who deserts his post stays at it bravely until his duty is over.
questions.why: To desert is to abandon a place or person that one should stay with.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word merit correctly?
options: Fahad poured himself a glass of cold merit to drink after his long morning run.
The merit of the storm flooded the low streets near the old harbor all night long.
The merit rolled off the kitchen table and broke into three sharp, shiny pieces.
The judges agreed that every design had some merit, but Lina's was the most creative.
questions.why: Merit is the quality of being good or worthy, which judges look for in a design.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use “desert” to mean “a dry, sandy land” or “to abandon”?

rows.text: Camels can walk for days across the desert without drinking water.
A loyal friend will never desert you when times are hard.
The Empty Quarter is one of the largest sand deserts on Earth.
The frightened guards deserted the gate and ran into the night.

questions.why: Context shows whether desert names a place or the action of leaving someone behind.

questions.stem: Which two sentences describe someone who has mastered a skill? Choose two.
options: Saud has just opened his first chess book and is learning how the pieces move.
After years of practice, Mona recites long poems from memory without a single mistake.
Ahmad can now type quickly and correctly without ever looking at the keyboard.
Rana tried the guitar once last week but has not touched it since then.
questions.why: To master a skill is to learn it so well that you can do it easily and correctly.

questions.stem: Away at university, Abdullah ____ for his mother's cooking and the noisy family dinners every Friday.
questions.why: To pine for something is to miss it and long for it.

questions.stem: Find the part that contradicts the meaning of “conquered” in this sentence about a climbing team.
segments: at the bottom of its slope.
questions.why: To conquer a mountain is to reach its top, not to stay at the bottom.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to “conquer” in “Huda worked hard to conquer her fear of speaking in public”?
questions.why: To conquer a fear is to overcome it.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to tell how Basma came to master the art of sadu weaving.
sequence: Basma pined to learn the weaving her grandmother did every evening.
Her first pieces were lumpy and crinkly, but she kept practicing.
After two years, she had mastered the bright sadu patterns.
At the school fair, the judges praised the merit of her rug.
questions.why: The paragraph moves from a wish to early struggles to skill to praise.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the grandfather's main message in “A Letter from Grandfather”?
options: Gardening is a useful hobby that every young person ought to learn.
Expensive shoes help new students make friends during the first week.
A new school is frightening, so Hamad should stay close to his home.
Good character and steady effort matter more than how things look.
questions.why: Each comparison in the letter points to character and effort over appearances.

questions.stem: Classify each comparison from “A Letter from Grandfather” as a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: Your mind is a garden
Fancy things are like desert mirages
Honesty is a lantern
like an old falcon watching for its rider

questions.why: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.

questions.stem: Part A: In “A Letter from Grandfather,” what does the comparison of fancy things to desert mirages suggest?

partA.stem: Part A: In “A Letter from Grandfather,” what does the comparison of fancy things to desert mirages suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: Things that look impressive may have no real value up close.

options.label: B
options.text: Hamad should travel to the desert to see real mirages.

options.label: C
options.text: Shining objects are always worth more than plain ones.

options.label: D
options.text: Expensive things are very difficult to find in the desert.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the letter best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Let me share what seventy years of experience have taught me.

options.label: B
options.text: Do not envy the boy with the expensive shoes or the newest electronic gadgets.

options.label: C
options.text: Fancy things are like desert mirages: they shimmer brilliantly from far away, but they vanish when you come close.

options.label: D
options.text: When you make a mistake, admit it immediately and honestly.

questions.why: A mirage looks real from far away but disappears, just like the value of fancy things.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “A Letter from Grandfather” uses a metaphor to show that honesty guides other people?

segments.text: Honesty is a lantern; people will follow its light long after they have forgotten your name.
When you make a mistake, admit it immediately and honestly.
Your mind is a garden, and every habit you practice is a seed.
Do not envy the boy with the expensive shoes or the newest electronic gadgets.

questions.why: A lantern lights the way, just as an honest person shows others the right path.

questions.stem: In “A Letter from Grandfather,” the grandfather calls a mountain “a crowd of stones” to show that great achievements are built from ____.
questions.why: The metaphor shows that small tasks, done well, add up to something great.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about effort and honesty with its type of figurative language.

pairs.left: Hard work is the key that opens every door.
Her promise was as solid as a stone wall.
The lazy afternoon whispered, “Rest a little longer.”
I have told you a million times to be careful!

questions.why: Recognizing figurative language helps readers find a writer's deeper meaning.

questions.stem: What does the metaphor “Merit is a key that no money can copy” mean?
options: Money can be used to copy any key that a person loses.
Keys are expensive, so people should save money for them.
People with merit always carry many keys in their pockets.
Real worth must be earned and cannot simply be bought.
questions.why: A key no money can copy stands for worth that only effort can earn.

questions.stem: True or false: In “My grandmother pines for her old village like a palm tree thirsting for rain,” the writer uses a simile to show how deeply she misses her home.
questions.why: The word like signals a simile, and a thirsty palm tree shows a deep longing.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence contradicts the word “crinkly”?
questions.why: Crinkly means full of small wrinkles, so the hands cannot be smooth.

questions.stem: A father writes, “Do not chase applause; chase the quiet satisfaction of a job done well.” Which two statements express his message? Choose two.
options: Pride in honest effort is a better goal than attention.
Doing good work matters more than being praised for it.
Jobs that are noisy and busy are usually the best jobs.
People should never clap for others at school events.
questions.why: The father contrasts outside praise with the inner reward of good work.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main message of “A Letter to Lulwa”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main message of “A Letter to Lulwa”?

options.label: A
options.text: Lulwa should never own a phone, even after she becomes an adult.

options.label: B
options.text: Lulwa should become an architect only because her mother wishes it.

options.label: C
options.text: Lulwa should guard her time so she can work toward her real goals.

options.label: D
options.text: Lulwa should reply to her classmates' messages much more quickly.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the letter best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I want your hours to belong to you, not to a glowing screen that never stops demanding attention.

options.label: B
options.text: I am saying "not yet."

options.label: C
options.text: I was exhausted after a long day at the hospital, and my answer was impatient, so let me reply properly now.

options.label: D
options.text: Yesterday evening you asked me why I refused to buy you the phone that everyone in your class seems to own.

questions.why: The mother wants Lulwa's time spent on her goals rather than lost to a screen.

questions.stem: In “A Letter to Lulwa,” what does the comparison “Time is a quiet thief” suggest?
options: Time moves so loudly that people always notice when it passes.
Time can be stolen back if a person locks the door carefully.
Time belongs only to people who own the newest kinds of phones.
Time is lost slowly and secretly, often without our noticing.
questions.why: A quiet thief takes things without being noticed, just as distractions steal time.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “A Letter to Lulwa” reverses its words to state the mother's message most memorably?

segments.text: When you are older, you will hold the phone, but I simply do not want it to hold you.
You aspire to become an architect, and that ambitious dream deserves to be your priority.
Those habits will carry you further than any number of superficial messages.
Time is a quiet thief.

questions.why: Switching who holds whom makes the warning about control easy to remember.

questions.stem: Which two activities does the mother in “A Letter to Lulwa” want her daughter to spend time on instead of a phone? Choose two.
options: thinking about why some rooms feel welcoming
buying a phone like the ones her classmates own
sending short messages to her classmates
questions.why: The mother lists activities that build toward Lulwa's dream of architecture.

questions.stem: In “A Letter to Lulwa,” is each phrase meant literally or figuratively?

rows.text: Time is a quiet thief.
measure the shadows of buildings
it slips away through a thousand small distractions
You aspire to become an architect

questions.why: Figurative phrases compare or exaggerate; literal phrases mean exactly what they say.

questions.stem: A father writes, “Never ____ your dreams when the road grows hard; a ship that holds its course reaches the harbor.”
questions.why: To desert something is to abandon it, which the father warns against.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence from a father's advice: “Be the palm tree, not the tumbleweed: put down deep roots, and the wind will not decide where you go.” What is the father's message?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence from a father's advice: “Be the palm tree, not the tumbleweed: put down deep roots, and the wind will not decide where you go.” What is the father's message?

options.label: A
options.text: Palm trees are more useful than tumbleweeds in desert farming.

options.label: B
options.text: Windy weather is dangerous, so stay indoors on stormy days.

options.label: C
options.text: Strong values keep a person steady when others try to push him.

options.label: D
options.text: A person should move often so that he can see many new places.

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the sentence best support the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the palm tree”

options.label: B
options.text: “not the tumbleweed”

options.label: C
options.text: “the wind”

options.label: D
options.text: “put down deep roots”

questions.why: Deep roots stand for firm values that keep a person from being blown around.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a simile to describe someone who has mastered a skill?
options: Huda had played that hard piece about a billion times and never made one slip.
The hard piece bowed politely and let Huda play it from start to end without a slip.
Huda was a falcon riding the wind as she played the hard piece without a slip.
Like a falcon riding the wind, Huda moved through the hard piece without a slip.
questions.why: A simile uses like or as; the other choices are a metaphor, personification, and hyperbole.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a paragraph that ends with the writer's message about conquering fear.
sequence: Many students fear speaking in front of the class.
Their hearts race, and their notes turn crinkly in their sweaty hands.
Yet fear is like a sand dune: it looks huge only until you start climbing it.
Every fear we face is a small mountain that we can conquer.
questions.why: The paragraph describes a problem, reframes it with a simile, then states the message.

questions.stem: Which part of this advice uses the word “merit” incorrectly?
segments: by the merit of her work,
not by the price of her shoes,
and then merit her loudly in the hallway.
questions.correction: and then praise her honestly in front of others.
questions.why: Merit means worth or to deserve; it does not mean to praise someone.

questions.stem: Match each word from a story about a new team member with its meaning: bigoted, bond, hostile, participate.

pairs.right: unfairly refusing to accept people who are different
a close connection that joins people together
unfriendly and ready to fight or oppose
to take part in an activity

questions.why: These words describe how people treat one another on a team.

questions.stem: The cousins' summer visits always ____ with the date harvest, so they help pick dates every year.
questions.why: To coincide is to happen at the same time as something else.

questions.stem: True or false: A bigoted coach judges players by where their families come from instead of by how well they play.
questions.why: A bigoted person unfairly judges others for being different.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word hostile correctly?
options: The hostile dog growled and showed its teeth whenever a stranger came near the gate.
The hostile kitten purred softly and curled up in Lama's warm lap for the whole evening.
The hostile breeze gently cooled the beach on that calm and pleasant summer evening.
Our hostile neighbors brought us a tray of sweets on our very first day in the house.
questions.why: Hostile means unfriendly and ready to attack, like the growling dog.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe two events that “coincide” or two events at different times?

rows.text: The school sports day and the science fair are both on Thursday morning.
The football match ended an hour before the awards ceremony began.
This year, Ali's graduation falls on the same day as his grandfather's birthday.
The museum trip is in March, and the book fair is in May.

questions.why: Events coincide only when they happen at the same time.

questions.stem: Which two sentences show a bond growing between two people? Choose two.
options: Hassan and Fahd argued about every decision and refused to work together.
Sharing a tent during the desert trip turned the two strangers into close friends.
The two players never spoke to each other outside of their weekly matches.
After months of training side by side, the two runners began to trust each other completely.
questions.why: A bond is a close connection that grows through shared time and trust.

questions.stem: Only students who sign up by Sunday may ____ in the regional robotics contest.
questions.why: To participate is to take part in an event.

questions.stem: Find the part that contradicts the rest of this sentence about a gymnastics judge.
segments: no matter where each one came from.
questions.why: A judge who scores only on skill is fair, not bigoted.

questions.stem: Which choice is the best antonym of “participate” in “Everyone was invited to participate in the class debate”?
questions.why: To sit out is to stay out of an activity, the opposite of participating.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to tell how a hostile rivalry between two classes turned into a bond.
sequence: Class 6A and Class 6B were hostile rivals who mocked each other at every match.
Their final game happened to coincide with the school's tree-planting day, so it was canceled.
Both classes had to participate in planting trees side by side.
By evening, the former rivals had formed a bond and planned a joint team.
questions.why: The events move from conflict to a surprise change to cooperation and friendship.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “My First Season”?
options: The narrator's father teaches him how to take a powerful left-footed shot.
The narrator learns that city players are always better than village players.
The narrator wins respect by answering cruelty with self-control and effort.
The narrator decides to leave the academy and return to his mountain village.
questions.why: The whole passage shows how calm effort turned mockery into respect.

questions.stem: Part A: What lesson does the narrator learn by the end of “My First Season”?

partA.stem: Part A: What lesson does the narrator learn by the end of “My First Season”?

options.label: A
options.text: Holding back anger can be a form of strength.

options.label: B
options.text: Practicing late at night is bad for young players.

options.label: C
options.text: New players should avoid speaking to their teammates.

options.label: D
options.text: Fighting back is the fastest way to earn respect.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: My boots were old, my accent was strong, and several of the city boys immediately decided that I did not belong.

options.label: B
options.text: I wanted to retaliate more than I had ever wanted anything.

options.label: C
options.text: I realized that restraint is not weakness; it is strength that has learned to wait.

options.label: D
options.text: Gradually, the laughter faded into silence and then into respect.

questions.why: The final sentence directly states the lesson about restraint.

questions.stem: Which two sentences from “My First Season” are the best evidence that the narrator answered unfair treatment with hard work? Select two sentences.

segments.text: For weeks, I answered every insult with hard work.
I arrived early, stayed late, and practiced passing until the sun disappeared behind the stadium.
My face burned with humiliation, and I wanted to retaliate more than I had ever wanted anything.
During my first practice, a tall defender pushed me to the ground and laughed.

questions.why: Strong evidence names the actual effort the narrator made.

questions.stem: Compare the tall defender at the beginning and at the end of “My First Season.” When does each detail describe him?

rows.text: pushes the narrator to the ground
asks to learn the narrator's left-footed shot
tells the narrator to go back to his goats
treats the narrator as someone with skills worth learning

questions.why: Contrasting the defender's actions shows how the narrator's self-control changed him.

questions.stem: At the beginning of “My First Season,” several city boys are ____ toward the narrator, but by the end of the season they respect him.
questions.why: Pushing and mocking the narrator shows that the boys were hostile, or unfriendly, at first.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph: “For decades, unfair laws kept Black players out of the major baseball leagues in the United States. These players formed their own leagues, which produced some of the greatest athletes in the sport's history.” Which sentence best states the main idea?
options: Excluded players built strong leagues of their own despite unfair laws.
Major league baseball has always welcomed every talented player equally.
The greatest athletes in baseball history all played in the major leagues.
Baseball was not a popular sport in the early part of the twentieth century.
questions.why: The main idea combines the unfair exclusion with the players' strong response.

questions.stem: Match each signal word with what it shows in a compare-and-contrast paragraph about two athletes.

pairs.right: points out how one differs from the other

questions.why: Signal words tell readers whether a writer is comparing or contrasting.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Like his older brother, Hamza chose to participate in the debate club, but unlike his brother, he never missed a meeting,” the brothers are compared in one way and contrasted in another.
questions.why: Like shows a similarity, and unlike shows a difference.

questions.stem: A student claims, “The new coach built a strong bond with the team.” Which two details are the strongest evidence for this claim? Choose two.
options: The coach had won three championships before he joined this school.
The captain said the coach listened to every player as if each one mattered most.
The players often stayed after practice to talk with the coach about their problems.
The team's new uniforms arrived during the coach's first week.
questions.why: Good evidence must connect directly to the claim about the coach's bond with the players.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to build a paragraph that states a main idea about teamwork and then supports it.
sequence: A team becomes strong only when every member feels welcome.
For example, a player who is treated in a hostile way may stop trying.
Similarly, a bigoted captain can split the team into angry groups.
In the end, a team forms a lasting bond only when everyone is invited to participate.
questions.why: A paragraph states the main idea, gives examples, and then sums up.

questions.stem: Part A: In “Two Tournaments,” how is the narrator's response at seventeen different from his response at twelve?

partA.stem: Part A: In “Two Tournaments,” how is the narrator's response at seventeen different from his response at twelve?

options.label: A
options.text: At seventeen he plays carelessly, but at twelve he makes very careful moves.

options.label: B
options.text: At seventeen he faces no unfair looks, but at twelve he faces many of them.

options.label: C
options.text: At seventeen he stays focused, but at twelve he is shaken by unfair treatment.

options.label: D
options.text: At seventeen he refuses to shake hands, but at twelve he greets everyone kindly.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I played my first international chess tournament when I was twelve.

options.label: B
options.text: In both tournaments, I faced the same unfair looks.

options.label: C
options.text: That year, I finished second overall.

options.label: D
options.text: I no longer let other people's prejudice decide how I would play.

questions.why: This sentence shows how he changed in the way he handled unfair treatment.

questions.stem: Which two things stay the same in both of the narrator's tournaments in “Two Tournaments”? Choose two.
options: The narrator loses three games in a row.
The tournaments take place in the same hall.
The narrator finishes in second place.
Some people treat the narrator unfairly.
questions.why: Similarities are details true of both events; the losses and second place happen only once.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of “Two Tournaments”?
options: Unfair treatment at chess tournaments disappears once a player becomes older.
Chess tournaments in Europe are much harder than tournaments at home.
The narrator wins second place because his opponents played carelessly.
Over time, the narrator learns that his self-respect depends on him, not others.
questions.why: The passage contrasts two tournaments to show the narrator's inner growth.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Two Tournaments” best explains why the narrator struggled at age twelve?

segments.text: At twelve, I believed that I had to win people's approval before I could win a match.
I remember the enormous hall in Vienna more vividly than any individual game.
Five years later, I returned to the same competition in the same hall.
That year, I finished second overall.

questions.why: Needing others' approval made him easy to shake, which explains his losses.

questions.stem: In “Two Tournaments,” does each detail describe the narrator at twelve or at seventeen?

rows.text: makes careless moves he would never make at home
extends his hand whether or not it is accepted
believes he must win approval before winning a match
finishes second in the tournament

questions.why: Sorting details by age makes the contrast between the two tournaments clear.

questions.stem: A writer's main idea is that hostile rivals can become true friends; the detail that best supports it is that the two former rival captains ____.
options: play for teams in different cities
questions.why: Training together shows the rivals became friends, which supports the main idea.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Although a bigoted official tried to keep the two friends off the same team, they kept practicing together every evening in the empty lot.” What does the sentence mainly show?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Although a bigoted official tried to keep the two friends off the same team, they kept practicing together every evening in the empty lot.” What does the sentence mainly show?

options.label: A
options.text: The friends were not allowed to see each other.

options.label: B
options.text: The official placed the friends on the same team.

options.label: C
options.text: The friends preferred practicing in the evening.

options.label: D
options.text: The friends kept their bond despite an unfair person.

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “in the empty lot”

options.label: B
options.text: “the two friends”

options.label: C
options.text: “every evening”

options.label: D
options.text: “Although a bigoted official tried to keep the two friends off the same team, they kept practicing together”

questions.why: The word although sets up the contrast between the unfair official and the loyal friends.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about two rival schools does not make sense with the rest?
segments: shared their equipment, cheered for each other,
questions.why: Schools that share and cheer for each other are friendly, not hostile.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence best supports the claim “Participating in team sports helps students form lasting bonds”?
options: Nora enjoys watching professional volleyball matches on television with her family.
Volleyball was first played in the United States more than one hundred years ago.
Nora's school volleyball club practices three afternoons a week in the large school gym.
Former teammates from Nora's school volleyball club still meet every month, ten years later.
questions.why: The best evidence shows friendships from a team lasting over time.

questions.stem: Is each statement about Jackie Robinson's era a fact or an opinion?

rows.text: Jackie Robinson joined the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947.
Answering hostile fans with silence is the bravest choice anyone can make.
Robinson's first major league season happened to coincide with the year he turned twenty-eight.
Every athlete should be required to participate in a lesson on fairness.

questions.why: Facts can be checked; opinions state beliefs or judgments.

questions.stem: Match each word from a story about a new student with its meaning: frowned, embarrassed, mispronouncing, deaf.

pairs.right: wrinkled the forehead to show displeasure
feeling awkward and ashamed in front of others
saying a word with the wrong sounds
unable to hear, or unable to hear well

questions.why: These words describe reactions and challenges that characters often face in stories.

questions.stem: The school hired a sign-language interpreter so that the two ____ students could follow the morning assembly.
questions.why: A sign-language interpreter helps people who are deaf understand spoken words.

questions.stem: True or false: A teacher who frowned at the noisy class was showing that she was pleased with the students.
questions.why: People frown when they are unhappy or displeased, not when they are pleased.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word plots correctly?
options: The baby plots loudly whenever she wakes up hungry in the middle of the night.
The plots of the cake melted quickly in the hot afternoon sun on the balcony.
Hamad wore his new plots to his cousin's wedding party last Thursday evening.
Many adventure novels have exciting plots full of chases, secrets, and surprises.
questions.why: The plots of stories are their series of events.

questions.stem: Does each reaction show that the character felt “embarrassed” or confident?

rows.text: Hind's face turned red, and she hid behind her book after calling the teacher by the wrong name.
Talal stepped up to the microphone and smiled at the audience.
Waleed mumbled an apology and stared at his shoes after spilling juice on a guest.
Asma raised her hand first and explained her answer clearly.

questions.why: Blushing and hiding show embarrassment; stepping forward and speaking clearly show confidence.

questions.stem: Which two sentences show that a character is embarrassed? Choose two.
options: Salem yawned and stretched after the long, quiet afternoon.
Huda's cheeks burned, and she wished the floor would swallow her.
Rana grinned proudly as she held up her winning certificate.
Majid laughed nervously and covered his face after his voice cracked.
questions.why: Burning cheeks and a covered face are signs of feeling embarrassed.

questions.stem: The referee ____ and shook his head, clearly unhappy with the players' rough tackles.
questions.why: Frowning and shaking one's head show displeasure.

questions.stem: Find the part that contradicts the rest of this sentence about a news reader.
segments: so she practiced it all afternoon.
questions.why: People practice a name because they are worried about saying it wrong, not proud of it.

questions.stem: Which phrase is closest in meaning to “deaf” in “The old cat is almost completely deaf now, so it does not come when we call it”?
questions.why: A deaf animal cannot hear, so it does not respond to its name.

questions.stem: Put these sentences in order to tell what happened when Kareem read the morning announcements.
sequence: Kareem stood nervously at the microphone with his paper.
He began mispronouncing the name of the visiting scientist.
The principal frowned slightly, and Kareem felt embarrassed.
He took a breath, said the name correctly, and finished strongly.
questions.why: The events move from nerves to a mistake to a reaction to a strong finish.

questions.stem: Which event is the turning point in “The Market Translator”?
options: The narrator becomes fluent in English during her very first year.
The narrator finds Mama studying English words alone at night.
The fruit seller makes a joke that makes all the shoppers laugh.
Mama and her daughter walk to the busy market on a Saturday.
questions.why: The story turns when Mama decides to learn instead of staying silent.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses a theme of “The Market Translator”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses a theme of “The Market Translator”?

options.label: A
options.text: Learning something new takes courage, especially when it feels embarrassing.

options.label: B
options.text: Children should always do the shopping and talking for their families.

options.label: C
options.text: Markets in big cities are noisy places full of strangers and jokes.

options.label: D
options.text: People who move to new countries can never truly feel at home.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the story best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Then he made a joke, and everyone laughed except Mama.

options.label: B
options.text: That night, I heard an unfamiliar sound from the kitchen.

options.label: C
options.text: She looked up, embarrassed, but did not close the book.

options.label: D
options.text: I had become fluent in English after just one year at school, but Mama still recognized only a handful of words.

questions.why: Mama keeps studying even though she feels embarrassed, which shows courage.

questions.stem: In “The Market Translator,” does each detail describe Mama or her daughter at the start?

rows.text: knows only a few English words
has become fluent in English in one year
does the talking at the market
feels like a guest in her own life

questions.why: Contrasting the two characters shows why the market is hard for Mama.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “The Market Translator” best shows that Mama feels left out at the market?

segments.text: Then he made a joke, and everyone laughed except Mama.
I had become fluent in English after just one year at school, but Mama still recognized only a handful of words.
That night, I heard an unfamiliar sound from the kitchen.
She looked up, embarrassed, but did not close the book.

questions.why: Being the only one who cannot laugh shows Mama is left out.

questions.stem: Put these events from “The Market Translator” in order.
sequence: The narrator translates the fruit seller's question for Mama.
Mama says she feels like a guest in her own life.
The narrator hears Mama whispering English words in the kitchen.
Mama asks the narrator to teach her.
questions.why: The plot moves from the problem at the market to Mama's decision to learn.

questions.stem: Match each part of plot structure with its example from a tale about a shy new student named Kenji.

pairs.right: Kenji arrives at a school in Riyadh where he knows no one.
Kenji is too shy to join the lunchtime football games.
Kenji finally kicks the winning goal in a class match.
Kenji's classmates invite him to play every day after that.

questions.why: Plot structure moves from introduction to conflict to turning point to ending.

questions.stem: In fiction, the ____ is the central message about life that a reader can take away and apply to real life.
questions.why: A theme is a lesson or insight about life, not just an event.

questions.stem: True or false: “Tamer frowns and stays silent whenever he must speak English, but his sister Hala jokes easily with her new classmates” contrasts two characters.
questions.why: The word but signals a contrast between Tamer and Hala.

questions.stem: Which choice states a theme about language rather than a topic?
options: A family moving from Jeddah to Canada and learning English together
Learning a new language in a new country
Words can build bridges between people who feel far apart.
A boy who learns to speak Spanish at his new school
questions.why: A theme is a complete statement about life; a topic is only a subject.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: “Hamid felt embarrassed about mispronouncing words when he read aloud in his new class. His twin, Zaid, volunteered first every time.” Which two statements correctly compare or contrast the twins? Choose two.
options: Both boys refuse to read aloud in front of the class.
Zaid is shy, while Hamid always volunteers first.
Hamid is shy about reading aloud, while Zaid is eager.
Zaid is more confident than Hamid about reading aloud.
questions.why: The details show that Hamid holds back and Zaid jumps in.

questions.stem: Part A: In “Sofia and Leo,” how is Sofia's way of learning Arabic different from Leo's?

partA.stem: Part A: In “Sofia and Leo,” how is Sofia's way of learning Arabic different from Leo's?

options.label: A
options.text: Sofia learns faster than Leo because she already knew some Arabic words.

options.label: B
options.text: Sofia studies quietly but fears speaking, while Leo practices aloud without worry.

options.label: C
options.text: Sofia learns from cartoons, while Leo learns only from his teachers at school.

options.label: D
options.text: Sofia practices aloud with friends, while Leo studies long lists of words alone.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the story best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither of them knew a single word of Arabic.

options.label: B
options.text: She memorized long lists of vocabulary every night, yet at school she stayed silent, anxious that one mistake would make her classmates giggle.

options.label: C
options.text: Sofia and her younger brother, Leo, arrived in Riyadh in September, when the afternoons still shimmered with heat.

options.label: D
options.text: Jana smiled and replied slowly so Sofia could follow.

questions.why: This sentence shows Sofia's quiet study and her fear of speaking.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the theme of “Sofia and Leo”?
options: Being willing to make mistakes helps people learn and connect.
Younger children always learn new languages faster than older ones.
Making friends at a new school depends on speaking perfectly.
Cartoons are the best tool for learning any new language quickly.
questions.why: Sofia succeeds only when she risks an imperfect sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Sofia and Leo” marks the turning point for Sofia?

segments.text: One afternoon, her classmate Jana dropped a notebook, and Sofia, without thinking, said a polite Arabic phrase as she handed it back.
Within two months, he was chatting with the neighbor's children in the courtyard.
Words that sounded perfect in her bedroom vanished the moment anyone looked at her.
Neither of them knew a single word of Arabic.

questions.why: Speaking without thinking is the first time Sofia breaks her silence.

questions.stem: In “Sofia and Leo,” does each detail describe Sofia, Leo, or both?

rows.text: arrived in Riyadh knowing no Arabic
repeats cartoon phrases loudly at dinner
stays silent at school
chats with the neighbor's children within two months

questions.why: Sorting details shows how the siblings are alike and different.

questions.stem: In “Sofia and Leo,” Leo is not ____ when he says words the wrong way; he keeps repeating cartoon phrases loudly at dinner.
questions.why: Leo never minds when people laugh at his pronunciation, so he is not embarrassed.

questions.stem: Find the part that does not make sense in this sentence about a deaf sprinter.
segments: because he could hear the starting gun clearly.
questions.correction: because he could not hear the starting gun.
questions.why: A deaf runner cannot hear the gun, so a flashing light signals the start.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “At the family dinner, everyone spoke English except Grandmother. She smiled and nodded, but her eyes kept drifting to the window.” What does the reader learn about Grandmother?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “At the family dinner, everyone spoke English except Grandmother. She smiled and nodded, but her eyes kept drifting to the window.” What does the reader learn about Grandmother?

options.label: A
options.text: She understands everything but chooses to stay quiet.

options.label: B
options.text: She is bored because the dinner has lasted too long.

options.label: C
options.text: She is waiting for a guest who has not yet arrived.

options.label: D
options.text: She feels left out because she cannot follow the talk.

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “everyone spoke English except Grandmother”

options.label: B
options.text: “her eyes”

options.label: C
options.text: “At the family dinner”

options.label: D
options.text: “She smiled and nodded”

questions.why: Not knowing the language keeps Grandmother out of the conversation, even at her own family's table.

questions.stem: Two stories share the theme “Home is found in people, not places.” How might the two stories most likely differ?
options: One must be set in a desert, while the other must be set in a big city.
One might show a family moving abroad, and another a boy at a new school.
Both must have exactly the same characters, setting, and plot events.
One might have a theme about home, and the other a theme about sports.
questions.why: Stories can share a theme while telling very different events.

questions.stem: Put these events of a tale about an embarrassed new student in the order of plot structure: exposition, rising action, climax, resolution.
sequence: Mei Ling joins a class in Dammam and understands little Arabic.
She feels embarrassed when she mispronounces words, so she stops speaking.
During a class play, she must say one line, and she says it perfectly.
Her classmates cheer, and she begins speaking more each day.
questions.why: The plot introduces Mei Ling, builds her problem, reaches a turning point, and resolves it.

questions.stem: Match each sentence from a story with the word that best describes the character in it: frowned, embarrassed, deaf, mispronouncing.

pairs.left: Ali glared at the broken kite and wrinkled his forehead in annoyance.
Dana's face turned red when she noticed her mismatched shoes at the ceremony.
Uncle Saad reads people's lips because he has never heard sound.
On his first visit, Peter kept saying “Jeddah” as “Jed-day.”

questions.why: Character details act as context clues for these describing words.

questions.stem: The sailors dropped the anchor so the boat would not drift away. What does “anchor” mean here?
options: a heavy object that holds a boat in place
a flag that shows the boat's name
a type of sail used in storms
questions.why: An anchor is a heavy object lowered into the water to keep a boat from moving.

questions.stem: A sudden wave hit the small fishing boat, and it capsized. What happened to the boat?
options: It turned over in the water
It was painted a new color
It was towed back to shore
questions.why: To capsize means to turn over in the water.

questions.stem: The sign told hikers to use caution near the cliff's edge. What does “caution” mean?
questions.why: Caution means being careful to avoid danger.

questions.stem: After the storm, Omar's clothes were still ____ from the sea spray.
questions.why: Damp means slightly wet.

questions.stem: Before leaving the boat, the captain made sure the ____ was lowered to hold it steady.
questions.why: An anchor holds a boat steady in place.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “anchor,” “capsize,” “caution,” and “damp.”

pairs.right: a heavy object that holds a boat in place
to turn over in the water

questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you understand stories about the sea.

questions.stem: Match each word with its meaning: “enormous,” “exhausted,” “intense,” and “rescue.”
questions.why: Knowing these meanings helps you understand stories about danger and survival.

questions.stem: True or false: An anchor is used to hold a boat in place.
questions.why: An anchor is a heavy object that holds a boat steady.

questions.stem: Does each sentence describe something “enormous” or something small?

rows.text: A whale swimming beside the fishing boat
A tiny shell on the sand
A mountain rising above the village
A single drop of rain

questions.why: Enormous describes something very large, like a whale or a mountain.
